○ Third, the specific elucidation of the characteristics of the fruit (in two parts): first, arising from the essence to manifest function; second, subsuming function back into the essence.
First, arising from the essence to manifest its function:
the pedestal is all-pervasive with a thousand petals, each petal representing one world, thus constituting a thousand worlds.
I transform myself into a thousand Śākyamunis to preside over these thousand worlds. Subsequently, within a single petal-world, there are further ten billion Mount Sumerus and ten billion [worlds].
There are a hundred million suns and moons, a hundred million sets of four continents, a hundred million Jambudvīpas in the south,
and a hundred million Śākyamuni Bodhisattvas sitting beneath a hundred million bodhi trees, each expounding for you the *bodhisattva-maṇḍala-bhūmi* that you have asked about. Furthermore,
each of the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis likewise manifests a thousand times a hundred million Śākyamunis, and they do so in the same manner.
The preceding section presented the characteristics of the fruit in general, clarifying the essence of the environment and its inhabitants;

this section specifically presents the characteristics of the fruit, clarifying the function of the environment and its inhabitants. That platform is a great lotus flower within the Great Fragrant Water Ocean.
Within the flower is a lotus pedestal, and upon the pedestal is a Buddha. This Buddha is Śākyamuni, the Original Buddha, who is the primary Reward Body (Sambhogakāya).
The "platform" (*tai*) refers to the lotus platform where Vairocana resides; it is the land of dependent retribution for the Buddha-body of both the original and the manifested.
This original lotus platform is surrounded by a thousand petals, each petal representing a world-system; thus, there are a thousand world-systems.

This reveals the land of dependent retribution for both the original and the manifested [bodies]. Furthermore, it manifests as the world of the land of dependent retribution for the manifested Buddha.

"World-systems. Regarding the statement "I manifest as a thousand Śākyamunis and so forth," this "I" refers to Vairocana himself; it distinguishes him from the provisional, limited, ordinary, or external "selves.

This reveals the Buddha-bodies of both the fundamental and the manifested. Furthermore, the manifested Buddha-body manifests as the teacher within the world-system that serves as the locus for the manifestation.
Each of these Buddhas within the individual world-systems is a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of Vairocana; therefore, it is said:
I manifest as a thousand Śākyamunis, each occupying a thousand worlds, and subsequently merge into one, manifesting my traces according to the land.

Furthermore, I manifest as the bodies of the trace-Buddhas and their dependent lands. Regarding the phrase "subsequently merging into one petal," this refers to taking the very last petal among the thousand petals as an illustration; this single petal of the trace-flower further manifests as...
There are ten billion flowers; each individual flower constitutes a single world, and thus there are ten billion worlds.
Within each individual world, there is a single Mount Sumeru, and thus there are ten billion Mount Sumerus.
In Sanskrit it is called Sumeru; here it is translated as "Wondrous High" (Miaogao).

Because it is composed of various jewels and rises above all other mountains, each individual Sumeru mountain has its own sun and moon that revolve around Mount Sumeru; thus there are ten billion suns and moons.
Each sun and moon travels through the four continents in one day and night; thus there are ten billion sets of four continents.
Throughout the world, in each and every four-continent system (*cāturdvīpaka*), there is one Jambudvīpa; thus, there are ten billion Jambudvīpas.
"Jambu" in the Sanskrit language means "excellent gold" (*jina-suvarṇa*); this is because the trees flow with molten gold and the rivers produce golden sand.
The "Śākyas" among these ten billion [Buddhas] are those who manifest the physical form of a Buddha. Furthermore...
The manifested traces of the Buddha’s body are the thousand Śākyamunis. Each one further manifests ten billion Śākyamunis as appropriate for those to be converted;
thus it is said: "Ten billion Bodhisattvas and Śākyamunis sit upon ten billion [thrones]," and so forth.

This concludes by revealing the Tathāgata’s compassionate heart (*vatsalya-citta*) in manifesting birth, renouncing the world, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and delivering sentient beings. Each and every one...
Śākyamuni manifested the eight phases of attaining enlightenment simultaneously with the other Buddhas;
none departed from beneath the Bodhi tree to ascend to the realms of the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and even up to the Brahma Heaven.

In all these places, they expounded the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground transmitted by Vairocana, emitting bodily radiance that stirred both humans and devas. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddhas] sat beneath ten billion Bodhi trees, each...
I have explained to you that which you asked regarding the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind (*cittabhūmi*). As for the remaining nine hundred and so forth:
previously, from among the thousand lotuses, one lotus was manifested; from among the thousand Buddhas, one Buddha was manifested.
What then of the remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis? Furthermore, since one lotus and one Buddha were manifested in this manner, then...
The remaining nine hundred and ninety-nine Śākyamunis, along with their respective environments and inhabitants, likewise each manifested themselves;
even their inquiries regarding the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground were exactly the same, without duality or distinction.
Second, subsuming function into essence:
The Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus is my transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis are the transformation bodies of those thousand Śākyamunis.
I am their source, and am named Vairocana Buddha.
This Śāntamati understands that ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle cannot penetrate the fact that function is identical to essence;

yet they claim there is a real distinction between the fundamental and the manifested, or between the original and the responsive manifestations. Therefore, he speaks of the "thousand times ten million Śākyas," asserting that these are the transformation bodies of the thousand Śākyas.
The Thousand Śākyas are the emanations of Vairocana. The passage beginning with "Ascending that platform" clarifies how the essence gives rise to function;
this is the function of the very essence itself. The subsequent section clarifies how function is gathered back into the essence; this is the essence of the very function itself.

This correctly demonstrates that the essence is not separate from function, and function is not separate from the essence; essence and function are non-dual. Therefore, it is said: "I take this to be the fundamental source."
Named Vairocana. This concludes the detailed answer regarding the characteristics of the fruit. II.
The detailed answer regarding the characteristics of the cause (in two parts): First, the citation of the question; second, the explanation of the name "Mind-Ground."
First, the introductory statement of the inquiry:

At that time, Vairocana Buddha, seated upon the Lotus-Womb Treasury Throne, extensively answered the questions regarding the Chapter on the Dharma of the Mind-Ground posed by the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis.
"At that time" refers to the moment when the fundamental and the phenomenal are revealed, the pervasive manifestations are fully displayed, and all functions are gathered back into the essence.
"Extensive answer" is said in contrast to the brief answer given above; the previous response was merely brief, stating only: "I have already cultivated the mind-ground for a hundred kalpas."

Furthermore, fearing that the assembly might not know what kind of "ground of mind" (cittabhūmi) this is, the interrogative statement is set forth at the beginning, which will be answered in detail below.
II. Explaining the Name "Ground of Mind" (in four parts): 1. Explaining the names of the Ten Abodes (daśavihāra). 2. Explaining the names of the Ten Practices (daśacaryā).
3. Explaining the names of the ten transferences; 4. Explaining the names of the ten stages.
First, explaining the names of the ten abidings:

"O Buddhas, you should know that within the stage of firm faith and patience, the ten minds of initial aspiration are directed toward the fruit: first, the mind of relinquishment; second, the mind of precepts."
1. The mind of patience; 2. The mind of diligence; 3. The mind of concentration; 4. The mind of wisdom; 5. The mind of aspiration; 6. The mind of protection; 7. The mind of joy; 8.
The mind of the summit.

This explains the names, virtues, and stages of the ten abiding minds (*daśa-vihāra-citta*). Regarding the phrase "All Buddhas should know," this refers to the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis;

they are addressed here because they are the appropriate recipients of the teaching. Within the stage of "firm faith and patience" (*adhimukti-kṣānti*), the ten "minds of departure" (*daśa-prasthāna-citta*) are directed toward the fruit.

As the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states: "The ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) and the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are called the 'abiding of the lineage' (*gotra-vihāra*). Here, "lineage" (*gotra*) refers to the seed.
"Son" (*putra*) carries the meaning of "generation. "Nature" (*gotra*) refers to one's "nature-portion," which signifies that which is self-defined and unchanging.

Because at the stage of the first abode (*prathamā bhūmi*), the seeds of the Middle Way are perfected and one dwells therein without regression or loss, yet progresses ever further, it is called the "abiding in the lineage" (*gotrabhūmi*).
The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "The three levels of worthiness (*trayaḥ pūjyāḥ*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmayaḥ*), and so forth—the various Bodhisattvas of Equality and Subtlety."

It is divided into six stages, each possessing five factors: nature (*gotra*), contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), wisdom (*prajñā*), firmness (*dṛḍha*), and patience (*kṣānti*). Each of these factors is further subdivided into six types according to the six stages.
Within these ten stages of abiding, this [first stage] is called the "nature of the cultivated seed" (*śikṣita-gotra*). "Cultivated" (*śikṣita*) means training;

it refers to the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) in order to destroy the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*). Among the six types of contemplation, this is called "abiding contemplation."
"Abiding" (*sthiti*) means to dwell securely; it refers to the mind’s convergence with principle, which is called abiding. "Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) means to observe and illuminate;

it refers to the thorough investigation and examination of all phenomena as being empty by nature through dependent origination, which is called contemplation. This refers to the practice of the principle of the contemplation of emptiness, which sweeps away all phenomena.
Because these two meanings are combined, it is termed "abiding-contemplation. Among the six types of wisdom, this is called the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Reaching the ears is called "hearing" (*śruta*); discerning is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*). Because one hears the principle of the Middle Way, all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) arises, enabling one to comprehend all phenomena and remain free from the characteristics of the two extremes.
Regarding the phrase "one who possesses firm faith and receptivity" (*kṣānti*), there are two meanings. As for "firm," among the six types of firmness, this is termed "firmness of faith. Faith is...
Faith is firm; that is to say, it is solid and substantial. This means believing that all phenomena are identical to ultimate truth because they are indestructible.

Regarding "patience" (*kṣānti*): among the six types of patience, this is called "patience through faith" (*śraddhākṣānti*). Faith is the mind of faith, and patience is the patience of equanimity (*anurakṣaṇā-kṣānti*).
This means believing that all phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent, and being able to accept, endure, and realize these empty phenomena through the two dharmas.

Taken together, these terms are called "the patience of firm faith" (*kṣānti*). Regarding the "middle," it means that within this patience of firm faith there are ten types of persons who simultaneously give rise to the vast mind of spreading the Dharma above and transforming those below, proceeding toward the ocean of Buddhahood without being able to regress.
The *Awakening of Faith* says: "As for the characteristics of the differentiated stages of progress on the path, this refers to the path realized by all Buddhas."
Because all bodhisattvas resolve their minds and practice for the sake of attaining the ultimate goal, the resolution of the mind is briefly explained as being of three kinds:

first, the resolution of the mind through the perfection of faith; second, the resolution of the mind through practice based on understanding; and third, the resolution of the mind through realization.

Regarding this resolution of the mind through the perfection of faith: it pertains to sentient beings of the indeterminate group who, by virtue of the power of cultivated roots of goodness, believe in the law of karma and its results.
In response: one gives rise to a mind of weary detachment and seeks the path to Bodhi. Having encountered various Buddhas, one personally receives their teachings and makes offerings to them.

After practicing for ten thousand kalpas, the mind of faith is perfected. Whether through being instructed by a Buddha or Bodhisattva to resolve upon the mind, or through the power of great compassion and vows, or due to the conditions of protecting the Dharma, one is able to resolve upon the mind spontaneously. Thus, with the perfection of faith, one resolves upon the mind and enters the correct [path].

The group of certainty (*niyata-rāśi*) never regresses; this is called abiding within the lineage of the Tathāgata. Because it is conjoined with the true cause, it is termed the "arousing of the mind through the perfection of faith.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of arousing the mind: first, the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*), because it correctly contemplates the dharma of *tathatā*;

second, the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), because it delights in accumulating all virtuous practices; and third, the compassionate mind (*karuṇā-citta*), because it desires to uproot all [suffering].

Because it is [free from] suffering, those who thus resolve their minds all attain non-retrogression; therefore, it is said that within the stage of "firm faith and patience" (*kṣānti*), the ten minds of "setting out toward the fruit" are realized.
What are these ten minds? The first is the mind of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*). Relinquishment means giving (*dāna*); it carries the sense of having no regret or attachment.
This refers to relinquishing all internal and external phenomena, thereby penetrating the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and signless (*animitta*), and entering [into realization].

Because of the *śūnyatā-samādhi*. Second is the mind of ethical discipline (*śīla*). "Discipline" refers to the precepts; it carries the meaning of protecting the wholesome and obstructing the unwholesome.
This means that because all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are without accumulation and without reception, and because all natures are detached, the single path is pure.
Third is the mind of patience (*kṣānti*). "Patience" means acceptance; it carries the meaning of enduring with immovability. This means by way of signlessness (*animitta*).

Wisdom-patience (*prajñā-kṣānti*). This is the patience of the emptiness of all emptiness (*sarva-śūnyatā-śūnyatā-kṣānti*), because the mark of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena (*dharma*) is unattainable.

Fourth is the advancing mind. "Advancing" (*pra*) refers to diligence (*vīrya*); it carries the meaning of moving forward without retreating. That is to say, within the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*)—
Ascending the Mountain of Non-arising, one enters emptiness and enters the provisional; yet there are no two distinct characteristics. Fifth is the concentrated mind (*samādhi-citta*).

Concentration is *dhyāna-samādhi*, meaning the state of being neither dull nor distracted. This refers to the mind’s contemplation being tranquil, whereby all evils are extinguished and all virtues are produced.
Sixth is the wise mind (*prajñā-citta*). Wisdom is *prajñā*, which clearly illuminates and realizes the non-... [the ultimate truth].

The meaning of "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) refers to the fact that by means of the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), which is ineffable, one enters the principle of the single truth of the Middle Way;

thus, the breaking of the hindrance of ignorance is entirely the function of wisdom. Seventh is the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta*). Aspiration is the sense of longing; it carries the meaning of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below.
This refers to first generating the mind of seeking, then practicing the path in the interim, and finally, when practice is perfected and the vow fulfilled, the fruit of Buddhahood is realized.
Therefore, the eighth is the mind of protection (*rakṣā-citta*). "Protection" means guarding and maintaining; it carries the sense of being able to effectively act as a dam.

This refers to protecting by means of the protection of signlessness (*animitta-rakṣā*), so that the eight inversions of the various non-Buddhists do not disturb right faith. One protects the root because the essence of the Dharma (*dharma-tattva*) is neither accumulated nor dispersed, and thus cannot be protected.
The ninth is the mind of joy (*muditā-citta*). "Joy" means rejoicing; it carries the sense of attaining happiness and leaving behind suffering.
That is to say, seeing others obtain happiness, one constantly gives rise to joy; this is the mind of tranquil illumination that delights in all phenomena because it takes all dharmas as its object.
Tenth is the "Crown Mind" (*mūrdha-citta*). "Crown" refers to the crown of the head; it signifies being most noble, with nothing superior above it.

This means that by means of the supreme wisdom of the crown, one extinguishes the wheel of non-self, severs the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), does not undergo the fruits of the six realms of existence, and dwells in the third stage, the "Crown."

One attains the clarity of right concentration. By initiating practice, one proceeds toward the reality of the nature of the Way; because one does not depart from right faith, these ten minds become perfectly luminous.
The contemplation of emptiness is accomplished, the rational nature gradually manifests, and the provisional establishment of ultimate truth ceases.

From this, one is liberated and advances toward the stages of practice (*bhūmi*). The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "By means of the six [substances]—copper, silver, gold, lapis lazuli, crystal, and agate—"

The six stages—wheel (*cakra*), facing (*abhimukha*), proceeding (*gati*), orientation (*ābhimukhya*), ground (*bhūmi*), and excellence (*praṇīta*)—are as follows. Regarding the "wheel," there are two meanings: first, turning;

second, crushing and grinding. This means that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas turn the Great Dharma Wheel (*mahā-dharmacakra*), they are able to crush and grind away the afflictions and karma of sentient beings.
Because they sever delusions and realize the truth, there are respective shallow and deep stages in their progression.
The same applies here; thus, the six wheels are correlated with the six stages. Question: To which wheel does this stage of the ten abodes correspond?
Answer: It corresponds to the copper-jewel wheel. Why copper? Because it resembles gold in color yet lacks the functional utility of gold.
Although it is free from the impurities of iron, it still possesses dross. However, if it is refined, polished, and tempered, it can become [gold].

Various vessels serve practical purposes in the world. It is said that the Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes cultivate only the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) to sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), which is like being freed from dust and grime.

Among the forty-two grades of ignorance (*avidyā*), those at the stage of the Ten Abodes sever one grade—the mark of extinction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*)—and ten grades of the mark of difference (*visabhāga-lakṣaṇa*).
If these ten preceding grades of the mark of difference have not yet been completely severed, [the Bodhisattva remains at this stage].
Just as copper contains dross, once delusion is severed, virtue is likewise revealed.

Thus, one can give rise to function according to the essence and manifest forms according to the species, transforming all sentient beings like a vessel that accomplishes the salvation of the world; therefore, [he possesses] the precious wheel of copper.
Regarding the ten stages of abiding (*bhūmi*).
Second, the explanation of the names of the ten practices (*caryā*):

"O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten minds of setting forth, one enters into the patience regarding the firmness of dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*), and the ten minds of nurturing advance toward [the next stage]."

The fruits are: first, the mind of loving-kindness; second, the mind of compassion; third, the mind of sympathetic joy; fourth, the mind of equanimity; fifth, the mind of generosity; sixth, the mind of pleasant speech;
seventh, the mind of beneficial intent; eighth, the mind of impartiality; ninth, the mind of concentration; and tenth, the mind of wisdom.
This explains the names and virtues of the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*). Within the six natures (*ṣaḍ-gotra*), this constitutes the nature-seed-nature (*prakṛti-gotra*).
This means that although one has realized the original nature of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one does not remain submerged in the principle of emptiness;
rather, one is able to discern all phenomena and transform sentient beings, causing them to enter the Buddha-way. Among the six contemplations, this constitutes the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*).

Contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the practice of cultivation. By cultivating the provisional practice of contemplation, one establishes all phenomena. Because these two meanings are combined, it is called "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

Among the six types of wisdom (*prajñā*), this is termed "wisdom born of reflection" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). "Reflection" (*cintā*) means critical reflection, superior reflection, and decisive reflection.

"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the discerning wisdom of awakening (*dharmapravicaya-bodhiprajñā*). Through reflecting upon the principles within [this wisdom], one gives rise to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
"Wisdom" (*prajñā*) refers to the transformation and edification of sentient beings. Because these two meanings are combined, it is called "contemplative wisdom" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

The two phrases beginning with "The Buddhas should know" conclude the preceding section. The phrase "entering into the patience of the firm dharma" (*dṛḍha-dharma-kṣānti*) and so forth initiates the subsequent section.

Why is it that the previous stage was called "firm faith-patience" (*dṛḍha-adhimukti-kṣānti*), while this practice is called "upright dharma-patience"? It is because the principle (*dharma*) previously cultivated is entered through faith, and faith arises from the principle.
Therefore, what was previously called "firm faith" (śraddhādhimukti) is here called "firmness in the Dharma" (dharmakṣānti).

Among the six types of firmness, this is named "firmness in the Dharma," meaning that one knows all phenomena are precisely the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) because they cannot be destroyed. Among the six types of patience (kṣānti), this is named "patience in the Dharma."
Although one knows that all dharmas are empty and devoid of any marks, one is nevertheless able to provisionally establish all dharmas in order to transform sentient beings.
Within these provisional dharmas, one endures and realizes them. Because these two aspects of dharma are spoken of in conjunction, it is called "Patience with the Firm Dharma" (dharmakṣānti).
In this stage, one penetrates deeply into the profound mystery of the truth of the ten abodes and relies upon the sublime practices of Bodhi.

Arising from principle, one exercises the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) and practices the four methods of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*) to benefit sentient beings, nurture the holy embryo, and perfect holy virtue toward the ocean of the Buddha-fruit. Therefore, it is called the "ten nurturing minds" directed toward the fruit of Bodhi.
What are the ten nurturing minds? The first is the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which cherishes and pities sentient beings so that its transformative influence covers all.
It can give rise to the state of right nature (*samyaktva*), for it does not rely on the teachings of Māra to attain the fruit of happiness. Second is the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*):

out of pity for sentient beings, through the emptiness of emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*), one personally extinguishes all suffering and bestows equal, singular happiness upon all sentient beings by giving rise to great compassion.
Third is the mind of joy (*muditā*): rejoicing in the happiness attained by others, through the joy of the emptiness of emptiness.
They cause all sentient beings to enter into right faith, abandon wrong views, and turn their backs on the suffering of the six realms; thus they rejoice. Fourth is the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*):
providing for all without stinginess, being without fabrication or signs, like space within the dharma of emptiness, where the essential nature of self and others cannot be apprehended;
thus they constantly cultivate equanimity with a mind free from arising. Fifth is the mind of generosity (*dāna*): bestowing universally and without parsimony.

The gift of body, the gift of speech, the gift of mind, the gift of material wealth, and the gift of the Dharma. He instructs and guides all sentient beings; he transforms them through conduct free from conceptual thought.
Having mastered principles and perfected giving, all marks appear before him. Sixth is the mind of pleasant speech: whatever he says is virtuous;
with compassionate and loving words, he gathers and transforms sentient beings, always acting in accordance with his heart to give rise to roots of goodness. Seventh.
This is the mind of benefit. It transforms sentient beings through supreme practice; it is the essential nature of true wisdom.

It extensively traverses the path of knowledge and manifests within the six realms of existence without regarding them as afflictions, benefiting others solely for their sake. Eighth is the "identical mind": concealing one's identity to gather and transform others.

Through the wisdom of the nature of the Path, one is identical with emptiness and the dharma of non-arising; through the wisdom of non-self, one is identical with all beings as being non-dual. Thus one enters into all...
The physical forms, karmic activities, and all matters pertaining to the six realms of existence are identical. By entering the Samādhi of Identical Dharma, one attains the ninth [stage]:
the concentrated mind. Sealed and maintained without distraction, one contemplates emptiness with the still wisdom of a single thought; nothing can disturb it.

One clearly perceives that the seeds of "self" and "person" among all sentient beings are devoid of both conjunction and dispersion, for their accumulation, integration, arising, and activity cannot be apprehended.

Tenth is the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*). It illuminates all things with unimpeded penetration, observing that the various fetters of false views and afflictions have no determinate intrinsic nature.

This mind enters the path of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and gives rise to the mind of non-arising (*anutpāda-citta*). From these ten minds, one’s practices proceed without contradiction;

concentration and wisdom become perfectly clear and bright, and neither the provisional (*saṃvṛti*) nor the empty (*śūnya*) are established. Observing through the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), one advances toward the stage of the candidate for the fruit (*pratipannaka*).
Furthermore, regarding the meritorious practice of this stage, among the six wheels, it corresponds to the wheel of silver treasure.

This means that the nature of silver is brilliant and pure, such that it does not receive dust or grime; even after being melted and refined, its nature remains eternally unchanged. Such is the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage of practice.

By cultivating the contemplation of the provisional and applying effort, one spontaneously and progressively severs the ten grades of the delusions, karma, and afflictions of differentiated characteristics within the middle [level].
This reveals the inherently pure nature, which is like the lustrous purity of silver that remains unchanged through smelting and refinement.
Therefore, the silver jewel-wheel corresponds to the stage of the ten practices (*daśabhūmi-pratipatti*).
○ Third, the explanation of the names of the ten transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*):
"O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten minds of nourishment, one enters into the firm cultivation of patience; [this is] the orientation toward the ten adamantine minds (*daśavajracitta*)."
The fruits are: first, the mind of faith; second, the mind of mindfulness; third, the mind of dedication; fourth, the mind of penetration; fifth, the mind of rectitude;
sixth, the mind of non-retrogression; seventh, the Mahāyāna mind; eighth, the signless mind; ninth, the mind of wisdom; and tenth, the indestructible mind.
This explains the names, virtues, and stages of the ten *pariṇāmanā-cittas* (dedication-minds). As for the dedication-mind:

based on all the practices and realizations of omniscience cultivated and attained in the two preceding stages, it does not fall, does not regress, and does not abide; neither emptiness nor the provisional is established.

Every moment of mind is dedicated within the equality of *tathatā* (suchness) and the principle of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm); this is called the dedication-mind. O Buddhas, you should know these two.

[This] phrase concludes the preceding [section]. Regarding the phrase "entering the firm cultivation of patience" and so forth, it initiates the subsequent [section]. As for the expression "from these," it refers to the ten practices mentioned above.

Just as a sprout grows and flowers, fruits, and seeds come to fruition, when the flowers have fallen and the fruit is about to be formed, one further increases the firmness and vigor of the mind so that it cannot be invaded or damaged by Māras or externalists.
This stage, among the six natures (*ṣaḍ-gotra*), is called the nature of the path-variety (*mārgākāra-gotra*). This is because of the cause.
One cultivates the Middle Way and attains penetration into the Buddha-dharma, for it is able to give rise to the seeds of the bodhi-path for all sentient beings.

Among the six contemplations, this is called "contemplation directed toward" (*mukha-vipaśyanā*), because it is directed toward the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Among the six types of wisdom, this is called "cultivated wisdom" (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because by cultivating the principle of the Middle Way, one generates untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom. As stated previously:

*Dṛḍhadharmanidhyānakṣānti* (Patience in Firmly Contemplating the Dharma). This is translated here as "Firm Cultivation Patience" (*dṛḍhabhāvanākṣānti*), which possesses two meanings. Among the six "firmnesses" (*dṛḍha*), it is called "cultivation firmness" (*bhāvanādṛḍha*);
that is, by practicing Madhyamaka, one realizes that all phenomena are precisely the Middle Truth (*madhyasatya*) and are thus indestructible.

Among the six "patiences" (*kṣānti*), this is called "cultivation patience" (*bhāvanākṣānti*); that is, by cultivating the Middle Way, one knows all phenomena in terms of both their facts (*vastu*) and their principles (*yukti*).
Harmonious and integrated, within this principle one accepts and realizes it; when these two meanings are combined, it is called "firmly cultivated patience.

These ten stages of the direction toward enlightenment (*adhimukticaryā*) constitute the arousal of the mind through practice and understanding. One enters the preceding ten stages of abiding (*vihāra*) by virtue of the fulfillment of faith.
These ten stages of dedication are entered by virtue of the fulfillment of practice.

Because this Bodhisattva is about to complete the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, there arises within them a profound realization of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness). Thus, in every thought-moment, the true mark of the mind is realized;
in every moment of mindfulness, there is *tathatā*; and in every action, there is perfect integration as they cultivate the diamond-like samādhi and gather [all merits] into one.
All practices of the Dharma-gate penetrate deeply into contemplation of principle, becoming increasingly clear and bright until one enters the ocean of the Buddha-fruit. Therefore, it is said:
"From these ten stages of the nurturing mind, one enters into firm cultivation of patience; the ten adamantine minds turn toward the fruit.
What are called the ten stages of the dedicatory mind? The first is the mind of faith: simply believing that one's own mind will certainly attain Buddhahood, forever free from doubt.
First, the mind of grasping. Second, the mind of mindfulness: in every thought-moment, one does not lose the right wisdom of all Buddhas;

regarding the six recollections of the Mahāyāna, one is constantly aware and constantly giving, because they are of a single unified character. Third, the mind of dedication: "dedication" means non-abiding.
Toward it, one immediately does not regress. Regarding this unsurpassed vajra bodhi, mind after mind enters emptiness, yet there is no coming or going;
for one receives the fruits through illusion and attains profound liberation of mind. Fourth is "penetrating the mind. To penetrate means to thoroughly comprehend.
It penetrates all without obstruction; internal and external are pure. It is the mark of emptiness within emptiness, the *tathatā* (suchness), because nothing can be apprehended therein.
Fifth is the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*). "Direct" means upright and straightforward. It directly illuminates equality and enters the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Regarding those born within the three realms—which are empty of ignorance and the divine self (*ātman*)—it does not undergo the bonds of affliction. Sixth is the non-retrogressive mind (*avinivartana-citta*). Non-retrogression...
Entering the stage of ordinary beings, one does not give rise to new or further nurtured false views, but constantly gives birth to a mind of emptiness.
This mind enters non-duality because it constitutes the non-retrogressive single path and single illumination. Seventh is the Mahāyāna mind:

understanding that all things are resolved within the single emptiness, one employs the wisdom of this single emptiness as both the vehicle of wisdom and the vehicle of practice. Carrying and utilizing this, one causes all sentient beings to enter together into the ocean of the Buddha.

Therefore: Eighth is the signless mind (*animitta-citta*). This is the mind being signless, liberated from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and illuminating the *prajñāpāramitā*, because it is free from the two marks.
Ninth is the wisdom-mind (*prajñā-citta*). Within the immeasurable *dharmadhātu*, there is no accumulation and no undergoing of birth;
though afflictions arise life after life, they do not bind, for its radiance illuminates the nature and enters into all phenomena. Tenth is the indestructible [mind].
The mind is indestructible by the eight māras. Entering the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, one manifests with sovereign mastery and shakes the great trichiliocosm.
Because the mind of the ground of equality in space is non-dual and undifferentiated, when these ten minds are perfected, the principle of the two kinds of emptiness is revealed.
Moved thereby, all Buddhas bestow their empowerment, and one attains the *mōdǐng* (crown-of-the-head) samādhi, realizing entry into the *dhāraṇī* of the equality of space.
This Dharma-gate is the entry into the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Within these ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the Golden Jewel Wheel (*suvarṇaratnacakra*) corresponds to this position.
This is because the substance of gold is precious and its utility for salvation is immense; it is refined by fire and its color remains unchanged.
This Bodhisattva practices only the Middle Way; their meritorious conduct deepens and their teaching and transformation of others become vast.
Although they mingle among the various defilements, they are not stained by those defilements; although they dwell amidst the five desires, they are not burned by the five desires.

Because they have completely severed the ten final grades of ignorance regarding distinct characteristics (*bhinnalakṣaṇa-avidyā*), they are matched with the Golden Jewel Wheel in the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). This...

Regarding the three preliminary practices of the sages (*śaikṣa*), although each cultivates a single contemplation, this is stated according to their fundamental stages as described in the *Yingluo* (The Garland).
In reality, however, the three contemplations are cultivated in a perfect unity; they are three while being one, and one while being three.
○ Fourth, the explanation of the characteristics of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
O Buddhas, you should know that from these ten adamantine minds, one enters into the firm noble patience (*āryakṣānti*) and attains the fruits of the ten stages:

first, the stage of the equality of essential nature; second, the stage of excellent wisdom of essential nature; third, the stage of radiance of essential nature; fourth, the stage of... [essential nature].

The second is the Ground of Blazing Wisdom; the third is the Ground of the Radiance of the Nature of Body; the fourth is the Ground of the Flower-Light of the Nature of Body; the fifth is the Ground of Fulfillment of the Nature of Body;

the sixth is the Ground of the Buddha’s Roar of the Nature of Body; the seventh is the Ground of the Flower Adornment of the Nature of Body; and the eighth is the Ground of Entry into the Buddha-realm of the Nature of Body.

O Buddhas, you should know that this single phrase designates Samantabhadra; it is spoken in response to the thousand transformation Buddhas to explain the names, virtues, and stages of the ten bhūmis.
From this single phrase, the preceding section—beginning with "entering the patience of the noble ones" (*āryakṣānti*) and so forth—is concluded, while the subsequent section is initiated.

Having previously practiced the noble conduct during the three stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), their merit becomes perfectly complete, and they attain entry into the *dhāraṇī* dharma-gate of the stage of true equality (*samyaktva-niyāma*). From here on...

This is called "sagehood" (*ārya*). Therefore, it is said that from these ten adamantine minds, one enters into the stage of firm sage-like patience (*kṣānti*) and attains the fruits of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Question: Why are the first three stages of the worthy ones (*puruṣapudgala*) called "minds" (*citta*), while the ten stages of the sages are called "stages" (*bhūmi*)? Answer: Regarding the stages of the three worthies...
As long as True Suchness (tathatā) has not been realized, it is not the locus of reliance. These ten stages of the noble ones (āryabhūmi), however, constitute the ground of the Buddha-realm;
they are the basis for all things, the nature of all virtues, and the source from which all virtues arise. Therefore, the mind is termed "ground" (bhūmi).
Among the six natures, this ground is the nature of perfect enlightenment (samyaksambuddhatva); that is to say, it is identical to the essence of the Buddha, being without distinction.
Therefore, among the six contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), this is the contemplation of the ground (*bhūmi-vipaśyanā*), meaning it is able to give birth to all things;

for by practicing the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), all the wisdom and merit of the Buddhas arise from it. Among the six types of wisdom (*prajñā*), it is the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*).
This refers to correctly knowing the principle of the Middle Way, wherein through emptiness and signlessness one is able to give rise to all untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

Regarding the term "firm noble patience" (*kṣānti*), there are two meanings. Among the six types of firmness, for Bodhisattvas on the stages (*bhūmi*), it is called "firmness of virtue" (*guṇa-dṛḍha*).
This means that by cultivating the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation, they destroy a portion of the obscurations such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and manifest [the truth].
It brings forth a portion of the three virtues of *tathatā* (suchness), which cannot be destroyed; therefore, it is called "Firm Virtue" (*guṇa-dṛḍha*).

Among the six types of patience (*kṣānti*), this is termed "Right Patience" (*samyak-kṣānti*). This means that one correctly destroys ignorance; because one endures, confirms, and realizes the principle therein, it is called "Right Patience.

When these two meanings are combined, it is termed "Firm Noble Patience" (*dṛḍha-ārya-kṣānti*). This is precisely what is called "the mind awakened through realization" (*pratyakṣa-bodhicitta*). That is to say:
Because they realize the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), they act solely to guide all sentient beings and do not rely on words and letters;

this has been extensively clarified in the *Awakening of Faith*. The above provides a general explanation of the meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Below follows a specific explanation of the meaning of the ten stages. What are the names of these ten stages?

First is the Stage of the Equality of Essential Nature (*dharmatā-samatā-bhūmi*); this refers to the bodhisattva’s realization and entry into the equality of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of all Buddhas.
Mahāmati, the Dharma-gate of reality gathers in and sustains sentient beings; for whatever they do, their wisdom is impartial.

Second is the Stage of the Wholesome Wisdom of Essential Nature: here, this Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates the great wisdom of the equality of the Dharma-body, because they have attained pure and clear penetration into all roots of goodness.
Third is the Stage of Radiance of Essential Nature: here, this Bodhisattva realizes and gives rise to...

The Radiance of the Ultimate Wisdom at the Margins: By means of the wisdom that understands through samādhi, one is able to know all the Dharma-gates of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, because of entering the radiance of the supernormal powers. Fourth is the Ground of the Blazing Body-Nature:
This Bodhisattva, by means of the flames of wisdom, burns the fuel of afflictions; by entering into skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they are able to teach and transform all sentient beings.
Because it causes one to see the essence of the Buddha, it is the fifth stage, the Ground of Wisdom Illuminating Essence.

This Bodhisattva, by means of the illumination of the wisdom of the ten powers, knows the two natures of existence and non-existence regarding good and evil, gives rise to all meritorious practices, and turns the ineffably ineffable Dharma-gates.
The sixth is the Ground of Flower-Light Essence. This Bodhisattva, by means of the flowers of great wisdom-practice...
At one time, they bloom simultaneously. Regarding the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers and Clear Wisdom":

manifesting their bodies to the assembly, they display various transformations that cannot be fully described even after hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas. Seventh is the Stage of Fulfillment of Essential Nature:
this Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the eighteen qualities of noble wisdom; throughout all lands, they act in accordance with the mental activities of sentient beings.
He manifests the attainment of Buddhahood by achieving enlightenment and turning the wheel of Dharma. This is the eighth stage, the Ground of the Buddha’s Lion’s Roar.

Here, this Bodhisattva enters the samādhi of the rank of the Dharma King; his wisdom is like that of a Buddha, and as a great Dharma teacher, he bestows the medicine of the Dharma upon all sentient beings.
He destroys the four māras, is fully endowed with the Dharma-body, and preaches the Dharma without fear, like a great lion.

Because of this roar. Ninth is the Ground of the Flower Ornament of Essential Nature (*dharmatā-puṣpavyūha-bhūmi*). This Bodhisattva attains the Flower Ornament of the Buddha and is well able to protect the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Through the majestic deportment of a Buddha and the Tathāgata’s Samādhi of the Sovereign King (*samādhirāja*), they enter and emerge from this sovereign concentration at no fixed time.
Simultaneously throughout ten billion sets of four continents, they attain Buddhahood, manifesting infinite bodies, speech, and minds, and preaching the Dharma without end.
The Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of Measurement: Being able to turn the realms of all Māras and enter the Buddha-realm, and turning the Buddha-realm and enter the realm of Māras;
because such matters are manifested simultaneously within a single thought-moment, it is the tenth stage of the nature of entering the Buddha-realm.
This Bodhisattva, having attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), enters the Vajra-samādhi.

His great wisdom is empty, empty again, and yet empty, like the nature of space. He is fully endowed with the ten categories of merit, as well as unspeakably many wondrous Dharma-gates, wondrous samādhi-gates, and dhāraṇī-gates, which are beyond the reach of the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings of the lower stages.
This is what is to be known. Only a Buddha can exhaust the source of the immeasurable body, speech, and mind of a Buddha.
From this point on, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are perfected, and one enters equally into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wondrous enlightenment.

Regarding the merits of a Bodhisattva at this stage, among the six wheels, it corresponds to the position of the lapis lazuli jewel wheel. Just as the Lapis Lazuli Jewel produces Mount Sumeru, so too does [this stage produce] all...
No multitude of jewels can destroy it; likewise, the reality realized by a Bodhisattva on this tenth stage cannot be shaken or destroyed by external Māras.
Therefore, the lapis lazuli jewel wheel is correlated with the ten stages. Regarding the contemplative practice, abandonment, and realization of these ten holy stages:
on the first stage, one abandons the superior grade of delusions and realizes the inferior grade of wisdom. From the second stage up to the seventh stage, [the process continues accordingly].

By severing the medium-grade afflictions, one realizes medium-grade wisdom; from the eighth stage through the tenth stage and so forth, by severing the low-grade afflictions, one realizes superior-grade wisdom.
This is precisely the transformation of the mental complex associated with the five sensory consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
The mental states associated with the transformation of the sixth consciousness become the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation;

the mental states associated with the transformation of the seventh consciousness become the Wisdom of Equality; and the mental states associated with the transformation of the eighth consciousness become the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.

When these four wisdoms are perfectly luminous, the three bodies manifest in their entirety—namely, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, the Stainless Wisdom, and the Wisdom that Arises Simultaneously, which universally...
It illuminates the dust-like lands throughout the ten directions. The above concludes the explanation of the names and characteristics of the "Mind-Ground.

Below, the conclusion summarizes the answer to provide an exhortation for practice. III. Conclusion of the Response to the Question (2): 1. Citing the Dharma and Stating the Causes; 2. Providing Exhortations for Practice and Realization.
First, the presentation of the Dharma and the statement of the cause:
these are the forty dharma-gates. In this chapter, I describe the roots and sources for entering the fruit of Buddhahood when I was formerly a bodhisattva.
This "Chapter on the Forty Dharma-Gates" summarizes the rules for the mind-ground to encourage practice.
"When I was formerly a bodhisattva" refers to citing the fruit to clarify the cause. "The source for cultivating entry into the fruit of Buddhahood" refers to the fundamental origin.
This illustrates that the cause gives rise to the fruit: if it were not a superior cause, one could not obtain a superior fruit;
and if it were not a superior fruit, how could it manifest a superior cause? Śāntamati points directly to the source as a model for sentient beings to cultivate and enter.
II. Encouraging Cultivation and Realization:
In this way, all sentient beings enter the stages of *prasthāna* (setting forth), *poṣaṇa* (nurturing), and *vajra* (diamond-like), and through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they shall realize the fruit:

the unconditioned, signless, great fulfillment, and eternal abiding; the ten powers (*daśabala*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), and the perfection of the *dharmakāya* and *jñānakāya*.

This provides a general answer to the previous two questions, clarifying the meaning of cultivation and realization. The two characters "thus" (*evam*) inherit from above that the source of one's own attainment of Buddhahood lies herein.

All sentient beings should likewise, as I did in the past when practicing the Bodhisattva path, cultivate the stages of the person, the stage of setting out, the stage of growth, the Vajra stage, and the ten bhūmis—the practices of the forty noble sages. To act in this way is...

By means of the mind of the causal stage, one attains the realization of the fruit to be accomplished: the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and signless (*animitta*), the great fulfillment and eternal abiding.

The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and Wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*) are fully endowed with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇavyañjana*). That which is unconditioned and signless manifests the Dharma-body; that which is the great fulfillment and eternally abiding manifests the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*);

and the ten powers (*daśabala*) and eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*) manifest the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The Dharma-body and Reward-body are inseparable—the three bodies (*trikāya*).
It manifests perfectly. This constitutes the fulfillment of the Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body.

By means of these three bodies, one attains the realized body as the fruit through cultivating the mind-ground during the causal stage. The *Zongjing lu* states: "By the transformation of the fundamental mind..."

One attains the realization of the *dharmakāya*. As for the fundamental mind, it is the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). It means that all phenomena, such as the wholesome and unwholesome, arise based upon this.
If one is deluded regarding this consciousness, there is birth and death; if one awakens to this consciousness, one attains *nirvāṇa*.

When this consciousness undergoes transformation, afflictions are simultaneously severed and extinguished entirely, and because one attains the realization of the *dharmakāya*, this is the second transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
The fundamental mind attains the realization of the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*). That which relies upon the fundamental mind is the seventh consciousness;
it arises based on the eighth consciousness. If one is deluded regarding this consciousness, all forms of ignorance arise; if one awakens to this consciousness, all forms of wisdom arise.
Therefore, when this consciousness undergoes transformation, one is liberated from all ignorance and immediately realizes the reward body.
Because of the body, the mind that engages in activity arises three times, whereby one attains the realization of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
This "mind that engages in activity" is precisely the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭhavijñāna*), which gives rise to discrimination in relation to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

By being deluded regarding this consciousness, one gives rise to all forms of greed, hatred, and ignorance, thereby harming sentient beings. By awakening to this consciousness, one cultivates all the categories of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
This benefits sentient beings. Therefore, when this consciousness undergoes transformation, one immediately realizes the nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).

For this reason, when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he teaches the various dharma-gates of the mind-ground not for any purpose other than to cause all sentient beings to sever evil and cultivate goodness, transform consciousness into wisdom, realize the three bodies, and perfect the ten titles. As for the ten powers: first, the knowledge of...

1. The power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*). 2. The power of knowing the retribution of karma in the past, present, and future (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñānabala*). 3.

The power of knowing all meditative absorptions, liberations, and concentrations (*dhyāna-vimokṣa-samādhi-jñānabala*). 4. The power of knowing the various dispositions and the degrees of the faculties of beings (*indriya-parāpara-jñānabala*). 5.

The power of knowing the various inclinations of beings (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*), also called the power of desire (*chanda-bala*). 6. The power of knowing the various elements or natures of beings (*nānā-dhātu-jñānabala*), also called the power of nature (*prakṛti-bala*).
7. The power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations; 8. The power of knowing past lives with the outflows extinguished; 9. The power of knowing the unimpeded divine eye; 10.
The power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows through the permanent severance of all habitual tendencies. Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*):
1. No failure in physical action; 2. No failure in verbal action; 3. No failure in mental action; 4. No [forgetfulness]...
1. A concentrated mind. 2. A mind free from divergent thoughts. 3. A mind that never lacks equanimity. 4. No decrease in desire. 5. No decrease in mindfulness.
6. No decrease in diligence. 7. No decrease in wisdom. 8. No decrease in liberation. 9. No decrease in the knowledge and vision of liberation.
10. Physical actions follow the movement of wisdom. 11. Verbal actions...
Fifteen: mental action follows the movement of wisdom. Sixteen: knowledge of the past is unimpeded.
Seventeen: knowledge of the present is unimpeded. Eighteen: knowledge of the future is unimpeded. Regarding these eighteen practices, why are they called "unshared"?
Because they are the realm of the noble wisdom of the self-awakened Buddhas, and are not [the domain] of provisional or lesser bodhisattvas.
It is not shared; furthermore, it is not a realm that can be known by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), hence it is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*).

○ Third, Huaguang’s Request for Explanation (2): First, a general indication of the *nirmāṇakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*; second, a specific clarification regarding the appropriate recipients of the teaching.
First, a general indication of the Reward and Transformation Bodies:
At that time, in the Lotus-Womb Treasury World (Padmagarbha-lokadhātu), upon the seat of the magnificent great radiance, was Vairocana Buddha, along with the Buddhas of the thousand petals,
the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas, and all the Buddhas of every world.
This serves as a general indication that essence and function are inseparable, clarifying the principle that the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are non-dual.

The phrase "at that time" refers to the original Vairocana Tathāgata; it indicates the moment for exhorting practice by citing the cause to clarify the fruit. This is the Vairocana upon the lotus pedestal.

The majestic and great seat of radiant light; the Buddha upon the thousand-petaled lotus; and the hundreds of thousands of myriads of Buddhas—all have already been explained and visualized in the preceding text.

As for the phrase "the Buddhas of all worlds," this refers to the Śākyamuni Tathāgata of the hundred-thousand-myriad transformations, who, through successive emanations, manifests as immeasurable and inexhaustible Wisdom Tathāgatas residing within all worlds and preaching the Dharma.
This benefits sentient beings. It signifies that from within the dharma of the precepts of the mind-ground, immeasurable and inexhaustible Buddhas of wisdom are born.
As the text of the lower fascicle states: "The multitude of Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust attain perfect enlightenment by means of this. This refers to that very point.
II. Specifically clarifying those suited to the teaching:
Within this assembly, there was a bodhisattva named King Flower Radiance, the Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom and Clarity. He rose from his seat and stood.

He addressed Vairocana Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, the Buddha has briefly opened up the characteristics of the ten stages of departure (*niryāṇa*), the ten stages of nurturing (*poṣaṇa*), the ten adamantine stages (*vajra-bhūmi*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*).
Within each of these individual meanings, they are not yet fully understood. We only pray that you will explain them;

we only pray that you will explain them—the Gate of All-Knowledge, the Sublime Ultimate Adamantine Treasure Store, which was already clarified within the Tathāgata’s Chapter on the Hundred Contemplations.”
This section of the text follows as a summary of the preceding meaning. From that time onward, Śākyamuni’s body emitted rays of wisdom-light, causing gods and humans to give rise to doubt.
The Lord of Profound Penetration and Radiance gathered the assembly by emitting light and inquired about the characteristics of the radiance.
Śākyamuni led the multitude to the abode of Vairocana, where he posed the two aforementioned questions on their behalf to resolve their doubts. Vairocana accepted and answered them. From...
All who reach the state of supreme sagehood take the mind-ground as their cause and shall thereby attain the fruit of Buddhahood. Within that fruit, each and every realm is clearly elucidated.

Furthermore, fearing that the great assembly, though they have heard that the mind-ground is the cause, may not know what kind of mind-ground it is, [the Buddha] extensively expounds its names and characteristics as the thirty minds and the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Since such names exist, such...

Such characteristics must necessarily have such meanings. If these underlying principles were not elucidated, it would cause practitioners to be ignorant of their direction, clinging to appearances and thereby deluding the mind, and clinging to phenomena and thereby deluding the principle. Therefore, the Bodhisattva Flower-Light King requested an explanation of these meanings;
this precisely refers to the fact that while the mind of nirvana is easy to understand, the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify. Within this assembly...
"One Bodhisattva" refers to the Bodhisattva at the stage of fruition among the thousand Buddhas seated upon the throne above.
Regarding "King Huaguang of Great Wisdom and Clarity," he was previously called the "Mysterious and Penetrating Lord of Huaguang," and here he is called "King Huaguang of Great Wisdom and Clarity."
This clearly reveals the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground Precepts. One who does not possess great wisdom cannot thoroughly inquire into it;
for the severing of delusions and the realization of truth must take wisdom as the foremost. Rising from his seat, he manifested the sincerity of his physical action;
addressing Vairocana Buddha, he manifested the sincerity of his verbal action; with body and speech in *tathatā* (suchness), his mind was in accord with reality.

This is the manifestation of the sincerity of mental action (*manas-karman*). The Buddha has briefly opened up the ten stages of setting forth (*prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*puṣṭi*), the ten adamantine stages (*vajra*), and the ten grounds (*bhūmi*)—these forty dharma-gates of names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).

Although these names and characteristics are numerous, when sought through their characteristics, the names and characteristics themselves become abbreviated; therefore, it is said they are "briefly opened. While the names and characteristics are brief, their meaning remains vast. Within this, one...
There is a single underlying meaning: the wisdom of cultivation and abandonment has never been understood. Therefore, one must request a detailed and clear explanation.
Thus it is said: "I only pray that you will speak of this; I only pray that you will speak of this. This repetition of the request expresses the utmost sincerity of the petitioner.

As for the phrase "the wondrous ultimate treasury of the vajra, the gateway to all-knowledge," this request concerns right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), which gives rise to skillful means (*upāya*) contemplation.
[This is] practice, because it aims at the fruit of Buddhahood. "Sublime ultimate" refers to the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
"Vajra" refers to firm and sharp wisdom. This means that if one is to reach the ocean of the fruit, nothing other than vajra-wisdom can do so. Once this wisdom arises, no phenomena can destroy it;
rather, it is able to destroy all phenomena—cutting off and exhausting all defilements and all seeds of evil without remainder.
Therefore, it is said: "The ultimate wondrous Vajra. Because this wisdom is fully endowed with all merits, it is called the "Treasury of Jewels.
Because it serves as the skillful means for the cultivation and abandonment of all worthies and sages, and as the root of contemplative wisdom, it is called the "Gate of All-Knowledge.

Part One: Explaining the Meaning of the Ten Abodes (2) I. General Introduction and Restatement of the Question II. Detailed Explanation of Their Meanings I.

General Introduction and Restatement of the Question At that time, Vairocana Buddha said: "O thousand Buddhas, listen attentively! Regarding what you previously asked as to what the meaning is of 'setting forth' (prasthāna):"

[In the] middle [section]. This passage cites the Bodhisattva Mahāprajñāloka and requests an explanation of its meaning; it exhorts the listeners and grants permission to expound the meaning of the contemplative practices for advancing through the stages of the ten abodes (*daśabhūmi*).
II. Detailed Explanation of the Meaning (Ten Sections). I.
First, the Explanation of the Stage of Equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*).
O Disciples of the Buddha, one renounces everything: kingdoms, cities, towns, fields, houses, gold, silver, bright pearls, sons and daughters, and even one’s own body.
All conditioned things are entirely relinquished; the unconditioned is signless. The notions of self, person, knower, and seer are merely provisional aggregations that constitute a master;
they give rise to the view of a self. Within the twelve links of dependent origination, there is no combination, no dispersion, and no experiencer.

Regarding the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and the five aggregates—all these are a single unified appearance, devoid of the marks of self or what belongs to a self. All phenomena are provisionally established; whether internal...
Regarding all phenomena and all external phenomena, neither abandoning nor grasping them, the bodhisattva at that time is said to be like a provisional assembly;
because they contemplate what is present before them, they abandon the [grasping] mind and enter the emptiness samādhi.

First, the meaning of the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) is explained; this is precisely the *dāna-pāramitā*. In other scriptures, it is called the "Stage of Resolving the Mind" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*).
This means that throughout various eons, one practices the ten minds of faith (*śraddhā*), refrains from holding false views, extensively seeks wisdom, and practices the mind of equanimity.

There are ten types of equanimity, which in total comprise only three: the relinquishing of wealth, the relinquishing of the Dharma, and the relinquishing of everything to the very end. Question: Regarding the "Mind-Ground" (*citta-bhūmi*)...
Regarding this Dharma-gate, there are forty stages. First, as for clarifying the mind of relinquishment: why is this? The answer is:
it is because one wishes to cause those who follow the path to Buddhahood to attain all-encompassing liberation; they must first aspire toward unsurpassed bodhi and nirvana without remainder.

If one cannot completely relinquish attachment to body, mind, and the world, then even if one is able to practice, one remains fundamentally an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). How can such a person enter the Way?

Therefore, it is shown at the outset that those whose primary concern is birth and death and who resolutely seek the Buddha-way should gradually practice relinquishing from the outside until they reach relinquishing from the inside, and finally relinquishing both the internal and external, even relinquishing that very relinquishment.

Such a person is called a "flesh-body Bodhisattva" and is thus able to enter the Way for their own benefit; through this perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), they are able to extensively gather others.
Sentient beings are also easily transformed. As for those at the stage of the three levels of worthiness (the *śaikṣa* stages), they merely abandon the coarse delusions of the two attachments;
however, they still possess subtle attachments to self and phenomena (*ātman* and *dharma*), which must also be completely relinquished before the fruit of Buddhahood can be realized.
Therefore, throughout all the stages of a bodhisattva, the relinquishing of one's position must invariably come first; thus, the "mind of relinquishment" is explained at the outset.

"If you, O Son of the Buddha" identifies the person capable of cultivation—one who is worthy of the Great Dharma and acts as the Buddha’s representative in transforming and guiding others, and is therefore called a "Son of the Buddha.

"Relinquishing everything" identifies the dharma to be cultivated: the realization of principle, the contemplative practice, and the three wheels [of subject, object, and action] in their essential unity.

"Empty. Regarding everything from the internal faculties and body to the external environment and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), one is able to relinquish them all without regard or attachment, and without any subsequent regret;
hence it is said, "relinquishing everything. The following two lines concerning the "Buddha-sons" (*jinaputra*) should be understood in the same manner.
From the section on "kingdoms and cities" up to "relinquishing everything," this passage precisely clarifies the mind of renunciation of the Buddha-sons.

Regarding the meaning of contemplating essence and function through observation: the mention of "the land and so forth" explains the aforementioned practice of relinquishing everything in order to manifest the gate of the contemplation of emptiness.
This means that when begging for the precious throne, one immediately relinquishes the kingdom, lands, and cities, and does not form the notion of exercising mastery over them.
If asked for the Pure Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), one immediately relinquishes fields, houses, gold, silver, and bright pearls, without conceiving thoughts of them as precious.

If asked for male or female servants, one immediately relinquishes sons and daughters, even unto one's own body, without conceiving thoughts of affection. Thus, one gives away everything that one possesses.
There is not even a hair’s breadth of attachment; rather, all conditioned things are entirely renounced.
Why is this? It is because one fulfills the *dāna-pāramitā* to adorn unsurpassed *bodhi*.

From the section on "the unconditioned and signless" up to "neither abandoning nor receiving," the meaning of the contemplation of universal renunciation is clarified, including [the relinquishing of] kingdoms, cities, and so forth.
External objects belong to the category of the distant; it is relatively easy to relinquish them. Men and women, however, belong to the category of the intimate;
it is extremely difficult to relinquish them. Furthermore, one regards one’s own body as even more intimate than men and women; how then can one relinquish what is so difficult to let go?
It is because this Bodhisattva has realized that the world and the self are entirely empty, fundamentally unconditioned and signless, and truly non-existent.
All phenomena arise through the successive manifestation of ignorance and non-awakening.
Within this state, regarding the marks of self and others, and the distinctions between self and other, that which is known by the emotions and seen by the eyes is falsely perceived as real.
Consequently, through the gathering of various conditions, one falsely assumes a sovereign self, designating it as "I" or "person. As the *Qianbi jing* says: "Through false conjunction..."
To establish the name "one who is born" (*jāti*), the primary term is used; it may also be expressed as "one who conceives birth.

This refers to not recognizing that dependent origination is like an illusion, yet instead clinging to a self and a person, constructing the view of a self, and engaging in various acts of grasping and rejecting.

Because of these constructions arising from the view of a self, one undergoes the cycle of birth and death, flowing and turning without rest; thus, the twelve links of dependent origination revolve without end.
The term "etc. refers to the provisional synthesis of names. The designation "arising" is established to reveal the meaning of dependent origination as emptiness in nature.

Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination: ignorance serves as the cause and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) serve as the condition; volitional formations serve as the cause and consciousness (*vijñāna*) serves as the condition;
consciousness serves as the cause and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) serves as the condition; name-and-form serves as the cause and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) serve as the condition. The six...
With entry as the cause, contact is the condition; with contact as the cause, sensation is the condition; with sensation as the cause, craving is the condition;
with craving as the cause, grasping is the condition; with grasping as the cause, becoming is the condition; with becoming as the cause, birth is the condition;

with birth as the cause, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair are the conditions. Thus, through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is the illusory arising of birth.

The separation of causes and conditions is called "extinction" in its conventional, false sense. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "From ignorance to old age and death, all exist by virtue of the condition of birth.
Since they arise from causes and conditions, they likewise cease through causes and conditions. "No union, no dispersal, and no experiencer" explains that causes and conditions are like illusions;
it reveals the meaning that the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally numinous, luminous, and beyond all dependence. Indeed...
This dharma of causes and conditions arises through the convergence of conditions; yet the essence of the dharma is fundamentally unarisen.

Because there is originally no dharma of birth, death, or cyclic transmigration, it is said to be without conjunction. When conditions are exhausted, it ceases; yet the essence of the dharma is fundamentally unceasing.
Because there is fundamentally no dharma that transmigrates through liberation, it is said to be "without dispersion.

Since there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor union nor dispersion, there is likewise no one within it who undergoes such arising and ceasing; therefore, it is said to be "without a recipient. As for the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and so forth:
The preceding discussion on the twelve links of dependent origination was a general enumeration of the causes and effects of arising and ceasing throughout the three periods of time.
From here below, the individual dharmas of the present are specifically explained, with the desire that all sentient beings may realize them at the gateway of these six sense faculties.
One will thus avoid seeking outwardly. As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "Transmigrating through birth and death, or realizing nirvāṇa—all these are your six sense faculties.

Therefore, one should realize [the truth] by means of the six faculties. Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*): they consist of the six faculties and the six objects, which mutually encompass and enter into one another.
They are also called the twelve bases (*āyatana*). That is to say: the eye is the base of visible forms; visible forms are the base of the eye. The ear is the base of sounds;
sounds are the base of the ear. This continues up to: the mind is the base of mental phenomena (*dharma*); mental phenomena are the base of the mind.

What is meant is that the sense organ does not stand alone, nor does the object arise in isolation; when the organ and the object encounter one another, they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
As for the eighteen *dhātus*, "dhātu" refers to a state or sphere; it is the boundary of the six organs, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses.

The five aggregates (*skandhas*), also called the five *upādāna-skandhas*, consist of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. That which possesses resistance and obstruction is called form (*rūpa*). To experience...

Feeling (*vedanā*) is called "receiving. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is called "contemplative concern. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are called "transmigration. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is called "discrimination.
As for why they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*), it is because these five kinds cover over the inherently existing true nature of ourselves.

As for why they are called "heaps" (*rāśi*), it is because through the accumulation and gathering of these five kinds, the deluded body and deluded mind are formed, whereby one undergoes immeasurable birth and death. This...
The five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements have been expounded by the Tathāgata in various places throughout the sūtras.

For those deluded regarding the mind, he opened the teaching on the mind by explaining the aggregates; for those deluded regarding form, he opened the teaching on form by explaining the bases; and for those deluded regarding both, [he explained the elements].

The aggregates (*skandha*) are opened up to explain the elements (*dhātu*). Regarding this method of opening and closing the three categories and five aggregates, it is not for any other purpose than to cause all sentient beings to know that these are illusory, like flowers in the sky.

If one can thoroughly understand these flowers in the sky to be false, then at that very moment, the cycle of birth and death will cease forever. All things that appear as a unified whole (*ekaghanākāra*)—
This clarifies the bodhisattva’s wisdom of contemplation, which uses the illusory to elucidate the meaning of the real.

That is to say, when one contemplates the body, mind, and world—all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*)—their essential nature is entirely empty. They are fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and signless (*animitta*), not formed through the combination of conditions;
therefore, it is said that "all is a single unified mark" (*eka-saṃghāta-lakṣaṇa*). The two characters "unified" (*saṃghāta*) precisely express non-existence.
It is the state of signlessness (*animitta*). This is different from the character "combination" (*saṃghāta*) formed by the union of the aforementioned provisional designations.

Since it is called "signless" and yet also called a "single combined mark" (*ekasaṃghātalakṣaṇa*), these are sublime expressions made within the totality of signlessness. The phrase "without the marks of self or what belongs to self" summarizes the preceding meaning.

As for that which is called the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and so forth— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; this translation reflects the portion available.*

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are of a single unified nature (*ekasaṃghātalakṣaṇa*). Who, then, possesses a self? When one investigates the characteristic of a single self, it is ultimately unobtainable.
Since there is no self, who possesses "what belongs to a self" (*ātmīya*)? When one thoroughly examines the characteristic of a single [possessive] entity, it is ultimately unobtainable.

For this reason, one knows that all phenomena produced by the conjunction of causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya-sāmagrī*) are merely conventionally established (*prajñaptisiddha*). Therefore, as for what is said: if...
All internal phenomena, such as the five aggregates, body, and mind, and all external phenomena, such as kingdoms, cities, men, and women—all these internal and external phenomena are entirely empty.

Therefore, although one relinquishes them, one does not perceive a self as the person who relinquishes, nor does one perceive any object as the phenomenon that is relinquished; for both natures are empty.
Within this, one does not perceive even oneself as a recipient of the gift; because these three wheels are empty in essence, it is said that "one neither abandons nor receives.
When the Bodhisattva is thus—as concluded below by the phrase "equal and downward"—it refers to the benefit of sustaining the contemplation of relinquishment.
