That is to say, when the Bodhisattva practices the relinquishment of the emptiness of the three wheels as described above, at that very moment, this is called "the manifestation of the contemplative observation of the illusory assembly of the provisional."
Because it precedes [the subsequent stages], it causes the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*) to realize and enter the Samādhi of True Emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*);

this is the benefit of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) and right meditative attainment (*samyak-samāpatti*). Regarding the phrase "as the contemplation of the provisional manifests before one":

this refers to these Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes who, having practiced the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), have swept away all phenomena so that no marks of existence remain; now, they cultivate the mind of equanimity upon these very provisional phenomena.

This resembles the contemplation of conventional reality; therefore, it is called the "contemplation that accords with conventional reality appearing before one. This meaning is explained extensively in the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara Sūtra).
Such a mind of relinquishment and such a practice of relinquishment are called the Bodhisattva’s contemplative observation of the essence and function of the signless mind of relinquishment.
II. Explanation of the Stage of the Mind of Precepts.
O Disciples of the Buddha, as for the precepts: they are not non-precepts, yet there is no one who receives them. The ten wholesome precepts have no teacher to preach them;
there is no one who accumulates deceit, theft, or even wrong views. Compassion, goodness, purity, uprightness, rectitude, truthfulness, right view, equanimity, and joy—these are the ten precepts.
The essential nature [of this precept] restrains the eight inversions, is free from all [dualistic] natures, and is the purity of the single path;
this explains the meaning of the "precept-mind," which is the Śīla-pāramitā. A separate sutra calls it the "Stage of Cultivating the Ground" (Caryā-bhūmi).
This means that one should constantly follow the mind of emptiness while practicing all dharma-gates to adorn the categories of precepts. These precepts generally comprise the three clusters;
the ten inexhaustible precepts, each of which contains thirty thousand and eight hundred thousand immeasurable precepts. This refers to the section "Non-Non-Precepts" below.
The section beginning with "Reaching the state of no-accumulation" correctly elucidates the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s contemplative observation of the essence and function of the precept-mind.
In the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Sutra), regarding this "non-non-precept," there are the two characters "non-precept.

To speak of "non-precept" refers to the great precepts of the Buddha's sons (*buddhaputra*), which differ from those of the various followers of the Lesser Vehicle who possess specific precept-characteristics to be maintained; it merely restrains their...
Although one possesses a body, one is unable to achieve ultimate clarity regarding the nature of the precepts. A sutra states: "The nature of the precepts is like empty space;

those who grasp at them are deluded. Only when the Bodhisattva Mahayana Buddha-precepts—whose essence is like empty space—are received without receiving and maintained without maintaining, do they become "non-precepts" (a-jie), yet because of this, one does not fall into the view of eternalism. This is what is meant by being "not non-precepts."
This refers to the great precepts of the Buddha’s sons. Furthermore, they differ from the various demons and non-Buddhists who discriminate between existence and non-existence.
Those who claim there are precepts immediately adopt the precepts of cattle, dogs, and so forth, hoping to be reborn in the heavens. Those who claim there are no precepts simply do not receive them;

they falsely discourse on the non-existence of precepts to be maintained, asserting that lust, anger, and delusion are all pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), and that harsh abuse and physical assault are likewise.

There is nothing that is not a Buddha-work. Even if one indulges in greed, anger, and ignorance; gives free rein to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; claims to have attained what has not been attained; claims to have realized what has not been realized;
and misleads sentient beings by causing them to doubt—thus deluding oneself and others as a person of great falsehood—the teacher and disciple alike shall fall into the evil realms.
Because this is the Great Precept of the Bodhisattva, it is received without receiving and observed without observing. Although it is thus...
The nature of the precepts is like empty space; fundamentally, it is free from defilement. This does not obstruct the practice of the precepts in accordance with that nature.

Therefore, it is said to be "not non-precepts," which is not the same as the view of nihilistic annihilation. Regarding the phrase "there is no one who receives [them]," the character "one" (*zhe*) specifically identifies the Buddha’s son (*putra*).
It means that one does not receive or practice any of the precepts belonging to the Hīnayāna, to demons, or to outsiders; hence it is called "no [recipient]."
Regarding the "recipient": the precepts of the ten wholesome actions clearly define the great precepts of the Buddha’s sons.

This means that the reason these Bodhisattvas do not receive or practice the various unwholesome precepts is that they personally and diligently uphold the pure and wondrous *prātimokṣa* of the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries as taught by the Buddhas of the three periods of time. As for the phrase "without a teacher":
Regarding the "Preacher of the Dharma," the *Qianbi jing* (Sutra of the Thousand Arms) states: it is called the "precept of preaching the Dharma without a teacher.
This is precisely the "Vajra Jewel Precept of Radiance. As for what is termed the "Ten Good Precepts," they are indeed the dharma-gate practiced by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
yet they are fully possessed within the fundamental nature of all sentient beings from the very beginning, and do not arise from being taught by a teacher. Therefore, it is said:

Regarding the precept of teaching the Dharma without a teacher, from deception and theft up to wrong views, there is no one who accumulates them. This clarifies that the essence of evil precepts is empty.
"Deception" refers to cheating; "theft" refers to stealing. Both are spoken of in relation to the precepts of demons, heterodox teachers, and external paths.
Regarding "not referring generally": the two characters "even unto" (*nàizhì*) are an elliptical expression. This means that the multitude of such unwholesome dharmas cannot be enumerated one by one;
therefore, these two words are used as a shorthand to encompass all unwholesome dharmas, such as sexual misconduct, killing, greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Wrong view" refers to incorrect and evil cognition and vision; it encompasses all sixty-two types. Regarding the statement "there is no accumulation":

even for the wholesome precepts of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there is neither upholding nor receiving; how much less could evil dharmas such as deception and the like be accumulated within the mind?
Therefore, it is said that "there is no accumulation. Benevolence, goodness, purity, and straightforwardness—these constitute the essence of the ten precepts.
The section on "Nature" clarifies the meaning of the essence and function of the Bodhisattva’s precept-mind. That which is called "compassion" (ci) means to have pity for all beings;
thus, there is no thought of killing. That which is "good" (liang) means being gentle, kind, and mature; thus, there is no act of theft.
That which is "pure" (qing) means that the substance is profound, clear, and stainless; thus, there is no conduct of defilement. That which is "straight" (zhi) means being upright and impartial.
Thus, there are no words of falsehood or deception. "Correct reality" means that all perversity, delusion, and frivolity are completely eliminated. Thus, there is no business of selling alcohol.
"Correct view" means that every iota of deviance and bias is removed. This one [precept] encompasses three:

namely, not speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly, not praising oneself or disparaging others, and not slandering the Triple Gem. "Renunciation" (śīla) refers to the ability to relinquish things without stinginess.
Thus, there is no mind of stinginess or further disparagement; this is "joy," meaning to rejoice without resentment. Thus, there is no mind of anger and no sense of regret.
The term "etc. refers collectively to the remaining dharmas; it means that these eight constitute the essential nature of the aforementioned ten wholesome, wondrous precepts.
Therefore, it is said: "These are the essential natures of the ten precepts, which restrain the three phrases of the eight inversions. This concludes the section.
This clarifies the benefit of the essence and function of the Bodhisattva’s precept-mind.

It means that these ten precepts, through the power of the great function of the entire body of the fundamental nature, are able to prohibit and utterly sever the eight kinds of inversions external to the ordinary person.
Regarding the "eight inversions," there are the four inversions of the ordinary person: reckoning the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure.

Purity. Regarding the four inversions of the Lesser Vehicle—reckoning the impermanent as permanent, the painful as pleasant, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure—these eight inversions arise simply because one does not fully comprehend the Tathāgata’s true, eternal four virtues.

As for the statement that "all natures are detached," this refers to the Bodhisattva’s realization of the precepts of the original source of self-nature; it means not merely abstaining from unwholesome conduct.
The essence of emptiness is itself good precepts, and its essence is likewise empty. Why is this? Because they belong to the realm of relative opposition.

Since both good and evil are of the nature of emptiness, how could there be anything [substantial] within it? Thus, in the nature of right precepts, the nature of wrong precepts, and the nature of possessing precepts, all are detached from inherent existence.

It is free from the nature of non-precepts; it is free from the nature of upholding precepts; it is free from the nature of violating precepts; it is free from the nature of attaining precepts; it is free from the nature of losing precepts;
and so on, until all natures such as dependence on others, false conceptualization, and inversion are forever and completely transcended.
Therefore, it is said to be "free from all natures. As for "the single path of purity," it means that since these natures of inversion have already been transcended.
Only by realizing the single path taught by no teacher— the pure essence, the luminous Vajra Jewel Precepts— do they manifest alone and clearly,
benefiting sentient beings through inconceivable activity. To maintain them in this way is what is called the contemplative illumination of the essence and function of the Buddha-son’s precept-mind.
III. Explanation of the Stage of the Mind of Patience.

O Disciples of the Buddha, patience possesses the essential nature of signless wisdom. It is the patience of the emptiness of all things, the patience in all places, and is called the patience of the practice of non-arising.
It is termed the patience regarding suffering because it is found in all places; it is an immeasurable practice, and each individual instance is named patience. There is no [end].

Sensation. No striking. No anger with staff or sword. All are suchness (*tathatā*). There is no single truth; there is one mark, yet no mark of non-existence. There is the mark of existence and non-existence;
it is not the mark of a non-mind. It is the mark of conditions and non-conditions. Standing, dwelling, moving, and stopping; self and person, bondage and liberation.
All phenomena are like the mark of patience; they are ungraspable.
This explains the meaning of the mind of patience, which is the pāramitā of kṣānti. In other sūtras, it is called the "dwelling in practice."
This refers to being able to practice the power of patience (*kṣānti*), thereby nurturing all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

"Patience" means remaining serene and composed amidst all circumstances, whether adverse or favorable; it is the powerful force for constructing the Path. There are many types of patience, and herein six are presented, which encompass them all.
From the section on the essence of wisdom regarding existence and non-existence up to the section on the signless (*animitta*) alone, [the meaning is] precisely as follows:
This clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s patient mind (*kṣānti-citta*) in terms of its essence and function, and the nature of the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*).
Regarding "the patience that is the emptiness of all things": the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara Sūtra) states, "This is called the patience of signless wisdom.

"Existence" (*you*) refers to that which is inherently present (*prakṛti-stha*), not obtained from without. "Signlessness" (*animitta*) is the principle of suchness (*tathatā*). "Wisdom" (*prajñā*) is the gnosis of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*). This refers to this bodhisattva...

Patience does not reside within the midst of phenomena, nor is it separate from them. In this state of neither separation nor identity, one takes as the foundation the essence of signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) and gives rise to the great light of signless wisdom.
One observes all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms as being entirely like empty space: devoid of material characteristics, without "that" or "this," and truly [as they are].
There is no duality of dharmas; there is only the single essence-nature (*dharmatā*). This nature is pure and devoid of substantiality.
By means of the capacity of signlessness (*animitta*), one transforms the locus of signlessness, penetrating into the emptiness of all emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Therefore, it is said:

"The essence-nature of the wisdom of existence and non-existence is the patience regarding the emptiness of all things (*sarva-śūnyatā-kṣānti*). Regarding the phrase "patience in all places," in the *Qianbi jing* (Sahasrabhuja-sūtra), it is called the "Universal Vow" (*samantapraṇidhāna*).
Practicing patience means the patience of the emptiness of all things. In every respect, there is nothing that is not patience.
By means of the mind of patience toward all things, one does not perceive the arising of even the slightest phenomenon, nor does one perceive the cessation of even the slightest phenomenon.
Because it is free from both arising and cessation, one enters into non-arising; therefore, it is called "patience in all places," which is termed "Non-existence."

This refers to practicing the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Regarding the statement that one is named after all objects of experience, as in "the patience of enduring suffering," the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara Sūtra) says it is called "the patience of enduring enmity.

Because the Bodhisattva accords with the practice of the patience of non-arising, he further cultivates and maintains three kinds of great patience for the sake of sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*.
Whenever he is subjected to the jealousy or harm of others, he perceives no suffering to be endured. The Bodhisattva...
All objects are but mind; the mind does not exist as mind of itself, for it arises because of objects. Objects do not exist as objects of themselves, for they arise because of the mind.

When mind and object are both empty and one, this is termed "patience like [the realization of] suffering. This is what is meant by: "Do not give rise to enmity or kinship because of slander or praise.
How could this not manifest the power of the compassionate patience of non-arising? Each and every one of the immeasurable practices is called "patience. [This is the power of] the Thousand Arms.

In the Sūtra, it is called "the patience of immeasurable practices. This expands upon the practice of patience, comprehensively encompassing all the aforementioned locations, as well as the mental faculty capable of enduring and the mental phenomena that are endured. Although there are thus immeasurable gateways of practice, [the following]...
These various differences all arise from the essence of signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*) as its basis for manifesting illuminating functions.
Therefore, what are called the "immeasurable practices" are each termed "patience regarding signless wisdom" (*animitta-prajñā-kṣānti*).

Regarding "no receiving, no striking, and no anger toward weapons or staves—all being suchness," this is designated in the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Avalokiteśvara Sūtra) as "patience in accepting suffering" (*duḥkhādhivāsana-kṣānti*), which clarifies [the point].
This is the conduct of the patience regarding suffering in all circumstances above.
That is to say, amidst what is difficult to endure and prone to anger, one clearly receives blows from knives and staves. The Bodhisattva realizes that the three spheres are empty in essence;
thus, examining within his own mind, he seeks even a single mark of "receiving," but finds it utterly unobtainable. Consequently, there is no mark of a self that receives the blows.
Therefore, if one investigates by tracing back to the external object, one cannot find a single characteristic of "striking";

since there is no characteristic of a person who strikes, there is no characteristic of a sentient being who is struck, for the sword or staff—when investigated within the act of striking—is fundamentally quiescent.
Furthermore, if one investigates by tracing back to the subject who strikes, the mind is fundamentally as-it-is; thus, there is no endurance of suffering.
The notion of a self within a mind of anger is what is meant by "no recipient," "no striking," and "no sword or staff"—that is, no mind of anger.
The phrase "all are suchness" explains the meaning of these three words "no" (*wu*) to reveal the emptiness and stillness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*).
The four characteristics have no source; therefore, it is shown that their general characteristic is that "all are suchness. There is not a single truth or a single characteristic.
In the *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Sutra), this is called "the patience of discerning phenomena" (*dharmakṣānti*). These two phrases clarify that all things are as they are. Question:
Since it is said that when one receives blows from swords or staves, the mind of anger and the objects of the senses are distinct and clear, for what reason is it further stated...?

[The questioner] asked: "Are the absence of receiving blows from knives or staves and the absence of a mind of anger both 'as-it-is' (tathatā)? [The respondent] answered: "Regarding what is called 'all is as-it-is':

within the patience of the essential nature of signless wisdom (*animitta-prajñā*), there are fundamentally no two dharmas—the worldly and the supramundane, or the ultimate and the conventional truths.

Therefore, it is said that there is not even a single truth; this is precisely not falling into the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). As for 'one mark,' it is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Although it is so called..."

There is no characteristic of two truths; one does not fall into the view of eternalism. Fearing, however, that one might again interpret this through the lens of nihilism, [the Buddha] reveals the single characteristic to demonstrate it, so that one does not fall into the view of annihilation. When Bodhisattvas of the ten stages practice the contemplation of emptiness, they contemplate all phenomena.

The essence of all things is entirely empty. There is neither the real nor the provisional; there is nothing that is not empty. Because it is solely emptiness and devoid of characteristics, it is called "the single characteristic.

That there is no "absence of characteristics" is a statement that doubly reaffirms the preceding meaning. Question: Since there is a "single characteristic," why is it called "no single [or multiple] truths"?
And since it is said there are "no single or multiple truths," how can there be a "single characteristic"? Is it still possible for a "single characteristic" to exist?
Question: If this is so, why do you say there is no single truth? Answer: To speak of a "single characteristic" is precisely to mean "no characteristic.

Where there is no characteristic, yet there is a characteristic, that characteristic is itself no-characteristic. In reality, not even a single characteristic can be apprehended; therefore, it is said that there is no "no-characteristic."

Regarding the passage from "The characteristic of existence and non-existence" to "The characteristic of having and not having objects as conditions," this section successively explains and refutes the biased conceptualizations of externalists (*tīrthika*) in order to conclude the meaning of the essence of the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*) within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*).

"The characteristic of existence and non-existence" refers to the total elimination of the characteristics of the phenomena being endured (*viṣaya*), such that they are unapprehendable. "Not the characteristic of non-mind" refers to the total elimination of the [subjective] mind that endures them.

The characteristic of the mind of patience cannot be apprehended. Regarding "the condition being without the characteristic of a condition": this means that both the subject and object are simultaneously dispelled, such that neither characteristic can be apprehended.
These three phrases are stated in close connection with the preceding word "non-" (*wu*), elucidating the meaning of the non-existence of even the characteristic of non-characteristic.
That which has characteristics refers to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). That which lacks the characteristic of existence is what is to be endured.
The Dharma is fundamentally empty, yet it possesses this mark of non-existence; furthermore, it is not the true emptiness. As for the "mark of mind," this belongs to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
As for the "non-mark of mind," it is the mind capable of endurance that is fundamentally empty, yet it is neither this non-mark of mind nor the true emptiness.
As for the "mark of conditions," this belongs to the Lesser Vehicle. The absence of marks of conditions is the original state of subject and object within the wisdom of endurance.
It is one emptiness. Yet, by taking this mark of non-conditioning as an object, it is not yet true emptiness.

Only when the Bodhisattva’s subjective mind and objective境 (objects) are both empty, and even that emptiness is further emptied, is it the signless true emptiness—the *dharmakṣānti* of the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Regarding "standing, dwelling, moving, and stopping," etc., this is a summary that reveals the mind of patience (*kṣānti*) and the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), which destroys the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and causes one to realize the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

It is the true nature (*dharmatā*). "Standing" (*sthita*) means to stand upright; "dwelling" (*vihara*) means to abide peacefully; "moving" (*gati*) refers to physical movement; "stopping" (*niṣadya*) refers to lying down or resting.

"Self" (*ātman*) is a designation used in relation to the characteristic of a person (*pudgala-lakṣaṇa*); "person" (*pudgala*) is a term raised in relation to the characteristic of a self (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*).

"Bondage" (*bandhana*) is the mundane characteristic of non-emptiness; "liberation" (*mokṣa*) is the noble characteristic of emptiness. Regarding these, there are all various [phenomena] such as existence and non-existence.
Regarding these marks: throughout the two sets of six periods and within the four modes of deportment, the Bodhisattva illuminates and penetrates each one.

Whether standing, sitting, moving, or resting, these marks possess no distinction between stillness and response. Regarding self and others, these marks possess no distinction between "this" and "that."
Regarding bondage and liberation, their characteristics possess no distinction between the noble and the ordinary. Since all characteristics are absent, how can there be any phenomena?
Since the dharma of patience is likewise absent, there remains only the essence of wisdom; illuminating and observing itself, this constitutes the practice of patience.
How, then, could there be any characteristic of patience? Therefore it is said: "All phenomena are like the characteristic of patience; they are unobtainable. This is what is meant.
"Not seeing even a single dharma is the Tathāgata; this is what is called Avalokiteśvara. The *Vajra* [Sūtra] says:

"If there are signs of a self or signs of a person, one is not a bodhisattva. Furthermore, the *Thousand-Armed [Avalokiteśvara] Sūtra* says: "Regarding all dharmas, they are entirely without marks (*animitta*).
They are clearly and distinctly understood as being empty and quiescent by nature, because they are unobtainable. All of these refer to this same meaning. As it is said:
This is the practice of patience. This is called the illumination and function of the essential nature of the signless wisdom-patience of the Buddha’s sons.
4. Explaining the Stage of the Mind of Diligence:
O Buddha-sons, whether in the four modes of deportment, at all times one practices subduing emptiness and provisionally accords with the dharma-nature, ascending to the state of non-arising.

Mounting [the mountain], one perceives all that exists and does not exist—whether as existent or non-existent—including the universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) of heaven, earth, blue, yellow, red, and white, up to the nature of the wisdom of the Triple Gem.

One enters into all the paths of faith and diligence, emptiness, non-arising, non-action, and non-wisdom. Arising from the state of emptiness, one enters the dharmas of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), yet these are without dual characteristics.
Continuously cultivating the mind of emptiness, one attains penetration and advances the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
This explains the meaning of generating the mind of progress; it is the *vīrya-pāramitā*.

In other sūtras, it is called the "Stage of Noble Birth" (*janma-kula-vihāra*), meaning that one is born into the family of the Buddhas because one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is pure. The Sanskrit term *vīrya* is translated here as "diligence" (*jingjin*).
This means being refined without admixture and advancing without retreat; it is the energetic application of the three preceding dharmas: generosity, ethical discipline, and patience.
"Without indolence" refers to the power of uninterrupted wisdom and practice.

From "whether in the four modes of deportment" up to "there are no two aspects" constitutes a section that precisely clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s progressive mind regarding the essence and function of contemplative observation. As for the "four modes of deportment":

One immediately practices the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—with diligence throughout all activities; thus, the character "conduct" (xing) symbolizes this state. "At all times" refers to the twelve periods of the day and night.
"Walking and subduing emptiness" is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). "Provisionally uniting with the Dharma-nature" is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*).

"Ascending the mountain of non-arising" is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*). These are the practices of the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*tri-kṣānti-bhūmi*).
This is called the stage of the Patience of Subjugation (*kṣānti*). In the first stage, *abhimukhī*, one subjugates emptiness; in the second stage, *caryāpratipatti*, one subjugates the provisional;

and in the third stage, *yogācaryā*, one subjugates the middle. Although these are divided into three, each is named according to its fundamental position; in reality, they are mutually inclusive and interpenetrating—three in one and one in three.
Regarding these practices, the Bodhisattva employs the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining—as dharma-gates, possessing a majestic presence that inspires awe.
One is able to subdue sentient beings through outward deportment that serves as a manifestation.

By gathering in sentient beings, one cultivates the path toward enlightenment at all times within these four modes of deportment, subduing the mind and entering into emptiness where no dharma can be apprehended.
Like reflections in a mirror, no marks can be grasped; this is precisely the practice of subduing through emptiness. This is called the "Dharma of Conventional Assembly."

Regarding "nature" (*xing*), this follows from what precedes. It means that although one constantly enters the true void and contemplates the essential nature of all phenomena, these are nonetheless formed through provisional conjunction;
they are true within the provisional, for apart from the true there is no provisional. This is precisely the subduing of the provisional through practice.

Within conventional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*), one should clarify the reality within their very substance; hence it is said that "conventionalities accord with the Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). As for the phrase "ascending the mountain of non-arising" (*anutpāda-parvata*):

this refers to the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the principle of non-arising, which is most supreme and most manifest. Abiding amidst the mundane yet transcending the mundane, it utterly surpasses the two extremes (*antadvaya*) and attains unimpededness.
Like ascending a mountain peak, it rises high above all without obstruction; thus it is called "ascending the mountain of non-arising."
Furthermore, since the Bodhisattva has already washed away all phenomena as empty (*śūnya*), they do not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that can arise;

yet, observing all phenomena as provisional (*prajñapti*), they do not perceive even a hair’s breadth of a phenomenon that can cease. Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, both emptiness and the provisional are true.
Thus, by simultaneously subduing [extremes] within the Middle Way of non-arising, the mountain-climbing is used as a metaphor. This clarifies the perception of all existence and non-existence.

Regarding the meaning of ascending the mountain of non-arising: throughout all times and in the four modes of conduct, the bodhisattva contemplates the principle of ultimate truth, giving rise to all untainted wisdom and clearly perceiving all internal and external four great elements.
There are the characteristics of existence and non-existence; the nature of all phenomena is emptiness, and emptiness possesses nothing. Therefore it is said:

"To see all existence and non-existence, as if they were existent or non-existent," etc. This refers to the formal determination of the various defiled and pure phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds that are to be observed.
First, one observes the phenomena of the mundane world with a mind of non-arising, seeing within heaven and earth the inclusion of blue, yellow, red, and white.
Whether long or short, square or round, whether as sense faculties or as objects, those that possess substantial form and are subject to mutual opposition are called all manifest matter (*rūpa*).

Whether as sense faculties or as objects, those that lack substantial form and are not subject to mutual opposition are called all non-manifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), such as [the bodies of beings] in the heavens of the four dhyānas.

The form resulting from meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) constituting a portion of the five sense organs, and the various objects of past and future mental recollection—though these appear as distinct counterparts in the present, they cannot be pointed out or expressed.
Although it is said that they cannot be expressed, they are nonetheless subsumed within the category of "form" (*rūpa*).

All phenomenal forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) are fundamentally devoid of substantial reality. Such is the nature of material phenomena; the same applies to mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*): they too are non-existent.

There is one dharma that is not the Tathāgatagarbha-mind; because its nature is a pure and luminous essence, it is said that "as if there were" or "as if there were not," for all things enter therein.
As for the phrase "the wisdom-nature of the Triple Gem," and so forth, this refers to the contemplation of supramundane dharmas.
The Three Jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Wisdom-nature (*jñāna-dhātu*) is the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Liberation.

All paths of faith and diligence are the path of sincere faith and diligent cultivation of all worthy ones and sages. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and non-conditioning (*apraṇihita*) are the meanings of the three gates of liberation.
This means that this Bodhisattva, by contemplating the true and pure essential nature of both the mundane and supramundane realms...
Principle is inherently pure and devoid of substantiality; therefore, one attains entry into the three gates of liberation. Regarding the gate of emptiness:
the Bodhisattva contemplates that all phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, and that their essence is fundamentally empty.
Thus, they awaken to the true emptiness of self-nature, which does not arise following causes and conditions, and thereby attain liberation.
The gate of liberation through non-arising (*anutpāda-vimokṣamukha*) is precisely the gate of liberation through signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).

Following the preceding [analysis], since one has observed that all phenomena are entirely empty and no signs can be apprehended, and because there are no signs, one realizes that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is eternally arising and does not perish according to causes and conditions;
thus, one attains liberation. The gate of liberation through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣamukha*) is precisely the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).
This is the gate of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). When a bodhisattva contemplates all phenomena as empty and signless (*animitta*), there is no longing or seeking.
Since there is no longing or seeking, one does not create the causes of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Because there are no causes for birth and death, there is no fruit.
Thus, one attains liberation. Liberation has the meaning of sovereignty (*vaśitā*); "gate" has the meaning of thorough penetration (*prativedha*). By means of these three—...
Liberation. Because one attains nirvana, it is called the "three liberations. Regarding "the absence of wisdom":
since the various dharmas observed above are unobtainable, how could the observing wisdom itself be obtainable? Hence, it is called "the absence of wisdom.

"Arising from emptiness and entering the conventional truth" regarding "dharmas" means that one has previously observed that the bodies of all dharmas—whether mundane or supramundane, existent or non-existent—are empty. That is to say:
He has realized and entered the samādhi of emptiness. This emptiness is not like the emptiness of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, which sinks into and stagnates in the quiescence of emptiness;

rather, it is the realization that within the principle of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a speck of dust can be established, yet in the gateway of this present world, not a single dharma is abandoned.

Although one realizes the patience of emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*), one does not dwell in or cling to it. Thus, emerging from the meditative concentration and patience that subdue emptiness, one arises and enters the phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Even though one thus enters both the ultimate and the conventional, there are no two distinct characteristics. To have no two distinct characteristics means that when entering the ultimate, one does not cling to the ultimate;

and when entering the conventional, one does not cling to the conventional. Therefore, it is said that there are no two distinct characteristics. One continues with a mind of emptiness and attains thorough penetration.
These two phrases conclude and clarify the mind of signless diligence and the benefit of the contemplative wisdom of essence and function.

"Continuing the empty mind" refers to entering emptiness from the conventional, entering the conventional from emptiness, and the perfect fusion of emptiness and the conventional, thereby attaining unimpeded penetration.
Because this is the mind that penetrates the true reality (*dharmatā*), it is called the "penetration of the continuing empty mind. [End of] Progression.
Regarding "dividing the roots of goodness": the root of goodness is the wondrous mind that is the very source of Bodhi, for it serves as the foundation of all virtues.

This very signless mind gives rise to various forms of diligence, continuing from heart-moment to heart-moment without interruption, progressing incrementally in every thought-instant, never regressing, and advancing toward the state of Buddhahood;
therefore, it is called "the division of roots of goodness leading forward. (From the *Qianbi* [Thousand-Armed] [Avalokiteśvara Sūtra]).

The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, when one cultivates the path toward Bodhi within the four modes of deportment, one immediately attains realization and entry into the wisdom-nature of all Three Jewels.
With this truly pure essential nature always manifest before one, one shall encounter the Buddhas in every successive birth."

One perceives the Dharma and perceives the Sangha. Through diligent effort in every lifetime, one studies the majestic deportment of the Buddha. Regarding the principle of the patience of subduing emptiness (*śūnyatā-kṣānti*), one does not even perceive the four modes of deportment.
One realizes the emptiness of non-arising (*anutpāda-śūnyatā*); thus, it is by not advancing that one advances upon the Path. Furthermore, the *Dharmapada* says:
"If one gives rise to a mind of diligent effort, this is delusion, not diligence. If one can remain such that the mind is not deluded, [this is true] diligence."
It is boundless. Such diligence is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the essence and function of the mind of progress.
○ Fifth, the explanation of the stage of the concentrated mind:
O Buddha-sons, it is quiescent extinction; signless and signless again; immeasurable practice; and the samādhi of immeasurable mind. This applies to both ordinary beings and sages.

There is no person who does not enter samādhi. Their essential nature is in accord. Because all things are due to the power of meditative concentration, the views of self, person, agent, and experiencer—all these bound views of nature—are the causes and conditions for obstruction.
The wind of dispersion agitates the mind; it is extinguished without being stilled. The eight inversions of emptiness have no objective basis.
By relying on the contemplation of quiescent wisdom, all provisional assemblies are seen to be extinguished moment by moment. All three... [samādhis].
The realms, fruits, and the nature of offenses are all extinguished through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and from this, all that is wholesome arises.
This explains the meaning of the concentrated mind; it is precisely the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.

In another sutra, it is called "abiding in the fulfillment of skillful means," which refers to the power of cultivating immeasurable roots of goodness. Through this, there is quiescent extinction, signlessness within signlessness, reaching the emptiness of emptiness.

The section on the eight inversions being without objective conditions correctly elucidates the essence and function of the concentrated mind of the Buddha’s heirs, as well as the meaning of contemplative observation.
"Quiescence" (寂滅) is the designation for the essence of concentration; in Sanskrit it is *dhyāna*, which here is translated as "quiescence. This refers to the one mind.

It is also called "meditative absorption" (*samādhi*), which is the meditation that takes suchness as its object; it is also called "tranquility," meaning that the faculties and their objects are in the state of suchness.

Neither identical nor separate. Because the mirror manifests forms, it is called "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*). "The signless is signless"—these two instances of signlessness explain the meaning of quiescent extinction.
The former "signless" clarifies the mind that is capable of concentration; the latter "signless" clarifies the object of that concentration.
Since both this mind and its object are signless, it is said, "the signless is signless. This refers to immeasurable practices.
Regarding the samādhi of the immeasurable mind: this clarifies the principle that for a bodhisattva, movement and stillness are one and the same.

Because at the time of entering meditative absorption there are no dualistic marks of subject and object, one is able to accord with the immeasurable mental activities and thus collectively accomplish samādhi.
This is precisely the constant illumination of dhyāna-contemplation within the four modes of deportment; as it is said: "The nāga is always in samādhi; there is no time when he is not in samādhi."
It is the time [of realization]. There is no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or sage (*ārya*) who does not enter samādhi. This statement means that the essence of concentration (*samādhi*) is equal;
it is not only sages who enter this samādhi, but ordinary persons also enter this meditative state. If this is so, why are they called "ordinary persons"?
It is because they are defiled by all the stains of cognitive-emotional consciousness (*vijñāna-vedanā*), and thus do not realize it themselves—just like a lamp within a garment.
The jewel [is within], yet one is unaware of it; wandering in poverty to other lands, one ultimately gains no benefit.

This is what is meant by being "perpetually in perfect enlightenment" while never having experienced perfect enlightenment—this refers to the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Why is this? Because their fundamental nature and essence are not in accord, how could they attain meditative concentration?
The Bodhisattva does not perceive a single dharma as being present before them; the objective realm is empty and the mind is tranquil, such that wisdom and principle are of one suchness.
Therefore, one is constantly in accord with the essential nature of all Buddhas.
By realizing the samādhi of that essential nature, at all times, through the power of noble concentration, one is able to clearly perceive all subtle selves, persons, agents, and experiencers.
This is delusive confusion. "I" refers to the view of self; "person" refers to the view of a person; "agent" refers to the mental activities of one's own mind, which is the view of a sentient being;
and "recipient" refers to the grasping and non-relinquishing of likes and dislikes, which is the view of a life-sustainer.
From these four views arise all forms of attachment and bondage. The nature of such false views is entirely a causal condition that obstructs the Path. Being thus...
The winds of the objects of distraction stir the ocean of the mind, causing it to follow the waves and drift through birth and death, endlessly and without cessation.
Therefore, it is said that "all are bound," and so forth. Regarding the statement that they are "extinguished without being pacified":

this means that these obstructing afflictions cannot be extinguished unless one relies on the power of the samādhi of right concentration, which illuminates through the cultivation of the contemplation of quiescence.
[This state] never ceases for even a moment. It is thought that this cessation is attained precisely through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in quiescence;

therefore, it is said to be "extinguished without being quiescent. The *Qianbi jing* (Sūtra of a Thousand Arms) states: "It is impossible for one who has not attained the power of meditative concentration in quiescence to be able to extinguish [the afflictions].
Regarding "emptiness, further emptiness, the eight inversions, and the absence of conditions": this refers back to the aforementioned power of meditative concentration.

Having already ceased the causes of the arising and ceasing of the view of self, the conditions for the arising and ceasing of the eight inversions of the śrāvakas, ordinary beings, and non-Buddhists naturally become empty;

hence it is said that "the eight inversions have no conditions. The passage from "relying on the contemplation of tranquil wisdom" up to "giving rise to all wholesome states" concludes by clarifying the meaning of the functional power of the illumination of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One relies on tranquility to still movement; one relies on wisdom to illuminate obscurity.

Using these two as the basis for contemplation, when concentration and wisdom are perfected and luminous, one serenely perceives that all phenomena involving the self and others are but provisional gatherings, composed of illusory transformations and the conditions of deluded thought; moment by moment, they are thus extinguished.

Once the inverted thoughts of arising and ceasing are emptied, then all the fruits of suffering—the karmic retributions within the three realms—as well as the natures of various evils and transgressions, will likewise [be extinguished].

All are extinguished by means of this power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Once the nature of suffering and its karmic retribution have been completely extinguished, they are fundamentally neither born nor extinguished;
likewise, untainted merit and wisdom are all produced by means of this power of meditative concentration. Therefore, it is said that "all that is wholesome is produced. This is what is meant by:
"When birth and extinction are both extinguished, quiescent extinction manifests before one. To practice dhyāna in this manner is to cultivate in such a way.
This is called the contemplation of the essence and function of the concentrated mind of the Buddha’s disciples.
Sixth, the stage of the wisdom-mind.
O Buddha’s disciples, the wisdom of emptiness is not without an object; that which knows the essence is named "mind. It discriminates all phenomena and is provisionally designated as the "subject."

This is to be in accord with the Way; to take up the fruit and practice the cause; to enter the state of the sage and abandon that of the ordinary person; to extinguish transgressions and give rise to merit.

Bondage and liberation are entirely the functions of this essential nature. All views—such as permanence, bliss, self, and purity—are due to the failure of the wisdom-nature to manifest within affliction.

Therefore, taking wisdom as the foremost, one cultivates the ineffable contemplative wisdom, entering the Middle Way of the Single Truth. As for the obstruction of ignorance against wisdom, it is not...
The marks do not come; they are not conditions, not offenses, and not the eight inversions. They are without arising or cessation. The radiant flames of wisdom-light illuminate the joy of emptiness.
Through the transformation of skillful means and supernormal powers, the functional activity of wisdom is realized by means of the essence of gnosis.
This explanation of the meaning of the mind of wisdom (*prajñā-citta*) is precisely the *prajñāpāramitā*. In other sutras, it is called the "Abiding in the Right Mind.
This is because one accomplishes the sixth dharma-gate of *prajñā*. In the Sanskrit language, *prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom" (*hui*).
Because this capacity can illuminate objects and wisdom can comprehend objects, one becomes clear regarding objects and free from delusion; thus, one is able to transform phenomena. Emptiness.

"Wisdom is not without an object. This section, up to the point concerning "the essence and function," precisely clarifies the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom-mind as the essence and function of contemplative observation.

To say that "empty wisdom is not without an object" means that this essence-nature of true emptiness, the wondrous primordial wisdom, does not arise without an object, nor does it arise from the objects themselves; rather, it is the original emptiness itself.
The essence of wisdom and spiritual insight is clearly known; this is called the mind (*citta*), because it does not depend on external conditions.
Since this is the essence of true knowing and awareness, it is fundamentally without discrimination. To say that it discriminates all phenomena is merely the illuminating function of the true mind.
This is not like the "extinguishing of the mind" and "obliterating wisdom" of the Two Vehicles, which do not take any arising phenomena as objects; nor is it like [the views of] other schools.
The discriminating consciousness-minds of ordinary beings and non-Buddhists are formed through the convergence of provisional causes and conditions.

They are provisionally designated as "masters," and their names are established conventionally; in reality, there is no sovereign controller. Although these are called false, they all arise based upon the True.
Just as waves depend upon water for their existence, so too do the various deluded minds, when illuminated by the wisdom of prajñā, appear clearly as non-dual with the ultimate Way;
they are of one single flavor, their essence being without distinction. Therefore, it is said that the nominally designated "master" is identical with the Way.
The phrase "taking the fruit and practicing the cause, etc. explains the illumination of the mind of wisdom.
Regarding the meaning of its application: it is said that this Bodhisattva directly transcends to the fruit of Buddhahood.

Relying solely on the fundamental wisdom of equanimity and emptiness to cultivate practices for the causal ground, one may thus enter the state of holiness and abandon ordinariness, extinguishing transgressions and giving rise to merit.

Ordinary beings, through the conceptualization of the mark of self (*ātman*), fail to attain liberation in every situation and are therefore bound; holy persons, being without self, are able to employ the wisdom of *prajñā*.

Illumination. Because one attains mastery everywhere, there is liberation. Thus, regarding these states of delusion and awakening, bondage and liberation among ordinary beings and sages, when a Bodhisattva observes them, they are entirely the functional manifestations of the fundamental nature. That which comes from the state of an ordinary being employs the conscious mind;
that which comes from the nature of a sage employs wisdom. Consciousness and wisdom originally have no dual essence; it depends solely on—
The difference lies only in their application. The section from "All views" up to "because they function as wisdom" clarifies the benefits of observing with the wisdom of emptiness.
Question: Regarding "all views," where does the distinction lie between the bondage and liberation of ordinary beings and sages?

Ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, and all those with inverted views do so because they fail to understand that the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity, his nirvāṇa without remainder, and the virtuous marks of True Suchness (tathatā) exist;
nor do they understand that this mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in these three respects, being equally and fully endowed [with them].
Consequently, they give rise to inverted views regarding the true permanence, true bliss, true self, and true purity of the mind.

Therefore, "permanence" (nitya) carries the meaning of never undergoing even momentary change. Its essential nature is empty and harmonious; it does not shift throughout the three periods of time and remains unchanging amidst the confusion of all phenomena.
Hence, it is called the virtue of permanence. "Bliss" (sukha) carries the meaning of peace, security, and quiescent extinction.
Because it is free from the suffering of the oppression of birth and death and realizes the bliss of the quiescence of nirvāṇa, it is called the quality of bliss (*sukha-guṇa*).
As for "self" (*ātman*), it carries the meaning of sovereignty and unimpededness; yet non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings falsely establish a sovereign master and cling to it as a self.
This is merely the false self (*mṛṣā-ātman*). If that which the Buddha possesses—the eight masteries (*aṣṭa-vaśitā*)—is taken as the self, then it is the true self;
therefore, it is called the "virtue of self. "Pure" (*viśuddha*) means being free from defilement and untainted; all afflictions have been completely eliminated, and it is profoundly serene and pure.
It is like a great, perfectly round mirror, entirely free from even the slightest obscuration; therefore, it is named "Pure Virtue.
Yet ordinary beings, deluded and ignorant of this, conversely reckon the impermanent as permanent, the permanent as impermanent, the non-blissful as blissful, and the blissful as non-blissful.
To regard what is not-self as self; to regard self as non-self; to regard the impure as pure; and to regard the pure as impure—these are called the eight inversions.
To regard the impermanent as permanent: all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world are entirely impermanent, being illusory and unreal;
yet one clings to them as truly existent. To regard what is not pleasure as pleasure: this refers to the pleasures of the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) in the world.
These are all causes of suffering. Because ordinary worldlings are greedily attached and do not relinquish them, they do not seek liberation.
Those who conceive of what is not-self as self: this body, a mere provisional combination of the four great elements, is fundamentally without a self;
yet within this illusory physical form, they forcibly assume mastery and falsely cling to it as "I. Those who conceive of the impure as pure: [this applies to] one's own body and that of others...
The body consists of thirty-six impure substances; this body of five kinds of impurity is fundamentally not pure. Yet, one conversely gives rise to greedy attachment, regarding it as pure.
Thus, these four views increase delusion and karma; they are called the "four perversions of the ordinary person.
Regarding those who constantly reckon the impermanent as permanent: the Dharma-body is eternally abiding and fundamentally undergoes no change or transformation. Yet, toward the Tathāgata...
Within the eternally abiding Dharma-body, they falsely conceive of there being change and transformation. Regarding that which is pleasure as not being pleasure:
because Great Nirvāṇa is free from all suffering, it is supreme bliss; yet they falsely conceive of this bliss of the Tathāgata’s Nirvāṇa as being suffering.
Regarding those who conceive of "no-self" where there is no self: the unborn true self (*bhūtātman*) is precisely the eternally real.

Failing to understand that within the dharma of non-self lies the Buddha-nature, the true self, they falsely conceptualize "no-self" within that very true self. Regarding those who conceive of the impure where there is purity:
the essential nature is truly pure and free from all defilements. Failing to understand the purity that is without delusion or obstruction, they [misconceive] regarding the Tathāgata...

Within the truly pure Dharma, they falsely conceptualize it as impure; thus, these four views belong to those of the Two Vehicles who contemplate phenomena such as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, thereby giving rise to the notion that afflictions have decayed and will not arise again—these are called the four views of withered inversion.
All actions performed by ordinary people under these eight inverted views are entirely [of this nature].
The power of afflictions and karma obscures and covers this nature of wisdom, preventing it from opening and thereby obstructing the attainment of true cognitive function.
That is to say, because the nature of wisdom is not clear due to afflictions, they are termed the two obstacles of affliction (*kleśa*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).
The obstacle of the phenomena of affliction obstructs principle; the obstacle of ignorance obstructs phenomena. Regarding the obstacle of affliction, it refers to this turbidity...

The nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) is to disturb and agitate the mind; because they obstruct the Right Path due to delusions such as craving, they are called the "affliction-obstruction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

As for the "ignorance-obstruction" (*avidyāvaraṇa*), it refers to all sentient beings who, from beginningless time, have been subject to various inversions and thus lack clear understanding regarding all phenomena;
this is called the ignorance-obstruction. This delusion is the seed of the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
Sons, [ignorance] is the root of afflictions. Because the nature of wisdom is not yet clear in those of the Two Vehicles, they are unable to sever this obstruction;
only Bodhisattvas can sever it. To destroy afflictions, one must take wisdom as the foremost priority.
To destroy ignorance, one must cultivate the inconceivable contemplative wisdom as an aid. Examine and scrutinize with great care the virtuous characteristics of wisdom.
Fundamentally, there is no transition and no change; this is the Tathāgata’s quality of permanence. There is no birth and no death; this is the Tathāgata’s quality of bliss.
There is no obstruction and no hindrance; this is the Tathāgata’s quality of selfhood. There is no barrier and no delusion; this is the Tathāgata’s quality of purity.
When various forms of contemplative wisdom continue in succession, uninterrupted and unceasing, one then realizes the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Wisdom arises and delusion perishes; thus, the obstructions of ignorance and delusion are suddenly shattered, and the originally inherent nature of wisdom is suddenly opened.
That which was previously called ignorance and affliction as an obstruction is precisely what obstructs the nature of wisdom. Therefore it is said:
Ignorance obstructs wisdom. Now, one clearly understands that ignorance obstructs wisdom; its very substance is entirely empty. How could it have any form or appearance?
Therefore, it is said to be "without characteristics. Since it is not a form or appearance, how could there be coming or going?

Therefore, it is said to be "not coming. Since there is no coming or going, it is not an object of the mind. Therefore, it is said to be "not an object. If there were an object, that would constitute the realm of the mind.
It is not empty; one forms inverted perceptions, gives rise to delusions, and creates karma, thereby incurring the sinful dharmas of birth and death through causes and conditions.
Now, since these are not conditions, they are likewise not sins. Furthermore, how could there be the eight inversions or birth and death?
Therefore it is said: "Without the eight inversions, there is no birth or death. This is solely the flaming radiance of the Bodhisattva’s wisdom, which serves as illumination and bliss.

Vastly penetrating and spiritually resonant, with immeasurable skillful means, unobstructed and unhindered, and possessing infinite transformations, various supernatural powers, and various wondrous functions—all these take the wisdom of equality as their essential nature; such is everything that is enacted and employed.
This is because there is nothing that does not function through the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*).

If one does not rely upon this essence of equalizing wisdom—the primordial source of the wisdom of emptiness—as the illuminating function, then whatever one does or undertakes will be driven solely by the power of the karma of ignorance.
May students know this and cultivate this wisdom; this is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of the essence and function of the mind of wisdom.

○ Seventh, the explanation of the stage of the Vow-mind (*praṇidhāna-citta*). O Disciples of the Buddha: As for the vow—it is a great seeking, a universal seeking, because one takes the fruit as the cause. The vow-mind is continuous; the vow-mind is continuous, persisting through a hundred kalpas.
Thus one attains Buddhahood and extinguishes transgressions. Seeking and seeking with a sincere mind, there is the single vow of non-arising emptiness. Contemplating and contemplating...

Entering meditative absorption, one perceives immeasurable fetters because of seeking the mind; one attains immeasurable sublime practices through liberation from that seeking; immeasurable merits have seeking as their foundation.
Having first generated the mind of seeking, one cultivates the path in the interim; because the practice fulfills the vow, the fruit of Buddhahood is realized.
One contemplates the Middle Way of the Single Truth, which is neither the aggregates, nor the elements, nor the realms of death and birth. Thus one sees.
It is not [mere] seeing; rather, the nature of the essence of the wisdom of understanding is the fundamental source of all practices.

This explains the meaning of the aspirational mind, which is precisely the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā*. In other sūtras, it is named the "Stage of Non-retrogression," because one enters the realm of ultimate emptiness where there is no arising.
As for "aspiration" (*praṇidhāna*), it means a solemn vow; it is the very act of generating the various great vows and bringing them to fulfillment.
The Buddha is the one who delivers sentient beings. "Wishing for great seeking" refers to the section on attaining Buddhahood and extinguishing transgressions;

this precisely clarifies the essence and function of the Bodhisattva’s aspirational mind (*praṇidhāna-citta*) and the meaning of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*). "Wishing for great seeking" means aspiring upward toward the fruit of Buddhahood;
"seeking all things" means transforming sentient beings downward. "Because one takes the fruit as the practice of the cause" explains the fulfillment of the aforementioned aspiration.

The Buddha resolved the doubts regarding the salvation of sentient beings. As the Sūtra says: "One who seeks first to save others before having saved oneself is a Bodhisattva who has resolved upon the path;
one whose self-awakening is already perfected and who can awaken others is a Tathāgata appearing in the world. Now, one first achieves self-benefit and subsequently benefits others. Why is this?
It is because one wishes to employ the awakening of the stage of fruition (phala-bhūmi) while practicing with the mind of the causal stage (hetu-bhūmi). This refers to ordinary worldly beings...
Regarding the supramundane, the tainted and the untainted, and the causes and effects of good and evil, there must be a resolute vow, such as that of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva,
who vowed not to attain Buddhahood until hell is emptied, or that of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who vows to deliver all sentient beings.
Only then does one realize Bodhi. In each of the forty-eight vows of Amitābha Tathāgata, he concludes by saying:
"If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha. Even Yama, the Son of Heaven, makes a vow to govern all sinners, and each is reborn according to their respective vows;
thus, in order to deliver sentient beings, one must first resolve to attain Buddhahood. This is the aspirational mind (*praṇidhicitta*).

Regarding "continuity": based on the aforementioned aspiration to practice the cause through the fruit, one must maintain mindfulness at all times, with every thought following the last without interruption.
Thus, in continuous succession, one practices for a hundred kalpas, enduring what is difficult to endure and relinquishing what is difficult to relinquish.
Externally, they renounce kingdoms, cities, wives, and children; internally, they renounce their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains.
Even throughout immeasurable worlds, there is not a space the size of a mustard seed where a bodhisattva has not sacrificed their body and life. Thus, the mind is devoid of both subject and object.
When both person and dharma are forgotten, and even this forgetting is forgotten, one is finally able to behold the Original Buddha and extinguish immeasurable sins;
thus it is said that "one attains the Buddha’s extinction of sin. To "sincerely seek, seek" means to reach the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood, thereby forming a single complete section.

This clarifies the meaning of the vow-mind from beginning to end, from cause to final fruition. Regarding "sincerely seek, seek," the first instance of the word "seek" refers to seeking upward [toward enlightenment].

"Buddha-fruit" (佛果). The character "seeking" (求) below refers to seeking to transform sentient beings. The two characters "sincere mind" (至心) refer to the mind that seeks the Buddha-fruit and the mind that transforms sentient beings;
these must be continuously cultivated and advanced until the great vows are fulfilled.
"Seeking nothing to seek" means that by means of the wisdom of non-arising emptiness, one accords with the principle of non-arising emptiness; thus, wisdom and principle are one. One.
The vow is impartial. Since there is no duality between the arising and the Buddha, it is said: "Non-arising, emptiness, and the single vow.

Regarding the statement "contemplation enters meditative concentration through illumination," this clarifies both contemplations together, revealing only the Middle Way. Because one enters the contemplation of the conventional from the contemplation of emptiness, there is illumination;

because one enters the contemplation of emptiness from the contemplation of the conventional, there is concentration. Thus, both contemplations are simultaneously relinquished; emptiness and the conventional do not stand, and concentration and wisdom are unified.

Perfect interfusion means that while there is illumination, there is constant stillness; while there is stillness, there is constant illumination. This is the illumination of the contemplation of contemplation, and the contemplation of the illumination of illumination.
Therefore, all boundless fetters of views arise from the great aspirational mind of seeking the higher and transforming those below.
Through the power of meditative concentration and wisdom that contemplate with equanimity, one attains liberation; this is precisely the aforementioned meaning of the eradication of offenses.

It is not merely that one is liberated from immeasurable fetters of views due to the seeking mind, but also that immeasurable sublime practices are likewise accomplished through such earnest seeking and aspiration, thereby attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; this is the aforementioned attainment of Buddhahood.
The meaning of this is that even the immeasurable merits equal to the sands of the Ganges, which accord with the nature of reality, all have the seeking of the mind as their fundamental basis;
this is precisely the meaning of the single vow of unborn emptiness. The statement "first giving rise to [the aspiration]" below encourages its certain practice.
Seeking the mind in this manner is not merely a matter of empty aspirations and desires; for it may happen that one lacks the practice that accords with those aspirations and desires.

Therefore, one must first give rise to the seeking mind, then cultivate the path in the interim, and finally fulfill the vows through the completion of practice. Thus, the fruit of Buddhahood is attained.
Thus, one attains accomplishment. The initial arousal of the mind seeking enlightenment is *ādikṣaya-bodhi* (initial awakening).

The intermediate cultivation of the path consists of *anupūrva-bodhi* (gradual awakening) and *yathābhūta-bodhi* (partial awakening). Because practice fulfills the vows, it constitutes *atyanta-bodhi* (ultimate awakening).

When these three types of awakening reach fruition and the myriad virtues are perfected, one is finally able to attain the fruit of Buddhahood and be called the Honored One of Two Feet (*dvipadottama*). By contemplating the Middle Way within the Single Truth, one reaches the state of oneness.

Regarding the section on "the source of all practices": this refers to the Middle Way contemplation and wisdom within the mind of the vow, which serves as the essential nature of the vow and the foundation of all practices.
As for "contemplating the Middle Way of the Single Truth," following from the preceding, it means that within the state of Buddhahood.
Contemplating the principle of the single truth of the Middle Way, one does not perceive the establishment of any vows. Fundamentally, there is no Buddha-way to be accomplished;
fundamentally, there are no sentient beings to be delivered. Originally, there is neither bondage nor liberation. Bodhi is inherently possessed; merit is inherently perfected.
It is the original Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness. Therefore, when contemplating the five aggregates, they are not the five aggregates; when contemplating the ten...

The eight elements, not the eighteen elements; contemplating arising and ceasing, yet not arising and ceasing; contemplating all views, yet not all views—therefore it is said that "seeing seeing is non-existent.
That the wisdom of understanding is the essential nature of the vow is precisely the faith, understanding, practice, and realization of the *Avataṃsaka*.

One of the four dharmas: when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of aspiration, they produce understanding through faith, give rise to aspiration through understanding, initiate practice through aspiration, and realize the fruit through practice.
Without this initial wisdom of understanding, there would be no way to enter; such is this wondrous wisdom.
It is the fundamental essence of all vows and the source of all myriad practices.
Therefore, when one aspires to attain Buddhahood and deliver sentient beings, one must do so through the Middle Way wisdom of the single vow of unborn emptiness.

By understanding the principle of the Middle Way of the single vow of unborn emptiness, one then gives rise to all manner of wondrous, signless practices based upon this, thereby realizing the state of Buddhahood.

The wondrous fruit of Bodhi and Nirvana is characterized by suchness. If one contemplates another or aspires for another, this constitutes deluded wisdom and deluded understanding. Let the student know this.
○ Eighth, the stage of protecting the mind.
If a disciple of the Buddha protects the Three Jewels and protects the merit of all practices, they shall cause the eight inversions and evil heterodox views of external paths to cease.
Not disturbing right faith, one extinguishes the fetters of the self and the fetters of views. Through non-arising, one illuminates and penetrates the two truths;

the contemplation of the mind manifests before one, thereby guarding the root. This is the protection of the signless; through emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness, one links the wisdom of the mind with wisdom.

One enters the path of non-arising, the path of emptiness, and the path of knowledge—all luminous, radiant light. Guarding contemplation, one enters emptiness and the provisional; part by part, they are illusory transformations. Illusory...
It arises through transformation; as there is no such thing as "non-existence," so too the gathering and dispersing of the essence of phenomena cannot be observed—such is the nature of the dharma.

This explains the meaning of "guarding the mind," which is the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*). In another sutra, it is called the "Abode of Youthful Truth" (*kumārabhūmi*), because one does not give rise to false inversions that would destroy the bodhicitta.
"Guarding" means to maintain and uphold [the mind], preventing demons or outsiders from invading and destroying it.

Because of the bodhicitta, one protects the Three Jewels. Regarding the section on protecting the root, this precisely clarifies the meaning of the Buddha-son’s contemplation of the essence and function of the protective mind.
The Three Jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakened illumination;
"Dharma" has the meaning of upholding; "Saṅgha" has the meaning of harmony. There are the mundane, sustaining Three Jewels, and there are the supramundane...
The Three Jewels are eternally present in the world. There are the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, which possess both a single essence and distinct characteristics.
Such Three Jewels are the parents of the Dharma-body and wisdom-life for all sentient beings, as well as their true friends and fields of merit. If one does not protect and uphold them...
The wisdom-life of the Dharmakāya would then be severed and extinguished, and all merits would have no source from which to arise.
Therefore, one must provide powerful protection and sustenance. To protect the Triple Gem is nothing other than to protect the six perfections and myriad practices cultivated by oneself.
What is called "merit"? It is, within the gates of practice, to be neither indolent nor lazy, and to possess a beginning.
To have an end is called "merit" (*guṇa*). To be without person (*pudgala*) or self (*ātman*), and without grasping or abandoning, is called "virtue" (*puṇya*).

Thus, they are termed "merit and virtue" (*guṇapuṇya*). The *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) states: "By protecting the fruit of Buddhahood and protecting the practices of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) in this manner, one ensures that non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not cause disturbance.
This clearly elucidates the meaning of protecting the Three Jewels (*triratna*). There are many kinds of non-Buddhists; generally, those who do not comprehend the mind [are included].
Those whose conduct follows the paths of the worldly realms and who seek externally are all termed "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).

As for the eight inversions, these are the deluded and perverted attachments of ordinary beings, followers of the Lesser Vehicle, and non-Buddhists. Because these various inverted views are unwholesome, incorrect, and sever the seed of Buddhahood, they are called "evil and deviant views.
Regarding "right faith": "right" is the opposite of "deviant," and "faith" refers to the removal of doubt; it means to rectify [one's mind].
That which is believed is called "right faith. What is meant by "protecting merit" is precisely this:

ensuring that various non-Buddhists, the ordinary and the small-vehicle practitioners, and their eight inversions, evil and heterodox views and knowledges, cannot disturb me. Such is the protection of right faith in the Triple Gem.
How can one cause evil views not to disturb right faith? There is no other method than simply to extinguish the bonds of the self.
They are bound by views, yet they believe their own [views] to be correct. This inverted false view arises from relying on the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Because they cling to a self, they are bound by that self. Because they are bound by the self, various views arise, and thus they are bound by those views.
Bound by the characteristics of the view of self, what they believe is not correct. When what they believe is not correct, the various Māras and outsiders gain entry. Māra...
A single external sense-base destroys all merit; when all merit is destroyed, it causes the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Sangha to be destroyed as well.
Therefore, protecting the Triple Gem is actually not a separate dharma; it consists solely in protecting the merit of one’s own practice.
By doing so, the fetters of the self and the fetters of views are extinguished; when the view of self does not arise, one immediately enters the unborn (anutpāda). Thus, by means of...

The wisdom of the principle of non-arising gives rise to contemplative observation. Contemplating emptiness, one does not sink into emptiness; contemplating existence, one does not stagnate in existence.
Being empty yet not empty, one does not fall into the view of annihilationism; being existent yet not existent, one does not fall into the view of eternalism.

Thus, by not stagnating in emptiness or existence, and not falling into annihilationism or eternalism, the two truths are perfectly integrated and mutually inclusive without obstruction. Therefore, it is called "non-."
The arising illumination penetrates the two truths; this very contemplation of the mind suddenly manifests before one.
By guarding this root—namely, right faith—one directly transcends to the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood without obstruction.
All merits and virtues grow from this; therefore, right faith constitutes the root.
By means of this protection and maintenance, there is no end; therefore, it is said that "the contemplation of the mind manifests before one.
This serves to protect the root, which is to say: the nature of the mind being undeluded is the Buddha Jewel; the essence of the mind being free from thought is the Dharma Jewel;
and not contradicting the principle is the Sangha Jewel. [This continues] through the section on "protection by means of signlessness" up to "all are the light of the luminous light."
This clarifies the benefits of the practice of contemplating non-arising. That is to say, by using the wisdom of non-arising to contemplate what is present, one protects the faculty of faith;
yet both this protective contemplation and the protected faculty of faith are each and every one without marks.
From a mind protected by signlessness, one practices conduct protected by signlessness; therefore, it is called "protection by signlessness.
By means of this protection by signlessness, the right faith that is protected becomes liberated in every respect.
Because of this liberation in every respect, one realizes signless true emptiness. Because one realizes signless emptiness, there is nothing created, and there is no...
Because there is no active construction, it is called "signless" (*animitta*). Thus, it is said to be empty, unconditioned, and signless.

Regarding the phrase "because the mind and wisdom are continuous," this follows from what precedes: since one has entered the principle of wisdom regarding the three gates of liberation—emptiness, the unconditioned, and the signless—one does not abide in or cling to liberation as the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) does; this very true emptiness is unconditioned and signless.
Within this wisdom-mind, continuing and connecting without interval or interruption, one immediately attains deep entry into the path of unborn emptiness and the path of unborn gnosis;
both are luminous, radiant, and brilliant. The path of unborn emptiness is the principle and fruit of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*;
