Within these six realms, there are various kinds of suffering: such as the suffering of the devas when the five signs of decline appear;
the suffering of humans, such as birth, old age, sickness, and death; and the suffering of asuras, such as anger and strife.
Suffering. In the hells, there are sufferings such as cold, misery, and piercing pain; among ghosts and spirits, there are sufferings such as being submerged in obscurity and sorrow;

among birds and beasts, there are sufferings such as harboring agitation and fear. Although a Bodhisattva manifests in forms corresponding to each category among the sentient beings of the six realms, they do not regard these immeasurable afflictions and distresses as a source of personal concern. This concludes the reason for the multitude [of manifestations].
As for not avoiding suffering: it is solely for the purpose of benefiting those within the *dharmadhātu* as one's own gain. This is the practice of the path of wisdom;
the essence of wisdom is itself empty. Although sentient beings are transformed, the nature of birth is non-birth.
Practice such as this is precisely the essence and function of the Buddha-son’s compassionate mind that embraces sentient beings through contemplative cultivation.
○ Eighth, the explanation of the stage of shared mind (*samacitta*).

O Disciples of the Buddha, by means of the wisdom of the nature of the Way (*mārga-dharmatā-jñāna*), one shares in the dharma of emptiness and non-arising; by means of the wisdom of non-self (*anātma-jñāna*), one shares in the non-duality of birth.

Emptiness and the source are the same in the objective realm (*ālambana-viṣaya*). The suchness-mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas is eternally arising, eternally abiding, and eternally ceasing; worldly phenomena continue in succession and flow on.
Transforming immeasurably, they are able to manifest immeasurable forms, bodies, colors, minds, and karmic activities. They enter all six realms of existence;

in all matters they are identical, in emptiness they are identical, and in non-arising they are identical. Because their bodies are divided and their forms dispersed, they enter the Samādhi of Identical Dharma.

This explains the meaning of "sharing the same mind" (*samānacitta*), which is precisely the inclusion through "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*). In other sutras, this is called the "difficult-to-attain practice," because it involves accomplishing roots of goodness that are difficult to attain.

From the passage beginning with "By means of the wisdom of the nature of the path" up to "reaching the state of non-duality with those born together," the text correctly clarifies the meaning of the contemplative practice regarding the essence and function of sharing the same mind. "By means of the wisdom of the nature of the path" refers to the benefit of the bodhi-path-nature.
This is the power of the wisdom of birth. This wisdom accords with and is identical to true emptiness; it is without arising and without cessation.
Within the dharma of signlessness, wisdom and principle are non-dual, perfectly integrating all things. Therefore, by means of the wisdom of no-self and no-person, one manifests a body;

this manifestation is identical to birth and non-dual. This wisdom of no-self is precisely the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Because this wisdom is without differentiation, it serves as the basis for...
This essence of wisdom is able to be co-arisen and non-dual. "Co" means that which is able to accord; "arisen" refers to that with which there is accord.
Regarding the term "non-dual," its meaning is twofold: first, because the self and others lack dual characteristics, they are hidden within a single category;
through various skillful means and various supernormal powers, one gathers in sentient beings without any sense of "self" or "other. Second, because [the self and others]... [text fragment ends]

I have no dual nature. Birth is itself non-birth; sameness is itself non-sameness. All are identical to the emptiness of non-birth. Therefore, they are "identical in birth," because their essence is without distinction.
"Emptiness and sameness share the same source and object" means that, following the preceding point, since it was stated they are "identical in birth," why [is this further explained]?

From the section on "reaching all phenomena as being identical," the meaning of the mind’s essence and function sharing the same source is clarified. Regarding "emptiness and sameness share the same source and object": having already stated above that they are "identical in birth," how...
They are called "non-dual. Since they are non-dual, how could they be "co-arisen"?
As for the statement that they are "co-arisen and non-dual," it means that those which give rise to the self are all fundamentally identical to the principle of unborn emptiness (*anutpāda-śūnyatā*).

Just as all waters are identical in their source, so too are all faculties and objects identical in the true realm. Within this principle-realm of non-dual true emptiness, there is in fact nothing [that arises].
Regarding the characteristics of the identity and difference between self and others, it is said that emptiness is the single source of the objective realm.

Since the suchness-characteristic of all dharmas is the true mark of reality for all phenomena, how could there be the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing? Fundamentally, they are without arising, without abiding, and without ceasing.
Non-arising is precisely non-non-arising; non-abiding is precisely non-non-abiding; non-ceasing is precisely non-non-ceasing.

Because there is no arising, abiding, or ceasing, it is therefore constantly arising, constantly abiding, and constantly ceasing. Regarding the phrase "the dharmas of the world" and so forth, this clarifies the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing.
A question is asked: Since it is said that they are constantly arising, constantly abiding, and constantly ceasing, how is this so?

Furthermore, is there a flux of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing? He replied: "It is because sentient beings do not recognize the dharmas of constant arising, constant abiding, and constant ceasing;
they are deluded regarding the truth and pursue the false, giving rise to afflictions and creating karma, and then receiving retribution according to that karma."
They revolve through the three periods of time, with birth and death being without end; hence it is said that worldly phenomena continue in succession, flowing and turning immeasurably.
Thus, the Bodhisattva observes that sentient beings in the world receive retribution according to their karma, undergoing immeasurable suffering without realizing it themselves.
Therefore, by means of the compassion and wisdom that share the same essence, they initiate the "sameness of purpose" (sabhāgatā) among the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Thus, they are able to manifest immeasurable forms of body, color, mind, and other activities, entering all six realms of existence. In all matters, they act in common with others;

according to whichever body is required for a being’s deliverance, they immediately manifest that very body. Dwelling together with all sentient beings in a single location, they preach the Dharma through various skillful means.

They cause beings to attain liberation. Like the Great Being of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha), they respond to conditions and reach those who call upon them, manifesting forms according to the various classes of beings;
thus it is said that they "enter the six realms," for in all matters they are identical. Regarding the phrase "identical with emptiness, identical with non-arising," etc.:

this is a concluding summary that clarifies the meaning of the identity between the mind and its essence and function. The single phrase "identical with emptiness, identical with non-arising" concludes the preceding section on being identical with the dharma of emptiness and non-arising.
This is the intended meaning. It refers to the non-duality of emptiness and non-existence; it is solely the single true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*).
Because this is the non-dual true emptiness, it is able to manifest all forms of emptiness. All that is manifested as emptiness is identical to the emptiness of non-arising (*anutpāda-śūnyatā*);

therefore, it is said that "emptiness is identical to non-arising. The phrase "I am identical to non-substantiality" concludes the preceding section, wherein through the wisdom of non-self (*anātma-jñāna*), one is identical with arising.
The meaning of non-duality is this: that which is called "self" is fundamentally without self; therefore, things are themselves without things.
Because there is neither self nor thing, one is able to manifest the forms of all things. Since the self is identical to non-existence, it is without things;
yet, because it divides its body and disperses its form, it enters the Samādhi of Identical Dharma. These two phrases conclude the preceding point: the ability to manifest immeasurable forms.

The passage concerning the karma of body, color, mind, and so forth means that only those who have attained this samādhi are able to enter the lands of all Buddhas, manifest the physical forms of all sentient beings, and engage in the activities of all sentient beings.
Because its name is manifested through these activities, it is called the "Samādhi of Identical Dharma" (*sādharmya-samādhi*).
Such wisdom and concentration constitute the Bodhisattva’s mind of "identical activity" (*samānārthatā*), which gathers in and sustains sentient beings.
This is the contemplative practice of essence and function.
○ Ninth, the explanation of the stage of the concentrated mind:

O Sons of the Buddha, furthermore, from the concentrated mind, one contemplates with wisdom to realize emptiness; every thought-moment rests in stillness upon the objects of perception regarding the dharmas of "mine," and consciousness...
Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), he remains unmoving; whether moving against or with the current, emerging or submerging, he constantly enters a hundred samādhis and the ten factors of dhyāna.
With the wisdom of a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇajñāna*), he perceives all "selves" and "persons," whether internal or external, as the seeds of sentient beings.
All are without conjunction or dispersal; though they are integrated, accumulated, initiated, and produced, they cannot be apprehended.
This explains the meaning of the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), which is precisely the practice of supreme concentration (*adhiprajñā-samādhi*).

In another sutra, it is called the "practice of wholesome dharmas" (*kuśala-dharma-carita*), meaning the teaching of the Dharma to others as the rule for attaining Buddhahood. Furthermore, from this concentrated mind, one proceeds through the section on the ten factors of dhyāna (*dhyānāṅga*).
This clearly explains the meaning of the essence, function, and contemplative practice of the concentrated mind. Regarding the phrase "furthermore, from the concentrated mind":
"furthermore" (fu) means "again" (you). This refers to having previously entered samādhi and right concentration within the desire realm;

now, one again arises from that concentrated mind of the desire realm to enter the two higher realms and manifest for the benefit of sentient beings. "Contemplation" (guan) means observation. "Wisdom" (hui) means discernment.
"Shine. Contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*) is the wisdom that realizes; "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) is the principle realized.
This means that this Bodhisattva, by means of a mind of tranquil concentration and contemplative wisdom, realizes the principle of emptiness within that concentration.

The emptiness thus realized is not like the cessation and liberation of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which cannot contemplate and realize that the root-body, the vessel-world, and the seeds of ignorance are entirely empty in their very essence. Bodhi...
Thus, he realizes emptiness yet does not dwell in or cling to the principle of emptiness. Within the principle of true emptiness, his mind and mental factors remain in tranquil contemplation.
Regarding all phenomena pertaining to "self" and "mine," he views them entirely as illusions. Following the nature of these illusory phenomena, he manifests an illusory body.
Within the realm of form and the realm of consciousness, he expounds the Dharma-gate of illusion to extensively transform illusory sentient beings. Nevertheless...
Thus it is. It cannot be moved or turned by the two realms of form and consciousness; it is not turned by external objects, but rather can turn them.

The realm of consciousness refers to the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the realm of form refers to the four heavens of the dhyāna realms (*catur-dhyāna*). That which is called "unmoved and unturned" is as follows:
That is to say, within the two upper realms, whether emerging in reverse order or in direct order, or dissolving in reverse order or in direct order—
by means of such entering and emerging, and appearing and disappearing— he constantly enters a hundred samādhis, the ten factors of dhyāna, and various supernormal powers.
He is sovereign and unimpeded; he is not defiled by the desires and evils of the lower realms, nor is he constrained by the emptiness and meditative absorptions of the two higher realms.
This so-called "retrograde and prograde movement" is unfathomable even to the gods. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"He enters right concentration within the body of a youth and emerges from concentration within the body of a maiden; he enters right concentration within the body of a maiden..."
The phrase "arising from meditative concentration within the body of a youth" refers to this. There are immeasurable names for samādhis; briefly stated, there are one hundred and eight.
Here, one hundred samādhis are cited in order to destroy the arising of the views of the hundred dharmas among sentient beings within the three realms.

As for the ten factors of dhyāna (dhyānāṅga): first, applied thought (vitarka); second, sustained thought (vicāra); third, joy (prīti); fourth, bliss (sukha); fifth, one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā); sixth, purity (śuddhi); seventh, equanimity (upekṣā); eighth, mindfulness (smṛti).
Ninth is wisdom; tenth is neither-pain-nor-pleasure. These ten constitute the meditative factors (*dhyānāṅga*) of the heavens of dhyāna.

By means of the wisdom of a single thought-moment, one reaches the point where not even a single factor can be apprehended. This clarifies the essence and function of the concentrated mind and its contemplative wisdom, as well as the meaning of each moment of mind being still and focused on its object.
One who employs the wisdom of a single thought-moment to form such a vision perceives that within the state of concentration, there is not even a single thought-moment.
Obstructing purity, wisdom shines forth in perfect illumination, seeing all things as they truly are:

whether it be the internal faculties and body, or the external vessel-world, the ripening consciousness of sentient beings, or the seeds and manifestations of ignorance—all are without conjunction or dispersion, without accumulation or formation, without arising or action; all are empty, like illusions and transformations, ultimately ungraspable.
It is said that the world is fundamentally without formation, abiding, destruction, or emptiness; sentient beings are fundamentally without birth, abiding, change, or extinction.
To contemplate in this manner is called the bodhisattva’s practice of contemplation regarding the essence and function of the entry and exit of the concentrated mind. Question:
What is the difference between this stage of the fixed mind—where contemplative wisdom destroys delusions—and the previous stage of birth? Answer: Briefly stated:
They are similar, yet each differs in its degree of depth. The former stage is fixed for destroying the coarse afflictions of conceptual discrimination;
this practice stage is fixed for destroying the subtle afflictions of conceptual discrimination. Thus, they are not the same.
○ Tenth, the stage of the Mind of Wisdom-Insight (*prajñā-citta*).

If, O disciples of the Buddha, one forms the mind of wisdom-insight, one contemplates the fetters of various false views, afflictions, and bonds as having no determinate essence or nature, because they accord with the emptiness of *anulomikī-kṣānti* (patience in conformity).
They are not the aggregates (*skandha*), not the elements (*dhātu*), not the sense bases (*āyatana*), not sentient beings, not a single self, and not cause or effect.

It is not a dharma of the three periods of time. It arises from the nature of wisdom. Light upon light forms a single flame; clearly and brightly it sees. It is empty and non-receptive. This wisdom and skillful means nourish and develop the mind.
This mind enters the path of the emptiness of emptiness and gives rise to the mind of non-arising. It ascends to the Chapter on the King of the Ocean Eye.
Thus has been explained the Hundred Dharmas Gate of Clarity for the Mind.
This explains the meaning of the "mind of wisdom" (*prajñā-citta*), which is precisely the practice of supreme wisdom (*prajñā-caryā*).
In other sutras, it is called the "practice of reality" (*tattva-caryā*), because the two truths are neither like [their conventional appearances] nor are they without characteristics.

From the section on the "mind that acts as the vision of wisdom" up to the passage concerning the "dharmas of the three periods of time," the text correctly elucidates the meaning of the essence, function, and contemplative practice of the mind of wisdom. The "mind that acts as the vision of wisdom" is the contemplative gnosis (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) that is capable of illuminating.
"Observing all false views and the like" refers to the delusions that are to be destroyed. "The agent" refers to the activity;
that is to say, this Bodhisattva’s great activity arises from the wisdom of the principle of quiescence as originally understood, giving rise to contemplative observation.

Through this observation, one perceives the deluded minds of oneself and others, and carefully examines the various evil false views, the bonds of afflictions, and the fetters arising from ignorance, just as follows:

One truly understands that there is no determinate intrinsic nature. Those with false views—namely, the various non-Buddhists who cling to permanence, cling to annihilation, cling to identity, cling to difference, and so forth—are those with such various attachments and views. Regarding the "bonds, afflictions, and fetters":

"bonds" refers to the eye being bound to forms and so forth; "afflictions" refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the eye, forms, and so forth, which give rise to the affliction of karma and cause [suffering].

Bound by the fetters of birth and death, one cannot attain liberation; therefore, they are called the afflictions of the knots and so forth. Regarding the phrase "having no determinate essence or nature":

it means that these afflictions arise from delusion regarding the *ālayavijñāna*. Upon reaching the stage after the seventh bhūmi, through the uninterrupted cultivation of the path, one attains liberation via *anulomikī-kṣānti* (conformative patience), whereby the *ālayavijñāna* becomes a single emptiness and is transformed into the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena). These various afflictions [are thus eliminated].

In that state of compliant patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*), all things are simultaneously quiescent; therefore, it is said that there is no determinate intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is because compliant patience is identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Thus, one contemplates the five aggregates (*skandha*) as not being the five aggregates; one contemplates the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) as not being the eighteen elements;

one contemplates the twelve bases (*āyatana*) as not being the twelve bases; one contemplates sentient beings as not being sentient beings; one contemplates the single self as not being a single self. One contemplates...
Cause and effect; non-cause and non-effect. Contemplating the dharmas of the three periods of time, they are not dharmas of the three periods of time.

All are non-existent; they are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. That is to say, within the true permanence of this nature, if one seeks for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, nothing at all can be found.
Therefore, they are not the five aggregates or other such dharmas. When the nature of wisdom arises, it reaches the point of giving rise to the unconditioned.

The arising of a single section constitutes the function of the contemplative observation of the wisdom-mind; it manifests the non-abiding provisional contemplation and thereby realizes entry into the contemplation of the Middle Way.
As for "the nature of wisdom arises," it is because this unconditioned, wondrous wisdom perceives that which arises from the mind.
It further develops the subtle function of contemplative wisdom; thus it is said that "the nature of wisdom arises. As for the phrase "each light is a single flame":

each light is *jñāna* (cognitive wisdom), and the single flame is *prajñā* (discriminating wisdom). *Jñāna* can illuminate objects, while *prajñā* can discern objects. By means of the flame of wisdom...
"To realize that the objects of conditions are empty and illusory" means that the one who sees clearly perceives them with perfect clarity.

"The void has no recipient" refers to the essential nature of this wisdom-illumination: it is unobstructed and unhindered, void-penetrating and spiritually penetrating, and does not receive any sensations.
Therefore, it is called "receiving emptiness" (*śūnyatā-anupādāna*). Regarding the phrase "his wisdom and skillful means are equal":

this refers to the Son of the Buddha who, through the illumination of *prajñā*-wisdom, clearly perceives that the essence of ignorance is empty. Consequently, the essence of his mind is void, pervasive, and unobstructed.
Because it is void, pervasive, and unobstructed, his wisdom further nurtures the *dharmakāya* through various ingenious and immeasurable skillful means, bringing it to completion.

Regarding the attainment of wisdom-life (*prajñājīvita*): it is not realized through another, but for the sake of accomplishment. This mind enters and gives rise to the path of emptiness-within-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), giving birth to the mind of non-arising (*anutpattika-citta*), like the growth of a sprout.
This mind is precisely the fundamental wisdom-mind. "Entering" (*praveśa*) means realization and entry; "arising" (*utthāna*) means initiation.

"Emptiness-within-emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) refers to the truth of the two-fold emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) which is realized. "Path" (*mārga*) refers to the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).
For, by means of the wisdom-mind employed since the past, one has now realized the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

Not only are phenomena such as the five aggregates empty, but there is also no agent that can empty those five aggregates and so forth. Regarding the principle of these two kinds of emptiness, there is likewise no dwelling.
Because there is no dwelling, one dedicates [merit] toward the Middle Way of the One Vehicle within the ocean of the *dharmadhātu*, giving rise to the non-arising [mind].
This is the mind, for it freely steers the vessel of compassion. As for the "unborn mind," because not even a hair’s breadth of phenomena is seen to arise or perish, it is called the unborn mind.
Only by giving rise to this mind can one universally carry and transport others, so that all may together realize the indestructible Vajra-mind.
Thus, the simultaneous application of compassion and wisdom constitutes the contemplative practice of the essence and function of the Bodhisattva’s mind of wisdom.
This is a brief explanation. Within the great treatise, in the "Chapter on the King of the Ocean-Eye" (*Sāgarakṣa-locana-rāja-parivarta*), these ten minds have already been explained;
they are each elucidated in detail within the "Gateway to the Clarification of the Hundred Dharmas" (*Śatadharma-vyākhyāna-mukha*), which is inconceivable.

As for the term "Gateway to the Clarification of the Hundred Dharmas," it refers to the gateway of the hundred and eight wisdoms. The mention of "hundred" here is used to indicate a large number. When the Bodhisattva is about to depart...

Explaining the Meaning of the Ten Transferences (2) 1. Citation of the Introductory Question 2. Correct Explanation of its Meaning.
First, the introductory statement and the question:
Vairocana Buddha said, "O thousand Buddhas, listen attentively. You previously stated that there are ten minds which are the diamond seeds."

This Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, addressed the Buddha who was ready to receive the teaching, admonishing him to listen and setting forth the inquiry; he then explained in detail the meaning of the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā-citta*).

This refers to how a Bodhisattva dwelling in the preceding stages of practice, having aroused great compassion to deliver sentient beings, must dedicate the wholesome deeds cultivated during those stages toward three destinations:
first, the *tathatā-bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality as suchness) which is realized; second, the... [unrealized] which is sought.

Third, regarding the dedication toward supreme enlightenment: by means of the mind that performs the dedication and the virtuous deeds dedicated, one directs them toward all classes of sentient beings to fulfill their pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) and cause them to enter equally into the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Furthermore, it is said that one dedicates phenomena toward principle, the small toward the great, and causes toward the fruit; for through the perfect fusion of phenomenon and principle, and the non-obstruction of the small and the great, [all are realized].

Because cause and effect are non-dual. Furthermore, it is said that one turns from the ultimate toward the conventional, and turns wisdom toward compassion, because the ultimate and the conventional are mutually integrated and wisdom and compassion are non-dual.
These two dharmas constitute the meaning of the three aforementioned types of dedication.
Regarding the statement that there are ten minds of the "vajra seed," this refers to these ten minds of dedication, which are the supreme contemplative wisdom and wondrous practice.
It is most firm and sharp; it cannot be destroyed by any afflictions, yet it can destroy all delusions and karmas.
Therefore, the mind of the tenth stage of dedication is called the "vajra-seed."
II. Correctly Explaining the Meaning (ten sections).
I. The Stage of Faithful Mind.
O Disciples of the Buddha, as for "faith," it is the foremost of all practices and the root of all virtues; it does not give rise to the ways of external paths.
With a mind of wrong views, one becomes attached to various perspectives and fetters; thus, by creating karma, one will certainly not attain liberation.

Upon entering the unconditioned dharma of emptiness, there is neither existence nor non-existence of the three marks: no arising of arising, no abiding of abiding, and no cessation of cessation. There is not a single dharma that exists; all are empty.

The wisdom of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is exhausted; it extinguishes the diversity of emptiness, the emptiness of form, and the emptiness of the subtle mind and mental factors.
Because the subtle mind and mental factors are themselves empty, every moment of faith is quiescent and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Even their conjunction has no basis.

Furthermore, regarding the "master"—the designation of "self" and "person" as functional entities—the "self" within the three realms is merely provisional. Since there is no obtainable characteristic of a collection [of aggregates], this is called the "faith of non-existence."

This explains the meaning of dedicating the mind of faith (*śraddhā-citta-pariṇāmanā*). A separate sutra states: "To rescue and protect sentient beings while remaining free from the notion of sentient beings is dedication.

This means that with a mind devoid of conceptualization (*animitta-citta*), one constantly traverses the six realms of existence and enters into their karmic retributions; yet, though experiencing them, one does not experience them as such.
If the "sons of the Buddha" are designated by persons, then "faith" designates the Dharma—namely, all practices culminating in the wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya-jñāna*).

This constitutes one section. It precisely elucidates the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s dedication of the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way—the essence and function of the mind of faith—within the stage of a Buddha-son.

Regarding the phrase "all practices" and so forth, it refers to the period beginning from the First Stage (Prathamabhūmi) and ending at Wondrous Enlightenment (Samyak-saṃbodhi), spanning three great eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

To cultivate the myriad practices and all virtuous qualities, if one does not first possess right faith as the primary foundation, one will inevitably be broken by the demons of emptiness and existence or by those outside the path.
Therefore, with the power of faith as a firm endurance, one subsequently gives rise to various sublime practices.
Thus, faith is that which can initiate, while all practices are what are initiated; this is because of the initiating power of right faith.
Faith gives rise to the wondrous practices that are initiated; through these initiated wondrous practices, one realizes the wondrous fruit that is beyond realization.
Therefore, faith is the source for entering the Path and the mother of all merit. Thus it is said: "All practices take faith as their head;
it is the root of all virtues. To not give rise to the mind of heterodox or false views is to manifest and clarify the emptiness of faith.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). There are ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist paths and sixty-two views; these are external false views.
Because they lack correct faith, they give rise to various kinds of delusions regarding the principle of namelessness, signlessness, and selflessness.
Now that fundamental correct faith has been established, once doubt is removed and attachment is abandoned, all such false views will forever cease to exist.
Therefore it is said: "Do not give rise to the heterodox views of external paths. Regarding the phrase "those who are attached to various views," this expresses the meaning of fundamental heterodoxy.
That is to say, ordinary people are attached to existence; externalists cling to permanence; the followers of the Two Vehicles are attached to emptiness;
and externalists cling to annihilation. All such views are termed "attachment. Wherever there is attachment, it is truly difficult to eliminate.
Naturally, one accumulates the causes of outflows, commits various evil deeds, and undergoes the fruits of those evil karmas.

Now, this son of the Buddha, having already established the roots of all virtues through right faith, employs the single illumination of the wondrous threefold gate of contemplation—emptiness, conventionality, and the Middle Way.
By this, the obstacles of affliction are instantly emptied. Once the obstacles of affliction are emptied, the obstacles of karma...
From what could they arise? Since even karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*) cannot be found, how could there be retributive obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*) to be experienced?

Therefore, it is said: "If one has formed the bonds [of afflictions], one must not create karma; if one enters into the unconditioned dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatāsaṃskṛtadharma*), the three marks do not exist.
This clarifies the meaning of non-experience. The previous mention of karmic and retributive obstructions as being "not necessarily experienced" is the faith of the Buddha-son (*jinaputra*).
Wisdom manifests before one, realizing that there is no agent who creates karma and no recipient who undergoes retribution.

Thus, the entire body has already entered into the unconditioned dharma of emptiness and is not bound by conditioned dharmas; yet, it is able to discern the three characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Because these are without movement and without arrival, it is said: "The three characteristics are non-existent. To say they are "non-existent" means that the three characteristics are what is to be negated.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is non-existent; there is no "non-existence" [of it]. This is the contemplative wisdom (*prajñā*) that can destroy it. Since that which is destroyed is non-existent, that which destroys is also non-existent.
Regarding "non-arising, non-arising," etc., this explains the various unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) such as faith and emptiness.
It means that not only are the three marks non-existent, but all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas are likewise non-existent. Within these very unconditioned dharmas, all [phenomena] are...

Even the Dharma cannot be apprehended. Regarding the repeated mention of "non-arising" and so forth: the former "non-arising" refers to emptiness—the principle realized through the exhaustion of all conditioned phenomena;
the latter "non-arising" refers to the elimination of the aforementioned wisdom that realizes non-arising, which is itself a "double emptiness."
It is said that they are originally unborn; why then should one further establish "non-arising" before designating them as "unborn"?
Therefore it is said: "Unborn, unborn. Such is the meaning of non-arising. "Non-abiding, abiding," and "non-extinction, extinction"—the meaning is likewise so.
There is not a single dharma that is empty [in the sense of being separate from this]. Following the preceding discussion of both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, all...
All phenomena are originally non-existent and entirely empty and quiescent; thus, there is no phenomenon that can be emptied, and therefore emptiness itself cannot be apprehended.
This summarizes and dispels the principle of the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional. Because it is the emptiness of non-apprehension, it is said:
"There is no emptiness of all phenomena" refers to the ultimate wisdom that exhausts both the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This is a summary that dispels the wisdom regarding these two truths: there is no wisdom of the conventional truth that can empty conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), nor is there ultimate wisdom that can empty unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). "Exhaustion" means the exhaustion of these two types of wisdom; that is to say, it is not...

However, when the objects of emptiness—the conditioned and the unconditioned, and the principles of the two truths—are found to be unobtainable, then the subject of emptiness—the wisdom that cognizes the conditioned and the unconditioned, and the two truths—is likewise exhausted without remainder. This is what is meant by "neither wisdom nor attainment.

From the passage beginning with "extinguishing the emptiness of difference" and "the emptiness of form," up to "even the combination has no basis," this section clarifies the dedication of the mind of faith.

"Meaning. "Extinction" (*nirodha*) refers to the act of eliminating; it is the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) that is capable of extinguishing. This is distinct from "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*).

"The emptiness of form" (*rūpa-śūnyatā*) refers to the form-dharmas that are to be extinguished—namely, what ordinary beings grasp as form while being deluded regarding emptiness, and what the Two Vehicles grasp as emptiness while being deluded regarding form. These are divided into two separate blocks.

Therefore, during the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*), one cultivates the contemplation of emptiness to shatter the ordinary person’s grasping at form and delusion regarding emptiness. During the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*), one cultivates the [contemplation of] the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Contemplation: This refutes the attachment to emptiness and delusion regarding form held by those of the Two Vehicles.

Now, the Bodhisattva of the Ten Dedications, by means of the wisdom of the contemplation of the equality of the dharma-realm, perfectly illumines the dharma-realm and simultaneously eliminates all divergent views of empty space, form, emptiness, the conditioned, the unconditioned, and sameness or difference.
Within the five aggregates, this refers to the aggregate of form and emptiness; that is to say, form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness...

"It is not different from form; form itself is emptiness, and emptiness itself is form. This refers to that [teaching]. Regarding "the subtle mind, the mind, and emptiness, etc.," this clarifies that the mental aggregates (*skandha*) which are to be extinguished are also empty.

That is to say, the aforementioned "different emptiness" (*visama-śūnyatā*)—once both the characteristics of form and emptiness are empty, then the "different emptiness" and the "form-emptiness" that could extinguish them are themselves empty. Thus, the mind of the subtle mind is also empty; hence it is called "subtle."

The mind and mind are empty. Furthermore, it is not only the mental activities of the subtle mind that are empty; even the subtle mind itself, upon which these activities depend, cannot be apprehended.
Therefore, it is said: "The subtle mind and the mind of the mind are both empty. As the *Nirvāṇa-samantabhadra-bodhi-sūtra* (Complete Enlightenment Sutra) states:

Do not seek or inquire. Even "harmony" (saṃghāta) has no basis. The single character "However" shifts the momentum of the text, stating that all ordinary beings and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) all derive [their views] from the self (*ātman*) and the person (*pudgala*), and thus establish names.
Establishing the function [of the self]. Because this is the person, between the names and functions, one makes distinctions for oneself, regarding them as "harmonizing" or "conjoining.

How could there be anything to be attained through cultivation or realization within the state where there is no self and no dharmas? How could a collection of wisdom be accumulated? Therefore it is said:

"Because there is no self, there is no attainment and no accumulation. Thus, one enters deeply with profound faith into the principle of wisdom: non-attainment, non-accumulation, and non-self. This is it.
This is called the "Buddha-son’s Signless State," the essence and function of the mind of faith, that which is to be dedicated.
II. The Stage of Mindfulness.
If a Buddha-son practices the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), he is constantly awakened, even unto constant giving; [he realizes] the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is empty and unattached.

There is no liberation. The characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing are unmoving; there is no arriving, nor going or coming. Yet, regarding the recipient of all karmic actions, one turns them over through the mark of total integration (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) into the wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*).
Wisdom and wisdom mount one another; vehicle after vehicle is quiescent extinction. Flame upon flame is impermanent; light upon light is non-existent.
Birth after birth does not arise; it transforms into the path of emptiness. It changes the former and turns toward the latter; it transforms and transmutes again and again, until it is transformed.
Transforming and transforming again; simultaneously abiding together; each flame having a single characteristic; arising and ceasing at one time;
already transformed, not yet transformed, and in the process of transforming—transformation also attains oneness, and sensation is likewise so.
This explains the meaning of dedicating the mind through mindfulness. A separate sutra names this the "Indestructible Dedication" (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*).

It means that one contemplates all phenomena as having reception and function, yet remaining non-abiding from moment to moment. When a disciple of the Buddha forms a mindful resolve and establishes it—extending from the six recollections up to the section on entering the wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*)—this precisely clarifies the Middle Way contemplation within the essence and function of the disciple’s mind of mindfulness.
Regarding the meaning of the dedication of wisdom: "to bring to mind" means that "bringing" refers to the act of initiating, while "mind" refers to clear recollection without forgetting.
The phrase "the six recollections," etc., clarifies the intent behind bringing something to mind. When it asks, "What does one bring to mind? it refers to these six recollections.

Answer: It refers to the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*): recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of the precepts, recollection of the devas, and recollection of giving.

From "constant mindfulness" (*sadā-smṛti*) up to "constant giving" (*sadā-dāna*), these represent the first and last of the six recollections; this is a method of abbreviation that encompasses the four intermediate ones.

Regarding the term "constant mindfulness," it refers to the recollection of the Buddha. This is explained according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* through the exposition of the six recollections, beginning with the recollection of the Buddha.

This refers to recollecting the ten qualities of the Buddhas: they are fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and the three mindfulnesses (*trismṛti*);
they are eternal, blissful, self, and pure. For this reason, they are called *Tathāgata*. They are eternally unchanging;
they are named the Great Śramaṇa, the Great Dharma Teacher, the Great Guide, and so forth, up to the *Bhagavat*. This is called the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva recollects the Buddha. As for recollecting the Dharma, it means recollecting and contemplating the Dharma taught by all Buddhas, which is most wondrous and supreme.
Because of this Dharma, sentient beings are able to attain present fruits. This True Dharma alone is without temporal limits;
it is that which is seen by the Dharma-body—neither arising nor ceasing, neither abiding nor perishing, neither beginning nor ending.
Even the dwelling places where all Buddhas roam are eternally unchanging; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Dharma.
As for mindfulness of the Saṅgha, it means being mindful of the noble Saṅgha of the Buddhas, who abide in accordance with the Dharma and uphold the True Dharma.
Practicing in accordance [with this], it cannot be seen, cannot be grasped, cannot be destroyed, and cannot be disturbed or harmed.
It is inconceivable; it is the excellent and auspicious field of merit for all sentient beings. Although it is a field of merit, it receives nothing.
It is even constant and unchanging—this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the Saṅgha and mindfulness of the precepts.
This refers to being mindful of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and contemplating that one possesses precepts that are unbroken, without leakage, indestructible, and unmixed.

Therefore, one should extensively expound the sublime Dharma for the sake of sentient beings and act as their protection; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the precepts (*śīla-smṛti*).

As for mindfulness of the deities (*deva-smṛti*), it refers to being mindful of the abodes of the Four Great Kings, up to and including the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

If one possesses faith, they shall attain the realm of the Four Heavenly Kings; I too have a share therein. If one possesses ethical discipline, learning, generosity, and wisdom, they shall attain the realms from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception; I too have a share therein.
Yet, these are not what I desire. Why is this? Because all realms, from the Four Heavenly Kings up to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, are impermanent.
Because they are impermanent, there are birth, old age, sickness, and death. For this reason, these are not what I desire.
They are like magical illusions that deceive the foolish; they cannot delude those of wisdom. The "foolish" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
I am not like ordinary, foolish people. I have heard that there is a "Heaven of the Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha-deva), which is eternal and unchanging.
