For the sake of sentient beings, I diligently seek this Heaven of the Ultimate Truth, so that I may enable them to sever and abandon their afflictions (kleśa), just as one acts according to their will.
Tree. If I possess faith, up to and including wisdom, then I am able to attain this ultimate heavenly state (*paramārthadeva*).
For the sake of sentient beings, I shall extensively analyze and explain this ultimate heavenly state; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s mindfulness of the heavens (*devānusmṛti*).
Regarding the recollection of giving (*dānānusmṛti*): it means to mindfully and deeply contemplate that this giving is the cause of *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddhas have cultivated this; I too shall cultivate it in the same way. If one does not practice generosity, one cannot adorn the fourfold assembly.
Although giving may not [immediately] sever all afflictions (*kleśa*), it can nonetheless eliminate present defilements, even unto the state of the Buddhas.
The Bodhisattva cultivates and accumulates this giving as a cause for Nirvana; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s mindfulness of giving.

Thus, from constant awakening up to constant giving, although there are six types of mindfulness in name, within the ultimate truth of emptiness and according to the principle of reality, there is truly no mindfulness to which one can cling, and truly no mindfulness that can [be apprehended].

As for liberation: why is this so? Where there is bondage, there is liberation; both are subject to arising and ceasing. Where there is neither attachment nor liberation, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because there is neither bondage nor liberation, there are no mental conceptions of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
Because there are no mental conceptions of the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, this is fundamentally unmoving and fundamentally unattainable.
Since the fundamental source is fundamentally unmoving, it does not arrive; thus, there is also no departing and no coming.
Where there is no coming, there is no mark of movement; one perceives that there is arising. Where there is no departing, there is no mark of arrival; one perceives that there is cessation.

Thus, being unmoving, non-arriving, non-departing, and non-coming, there are therefore no three marks of arising, abiding, and ceasing. [Consequently,] there is no performing of karma or receiving of retribution.

All things are empty. To be able to dedicate all performed actions, as well as the agent who performs them, as a single unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*) is to enter the wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*).
This dedication as a single unified whole is a state of mindfulness in which there is neither subject nor object;
subject and object are non-dual. There is no bondage and no liberation; bondage and liberation are non-dual. There is no arising and no cessation; arising and cessation [are non-dual].
There is no duality. There is no movement. There is no arrival. Movement and arrival are non-dual. There is no coming. There is no going. Coming and going are non-dual.
There is no karma. There is no retribution. Karma and retribution are non-dual. This is the dedication of the "unified mark. Regarding the wisdom that enters the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*):
"entering" has the meaning of "tending toward. The "Dharma-realm" refers to the ten Dharma-realms; it is the very nature of all sentient beings.
The mind that exists is the principle realized by all Buddhas; that is to say, there is no difference between the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings.

Wisdom is the wisdom capable of realizing the equality of the *dharmadhātu*. One turns the principles of the two truths toward the entry into the principle of the equality of the *dharmadhātu*, and turns the wisdom of the two truths toward the entry into the wisdom of the equality of the *dharmadhātu*. By means of this...

The wisdom of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-jñāna) accords with the principle of the dharma-realm; by means of the principle of the dharma-realm, it immerses itself in the wisdom of the dharma-realm. Thus, wisdom and principle are perfectly interfused.

There are no signs; one enters the Dharma-realm. There are three stages because, depending on whether the faculties of various bodhisattvas are sharp or dull and their practices are shallow or deep, that which they enter differs. The first is the initial mind of the ten abodes for those with sharp faculties.
One is able to destroy ignorance and immediately attains realization and entry into the principle of the equality of the *dharmadhātu*, thereby reaching the stage of non-retrogression.

Second, at the final mind of the tenth stage of dedication (*daśabhūmi-pariṇāmanā*), all practices have become fully matured; by destroying the two obstacles (*dvividhāvaraṇa*), one thus attains realization and entry into the principle of the equality of the *dharmadhātu*.
Third, at the initial mind of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), one is endowed with the ten qualities of the preceding stage of dedication.
Regarding the stages: upon entering the Dharma-realm at the initial mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*), the three virtues are perfectly integrated and the three bodies are sovereign.
This is called "entering the Dharma-realm through the three stages. This constitutes the second [aspect], entering the Dharma-realm through the final mind.
Wisdom upon wisdom multiplies, reaching the point where arising and ceasing are simultaneous and unified; this clarifies the single, harmonious dedication, whereby one enters the Dharma-realm.
Meaning (*artha*). When wisdom (*prajñā*) and wisdom mutually ride upon one another, this is knowledge (*jñāna*). When vehicle (*yāna*) and vehicle are quiescent, this is principle (*tattva*).
Because of the wisdom that enters the *dharmadhātu*, the wisdom-vehicle of the six recollections is transformed into the wisdom-vehicle of entering the *dharmadhātu*;

the principle-vehicle of the six recollections is transformed into the principle-vehicle of entering the *dharmadhātu*. That which is said to be as vast as the *dharmatā* and ultimately like empty space, exhausting the future...
Because there is no interruption in the future limit, [the flames] blaze on and on, impermanent; the lights shine on and on, non-existent.
These two phrases represent the image of wisdom destroying delusion. "Blazing on and on" and "shining on and on" refer to the wisdom that is capable of extinguishing;
"impermanent" and "non-existent" refer to the ignorance that is to be extinguished. The wisdom of the Bodhisattva is like the flame of a fire; sentient beings...

Afflictions are like firewood being burned. With the flame of wisdom, one burns the firewood of afflictions until they are completely exhausted without remainder, just as the flame of a fire can burn the grasses and trees of the great earth until they are completely exhausted without remainder. Furthermore, by means of the bodhisattva’s wisdom—
Just as the light of fire dispels the darkness of a room, so does the light of wisdom illuminate the darkness of ignorance within sentient beings, leaving no hidden corner unilluminated.
By means of the Middle Way contemplation and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), the Bodhisattva shatters the delusions of ignorance.

There is no obstruction that is not removed, and no principle that is not revealed. Regarding the phrase "birth after birth does not arise," since every flame is impermanent and every radiance is non-existent, this constitutes birth without birth and arising without arising.

Thus, being without birth and without arising is precisely the path of the transformative emptiness (*pariṇāmanā-śūnyatā-mārga*). What is called the "path of transformative emptiness" carries the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

"Transforming" means turning back; "changing" means shifting direction. It transforms ignorance into true suchness (*tathatā*), transforms afflictions into awakening (*bodhi*), and transforms birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) into nirvāṇa. Because its transformation and change are thus, it transforms yet does not transform.

It revolves without revolving; thus it is able to transform what precedes and revolve what follows. The phrase "transforming what precedes and revolving what follows" refers to transforming the ignorance of the characteristic of extinction (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) into the characteristic of non-extinction.

The phrase "transforming, revolving, and transforming through transformation" refers to transforming the ignorance of the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) into the characteristic of non-abiding.
The phrase "transformation, revolution, and transformation" refers to transforming the ignorance of the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) into...

Regarding the characteristic of non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*): the reason it does not mention the characteristic of transformation (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*) is that this is precisely what is refuted in its own primary context; therefore, it is not mentioned.
As for "simultaneous co-residence" and so forth, this explains that the four characteristics exist in mutual dependence, as they share the same awakening (*ekabodha*).

Thus, each momentary flash (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*) is a single characteristic; arising and ceasing occur at one and the same time. Each momentary flash is a single characteristic, such that the beginning and the fundamental nature are non-dual, being one and the same.
Because of awakening, arising and ceasing occur simultaneously; the four characteristics are equal, like reeds leaning against one another.

The five phrases beginning with "already transformed" collectively summarize the equality of the four characteristics—birth, abiding, change, and cessation—and the non-duality of the three types of awakening.
"Already transformed" refers to past arising and ceasing; "not yet transformed" refers to the future... [text truncated]

"Coming and going" refers to arising and ceasing. "Transformation upon transformation" refers to the arising and ceasing that occurs right before one's eyes. "Transformation also attains the One" concludes the preceding point by analogy:
although it is said that the three periods of time shift and succeed one another, when illuminated by the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, there is in reality no movement, arrival, coming, or going;
the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) are equal. Therefore, it is said: "Transformation also attains the One," meaning that as soon as there is birth, there is immediately cessation.

It is not for the sake of the foolish that this is taught. "Reception is also like this" means that, following what was stated above regarding the phenomena of arising and ceasing transformed throughout the three periods of time, one also attains the One.
This is because the mind capable of awakening to arising and ceasing also attains the One;
therefore it is said, "Reception is also like this. Such a mindful mind is the turning back of the son of the Buddha’s signless mindful mind.
Dedication. ○ Third, the Stage of Profound Mind (also called the Stage of the Mind of Dedication).

O Disciples of the Buddha, as for the "profound mind," it is the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Through the wisdom of the emptiness of real dharmas, it illuminates the existence of the ultimate truth (*satya*) and karma.

The continuity of the Way is the Middle Way within causes and conditions; this is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The provisional designations of all phenomena—such as self, person, and master—are called worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Within these two truths, one penetrates deeply into emptiness, wherein there is no coming or going. Like a magical illusion, one experiences the fruits of karma yet remains without a recipient;
thus, through deep and profound penetration, the mind attains liberation.
This explains the meaning of dedication with the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*).

A separate sutra names it "Dedication Equal to All Buddhas," because one is able to practice it at all times throughout the Buddha-dharma of the three periods. If, O Son of the Buddha, the term "profound mind" consists of two phrases that establish the definition;
from the first principle of emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) down to the section on "deeply penetrating emptiness," this correctly clarifies the dedication with the profound mind.
Regarding the term "profound mind" (*gambhīra-citta*): it is not spoken in contrast to the shallow; rather, it is the most profound of the profound, and is thus called the "profound mind.
As for "emptiness of the primary meaning" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), this is the one true *dharmadhātu*, the principle of great emptiness.

Regarding "the wisdom that knows the emptiness of real dharmas," this is the wisdom of the one true *dharmadhātu*, the wisdom of great emptiness. By means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, one enters the principle of the *dharmadhātu*.
Wisdom and principle are perfectly integrated; the Dharma-realm is unimpeded. By means of this wisdom and principle of the Dharma-realm, one gives rise to illuminating insight.

This illumination perceives the "existent" and the "real": "existent" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and "real" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). However, this ultimate truth does not exist apart from the conventional truth;
rather, it is precisely within the continuity of karmic paths, ignorance, old age, death, and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Within the dharma of the harmony of causes and conditions, the path that is fundamentally non-transmigrating and immutable is called the True Truth (satya).
The karmic path is the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*, which is termed the "karmic aspect" (*karma-lakṣaṇa*). Continuity is the seventh *manas-vijñāna*, which is termed "continuity.
This collectively encompasses the dharmas of the three subtleties and six coarsenesses; the causes and conditions refer to these three subtleties and six [coarsenesses].
*Coarseness* (*cūla*) is a term for the conjunction of arising and ceasing. This refers to what is called: "Due to the non-awakening of ignorance, the three subtle [states] arise;
with objective conditions as their cause, the six coarsenesses develop. It is also called the *karmic paths*, which are the wholesome and unwholesome actions performed by body, speech, and mind.

This means that these various karmas serve as the causes that lead to the reception of the fruits of all karmas pertaining to birth and death. *Path* (*mārga*) refers to a road, that which enables passage.
The meaning of this is that these three paths mutually interconnect: from afflictions they lead to karma; from karma they lead to suffering;
and from suffering they again lead back to afflictions. Thus, as they circulate and interpenetrate one another, birth and death continue without end.

This is the continuity of the paths of karma, the dharma of the conjunction of causes and conditions. Through the conjunction of these causes and conditions, all phenomena are designated by provisional names.
This leads ordinary people and non-Buddhists to falsely conceptualize a self and a person, grasping at them as a master;

this is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Conventional truth refers to that which is subject to flux and is unreal. Regarding these two truths of existence, the Bodhisattva [penetrates] deeply...

Entering emptiness. Regarding the second, the "truth of existence" (*satya-satya*): this refers to the aforementioned two truths, the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). As for why the ultimate truth is also called the "truth of existence":

it is because the term "ultimate" is established in contrast to the conventional; by positing the ultimate, one negates the conventional. Since both belong to the realm of relative opposition, they are not the truly ultimate.
Therefore, it is also called "the truth of existence" (*satya*). This means that while false speech reveals the various truths, both the false and the true are equally false.
Furthermore, regarding the two types of existence: "existence" refers to original existence, which is true, eternal, and unchanging;

therefore, it is also called existence. As it is said: "This Dharma abides in its own position; the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. It is also said: "The dharmas produced by causes and conditions—I say they are..."

This is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is also termed "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*), and it is also termed the meaning of the "Middle Way. To say "deeply entering emptiness" clarifies the meaning of dedicating with a profound mind.
Building upon the preceding, the Bodhisattva, by means of the wisdom of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*), illuminates the true and realizes the true;
illuminates the conventional and realizes the conventional. Regarding these two truths, they realize there are no two separate dharmas, which are unified as a single principle. Deeply...
Dedication. This is the principle of the one true dharma-realm and the great emptiness of equality; thus it is said: "Entering deeply into emptiness. That which is meant is:
"The real does not stand, the delusory is fundamentally empty; both existence and non-existence are discarded—this is the 'not-empty' emptiness.
As for the phrase "without coming or going," this summarizes the meaning of dedication through the profound mind. Since there are these two [aspects] herein...
The Truths. One enters deeply into emptiness; yet within the principle of emptiness, there is inherently no arising or ceasing, no coming or going.

Although one undergoes illusory transformations and receives retributions, because there is no receiving of the retribution of illusory transformations, this is called the profound liberation of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding the profound liberation of the mind: the Śrāvakas cultivate the Dharma of the four truths of arising and ceasing, and realize the emptiness of the person.

The principle [of the Śrāvaka] is called "shallow liberation. The Pratyekabuddha cultivates the dharma of the four truths of non-arising and realizes the principle of the emptiness of dharmas; this is called "deep liberation.
The Bodhisattva, by means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, perceives that emptiness and the provisional are non-dual and that the ultimate and the conventional are mutually integrated;
because this is profound within the profound, it is said to be the "liberation of the deeply deep mind."
○ Fourth, the Stage of Penetrating Mind.
O Disciples of the Buddha! Those who have attained penetrating illumination endure and accord with the true nature of all things. In every nature, there is neither bondage nor liberation.

They attain penetration into the unimpeded Dharma, penetration into meaning, penetration into words, and penetration into the methods of teaching and transforming others. They penetrate the causes and effects of the three periods of time and the faculties and practices of all sentient beings, remaining in suchness.

Conjoined, yet not dispersed; without practical utility, without function, and without the function of names. Every function is empty. This emptiness of emptiness illuminates and penetrates emptiness;
this is called the thorough penetration of the emptiness of all phenomena. Emptiness of emptiness is suchness (*tathatā*); its marks cannot be apprehended.

This explains the meaning of the dedication that penetrates the mind (*citta-pariṇāmanā*). A separate sutra names this "the dedication that reaches all places" (*sarvatragatā-pariṇāmanā*), which means entering all Buddha-lands through the power of great vows in order to make offerings to all Buddhas.

If a disciple of the Buddha is one who attains clear illumination (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), it is defined as being established in patience and compliance with the true nature of all things; from the section on reaching and teaching others up to the point of attaining penetration, this precisely clarifies clear illumination.
The meaning of dedicating the wisdom of contemplation on the Middle Way of essence and function: "Penetration" (*da*) means thorough understanding; "illumination" (*zhào*) means clear illumination.

This refers to penetrating both phenomena and principle, and illuminating them with unimpeded clarity. Because these two meanings are combined, it is called "penetrative illumination. This is the wisdom that realizes.
"Enduring and conforming to all true natures" refers to the principle that is realized. "Endurance" (*ren*) means patient acceptance.

It can be realized through patience (*kṣānti*). "Conformity" (*anuloma*) means to follow along without opposition. By means of this patience, one realizes the principle of the *dharmadhātu* and conforms to the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Consequently, one is able to thoroughly understand that the nature of all phenomena is none other than the true nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
Therefore, it is said: "Patience conforms to the true nature of all things. In each and every nature, there is neither bondage nor liberation.

The third phrase follows from the above: since one has observed that the nature of all phenomena is entirely the nature of the Dharma-realm, this very nature of the nature of all phenomena is, from the beginning, suchness (*tathatā*).
It is originally without bondage and originally without liberation. Being without bondage means there is no birth-and-death;
being without liberation means there is no nirvana. As a sutra says: "All sentient beings are, in their essence, none other than nirvana. From the beginning...
It arises from cessation and does not cease again. Because this sentient and insentient world is of one essence without distinction, being fundamentally pure, it is called "the nature of natures.
Regarding the statement that there is neither bondage nor liberation and that the unimpeded Dharma is realized, this clarifies the meaning of penetrating illumination.
The preceding section clarified that when observing all phenomena, their essential nature is without distinction; this section clarifies the observation of all phenomena [in their manifestation].

The characteristics and functions are not distinct. The two characters "unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa*) run through the following four types of unimpeded knowledge: unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), expression (*nirukti*), and teaching (*pratibhāna*).
Regarding "unimpededness regarding phenomena": this is the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
It means that by attaining this knowledge, one is able to thoroughly penetrate and analytically explain the distinctions among the names of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane.
"Attaining mastery of meaning" refers to the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

This means that upon attaining this knowledge, one is able to fully comprehend the distinct names, meanings, and subtle principles of all phenomena, proclaiming them in accordance with reality without impediment.

"Attaining mastery of expression" refers to the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*). This means that upon attaining this knowledge, one is able [to master] the names of all phenomena...

Regarding the meaning of words and principles: in accordance with the various faculties and natures of all sentient beings, and their diverse dialects and languages, he expounds the teachings for them, enabling each being to attain understanding.
Because he possesses unimpeded discernment and exposition regarding the nature of all phenomena, he teaches those who have attained realization;
this is the *pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid* (unimpeded knowledge of eloquence), by which one is able—upon attaining this wisdom—to...
He teaches in accordance with the various faculties and natures of all sentient beings and the specific dharmas they delight in hearing;

for he has attained thorough penetration and perfect integration, free from all obstructions. Regarding the phrase "equal throughout the three periods of time," this provides a detailed explanation of the aforementioned meaning.

As for the expression "causality across the three periods of time," it explains the aforementioned sense of "penetrating the Dharma. That is to say, this son of the Buddha, among all phenomena, fully comprehends the past...
The causes of good and evil in the present and future immediately evoke the fruits of suffering and happiness in the past, present, and future.
Thus, the causality of the three periods of time continues without end. Because each [factor] is thoroughly understood, the faculties and conduct of sentient beings are explained;
the term "teaching and transforming" (*śāsana*) conveys two meanings: namely, that the faculties and conduct of all sentient beings involve karmas such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
There are sentient beings bound by suffering; there are sentient beings possessing the bliss of liberation through morality, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth.

Among these sentient beings, some possess sharp faculties and others dull faculties; some possess neither dull nor sharp faculties; some possess a virtuous nature and others an evil nature; and some possess neither virtuous nor evil natures.
Due to these various distinctions among the seeds of their diverse faculties and natures, they give rise to various differences in their manifest activities (*samudācāra*).
Distinct. Because the Bodhisattva observes the faculties [of beings] and adapts the teaching, penetrating each and every one through skillful means (*upāya*).
"As it is" (*tathatā*): neither conjoined nor dispersed. These three phrases collectively explain the three types of meanings mentioned above;

that is, to thoroughly comprehend that all dharmas—the causes and effects of the three periods of time, the faculties and conduct of sentient beings, the mundane and supramundane, and arising-extinction and defilement-purity—are all *tathatā*.
Regarding suchness: fundamentally, there is no cause and effect across the three periods of time; fundamentally, there are no faculties or practices of sentient beings.
It is primordially equal, neither conjoined nor dispersed; it is without arising and without cessation. Non-conjunction is precisely non-arising; non-dispersion is precisely non-cessation.

Therefore, it is called "suchness" (tathatā), which is neither conjoined nor dispersed. Regarding the phrase "without practical utility," etc., this is a successive explanation clarifying the meaning of being neither conjoined nor dispersed.
That is to say, once one has realized that there is neither conjunction nor dispersion, then all phenomena (*dharma*) are, in their very essence, fundamentally empty.
How could there be any practical utility? Therefore, they lack practical utility. To have no utility is to have no named utility; utility and non-utility are one.
Regarding "the emptiness of all things": this refers to the fact that reality is manifested through names, and names function according to their utility.
These names and their functions are established based upon reality; since there is no substantial entity, there is no practical utility. Since there is no practical utility, there are no names.

Both names and reality, as well as their two respective functions, are all provisionally established. Each lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and each lacks self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); thus, all are empty.
Fundamentally, it is suchness (*tathatā*). How could there be its name? How could there be its function? Therefore, every function is empty.

As for "emptiness-emptiness illuminating and penetrating emptiness": this means that since all phenomena (*dharma*) which are illuminated have no substantial reality and no substantial names, then this observing wisdom (*prajñā*) which performs the illumination likewise has neither illumination nor penetration. This is called "penetrating oneness."
Regarding "the emptiness of all dharmas": because this emptiness of emptiness illuminates and penetrates emptiness, it is called "penetrating the emptiness of all dharmas.
As the Sūtra says: "If a person penetrates the dharma of non-self, the Tathāgata calls them a true Bodhisattva.
This refers to that very point. Emptiness of emptiness is suchness; its characteristics cannot be apprehended. These two phrases summarize the absence of [intrinsic nature].
They illuminate one another to reach the meaning of dedication. "Emptiness of emptiness" (kōng-kōng) is the principle of the Dharma-realm; "suchness" (rúrú) is the wisdom of the Dharma-realm.
By means of this path of such-principle and such-wisdom, one is detached from all marks of names, verbal expressions, mental objects, and conditions;
therefore it is said: "The marks of emptiness of emptiness and suchness cannot be apprehended."
V. The Stage of Upright Mind.
O Disciples of the Buddha, "upright" means upright illumination. Taking the self as the object of perception, one enters the wisdom of non-arising; thus, the self of ignorance is seen to be empty.
The sky is empty; the mind that realizes the principle of the emptiness of emptiness abides in both existence and non-existence, yet does not destroy the seeds of the Path.
Through the single contemplation of the untainted Middle Way, one teaches and transforms all sentient beings of the ten directions, turning them all toward *sarvajñā* (omniscience).
Being upright in emptiness, upright in nature, and upright in conduct, those born within the three realms of emptiness encounter fetters and bonds but do not undergo suffering.
This explains the meaning of the dedication of the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*).

In another sutra, it is called the "Dedication of the Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit" (*akṣaya-puṇya-kośa-pariṇāmanā*), because the Bodhisattva constantly bestows the eternally abiding Great Dharma upon others. O Son of the Buddha, "straightforward" (*ṛju*) is the defining designation.

"Direct Illumination" (*zhàozhào*). This section, situated within the untainted Middle Way (*anāsrava-madhyamā-pratipad*), precisely clarifies the meaning of dedicating the wisdom of contemplation—the Middle Way of the essence and function of the direct mind.
What is termed "direct illumination" refers to the sense of illuminating objects with straightforwardness and rectitude, free from partiality or crookedness.
When a Bodhisattva realizes and enters the Middle Way Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), they give rise to contemplative observation; they directly illuminate all phenomena.
The Dharma is such that the essential nature of self and others is entirely equal, devoid of any crookedness; this is the direct illumination of the upright person.
The two phrases, "grasping at conditions" and "the divine self entering the wisdom of non-arising," explain the meaning of the aforementioned direct illumination.
"Grasping at conditions as a divine self" refers to the self discriminated by the sixth consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it functions as the grasper and the subject of cognition.

The name "appropriating conditions" refers to the six consciousnesses. Those who call these the "spiritual self" (ātman) are followers of the Two Vehicles who do not understand that there are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses;
instead, they rely upon the six consciousnesses at the gates of the six sense organs and the three poisons to establish the root of defilement and purity.

For this reason, they designate these six consciousnesses as the "spiritual self. This is simply because the ālayavijñāna is difficult for people to fathom. As for the phrase "entering into non-existence":

Regarding "the arising of the wisdom of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*): this refers to the bodhisattva on the ten stages (*bhūmi*) who, by means of the wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*, observes that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of ignorance and afflictions is fundamentally empty.
When about to ascend to the first stage (*bhūmi*), they have already abandoned the dualistic attachments to a self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) based on conceptualization;

therefore, it is said they "enter the wisdom of non-arising. As for the emptiness of the divine self of ignorance, this refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*), which is the innate (*sahaja*) grasping within oneself.
This [self] arises from the perfuming of ignorance; it is subtle and difficult to know. Only after reaching the seventh stage does one finally abandon the attachments of the various non-Buddhists.
This eighth storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is called the *svabhāva-tattva* (the principle of self-nature) among the twenty-five *tattvas*.
Taking this storehouse consciousness as the *avyakta-ādi-tattva* (the unmanifest primordial principle), this consciousness is not something known by ordinary beings. Furthermore, it is...
This is not that which can be awakened to by the wisdom of the two vehicles. It means that based on a bodhisattva’s initial correct faith, they resolve their mind and engage in contemplation;

yet even if they realize the dharma-body, they obtain only a partial knowledge, and until the final stage of the bodhisattva grounds is reached, they cannot know it exhaustively—it is only the Buddha who fully comprehends it.

Therefore, the bodhisattvas of the three stages of worthiness give rise to the understanding of true contemplation and deeply contemplate the dependent origination of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Although one has not yet suddenly shattered ignorance (*avidyā*), one nevertheless realizes that the essence of dependent origination is empty; thus it is said: "Ignorance and the divine self (*ātman*) are empty;
within emptiness, even emptiness itself is absent. This explains the meaning that the essence of ignorance is fundamentally empty.

It means that within the essence of this *prajñā*—the true reality (*dharmatā*) of ultimate emptiness—even the characteristic of the emptiness of ignorance cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be the characteristic of ignorance itself? Therefore...
"Clouds are empty within emptiness; the principle of 'emptiness-of-emptiness' is equal to the mind. This explains the meaning of "the essence of illumination is not empty.
It means that the aforementioned emptiness of ignorance is the emptiness of existence (*bhāva*). The emptiness within emptiness is the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva*).
While such emptiness can still be subverted by existence and non-existence, this principle-mind of the emptiness-of-emptiness does not stagnate in existence when it is in a state of existence.
It is not destroyed by existence; it does not abide in non-existence. It does not sink into non-existence, nor is it destroyed by non-existence. Therefore it is said:
whether in existence or in non-existence, one does not destroy the seed of the Path. This "seed of the Path" is precisely the nature of the Bodhi-path, the Vajra-seed.
Because this essence of the Middle Way serves as the true seed for attaining Buddhahood, it is eternally unchanging. It is non-existent [in the sense of being devoid of self-nature].
Through a single contemplation of the untainted Middle Way, one reaches the point where one does not undergo even a single segment of the fetters and bonds;
this clarifies the function of the essence of the direct mind. It concludes by manifesting the benefit of the wisdom of the Middle Way contemplation.

As for what is called "not destroying the seeds of the Path," it means that by means of the single contemplation of the equality of the untainted Middle Way, one illuminates everything perfectly through that single contemplation; therefore, one remains within existence.

It revolves existence; yet while abiding in non-revolution, it is non-existent. Nevertheless, it is able to teach and transform all sentient beings throughout the ten directions who cling to existence or non-existence, causing them to leave behind the marks of existence and non-existence.

It leads all sentient beings together into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), the great emptiness of equality, and the *nirvāṇa* without remainder—the path of directness. For this reason, it cannot be destroyed by external things, yet it is able to destroy them.

Objects cannot turn a person, but a person can turn objects; such is the Bodhisattva. Through their upright nature and upright conduct, they perfect themselves and others, entering into *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Regarding the phrase "equal to emptiness," it explains the meaning of upright nature and upright conduct.
When Bodhisattvas manifest birth, coming and going within the triple world, they arrive in accordance with conditions and depart in accordance with conditions—all by means of [their upright nature].

Possessing a direct nature, one practices the direct path; one is neither bound by the Dharma nor seeks liberation from the Dharma. One does not loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), nor does one crave *nirvāṇa*.
Being without any hindrance, one is like empty space. This is what is meant by "not being like the three realms while perceiving the three realms. Therefore it is said:
"For those born within the three realms that are [inherently] empty, they encounter fetters but do not undergo them."
○ Sixth, the Stage of the Non-Retrogressive Mind.
If, O Disciples of the Buddha, one possesses the non-retrogressive mind, they do not enter the stage of any ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

They do not give rise to new or nurtured views, nor do they give rise to the accumulation of causes—the semblance of a self (*ātman*) or a person (*pudgala*)—which lead to the karma of the triple world. Furthermore, they practice emptiness and yet...

Abiding in liberation from regression, one practices the unified path of the primary Middle Way; therefore, one does not practice regression. Because the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is non-dual, one does not even conceive of regression.

As the wisdom of contemplation arises from emptiness in accordance with suchness (*tathatā*), one continuously rides upon the vehicle. The mind enters non-duality, constantly giving rise to a mind of emptiness.
Being the single path and the single purity, it constitutes the non-regressing single path and the single illumination.
This explains the meaning of the dedication of the non-retrogressive mind. A separate sutra names it "The Dedication of Entering All Equal Roots of Goodness.
This means that one practices untainted roots of goodness because they are non-dual. O Disciples of the Buddha, as for the non-retrogressive mind:

The heading is established. From the section "Not entering the stage of any ordinary person" up to "also practicing emptiness," this precisely clarifies the meaning of dedicating the Middle Way contemplative wisdom—the essence and function of the non-retrogressive mind.
As for the "non-retrogressive mind," it refers to not retrogressing into the stage of any ordinary person.
"All ordinary persons" is a collective term for all sentient beings within the three realms. The Bodhisattva, by means of illumination...

Having shattered the afflictions of the three realms, such as the delusions of views and thoughts, one stands on the verge of the stage of the Sages; therefore, one does not enter [the realm of ordinary beings].
Since one has already not entered any stage of an ordinary person, one does not give rise to the various views nurtured by external paths.
Not only does one not give rise to what is nurtured, one also does not give rise to the accumulation of causes—meaning that the causes are exhausted and the fruits are lost.

Although he manifests birth within the three realms, he is in reality not bound by karma; though it appears as if there were a self or a person, the karma of the three realms likewise proceeds in emptiness.
This above has generally clarified non-retrogression; below, non-retrogression is specifically clarified, and its meaning comprises three points.
First, non-retrogression in position; second, non-retrogression in practice; third, non-retrogression in mindfulness.
Regarding "not abiding in retrogression from liberation," this specifically clarifies the meaning of non-abiding in the stage of retrogression.

It means that this Bodhisattva’s precious position is not like the positions of the Śrāvakas, who abide in and cling to liberation and *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called "not abiding in liberation. Question: What is meant by "non-retrogression"?
Answer: This bodhisattva practices in unison within the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); therefore, they attain non-retrogression from their stage.
Regarding "non-retrogression in practice," this specifically clarifies the meaning of non-retrogression in conduct; that is to say, the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Unlike the practices for the cessation of the four truths, which involve both abiding and regression, this [practice] penetrates fundamental bodhi, the true suchness (*tathatā*), and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because wisdom and principle are of one suchness in a non-dual practice, one attains non-regression in practice.

As for "not thinking of regression," this specifically clarifies the meaning of "non-regression in thought" (*nien-bu-tui*): it means that the thought of this bodhisattva is not like [ordinary thought].
One contemplates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; there is mindfulness and non-mindfulness, and the discrimination of grasping and abandoning.

This gives rise to the wisdom of contemplation through emptiness, which clearly illuminates all phenomena as being the mark of suchness. Therefore, one is mindful while being without mindfulness, and without mindfulness while being mindful.

By means of the realm of non-thought, this is called "non-retrogression in mindfulness. The two phrases, "continuously mounting the vehicle" and "the mind entering non-duality," follow from what precedes;
they mean that not only does one practice non-retrogression in mindfulness, but one also does not abide [in it], because one is able to continuously mount the vehicle and the mind enters non-duality.
As for the phrase "continuously mounting the vehicle," it refers to the practice of non-retrogression in mindfulness.

It recedes without any interruption; therefore, it is called the "successively mounting vehicle" (*anupūrva-yāna*). Regarding the statement that "the mind enters into non-duality," this means that the object and wisdom are suchness (*tathatā*).
As for the phrase "the mind constantly arises as empty," this explains the meaning of the emptiness of self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) within the previously mentioned successively mounting vehicle.
Regarding the phrase "one path and one purity," etc., this explains the meaning of the mind entering non-duality through the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).

"One path" refers to the Middle Way contemplation (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*); "one purity" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Thus, by being empty yet not empty, one is able to achieve the non-retrogressive single path and single illumination.
"One path" is the Middle Way contemplation; "one illumination" is the contemplation of the conventional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*). Consequently, one does not abide in either of the two extremes.
The Middle Way is not established as a fixed position; one proceeds directly toward the ocean of the fruit of Great Nirvana, which is non-dual and without remainder.

This is what is meant by "one should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. To abide, maintain, practice, and contemplate in this manner is called the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s dedication of the non-regressive mind.
○ Seventh, the stage of the Mahāyāna mind.
O Disciples of the Buddha, those who possess exclusively the Mahāyāna mind understand that all things are one emptiness; therefore, all practices of the mind are called the One Vehicle.

One mounts the vehicle of empty wisdom (*śūnyatā-jñāna*). This is the vehicle of wisdom and the vehicle of practice; it is the vehicle of the mind that takes wisdom as its object. It functions through both the capacity to carry and the capacity to employ. Regarding the capacity to carry:
it carries all sentient beings across the river of the three realms, the river of fetters, and the river of birth and cessation. As for the practitioner:

while seated upon this vehicle, they employ its function by mounting the vehicle of wisdom in order to enter the ocean of the Buddhas. Therefore, all sentient beings who have not yet attained the employment of the capacity of empty wisdom are not so named [as practitioners].
It is for the sake of the Mahāyāna; it is simply called a "vehicle" because one thereby crosses the ocean of suffering.
This explanation specifically clarifies the meaning of dedicating with the Mahāyāna mind.

In another sutra, it is named the "Dedication that is Equal and Accordant with All Sentient Beings," which means observing all good and evil as being without dual characteristics. If a disciple of the Buddha... [the second part].

The phrases establish the definition. Because each and every [phenomenon] is understood as being one in emptiness, from the section on the "Vehicle of Ultimate Wisdom" and the "Vehicle of Practice," there is a clear exposition of the meaning of dedicating the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way—the essence and function of the unique Mahāyāna mind. As for what is called the "unique Mahāyāna mind":

This means that it is uniquely great and has nothing external to it. "Great" (Mahā) is a name established based on its essential nature, while "Vehicle" (Yāna) is a designation used according to its function.

Its function is to transport and carry; its meaning is vastness and breadth. It distinguishes itself from the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as from the vehicles of the stages of abiding and practice;
rather, it is the Middle Way Mahāyāna at the ultimate stage of dedication. Regarding the phrase "each and every [phenomenon] is one emptiness," this is precisely...
To explain the meaning of the "exclusive Mahāyāna mind": the upper interpretation refers to the wisdom that is capable of understanding the vastness of the *dharmadhātu*;

the lower interpretation refers to the vast principle of the *dharmadhātu* that is understood. Because wisdom accords with principle, both are equal, and there is no longer any distinction between subject and object;
therefore, it is said that "the understanding and the object of understanding are one and empty. All practices and minds are thus called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
This means that by means of this very wisdom of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-jñāna*), one gives rise to the mind of dharma-realm practice.
Therefore, all practices are the practice of the dharma-realm, and all minds are the mind of the dharma-realm. Hence it is said:

"All practices and minds are called the One Vehicle. Regarding the phrase "riding upon the single wisdom of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), this explains the meaning of the simultaneous operation of wisdom and practice.
This means that by means of the wisdom of emptiness of the One Vehicle, one manifests the principle of emptiness of the One Vehicle.

Because of the principle of emptiness of the One Vehicle, one gives rise to the practice of emptiness of the One Vehicle. By means of the practice of emptiness of the One Vehicle, one brings forth the principle of emptiness of the One Vehicle.
Were it not for the wisdom of emptiness of the One Vehicle, one could certainly not shatter the firm [delusions] of sentient beings.
The delusions of sentient beings cannot be dispelled unless one practices the emptiness of the One Vehicle; likewise, the true virtue of sentient beings cannot be perfected otherwise.
Therefore, when wisdom arises, delusions perish; when practice flourishes, the Way is accomplished. By means of this dual vehicle of wisdom and practice, [the goal is attained].
Extensively transforming sentient beings, they reach the city of nirvāṇa without encountering any difficulties. This is like a bird with two wings, soaring ten thousand *li* in a single flight;

it is also like the eyes and feet assisting one another to reach the central hall directly. Therefore, it is said: "Riding upon the single wisdom of emptiness. This refers to the vehicle of wisdom and the vehicle of practice.
By riding upon the mind of wisdom, one proceeds until entering the ocean of the Buddhas; thus, this section clarifies its unique greatness.
The meaning of "vehicle" (*yāna*). "Vehicle" refers to the wisdom-mind that carries and employs. These two phrases follow from what precedes:
because one rides upon the wisdom of the emptiness of the Great Vehicle, one is able to endure and apply the mind to the Great Vehicle, carrying and employing it as one wills.
As for "carrying and employing," it means to carry all sentient beings across the river of the three realms, as well as their fetters and bonds.

The "river" refers to the river of arising and ceasing. When it says "all sentient beings," this generally includes both ordinary people and sages, as well as those of provisional and limited capacities.
Regarding the phrase "crossing the river of the three realms": "crossing" means to deliver and liberate; "three realms" refers to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm;
and "river" carries the meaning of drifting and drowning. This is because all ordinary worldlings drown in the river of craving and are unable to achieve liberation.
Now, by causing them to board this Great Vehicle, they are enabled to emerge from the triple world and avoid being submerged; this is because of the river of fetters and bonds.
This refers to crossing over the non-Buddhists who are bound by the grasping of views and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Since these non-Buddhists possess various fetters of false views, they are unable to escape the ocean of suffering of birth and death. Now, by causing them to board this Great Vehicle, they attain liberation.
Because it is liberated. Regarding the "river of arising and ceasing," this refers to crossing over the dual-vehicle (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) understanding of arising and ceasing.

Since practitioners of the two vehicles have not yet eliminated their understanding of arising and ceasing, they are enabled to ride upon this Mahāyāna to transcend the death and rebirth of *pariṇāma-nirvāṇa* (transformation).
The above clarifies the meaning of "bearing a load"; below, it clarifies the meaning of "employing. As for "employing," it means that this practitioner, while seated...
Riding upon the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), one acts at will, moving freely and without obstruction.

Because it can thus carry and employ [all beings], it is solely by means of the vehicle of the wisdom of emptiness that one enters the ocean of the Buddhas. This "ocean of the Buddhas" refers to the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The phrase "all sentient beings are equal" concludes and clarifies the meaning of the mind of the Mahāyāna alone, thereby distinguishing it from the Hīnayāna.

One must not arrive at this [stage]. Why? Because as long as all sentient beings have not yet attained the vehicle of the single emptiness-wisdom (*ekāśūnyatājñānayāna*) capable of carrying and employing them, it cannot be called the Mahāyāna;
it is merely called a "vehicle" that enables one to cross the ocean of suffering and dwell securely in the *nirmita-pura* (the conjured city), being well-off for oneself alone.
Therefore, the Bodhisattva does not share the same status as those of provisional capacity; hence, it is called "unique."
This is the Mahāyāna mind.
○ Eighth, the Stage of the Signless Mind:
O Disciples of the Buddha, as for the signless mind, it is liberation from false conceptualization; it illuminates the Prajñāpāramitā as non-dual and one.
Severing all karmic bonds, one practices within the non-arising emptiness of the dharmas of the three periods of time, which are identical to suchness and the single truth.

Knowing for oneself that one shall attain Buddhahood, one recognizes that all Buddhas are one's teachers and all worthy sages are one's fellow students, for they are all equally identical to non-arising emptiness;
this is called the signless mind.
This explains the meaning of the dedication of the signless mind (*animitta-citta-pariṇāmanā*).

A separate sutra names it the "Dedication of the Aspect of True Suchness" (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa-pariṇāmanā*), meaning that the mind attains mastery and becomes equal to the Buddhas of the three periods of time by constantly illuminating both existence and non-existence. The two phrases beginning with "If a son of the Buddha...
serve to establish the framework; from "liberation from false conceptualization" up to "True Suchness, the single truth," this section precisely clarifies the signless mind.
The meaning of dedicating the wisdom of contemplation on the Middle Way of essence and function:

as for the "mind without marks," it refers to being free from deluded thoughts and the discriminating mind of liberation. Deluded thoughts are the phenomena of birth and death; liberation is the phenomenon of nirvana.

Birth and death are this shore; nirvāṇa is the other shore. Because ordinary beings dwell perpetually on this shore of birth and death due to their deluded imaginings, while those of the two vehicles, having already attained liberation, abide attached to the other shore of nirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva uses the great wisdom of prajñā to illuminate both birth and death and nirvāṇa, [abiding] within this signless...
If, within the *pāramitās*, there are truly no two dharmas, it is said that the illumination of the *prajñāpāramitā* is non-dual.

Once one realizes that deluded thoughts are liberation because there are no two dharmas, then all phenomena of karmic fetters and the laws of cause and effect across the three periods of time are all identical to the single truth of *tathatā* (suchness), which is the principle of non-duality. Thus, one practices within the emptiness of non-arising.
The section beginning with "Because they all equally share non-arising and emptiness" clarifies the meaning of dedicating the practice of signless mental contemplation.

This means that since one has already realized that deluded thoughts and liberation are both the single truth of suchness, one does not dwell on this shore of birth-and-death, nor does one dwell on that shore of nirvana. Because of this non-dwelling, one is able to constantly...

They practice within the emptiness of non-arising. Because they practice within the emptiness of non-arising, they know for themselves that they will certainly attain faith and achieve Buddhahood in the future.

They also know that all Buddhas who have already perfected the Way of the Buddha are their original teachers, while all those of the three stages of worthiness and ten stages of sainthood, who have not yet perfected the Way of the Buddha, are their fellow students.
Why is this? Because they are all equally the emptiness of non-arising (*anutpāda-śūnyatā*).

As for what is called "all being equally the emptiness of non-arising," it means that all the worthy ones and sages cultivate this emptiness of non-arising, and all Buddhas realize this emptiness of non-arising;
therefore, it is said that they are all equally the emptiness of non-arising. Thus, it is summarized and designated as such.

This is the signless mind. The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "When Śākyamuni Tathāgata was on the bodhisattva path, during a time long ago in past kalpas, he made offerings of the four requisites to immeasurable and boundless Buddhas and all their disciples."
There was no one who passed by in vain. Yet, none of these Buddhas bestowed upon me the prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood. Why was this?

It was because I harbored the notion of attainment. It was not until I made my final offering to the Tathāgata Samantaprabhāsa that he finally granted me the prediction: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni."
"O Bhikṣuṇī, why is this? It is because I have nothing to attain. That which has nothing to attain is the constant practice of the emptiness of non-arising.
That which is the emptiness of non-arising is the mind of signlessness."
○ Ninth, the Stage of the Mind of Wisdom.
O Disciples of the Buddha, as for the wisdom of suchness: it is the immeasurable dharma-realm, without accumulation and without the arising of birth; yet afflictions arise in every birth.
Yet they are not bound. All dharma-gates, the path practiced by all the worthy, the dharmas contemplated by all the noble ones—all these are likewise.
All the Buddha’s skillful means for teaching and transforming, I have gathered entirely within my mind.

As for all the treatises of non-Buddhists, the functions of those fixed in false determination, illusions, the teachings of Māra, and the teachings of the Buddha—all are distinguished as entering the sphere of the two truths.
It is neither one nor two; it is devoid of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases. It is the radiance of wisdom. This radiance illuminates the nature and enters into all phenomena.
This explains the meaning of dedicating the mind of wisdom. In another sutra, it is called the "characteristic of liberation that is unbound and unattached."
Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). This means that by means of *prajñā*, one illuminates all phenomena of the three periods of time as being a single unified whole (*ekapiṇḍa-lakṣaṇa*).

The two phrases beginning with "If a disciple of the Buddha... establish the premise; the section from "the immeasurable dharma-realm" up to "all things are likewise so" correctly elucidates the meaning of dedication through the contemplative wisdom of the Middle Way—the essence and function of the mind of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-prajñā*). As for what is called "suchness-wisdom":

This refers to the wisdom of the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*). It means that when this Bodhisattva is about to personally behold the Way of True Suchness, the characteristics of True Suchness manifest before them.

Within their heart of wisdom, they clearly comprehend the ten realms of existence—the phenomena of both the environment and its inhabitants—as being mutually inclusive, perfectly interfused, sovereign, and unimpeded.
This is what is meant by "truly attaining that which is such," being unobstructed throughout the ten directions; it is for this reason that [they attain it].
This wisdom of suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*) is able to manifest bodies within the immeasurable ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) to benefit sentient beings.
Although it manifests bodies to benefit beings, it has no accumulated causes and no experienced fruits; it is without birth and death, and without afflictions (*kleśa*).

It is like an empty valley responding to an echo; in reality, there is no body or mind that undergoes birth and death. Therefore, it is said that within the immeasurable dharma-realm, there is no accumulation and no taking of birth.

As for the two phrases, "giving rise to afflictions in every life yet not being bound," their meaning is as follows: [the former refers to the non-arising of afflictions, while the latter refers to the absence of bondage despite their arising].
This means that one does not cease from the dharmas of the six realms of ordinary beings, yet is not bound by them; this refers to the four noble realms.

All dharma-gates of cultivation and realization are likewise without attachment and without bondage. As for what are called "all dharma-gates," they refer precisely to all three stages of the worthy ones (śaikṣa).

The path of enlightenment practiced, the True Suchness (tathatā) contemplated and realized by all the ten types of noble ones—meaning that all such dharma-gates of the worthy and noble—are likewise entirely without attachment or bondage; therefore it is said, "all things are also thus.
This section, extending from "the skillful means of teaching and transforming employed by all Buddhas" up to "non-existent aggregates, elements, and sense-bases," is now explained.
This clarifies the meaning of the contemplative illumination of the mind of suchness-wisdom (*tathatā-jñāna*).

Since all dharma-gates whatsoever are neither attached to nor bound by anything, the Bodhisattva is likewise able to gather within the mind of suchness-wisdom all the skillful means (*upāya*) through which all Buddhas teach, transform, and guide sentient beings;
these are integrated and unobstructed. How much more so, then, for the Buddhas themselves?

The Dharma-gate is harmoniously integrated and non-dual. It immediately enters into all the dialectical arguments of external paths, all the functional efforts of false concentrations, and all manner of illusory transformations—whether spoken by Māras or spoken by Buddhas, whether seen by Māras or seen by Buddhas.
I am able to harmonize them. The mind of suchness-wisdom is vivid and luminous; all these distinctions enter into the locus of the two truths.

The two truths are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding these two truths, one ultimately has no delusion; they are neither one nor two. Why are they not one?
It is because there is the claim that "what the Māra says is not what the Buddha says," and "what the Buddha says is not what the Māra says. As for the Māra’s sayings...

That which is the teaching of Māra is wrong view; that which is the teaching of the Buddha is right view. Therefore, they are not one. How are they not two? What Māra teaches is in reality not the teaching of Māra;
what the Buddha teaches is in reality not the teaching of the Buddha. Thus, the teachings of Māra and the Buddha are truly without two distinct dharmas.
The vision of Māra and the vision of the Buddha are truly without two distinct essences. Therefore, they are not two. Furthermore, there are no aggregates, elements, or bases.
As for this, it means that since Māra and the Buddha are neither two nor different, how could there be the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), or sense bases (āyatanas)?

Therefore, one contemplates the five aggregates as not being five aggregates; one contemplates the eighteen elements as not being eighteen elements; and one contemplates the twelve sense bases as not being twelve sense bases.
These three phrases of the light of wisdom conclude the contemplative wisdom of the essence and function of the mind of suchness (tathatā).
Regarding the meaning of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), following from the above: Question: Since all phenomena (*dharmas*) are entirely non-existent, what kind of realm is this?
Answer: It is precisely the luminosity of the wisdom of suchness (*tathatā*). This very luminosity illuminates the nature of the *dharmadhātu* and enters into all phenomena;
for within the fundamental *dharmadhātu*, there is no duality or distinction. Such wisdom and such contemplative illumination—this is [the dedication].
This is called the dedication of the mind of the Buddha-son’s suchness-wisdom.
○ The Tenth Stage: The Stage of the Indestructible Mind.

If a Buddha-son possesses an indestructible mind, they enter the wisdom of the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), draw near to the state of liberation, and attain the true gateway to the Way. This is clarity.

The bodhicitta conforms to emptiness through the patience of subduing; it cannot be destroyed by the eight māras. The various sages touch its crown with their hands, and all Buddhas exhort its arousal.
It enters the samādhi of the touching of the crown, emitting bodily light that illuminates the Buddha-fields of the ten directions.

Entering the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, it appears and disappears with mastery, shaking the great trichiliocosm. It is non-dual and indistinguishable from the mind of the stage of equality, yet it is not the path of knowing through the Middle Way.
By the power of samādhi, one beholds the Buddha within the light, who manifests throughout immeasurable lands to preach the Dharma for them.

At that time, one immediately attains the *mūrdhan-samādhi* (Crown Samādhi) and realizes the stage of the equality of space (*ākāśa-samatā-bhūmi*). One masters the dharma-gate of *dhāraṇī*, fulfilling the noble practices (*ārya-caryā*).

Mind after mind acts within emptiness; through the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness and the Middle Way, because there is illumination without marks (*animitta*), all marks are extinguished, and one attains the *vajra-samādhi*.
Gate. Entering the gate of all practices; entering the stage of the equality of space, as explained in detail in the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*.

This explains the meaning of the dedication of the indestructible mind. A separate sūtra names this the "Infinite Dedication of Entering the Dharma Realm," because one awakens to the fact that all phenomena are signless within the Middle Way.
The two phrases beginning with "If a child of the Buddha... serve to establish the definitive framework.

From "Entering the wisdom of the noble stages" down to "the Middle Way knows that the path is one," this section precisely clarifies the meaning of dedicating the contemplative wisdom of the non-deteriorating essence and function of the mind.
Regarding what is called the "non-deteriorating mind," there are six meanings.
Therefore, one attains non-destruction. One enters the wisdom of the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), draws near to the state of liberation, and attains the correct gateway to the Path.

One clarifies the bodhicitta, subdues through patience in accordance with emptiness, and remains unshakable by the eight māras. Because these six meanings are present, it is called the "indestructible mind."

The "Awakening Mind" (*bodhicitta*). This is the third among these five types. It refers to the final mind of these ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*), when one is about to ascend to the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*) and clearly realize the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Because the aggregates act as a covering and "heaps" imply accumulation, the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates prevents practitioners from attaining transcendence;

If a practitioner diligently cultivates supreme goodness, desiring to transcend the cycle of birth and death within the triple world, this celestial Māra will create obstacles for them, instigating various forms of disturbance so that the practitioner cannot achieve the causes and fruits of happiness—both mundane and supramundane.
For this reason, he is called a celestial Māra. This single category of celestial Māra constitutes the external [obstacle].
Māra. The first seven types are internal Māras. In Sanskrit, *māra* means "life-taker" (*prāṇahara*) or "slayer" (*ghātaka*);

The Main Gate: Clarifying Bodhicitta. Subduing patience in accordance with emptiness, one realizes that deluded thoughts are *tathatā* (suchness).

Understanding ignorance as being identical to Buddha-nature, the eight māras cannot destroy it. Because the māras are unable to destroy it, all the sages touch his head in blessing to comfort his mind;

Following what was stated above, since this is neither the knowledge of the Middle Way attained at the first bhūmi, by what power does it arise?
It is said that although this bodhisattva has not yet attained the knowledge of the Middle Way, they do so through the water of the samādhi-concentration of all Buddhas.
By the power of this empowerment, one is also able to see within the light of one's own body all the Buddhas of the ten directions,
manifesting throughout immeasurable lands to preach the various sublime Dharmas for the sake of sentient beings. Because of seeing these Buddhas and hearing the Dharma,

The Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) is the gateway of total retention (dhāraṇī). As for the gateway of total retention, it means to encompass all phenomena and maintain immeasurable meanings.
The *Ratnavyūha-sūtra* states: "The name 'stage' (bhūmi) signifies 'retention' (dhāraṇī), because one retains all the merits and wisdom of hundreds of thousands of millions of asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

To say that "the mind and its mental activities are empty" means that the thirty minds of the stages of abiding, advancing, and entering—the mental activities involving the conceptual discrimination of the two attachments to self and phenomena—have all become empty upon reaching this point;

"Emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) refers to the principle of the threefold emptiness—the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena—which is that which is realized.

Regarding the phrase "because it illuminates," this explains the meaning of the Middle Way of the wisdom of emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

That is to say, by means of the wisdom of the signless Middle Way, one illuminates the principle of the signless Middle Way. There is no principle that is not revealed, and no sign that is not extinguished.
Therefore, all characteristics such as the obstacles of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are extinguished without remainder; this is what is called the equality of space.
The Ground (*bhūmi*) is the principle of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of intrinsic virtue, which is perfectly accomplished and all-encompassing; its measure has no exterior.
The differentiated characteristics of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*) are utterly unobtainable. Because it illuminates through the absence of marks (*animitta*), all marks are extinguished.
Since these obstructions are thus extinguished, one immediately attains the *vajrasamādhi*, the gateway of correct reception (*samāpatti*).
All appear simultaneously; by virtue of this simultaneous manifestation, one is able to enter the ten stages (*bhūmi*) with all gateways of practice fully perfected at once.
This is called "realizing entry into the stage of the equality of space. This is a brief explanation, as set forth in the *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*.

First, the meaning of abandonment and realization is clarified.
The *Huayan shu* states: "Bodhisattvas of the ten stages abandon ten kinds of obstacles and realize ten kinds of true suchness (*tathatā*).

Although the essential nature of true suchness is in reality without differentiation, ten types are provisionally established according to their superior virtues. Even within the first stage, [this is already attained]..."
Although all [aspects] have been realized, the suchness that is to be realized is not yet perfected; therefore, it is established in successive stages so as to bring it to perfection.

Furthermore, although in the first stage one is free from the dualistic conceptual grasping of self and phenomena, one is only able to distance oneself from the coarse afflictions of the six consciousnesses.
There still remain the subtle, co-emergent (*sahaja*) dual attachments to self and phenomena within the seven consciousnesses, which have not yet been emptied.

Regarding the dual attachments of the sixth [consciousness] of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), from the time one first arouses the mind in the stage of Faith, one cultivates the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

By the seventh stage of Faith, one has already severed the conceptual attachment to a self and subsequently enters the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Having passed through the three stages of the Ordinary Beings (*tri-kṣānti*), upon reaching the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), one [attains] partial...

The grasping at phenomena as distinct entities is likewise severed. Regarding the seventh [point]: the two types of innate grasping (*sahaja-grāha*)—from the first stage (*bhūmi*) onward, one constantly dwells within the contemplation of the twofold emptiness—until the final moment of the seventh stage, when one finally relinquishes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

Upon the initial moment of the eighth stage, one attains effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*). Thus, the active manifestation of innate self-grasping (*sahaja-ātma-grāha*) is forever suppressed. Innate...
The attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) arises intermittently until the stage of the final moment of the path of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).

At the time when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, within a single kṣaṇa, the ignorance of the characteristic of birth (*jātilakṣaṇa-avidyā*) and its seeds of maturation (*vipākavāsanā*) are finally severed completely, leaving nothing behind.
Regarding what is called the "ten stages" (bhūmis), wherein ten types of obstructions are severed and ten aspects of true suchness (tathatā) are realized: how is this so?

For example, on the first stage, one severs the obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (pṛthagjana). This obstruction arises from the active manifestation of the conceptual grasping at a self (ātman) held by ordinary worldlings.

Therefore, it is called the "obstruction of the nature of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanatva*). It simultaneously eliminates two kinds of deluded attachments: first, the delusion of clinging to a self and dharmas; second, the delusion of the defilements of the evil realms.
These three factors can obstruct the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*); only by severing these delusive obstructions does one ascend to the First Ground.

At this stage, the Bodhisattva, from the stage of the Worthy (*kalyāṇa*), first realizes the principle of nature (*dharmatā*) and for the first time attains the flavor of the Dharma (*dharmarasa*). This constitutes realization.
Regarding the principle of the two emptinesses: now that the contemplation of the two emptinesses manifests before one, one is able to sever [the obstacles] forever.
Once the delusive obstacles are severed, one is able to benefit oneself and others, giving rise to great joy; thus it is named the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

That which is realized therein is called the "Universal Pervasive True Suchness" (*sarvatraga-tathatā*), because it can universally pervade both defiled and pure phenomena. The Bodhisattva’s station is entrusted to that of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin-rāja*), who extensively cultivates...
Because they transform and guide sentient beings through dharmas such as compassion, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Among the ten pāramitās, the bodhisattva Joyful (Pramuditā) regards the dāna-pāramitā as most supreme; it is not that he does not cultivate the others, but he is able to do so only according to his power and capacity.
The meaning of the remaining nine perfections should be understood by analogy with this.
II. The Correct Explanation of its Meaning:
O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas enter the ground of the essence of equal wisdom (*samatājñāna*). They are transformed by the true Dharma; the radiant blossoms of all practices are fully perfected.

Through the functional application of the vehicle of the fruits of the four heavens, they respond to transformations without fixed direction. Their spiritual powers (*ṛddhi*) transform through principle, and they possess the ten powers (*daśabala*).
The ten titles, the eighteen unique qualities, dwelling in the Buddha’s pure land, immeasurable great vows, eloquence and fearlessness,
and all treatises and practices— I have attained entry into them all.
"O Sons of the Buddha" is the designation of their names; "Bodhisattvas" reveals their virtues. "Entering the stage of equality" indicates their virtuous rank and position.
Within each stage, there are three types of mind: first, the mind of preparatory application, which, through the power of its courage and vigor, exerts itself without timidity.

Because one enters by deeply realizing *tathatā* (suchness); because one serves the Buddhas with intense practice through an uninterrupted mind in the interim, providing guidance throughout the ten directions without ceasing;
and because one attains liberation through a subsequent mind of liberation that fulfills *bodhi* via non-abiding practice and returns to the state of non-attainment.
The three phrases beginning with "If you are a son of the Buddha" indicate their names and virtues.
This stage clarifies the meaning of the mind of superior progress. *Bodhisattva* is translated in Chinese as "Awakened Being" (*jue youqing*).
This is because there is awakening to be sought and sentient beings to be delivered. Regarding "entering the ground of the essence of equal wisdom": "entering" means to realize and penetrate it.

“Equality” refers to the principle of the Dharmakāya; that is, it signifies entering into the equality of True Suchness (tathatā), because it is the principle of the Dharmakāya, which neither increases nor decreases.
This is the principle of the non-differentiation of the three—mind, Buddha, and sentient beings. “Wisdom” refers to the wisdom of the Buddha.
This refers to the very realization and entry into the wisdom that is equal to that of all Buddhas. Consequently, whatever actions are performed, that wisdom remains impartial.
Therefore, it is said that one enters the ground of the essence of equal wisdom (*samatājñāna-svabhāva-bhūmi*). In other sutras, this is called the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).

The Bodhisattva’s wisdom is identical to the Buddha’s wisdom, and their principle is equal to the Buddha’s principle. Having thoroughly perceived the Great Way and fully exhausted the realm of the Buddhas, they attain the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*).

One ascends to the first stage; therefore, it is named the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "the true Dharma, transformation, and so forth," this indicates the dharmas that are realized.

"True" (*satya*) means without falsehood. "Real" (*bhūta*) means not empty. "Dharma" refers to the teaching (*śāsana*). "Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to the act of gathering and transforming beings.
"Speech" refers to turning this realized reality—the great Dharma of equality—to transform and enlighten sentient beings, thereby leading them to attain perfect awakening.
"The full radiance of all practices" means that "practices" refer to the six perfections and the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*).
"All practices" refers to the flowers, which are the causal flowers; "light" refers to the light of wisdom.

When a Bodhisattva reaches this stage, they attain all of these because they have become fully perfected. Regarding the "fruit-vehicle of the four heavens," the "four heavens" refers to the four continents of Mount Sumeru.
This refers to a Bodhisattva on the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), who frequently becomes a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).

He upholds the True Dharma, is capable of great generosity, and provides for the destitute and the solitary. He transforms the world through the Dharma, enabling all beings to constantly cultivate virtuous conduct.
In all his actions, he never departs from mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha. He rules as the sovereign of Jambudvīpa. Seven.
