Endowed with jewels, he travels through the four continents in a single day and night; hence it is said: "The vehicle of the fruit of the four heavens is used. Regarding "transforming beings without fixed direction":
one transforms beings according to one's will, responding solely to the conditions of their capacity, without any fixed location; hence it is said: "Transforming beings without fixed direction.
Regarding "the spiritual power of transformation according to principle": transforming in accordance with the truth. What kind of person is this? What do they preach?
The Dharma is entirely non-contradictory with the true mark (*dharmatā*). By means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he subdues arrogance and causes beings to believe and accept it.
That is to say, he subdues those who should be subdued and gathers in those who should be gathered in.

Whether through compassion or through majesty, he causes all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness; therefore, it is said: "Transformation through principle and supernormal powers."

Regarding "the ten powers and so forth": this means that one not only attains the fruits and virtues of the four heavens to perform transformative teachings, but further attains the Tathāgata’s ten kinds of intellectual power (*jñānabala*), the ten holy titles, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), and so on.

One dwells eternally in the Buddha’s pure land (*buddhakṣetra*), manifesting transformations according to the various classes of beings. There are four types of pure lands, which together constitute three lands. This...
The Bodhisattva of the Grounds dwells in the second [level], the Enjoyment Land of Other-Enjoyment.
Dwelling in this Pure Land, the Bodhisattva extensively proclaims boundless great vows and, through the four types of unimpeded eloquence, teaches all Dharma-gates without fear.
There are five general types of fear, with immeasurable specific varieties. All...
All are non-existent; therefore, it is called "fearlessness. "All treatises" refers to the four vidyās and the five vidyās—indeed, all such treatises.
"All practitioners" refers to the ten stages (*bhūmis*) and so forth—the wondrous and sublime practices of all great Bodhisattvas.
The phrase "I have entered them all" serves as a summary of the preceding text. Such various Dharma-gates as these—this...
The Bodhisattva of the Grounds has no lack of thorough penetration; therefore it is said, "I have attained entry into all.
Born into the family of the Buddhas and seated upon the ground of the Buddha-nature, one shall ultimately never again undergo any obstacles or the causes and effects of ordinary beings.
With great joy and rapture, they enter immeasurable Buddha-lands from a single Buddha-land; they enter immeasurable eons from a single eon.
They transform that which is inexpressible into expressible Dharma, and by reflecting back, they perceive all dharmas; they perceive all dharmas both in their forward and reverse sequences.

Constantly entering the two truths, yet abiding within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they employ a single wisdom to know the sequence of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and manifest each of these matters to sentient beings;
while their minds always abide in the Middle Way, they employ a single wisdom to know the diverse qualities of all Buddha-lands.
Furthermore, regarding the Dharma taught by the Buddha, their body and mind remain unchanging.

With a single wisdom, they know the twelve links of dependent origination and the nature of the ten non-virtuous actions, yet they constantly abide in the good realms. With all-encompassing wisdom, they perceive the two aspects of existence and non-existence;

with a single wisdom, they know how to enter the factors of the ten dhyāna stages and the thirty-seven limbs of enlightenment, while manifesting all physical forms throughout the six paths of rebirth. With all-encompassing...
Wisdom: knowing that the various forms of the ten directions arise moment by moment, entering into the retribution of form while the mind remains unbound.

This explains the meaning of abiding in the uninterrupted mind (*anantarya-citta*). It means that, as described above, by attaining noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), one enters the noble stage (*ārya-bhūmi*), realizes the noble principle (*ārya-tattva*), and accomplishes the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*).
Therefore, one is born into the Buddha-family and sits upon the ground of the Buddha-nature (*buddha-bhūmi*). Thus it is said: "born into the Buddha..."
"Born into the family" means being born and raised within the Buddha-family. For example, Lady Māyā;
whenever a Buddha appears in the world, she serves as his mother and Rāhula as his son. Therefore, it is said that one is "born into the Buddha-family.
Regarding "sitting upon the ground of the Buddha-nature," this means that the realm of True Suchness realized by this Bodhisattva is equal to that of all Buddhas.
They are equal and without distinction. That is to say, the Dharma-body of all Buddhas enters my own nature; my nature is identical and united with that of the Tathāgata.
Just as when the World-Honored One was born, he pointed one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, gazed in the four directions, took seven steps, and said:
"Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored; in the world and beyond the world, this Dharma is supreme."
It is supreme; therefore, it is said that one "sits in the Buddha-ground. All obstacles—the causes and effects of ordinary beings—are ultimately not received.

These three phrases precisely clarify the meaning of severing hindrances. Since it is said that one has been born into the family of Buddhas and sits in the Buddha-ground, then all obstacles of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) and all tainted (*sāsrava*) causes and effects of ordinary beings are already liberated.

Therefore it is said: "Ultimately not receiving" refers to those who possess great bliss and joy. Having forever abandoned all obstacles, they immediately attain the supramundane mind, a phenomenon never before experienced; for this reason, they possess great bliss and joy.
That which is called the discrimination of the two obstacles is utterly non-existent in them. "From one buddha-field, entering immeasurable buddha-fields" clarifies their body.

Regarding the meaning of the non-obstruction and perfect interfusion of lands: since the Bodhisattva has already abandoned all hindrances and attained bliss, he is able to manifest the bodies of a hundred Buddhas and their hundred Buddha-lands, or even the bodies of hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas and their hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-lands.
Thus, they are produced in a single location yet appear simultaneously throughout the ten directions. Therefore, the body does not obstruct the land, and the land does not obstruct the body.
Because every atom interpenetrates and every land is perfectly interfused, one can enter from a single kalpa into immeasurable kalpas.
This clarifies the meaning of the perfect interfusion and non-obstruction of time and kalpas;

that is to say, since one is able to manifest bodies and lands, one can thus transform a short duration into a long duration, and a long duration back into a short duration—just as within a single sitting of the World-Honored One.
Passing through sixty minor kalpas, he again made sixty minor kalpas appear as brief as a finger-snap, even unto a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
This refers to one who turns the Great Dharma Wheel throughout the three periods of time.

To take that which is inexpressible and make it expressible—this clarifies the meaning of the perfect, unimpeded nature of preaching the Dharma. For this True Suchness (*tathatā*) is, by its very nature, the Dharma.
There is no verbal expression; fundamentally, there are no names or signs. Yet, in accordance with the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, skillful means are artfully established;
thus, within the dharma that is without names or signs, one speaks by means of names and signs, and within the dharma that is without speech, one speaks by means of language.
Therefore, "reflecting back to see all dharmas" refers to this bodhisattva who realizes the Buddha’s impartial great wisdom and, through such reflective seeing, [perceives all things].

From the stage of an ordinary person, one turns away from delusion and returns to the truth; by means of the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣaṇabodhi*), one extinguishes all defiled phenomena and gives rise to all pure phenomena.
Thus, "seeing all phenomena in both their adverse and favorable aspects" means that, through the Buddha’s wisdom of equality, one perceives the fundamentally self-originated, intrinsically pure mind.
Due to ignorance (*avidyā*) and non-awakening, it undergoes a single moment of deluded movement, thereby moving contrary to True Suchness (*tathatā*).
In principle, it follows the flow of ignorance, thereby extinguishing all pure dharmas and giving rise to all defiled dharmas.
To "constantly enter the two truths while abiding within the ultimate truth" means that although one constantly illumines the absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one does not sink into emptiness.

Illuminating the conventional without being obstructed by existence, the two truths are perfectly interfused; they are understood to be without dual characteristics, yet it is constantly within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), for they are neither identical nor separate.

From the section "By means of a single wisdom, reaching the point where mind after mind is without bondage," the meaning of the essence and function of wisdom abiding in the uninterrupted mind (*anantarya-citta*) is extensively clarified.
Having already entered into lands and eons above, one expounds the wisdom of the Dharma.
It illuminates while constantly abiding within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

By means of the wisdom that realizes the principles within the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it gives rise to six kinds of wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) to reveal the supreme goodness of both the mundane and supramundane realms.

It instructs sentient beings, causing them to enter the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) and forever leave behind the miserable destinies (*durgati*). What are these six kinds of wondrous wisdom? The first is this single wisdom.
One is able to enter the first stage (*bhūmi*) and thoroughly understand the sequence of the ten stages, the severing of hindrances, and the realization of reality.
Although the practitioner’s rank is currently only that of the first stage, the wisdom and principles of all ten stages have already been fully encompassed;

therefore, one can point out the dharma-gates of the ten stages to sentient beings while constantly abiding in the Middle Way within every moment of mind. Second, by means of this single wisdom, one realizes...
One knows that all buddha-fields have various grades, and that their defilement and purity are not uniform;
one also knows that all buddhas preach various dharma-gates of defilement and purity for the sentient beings of those defiled and pure lands—
just as the Buddha of the Sahā world preaches for the sentient beings of the Sahā world, and the Buddha of the Sukhāvatī world preaches for the sentient beings of the Sukhāvatī world.
Although he understands each one individually, his body and mind have never undergone any change.

Third, with a single wisdom, he thoroughly understands the twelve links of dependent origination—from ignorance to old age and death—including their arising and ceasing, their beginning and end; he likewise knows all sentient beings.
The three karmas, the six sense faculties, the ten non-virtues, and the manifestation of differences in spiritual lineage, yet remaining constantly established in the good realms.
Fourth, by means of all-knowledge, one clearly perceives that non-Buddhists cling to the mark of existence as eternal and cling to the mark of non-existence as nihilistic.
Although they are divided into internal and external, within the essential substance of true suchness (tathatā), there is fundamentally no distinction;
all are non-contradictory with the reality-mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and share the same dharma-nature (dharmatā), for one does not perceive the dual characteristics of existence and non-existence.

Fifth, by means of this single wisdom, one knows how to enter the contemplative practices of the ten meditative factors (dhyānāṅga) of the four dhyāna heavens, as well as the three [perfections] that assist bodhi through provisional and limited [teachings].
Through the dharma of the seventeenfold path, he manifests all physical forms, appearing in bodies according to the various classes of beings and entering the six realms of existence.

He causes those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them, and causes those who have already planted roots of goodness to increase them, so that all may enter meditative concentration and cultivate the Way.
Sixth, by means of omniscience, he thoroughly understands the ten directions and the Dharma-realm, relying upon—
Retribution, direct retribution, internal form, external form—all these are illusory transformations, characterized by their successive cessation and arising.

Entering into the experience of the retribution of form, one reveals the distinctions of dependent origination to sentient beings; yet, at the juncture of every thought-moment, there is ultimately no attachment or bondage.
The light shines upon all things; therefore, the patient acceptance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the wisdom of emptiness are constantly present before one.

Because one practices all the dharma-gates from the first bhūmi through the second up to the Buddha-realm simultaneously, this is a brief exposition of the merits of the Ground of Equality (*samatā-bhūmi*).
The ocean-treasury of conduct and vows is like a single drop of seawater, or a mere hair-tip’s worth of the whole.
This section establishes the merits of the stage, thereby clarifying the mind of liberation. Regarding "the light shines upon all":
these six kinds of wisdom-light shine universally upon all phenomena—both mundane and supramundane, whether defiled or pure—their very substance being the mark of suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, there is the patient acceptance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and the wisdom of emptiness of non-arising, which are ever-present.
It manifests before one. Because it is constantly present before one, one attains liberation.
By virtue of this liberation, one proceeds from the first stage through the second, up to the tenth stage, entering the realm of the Buddha.
Within that interval, all the dharmas of noble practice can be fully enacted at once. Regarding the phrase "briefly set forth," etc., this clarifies what has been explained above. It has not yet...

This is as much as can be said. Indeed, the merit of this ground of equality and its oceanic treasury of practices and vows are as profoundly deep as the sea, immeasurable and boundless, and difficult to describe in full.
What has been spoken here is like a single drop from the great ocean, a matter no larger than a hair-tip;
it is the most ultimate and subtle of points, and thus it is said to have been presented only in brief.
II. The Ground of Wholesome Intelligence (Sādhumatī-bhūmi) (2) I. Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization II. Correctly Explaining the Meaning of the Text I.
Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization
The Bodhisattvas on this stage eliminate one type of obstacle to improper conduct (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*).

This obstacle consists of a portion of the innate grasping at phenomena (*sahaja-dharmagrāha*) within the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which arises from the commission of transgressions in the three types of action;

therefore, it is so named. They also eliminate two types of deluded attachments: first, the delusion of subtle transgression; and second, the delusion regarding the various courses of karma. These three factors—
It can obstruct the second bhūmi; only by severing this delusive obstruction does one ascend to the second bhūmi.

The bodhisattva now attains the superior perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), becoming fully endowed with natural morality (*prakṛti-śīla*) and remaining far removed from transgressions through negligence.

Since the delusive obstruction has been severed, it is called the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*). The *tathatā* realized therein is termed the "Supreme *Tathatā*. This nature of *tathatā* is endowed with...
Regarding the virtue of the limit (*antaguṇa*): because it is the most preeminent among all dharmas, the Bodhisattva’s station is entrusted to the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Therein, he provisionally cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action and other dharmas to transform and guide sentient beings. Among the ten *pāramitās*, the *śīlapāramitā* (perfection of ethical discipline) is the most supreme.
II. Correctly Explaining the Meaning of the Text:
O Disciples of the Buddha! Bodhisattvas, at the stage of the nature of excellent wisdom, clearly and purely understand all roots of goodness.
That which is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*)—these are the root of all merit.

Entering from contemplation into the wisdom of the Great Emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*), through the knowledge of the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga-jñāna*), one perceives that among all sentient beings there is none who is not subject to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); they all possess a conscious mind. [This applies even to those in] the three evil realms, who are subjected to swords and staves.

All forms of suffering and affliction arise from conditions; this is termed the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Regarding the three characteristics of suffering: first, as for "the nature of suffering" (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), it is like the initial sensation in the body arising from weapons or staves.
From these two conditions—the physical form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the external object—sensation arises; this constitutes the condition for the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

Next, the sensation on the mental plane (*manobhūmi*) takes the objects of the bodily sensation as its own objects, and because it encounters phenomena such as weapons, staves, and bodily sores or swellings, it experiences the sensation of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
Because it is heavy, it is the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Next, the two minds of sensation and perception take the physical aggregate (*rūpa-skandha*) of the body as their object;

because they give rise to the perception of suffering within the context of decay, this is called the condition for the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Thus, through these three perceptions, three minds arise in succession; therefore, this constitutes the suffering of suffering of suffering.

The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" designate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages [of the bodhisattva], thereby clarifying the meaning of the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).

Regarding the phrase "the stage of the nature of excellent wisdom" (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*): "excellent" (*sādhu*) means capability; "wisdom" (*mati*) means clarity. This refers to the Bodhisattva who has skillfully cultivated the great wisdom of equality within the pure *dharmakāya*;
thus it is named the Stage of Excellent Wisdom. In another sutra, it is called the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*). Within the causal state...
Maintaining the precepts, practicing the pure Brahma-conduct, and having a body free from defilement is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Being pure and clearly penetrating refers to the meaning of "excellent wisdom" (*sādhumatī*) being free from defilement; this precisely clarifies the essence and function of what is realized and attained.
"Purity" is the principle of the Dharmakāya that is realized, while "clear penetration" is the Bodhi-wisdom that realizes it. All roots of goodness are the functioning of this wisdom. What is...

The phrase "namely, equal and below" refers to the emergence of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). What are these roots of goodness? They are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Loving-kindness is to bestow happiness upon sentient beings. Compassion is to be able to extract them from their suffering. Sympathetic joy is to rejoice in the well-being of oneself and others. Equanimity is the liberation of both self and others.
Wisdom is to discern the capacities of beings and preach the Dharma accordingly. Such are the foundations of all meritorious qualities.

The Five Contemplations. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the six perfections, the four means of integration, the three bodies, the four wisdoms, and the immeasurable, Ganges-sand-like merits that accord with the nature—all take the wisdom of the four immeasurable minds and the dharma-gate of the five contemplations as their foundation;
therefore, it is said they are the root of all merit. Regarding the phrase "entering the great wisdom of emptiness through contemplation," this clarifies the meaning of compassion (*maitrī*).
The meaning of these five contemplations is as follows: The "Great Wisdom of Emptiness" refers to the essence of the profound, signless, great emptiness of *prajñā* realized by the Buddha.
It perfectly illumines the *dharmadhātu*, wherein mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-dual and without distinction;
there is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither arising nor ceasing. Yet all sentient beings are deluded and lack awakening. For this reason, the Bodhisattva gives rise to compassion.
Cultivate compassion. Extract suffering and bestow happiness. From this contemplation, enter the essence of the great wisdom of emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā-prajñā*).

Within the functioning of the wisdom of the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga-jñāna*) that arises based on that essence, contemplate and perceive the twenty-five states of existence within the triple world, the four modes of birth, the six realms of rebirth, and the twelve classes of living beings—all of whom are deluded regarding the essence of the fundamental great emptiness.
They mistake the delusive, conditioned mind for reality, giving rise to the discrimination of consciousness and creating greed and hatred.

Delusion, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth—through these light and heavy, wholesome and unwholesome karmic wheels, sentient beings fall into the six realms and transmigrate through the three existences.
Since these beings have not yet emerged from the burning house of the triple world and suffer in all six realms, it is said that there is nothing but the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

When one investigates the causes and conditions of this Truth of Suffering, they all arise from the karma created by the six consciousnesses and the retribution received by the six consciousnesses; therefore, it is said:
All possess conscious minds. Among the six realms of existence, let us set aside the three fortunate paths for now;

speaking instead of the three evil paths—namely, hell, hungry ghosts, and animals—we shall take the two objects of experience, such as being struck by knives and clubs, as examples for all forms of extreme suffering and affliction.

Consciousness arises conditioned by these factors. Because consciousness is not yet empty, it is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). This suffering is immeasurable and is subsumed within the three types of suffering:

the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). Regarding the characteristics of these three sufferings, they act as mutual causes and conditions.

Due to past karma, one experiences the present five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a contaminated physical body. The five aggregates undergo constant flux, and the four marks of existence do not cease; this is termed [the Truth of Suffering].

This constitutes the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). When this is further intensified by contact with the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), it becomes associated with painful feelings (*duḥkhā-vedanā*) that are difficult to endure or bear;

this is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). At the end of one’s lifespan, when the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are about to disperse, the difficulty of parting and relinquishing is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
These three types of suffering revolve without interruption; no one except those of great wisdom can fully comprehend them.

The three characteristics of suffering. Space is not real. First, the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) is elucidated. "As" (*yathā*) is a term used for specification;
it means, for example, as when the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*) first experiences sensation. What is this "first experience"?

It arises from external objective conditions such as weapons or staves, and internally from the sentient being’s body-faculty, which is part of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*). When these two conditions—the faculty and the object—come into contact, that contact gives rise to sensation.

This awareness has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure; it consists only of recollection (*anusmṛti*) and lacks discursive deliberation (*vikalpa*). It is therefore designated merely as the condition for the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Thus, the first five consciousnesses serve as the gateways for the clarity of the sixth consciousness, while the sixth consciousness serves as the basis for the discrimination of the first five.
If the first five consciousnesses do not illuminate their objects, the sixth would have nothing upon which to depend. As for the sixth...
If one does not continue to conceptualize them, the first five [consciousnesses] are exclusively direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), and all eight consciousnesses attain liberation.

Therefore, the triad of the first five faculties, their objects, and their consciousnesses collectively constitute the conditions for the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). Next, regarding "awakening on the mental ground" (*manobhūmi-vedana*): this clarifies the meaning of the conditions for the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
It refers to the sixth consciousness awakening to the images of the five sense-objects as perceived by the first five consciousnesses, in a single moment.
That [feeling] flows into the mental ground (*manobhūmi*) and is sent into the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), where it suddenly arises as manifest activity (*samudācāra*).

It then takes as its object the preceding five [consciousnesses], perceiving the objects of the body-sensations. Because one encounters the conditions of knives and staves being applied to the body, and because one experiences the phenomena of bodily sensations such as wounds and swellings from knives and staves, one further perceives the conditions of that suffering as suffering.
Since it is suffering within suffering, it is called "suffering of suffering" (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) due to its intensity. Next—

Regarding the two minds of "feeling" (*vedanā*) and "discernment" (*saṃjñā*): this clarifies the meaning of the conditions for the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). The two minds of discernment and feeling are as follows: 1.

Discerning that the body experiences swords and staves is the mind of discerning the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*). 2. Discerning the phenomena such as the swellings and sores upon the body inflicted by swords and staves is the mind of discerning the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*).
This, moreover, takes as its object the physical form (*rūpa-skandha*) of the bodily sores at the moment it is about to perish; from within that perishing sore...

Because it gives rise to the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*), it is called the condition for the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Thus, through these three perceptions, three types of mind arise in succession;

therefore, they constitute the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). Regarding the three perceptions and the three minds: first, the perception of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) gives rise to the mind that perceives suffering;

second, the perception of the suffering of suffering gives rise to the mind that perceives the affliction of the wound of sensation (*vedanā-gaṇḍa*); third, the perception of the suffering of change immediately gives rise to the mind that suffers from change. These are the three minds.

Because the mind is entirely suffering, it constitutes the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). If there are sentient beings with spiritual faculties who clearly understand the three types of awakening and the three types of suffering, and realize that the deluded body and deluded mind are like illusions and transformations, they will not give rise to delusions or create karma.

At that very moment, they will forever sever the cycle of saṃsāra. Although all things are suffering, they immediately transform this into self-awakening, awakening others, and the perfection of the practice of awakening. This is...
They are non-dual and indistinguishable from all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. The three types of suffering mentioned above clarify the Bodhisattva’s wisdom of contemplation and compassionate mind;
the three types of suffering mentioned below clarify the meaning of the Bodhisattva manifesting in form to benefit sentient beings.
All sentient beings with minds perceive these three kinds of suffering and give rise to immeasurable causes and conditions for affliction.

Therefore, within this state, I enter the Samādhi of the Path of Transformation and manifest all forms of physical bodies. Within the six realms of existence, through ten kinds of eloquence, I expound various Dharma gates, namely:
the consciousness of suffering, the conditions of suffering, the conditions of swords and staves, the practice of the consciousness of suffering, and the festering sores upon the body.

The arising and destruction [of phenomena] occur within internal and external contact; these may be complete or incomplete. When consciousness arises from the presence of two conditions, that consciousness acts as consciousness and experiences [its object].

This contact with consciousness is termed the "operation of suffering-consciousness. Due to these two conditions, the mind takes form as its object; when the mind contacts and is afflicted by it, and one experiences the poison of distress, this constitutes "suffering-as-suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

When the mind takes consciousness as its object, the initial state of awareness based on the sense-faculties is termed "suffering-as-awakening" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); the mind thus acts upon the mind.
Feeling arises from contact and consciousness. When one has not yet experienced the poison of affliction, this is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

When pressure gives rise to sensation, it is like sparks struck from stone; it arises and ceases moment by moment within body and mind. As the body disperses and decays, undergoing transformation, consciousness enters into decaying conditions.

Conditions gather and disperse; the mind suffers and is distressed. One feels attachment toward subsequent objects, and thought after thought does not let go—this is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).
The truth of suffering of all within the three realms.
This explanation establishes the state of uninterrupted mind (*ānantarya-citta*) to reveal the meaning of benefiting sentient beings through the practice of compassionate contemplation.

"All sentient beings who possess mind" refers specifically to the four modes of birth and the six paths of existence—the twelve classes of living beings—and excludes those without sentience. As it is said:

All who possess a mind shall surely become Buddhas. Yet these sentient beings, because they cannot thoroughly comprehend that this suffering is illusory, false, and unreal, perceive these three types of suffering and instead give rise to immeasurable causes and conditions for further affliction.
They commit various evil karmas, resulting in birth after death and death after birth, revolving like a whirling firebrand without any respite.
Therefore, this Bodhisattva, amidst the immeasurable causes of suffering and affliction for all sentient beings, gives rise to loving-kindness and exercises compassion;
he employs the means of integration through shared activities and enters the Samādhi of the Path of Transformation.

Manifesting every form of physical body, within the six realms of existence, he uses ten kinds of wondrous eloquence to expound the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—and first demonstrates [this to them].

By means of the characteristics of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one intends to cause all sentient beings to first recognize this as suffering, to become weary of suffering and seek happiness, to sever the origin (*samudaya*) and cultivate the path (*mārga*), and thereby realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*). What are the characteristics of the Truth of Suffering? They are the consciousness of suffering and the conditions of suffering.
This extends even to such signs as the breaking open of sores and swellings. "Painful consciousness" refers to the first five consciousnesses;

because they serve as the gateway through which the sixth consciousness experiences suffering, they are called "painful consciousness. "Conditions of suffering" refers to the conditions of the internal five sense organs and the body, for the body is the root of all sufferings;
thus, they are called "conditions of suffering. "Conditions of swords and staves" refers to external objective conditions, for these objects have the power to pull the mind toward them.
Regarding the function of karma, it is therefore called the "condition of knives and staves. The character "complete" (*ju*) penetrates both above and below:

it penetrates above the condition of the root of suffering-consciousness (*duḥkha-vijñāna*), and it penetrates below the breaking out and rotting of sores. To say "complete with the practice of suffering-consciousness" refers to the condition of the suffering of formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*).

The "sores on the body" refer to the condition of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*). The two characters "breaking out" and "rotting" refer to the condition of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*). This collectively clarifies the three types of suffering.

Characteristics. These three characteristics of suffering must necessarily be present within internal and external contact (*sparśa*). "Internal" refers to the sense faculties and consciousness; "external" refers to the objects and consciousness.

Within the contact formed by the harmonious conjunction of these various internal and external conditions, this suffering is produced; hence it is said to be "within internal and external contact. As it is said: "Eye-consciousness arises from nine conditions;
ear-consciousness only from eight; nose, tongue, and body from seven; and the last [mind-consciousness] from five or three."

34. If equal and immediate conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*) are added, one is increased for each starting from the beginning. This is because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) rely on causes and depend upon conditions;
they do not arise if these are deficient. This is precisely the meaning [of this verse]. Therefore, this suffering is produced when the various conditions are fully assembled.
If the various conditions are not complete, then this [consciousness] does not arise. First, it is explained that consciousness arises from the presence of two conditions;

although these conditions consist of both the sense faculty (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*), among these two combined, the five consciousnesses arise first. Although these consciousnesses do arise, their nature is not constant or uniform.

Because there is interruption, one neither creates nor experiences [the result]. This suffering is created by the sixth consciousness alone; it is also the sixth consciousness that receives the retribution.
Therefore, it is said that "consciousness creates and consciousness receives. Below, this will be further clarified through successive analysis regarding what is created and what is not.
Question: For what reason do the first five [consciousnesses] not create? Answer: The first five are contact-consciousnesses; they arise because of contact. Therefore, it is said:

Contact-consciousness (*sparśa-vijñāna*). This consciousness lacks deliberative thought; it is simply termed the "operation of painful consciousness. Because it possesses only the two conditions of faculty (*indriya*) and object (*viṣaya*), it neither creates karma nor undergoes its retribution.
This corresponds to the aforementioned "painful condition. Regarding "each moment of mind taking form and so forth as its object": this refers to the mind of the six consciousnesses.
This mind takes the aforementioned aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)—phenomena such as sores and swellings—as its object, perceiving each single contact one by one.

The mind is touched and the mind is afflicted. When one has already deeply experienced this poisonous affliction, because two kinds of suffering burn together, it is called "suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Because it is more severe than the aforementioned [types of suffering], it corresponds to "suffering as suffering. Regarding "the mind taking consciousness as its object," this explains the dependent origination of the production of feeling;

that is, the six consciousnesses of the mind take the five consciousnesses of the mind as their objects. Initially, when the five sense organs perceive an object, such as a sword or staff being applied to the body, in a single thought-moment—
Because discrimination has not yet arisen, it is simply termed "suffering-consciousness. Due to the six consciousnesses, the mind fails to realize that the objects before it are illusory and false;
instead, it is tossed about by the winds of those objects, giving rise to mental grasping and attachment, thereby creating the suffering of karma.

The mind itself experiences this, which is why it is said that "the mind creates and the mind receives. As for the statement that "contact-consciousness perceives contact," this refers to the first five types of contact.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) merely perceives the objects of contact; it has never experienced the intense suffering of the poison of afflictions, nor does it create or undergo them.

This alone is termed the single category of "suffering inherent in conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Thus it is said: "Contact-consciousness perceives contact; the arising of perception through oppression.

This explains the aforementioned "the mind acts and the mind receives" by means of a combination of doctrine and metaphor. As for the term "one who creates karma," this constitutes the sixth mind. Due to...
The first five consciousnesses take as their objects present shadows—whether adverse or favorable—which, in a single kṣaṇa, flow into the mental ground (manobhūmi).
There, they press against it to produce cognition, causing the mind to experience afflictive poison. It is like fire produced from striking stone: as one strikes, the fire emerges;
thus, within body and mind, it flows incessantly, arising and ceasing in every thought-moment. Therefore, it is said that "pressing produces cognition. The above clarifies what precedes.
Five do not create [karma]; only the sixth does. Regarding the "dissolution and disintegration of the body": this refers to the time when life ends.

The four great elements separate from one another, and the physical form of the body dissolves and disintegrates, undergoing transformation and transition. Consequently, the ālayavijñāna is led by the牵引 (induction) of karma and enters into the conditions of dissolution.
That is to say: through the conjunction of causes and conditions, there is false arising; through the separation of causes and conditions, there is false [cessation].
It is called cessation. Birth follows from habitual tendencies; death follows from the flow of transformation.

At the moment of passing away, before warmth and tactile sensation have been relinquished, the mind is distressed and troubled, experiencing only the conditions for the final thought-moment, which is deeply stained and deeply attached, persisting in every thought and every moment.
One cannot abandon it; this is the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*). This corresponds to the aforementioned conditions for the suffering of change.

These three types of suffering are the root of all sufferings. Since sentient beings within the three realms have not yet attained liberation from them, they are called "the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) throughout the three realms.
This explains the dharma-gate of the truth of suffering; what follows clarifies the dharma-gates of the remaining three truths: origin, path, and cessation.

Furthermore, one contemplates ignorance (*avidyā*): it accumulates immeasurable states of mind and performs all karmic actions, continuing and linking together in an unbroken succession. This accumulation of causes and conditions is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Through right view, there is liberation; the path of the wisdom of emptiness within emptiness—each moment of mind being designated as the path of wisdom—is the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

All have retribution; all have causes. Pure and singular illumination is the wondrous wisdom of the essential nature. Quiescent extinction is the single truth. The perfection of the category of wisdom is called the root.
All natures of wisdom arise from emptiness and enter into contemplation; this is the first wholesome root.

This is the investigation of the cause of the Truth of Suffering, intended to lead one to know suffering, abandon its origin, cultivate the path, and realize cessation—thereby attaining happiness by being free from suffering.
As for the phrase "further observing," it refers to tracing back the cause, asking: "From what do these sufferings arise?"
This means that suffering exists because it arises from the illusory delusions based on ignorance (*avidyā*). As for this ignorance, it is simply a lack of clarity.
Because True Suchness (*tathatā*) does not maintain its own nature, there is a single moment of deluded movement, giving rise to the three subtle states.

Failing to comprehend the external objects before one, the six coarse states increase; therefore, it is called ignorance. Due to the existence of ignorance, immeasurable varieties [of suffering] subsequently accumulate.
The mind that clings to various false imaginings gives rise to the conditions for all manner of evil karma, which draws forth the fruits of suffering in an uninterrupted succession.
Past causes produce present effects; present causes draw forth future effects.

Thus, through the accumulation of causes and the accumulation of those causes, one gathers the causes and effects of the three realms; this is called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). To speak correctly—
"Seeing liberation" refers to the Dharma-gate of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

This means that since one has already understood all forms of suffering (*duḥkha*) as being produced through the influence of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), which is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*), one must destroy ignorance and sever the cause of origination in order to attain liberation.
To sever the cause of origination, one must cultivate the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*); thus, by means of right knowledge and right view, one recognizes oneself.

This is the fundamental source-ground of the mind. By seeing through the delusory body and delusory mind and remaining far removed from perverse thoughts, one thoroughly realizes that all things arise through conditions and are empty and illusory.
Thus, one does not give rise to delusions, does not create karma, and consequently does not experience its fruits; thereby, one attains liberation.
Therefore it is said: "Right view is liberation. Liberation is emptiness. With this wondrous wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness, one cultivates the various factors of the path, moment after moment.
The mind enters the path of wisdom; this is called cultivating the path of wisdom, and it is termed the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Regarding the phrase "exhausting the retribution of existence and so forth," this explains the Dharma-gate of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*). Building upon the preceding point, it is only by means of cultivating the Truth of the Path that one can exhaust the retribution of existence and the causes of existence.
The non-forgetting of cause and effect constitutes "existence" (*bhava*); this refers to the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*), form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless (*ārūpyadhātu*).

The realms (*dhātu*). Because the afflictions such as views and thoughts cause one to transmigrate through the three realms and prevent escape from all suffering, they are called "existence" (*bhava*).
By means of correct knowledge and correct view, one practices the Noble Path and does not give rise to greed, hatred, delusion, pride, or doubt.

One does not give rise to any false views regarding the body or the self. Therefore, within the twenty-five realms of existence across the three worlds, the afflictions of view, the afflictions of thought, the *pāṃśu* (dust-like) afflictions, and so forth—both the fruits of suffering and the causes of suffering—are entirely empty and quiescent. Because they are empty and quiescent, there is a pure, singular illumination.

This is the wondrous wisdom of the essential nature; its substance is fundamentally pure, and its nature is free from all defilements. By means of this wondrous wisdom, one illuminates and penetrates [reality].
All things—both cause and effect—are empty. To realize the principle of emptiness, which is empty and quiescent, is called the "Single Truth of Quiescence.
This concludes the passage on the Four Truths above. The following text summarizes the contemplation of compassion to clarify the meaning that wisdom is the root.
That which is said to be "endowed with the root" refers to the perfection of the category of wisdom, namely the Great Emptiness (mahāśūnyatā), which is fully endowed with compassion, mercy, and joy.
The six perfections, the four means of integration, immeasurable merits, and the gates of expedient practices all take the category of Great Emptiness Wisdom as their root.

Therefore, it is said that the fulfillment of the category of wisdom is called the "root. Regarding the two phrases, "All natures of wisdom arise from emptiness and enter into contemplation," the meaning is as follows:
since the aforementioned [four immeasurables] are themselves compassion, joy, equanimity, and renunciation, all natures of wisdom are...
Relying upon the wisdom of great emptiness, one gives rise to the contemplation of emptiness and manifests within the six realms of existence.

For the sake of sentient beings afflicted by various sufferings, one expounds the Dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths, enabling all beings to know suffering, sever its origin, cultivate the path, and realize cessation;
this is called the first root of goodness.
Second is the contemplation of equanimity (*upekṣā*). All modes of attachment are entirely equal and empty. One contemplates all phenomena with an objectless equanimity;
they are of a single characteristic within the limit of emptiness (*śūnyatā-koṭi*). I contemplate the earth and soil of all ten directions as all being the old soil used by my former bodies;
the waters of the four great oceans are my former water; and all the fires at the end of eons are the fire used by my former bodies.
Fire and all wind-wheels are the breaths formerly employed by me. I now enter into this earth-element; my Dharma-body is fulfilled, and I cast off my former body.
Ultimately, I shall no longer receive the impure, segmented body composed of the four great elements. This is the fulfillment of the Chapter on Casting Off.
This is the explanation of the dharma-gate of relinquishing through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Indeed, it is for your sake that I have taught this dharma-gate of the Four Noble Truths;
it is that which I myself relinquished in the past upon realizing delusion, thereby attaining liberation and being able to realize the state of quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
For this reason, I now exhort you to practice and realize it accordingly as well. As for what is to be relinquished: what is it? It is the relinquishing of [clinging] from beginningless time.
Since [this time], while you were still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), all manner of greedy attachments and various unwholesome dharmas arose from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Because of that past greed and attachment, the Dharma-gate of practice and liberation was taught for you;
yet, since greed and attachment and liberation are both relative and thus unequal, now that you have completely abandoned them all, then...
All dharmas are entirely equal. Because they are equal, that which can be relinquished and that which is relinquished are both empty in their dual nature as conditions;
thus it is said that relinquishment has no object. Viewed from this perspective, all dharmas—whether defiled or pure—are of one mark within the limit of emptiness.
Within the principle of equality, no mark can be apprehended. Therefore, when I contemplate all the earth and soil of the ten directions, they are all my own.

The earth upon which my former body once rested is now the great waters of the four oceans; it is my former body’s old earth. The waters of the four great seas are the old water used by my former body.
All the fires of the kalpas are the old fire used by my former body. All the wind-wheels are the old air used by my former body.
Now that I have entered this Stainless Ground (Vimalā-bhūmi), my Dharma-body is perfected, and I cast off my former [body].
It is the body. To say that the *dharmakāya* is fulfilled refers precisely to this stage of the Stainless (*vimalā-bhūmi*), which is the body of the most excellent *tathatā*-nature realized therein.
Because the three virtues are perfected and the three bodies are complete, it is called the fulfillment of the *dharmakāya*.
Regarding the phrase "abandoning my former body" and so forth: this refers to the obstacle of improper conduct (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*) that is severed within this very stage.

Because one realizes the truth by severing this obstacle, one ultimately no longer receives a body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which is subject to segmentation and is impure and defiled.
Therefore it is said: "I abandon my former body because I do not accept it. This constitutes the perfection of the Chapter on Abandonment (*prahāṇa-varga*).
This is the second contemplation on the meaning of abandoning the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*).

The third contemplation: bestowing upon all sentient beings to be transformed the happiness of humans and devas, the happiness of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the happiness of being free from the fear of the ten non-virtuous actions, the happiness of attaining the *Sukusuma-samādhi*, and even the happiness of Buddhahood. One who contemplates in this manner is fully endowed with the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

This explains the meaning of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). Regarding the phrase "the third contemplation, etc.," it refers to the fact that when Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, they invariably bestow happiness according to the capacities and circumstances of those beings. Therefore, one next contemplates the various root-natures (*indriya*) of all the beings to be converted:
for those who seek the happiness of humans and devas, one provides the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, and the Ten [Precepts].
Excellent. May they be caused to attain the fruits of rebirth in the human or celestial realms and experience supreme, wondrous bliss.
For those who seek the Bodhisattva vehicle, provide them with the six perfections, the four means of integration, and so forth, so that they may realize the bliss of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

As for those who fear the ten unwholesome actions, because they previously committed impurities through the three types of karma, they will inevitably fall into the terrors of the three miserable realms.
By reversing these ten evils and causing one to cultivate the ten wholesome deeds, one attains rebirth among humans and devas and experiences the bliss of the ten wholesome deeds;

therefore, it is said that by leaving behind the fear of the ten evils, one obtains the bliss of the *Miaohua Samādhi* (Wondrous Flower Samādhi), which means to resolve upon the Bodhisattva mind and cultivate the Bodhisattva path.

The myriad practices are the flowers of the cause; samādhi is right concentration. By mounting this wisdom-concentration, one realizes the fruit of the ten stages and thereby attains the bliss of the *Miaohua* (Wondrous Flower) Samādhi, even unto the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood and the ultimate bliss of *nirvāṇa* without remainder.

One who contemplates in this manner is said to be fully endowed with the category of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). The five preceding sections of the sūtra text alternately clarify the meaning of the practice of contemplation while abiding in an uninterrupted state of mind.
The following section summarizes these points to reveal the meaning of the liberated mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwells within this stage, free from delusion, free from greed, and free from hatred. Entering the wisdom of the single,
equal Truth— the root of all practices— they traverse all Buddha-worlds and manifest immeasurable Dharma-bodies, as described in the "Chapter on the Heavenly Flowers of All Sentient Beings."
At that time, when the bodhisattva dwells in this second stage, because they are fully endowed with the category of wisdom, there is no characteristic of delusion;

because they are fully endowed with the category of relinquishment, there is no characteristic of greed; and because they are fully endowed with the categories of loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy, there is no characteristic of hatred.
Because they are free from greed, hatred, and delusion, they realize and enter the category of the wisdom of the great emptiness of equality—the noble gnosis of the Single Truth.
Thus, the wisdom and principle of the equal Single Truth serves as the root of all myriad practices.
By means of the dual integration of this wisdom and practice, one is able to traverse all Buddha-worlds, serve all Buddhas, and manifest emanations.

The immeasurable Dharma-body embraces and gathers in all sentient beings. The meaning of this passage is explained extensively and clearly in the great treatise, such as in the "Chapter on the Celestial Flowers of All Sentient Beings."
III. The Ground of the Radiance of Essential Nature (2). First, clarifying the meaning of abandonment and realization; second, the formal explanation of the textual meaning.
Regarding the first, clarifying the meaning of abandonment and realization:

The Bodhisattvas on this stage sever one type of dullness-obscuration. This arises from a portion of innate clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) within the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that is characterized by dullness;
through hearing, reflection, and meditation, as well as through dhāraṇī and sublime wisdom, they prevent it from manifesting.
Therefore, it is so named. It simultaneously severs two kinds of deluded attachments: first, the delusion of sensual craving; second, the delusion regarding *dhāraṇī*.
These three factors can obstruct the third stage (*bhūmi*); only by severing these delusive obstructions does one ascend to the third stage.
Now, this Bodhisattva, through the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retention, brings the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) before him and is thus able to permanently sever these delusive obstructions.
Because these have been severed, it is named the Ground of Radiant Light (*prabhākarī-bhūmi*).

The *tathatā* realized therein is called the "Excellently Flowing *Tathatā*" (*viśeṣa-srotas-tathatā*), meaning that this *tathatā* causes the teachings that flow from it to be most excellent. The Bodhisattva takes up the station of the King of the Yāma Heaven.

Provisionally practicing dharmas such as the ten wholesome paths of action to transform and guide sentient beings—among the ten *pāramitās*, the *kṣānti-pāramitā* (perfection of patience) is the most supreme.
[Section Two: Correctly explaining the meaning of the text.

If, O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, by means of the ground of the luminous essence-nature and through the wisdom that understands via samādhi, know all the dharma-gates of the Buddhas of the three periods of time—the twelvefold division of the Dharma: names, phrases, syllables, repetitions, prophecies, direct prose, and verses.
Unrequested discourse; the Vinaya precepts; parables; the Buddha-realm; past events; the square and upright; the marvelous;

such talk as this constitutes the essence, nature, names, and all distinct meanings of these dharmas. This is called the flavor within the phrases that explains all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*):

their successive arising, the initial entry of consciousness into the womb, the growth of the four great elements, form, and mind—this is termed the six stages (*ṣaḍ-vihāra*). Within the faculties (*indriya*), reality arises.

To perceive, yet not yet to distinguish between suffering and pleasure, is called the consciousness of contact (*sparśa-vijñāna*). Furthermore, the consciousness that perceives suffering and pleasure is called the three feelings (*tri-vedanā*). Continuous perception constitutes endless feeling (*vedanā*).

With the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the existence of good and evil, the initial stage of consciousness is called birth (*jāti*), and the final stage of consciousness is called death (*maraṇa*).
These ten categories are the results of the causes and conditions of present suffering. Contemplating these modes of activity as the Middle Way, I have long since been detached from them;
therefore, they lack intrinsic nature.
The three phrases "If a Buddha-son" indicate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages, thereby clarifying the meaning of the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*). Radiance.

Regarding the Ground of Essential Nature (*Svabhāva-bhūmi*): it refers to this Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and the great dhāraṇī of the Dharma, which enables the radiance of boundless wisdom to arise;

hence it is called the Ground of Radiant Essential Nature. In another sutra, it is named the Ground of Emitting Light (*Prabhākari-bhūmi*), meaning that through the power of practicing the patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) of all dharma-realms during the causal stage, great wisdom is manifested upon the resultant ground.
Because its wisdom-light shines forth, it is called the Ground of Luminous Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

From the section on "attaining birth in each respective realm" up to the end of the passage, the text correctly elucidates the essential nature of the ground of luminosity, thereby manifesting the meaning of the realization attained and the contemplative observation of its essence and function.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the wisdom that understands through samādhi": *samādhi* is a specific name for the *nāga-samādhi*.

Furthermore, it means that from this supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one gives rise to the light of great wisdom, which is able to understand and comprehend the dharma-gates through which all Buddhas of the three periods and ten directions guide and transform beings.
Because a Bodhisattva at this stage penetrates each and every one of these, it is called "the wisdom of understanding" (*prativedha-jñāna*).
Regarding the "twelve categories of dharmas" (*dvādaśa-dharmapada*) and so forth, this explains the meaning of the aforementioned "all Buddha-dharma gates. (10)

"Two" refers to the number. "Dharma" (dharma) means the rule or standard. "Section" (piṇḍa) means following a category. "Name" (nāman) refers to the collection of names (nāmakāya). "Phrasing" (vyañjana) refers to the collection of phonemes (vyañjanakāya).
"Sentence" (pada) refers to the collection of phrases (padakāya). These refer to all the provisional and ultimate Dharma-gates taught by the Buddhas, which collectively constitute the Three Piṭakas.
In the twelve divisions of the teachings, within the sections on the Dharma of the Half and the Full, there must be the text to carry the meaning, and the meaning is established by means of the text;
thus, text and meaning mutually complete one another to form the scriptures. Within them—whether names, meanings, flavors, phonetics, or phrases;
whether phenomena, principles, causes, results, expedient means, reality, the manifest, or the esoteric—by means of these ten...
These two categories of scripture exhaust its meaning. What are the twelve? First is *geya* (Sanskrit), which in Chinese is called *ying-song* (corresponding verse) or *zhong-song* (repeated verse).
This is because the meaning of the prose sections is not fully exhausted; it is intended for future disciples so that the meaning may be proclaimed again.
Second is *sūtra*, which in Chinese is called *qijing* (agreement sutra); "upper" refers to agreement with...

The principle of the Buddhas accords with the capacities of sentient beings below; it consists solely of prose (*gadya*) and lacks verse (*gāthā*), such as the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Heart Sūtra*, and others.
Third is *vyākaraṇa*: in Sanskrit, *vyākaraṇa*; in Chinese, "prediction" (*shouji*).
This refers to the Tathāgata’s bestowing of predictions upon the great Bodhisattvas and Śrāvaka disciples that they will become Buddhas in future lives, including the names of their kalpas and lands.

The *vyūha* (ornamentation) and so forth are examples of this. Fourth is the *gāthā* (verse). In Sanskrit it is called *gāthā*; in the language of China it is called "recitation" (*fèngsòng*). It is also termed "isolated" (*gǔqǐ*), as it should not follow prose.
It consists of verses spoken directly, such as the "Chapter on Emptiness" in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* and others.

Fifth is the *udāna* (unasked discourse). In Sanskrit it is called *udāna*; in the language of China it is called "self-spoken" (*zìshuō*). It refers to that which the Tathāgata speaks without anyone having asked.

Using the knowledge of others' minds, he observes the capacities of sentient beings and proclaims the teaching himself. This is as described in the *Buddhapiṭaka-sūtra* regarding the five aggregates as demons (*pañca-skandha-māra*).
Furthermore, in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, it is likewise stated that [the Buddha] spoke to his disciples of his own accord, without waiting for a request.

Sixth is the Vinaya precepts. The Vinaya precepts mostly concern causes and conditions; the Sanskrit term is *nidāna*, which in the Chinese language means "causes and conditions. As it says in the sūtras:

Because there were those who asked questions therein, he spoke of these matters. Just as in the Vinaya there are matters concerning observance and violation, gain and loss, as well as the origins of the establishment of the precepts—namely, all that was spoken by the Tathāgata, including the fundamental origins, the causes and conditions of good and evil, and their karmic retributions—it is thus.
Seventh is "Parable" (Avadāna): using words based on metaphors to instruct and enlighten, employing the shallow to illustrate the profound.
The "Deep" (Gambhīra) is a metaphor established by the Tathāgata for those of dull faculties; it refers to those who, being wise, must rely on parables to achieve understanding.
The eighth is the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu*). In Sanskrit it is called *jātaka*, and in Chinese it is called "Original Birth" (*ben-sheng*).
This refers to the Tathāgata’s recounting of the events of the births taken by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas while they were still in the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). It is also...
It describes the matters of taking birth during his own stage of the causal ground (*hetubhūmi*). As it says in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that in the past I was a *tsha-pa* (wild ass), a deer, a bear, and even a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*), and so forth.
Ninth is the *itivṛttaka* (Past Deeds). In Sanskrit, it is called *itivṛttaka*; in Chinese, it is called *benshi* (Past Deeds). It refers to when the Tathāgata [described] the various bodhisattvas...
The stage of the Bodhisattva’s discipleship consists of the practices of asceticism undertaken for the sake of seeking the Dharma of the path to Bodhi. These include, for example:

gathering fruit, drawing water, collecting firewood, preparing food, covering mud with one's hair, using one's own body as a seat, lighting lamps to seek a verse, cutting off flesh and sacrificing the body, and even becoming a Golden Wheel-Turning King and giving away a thousand heads, and so forth. This is the tenth.

*Vaipulya*. In Sanskrit, it is *vaipulya*; in Chinese, it is translated as "Great, Square, and Vast" (*dà fāngguǎng*). "Great" refers to the greatness of essence (*tǐ-dà*); "Square" refers to the greatness of characteristics (*xiàng-dà*);
and "Vast" refers to the greatness of function (*yòng-dà*). This refers to the Mahāyāna *vaipulya* sūtras preached by all Tathāgatas;
their meaning is like empty space—broad, expansive, and inclusive, encompassing everything without exception. Eleventh is the *Adbhuta-dharma* (Marvelous). In Sanskrit... [text continues].
It is called *Abhūta-dharma*; in the language of China, it means "unprecedented" or also "rare.
This refers to when the Buddha was first born, he looked toward the four quarters and took seven steps. Wherever his feet trod, lotus flowers appeared.
He emitted a great radiance that illuminated the ten directions and uttered these words: "I am the one who shall deliver all beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death."
Regarding "suffering": the great earth trembles, the heavens rain down various flowers, and trees produce sounds like celestial drums and music.
Such rare occurrences as these—never before heard or seen—are all termed "rare. Twelfth is "discourse" (*upadeśa* in Sanskrit;
*lun yan* in Chinese), which refers to all questions and answers found within the various sūtras.

The discussion of the meanings of various dharmas is all termed "discourse" (*upadeśa*). For example, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa engaged in discourse with Mañjuśrī regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other such teachings.
The above has extensively clarified the names and characteristics of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Hereafter, the general meaning of these twelve divisions will be presented. Regarding the phrase "these dharmas and so forth," the commentary follows from what precedes it.
Meaning refers to the essential nature of the twelve categories of phenomena (*dharmaskandha*). They are of one single flavor and, in reality, without distinction.
Because the minds of sentient beings are immeasurable, the Dharma-gates are likewise immeasurable. That is to say:
"If I were without any mind, what use would I have for any phenomena? Because there is a mind, there are phenomena. Because there is...
Because all phenomena (dharmas) exist, the designation "all" is established. Because there is the designation "all," the meaning of "all" is established.

Because the meaning of "all" is established, all phenomena are revealed. Therefore, it is said: "This is the name for the essential nature (svabhāva) of phenomena; 'all' refers to their various distinctions.
Regarding "names, phrases, and syllables" (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*), this refers to the twelve categories of dharmas (*dvādaśa-dharmaskandha*); it distinguishes between names, phrases, and syllables.

This is distinct. It is not merely to reveal that all sentient beings, by deluding themselves regarding principle, give rise to phenomena; by deluding themselves regarding wisdom, they give rise to consciousness;
and thus experience the meaning of taking up and discarding birth, moment by moment, within all conditioned dharmas subject to arising and ceasing.

It is intended to cause sentient beings to know that the True is inherently present and to recognize that the delusory is fundamentally non-existent. Regarding the phrase "initially entering the consciousness-womb" and so forth, this explains and clarifies the process of taking up birth moment by moment.

Regarding the meaning of "birth": what is called "receiving birth part by part" refers to the initial moment of entering the consciousness into the womb, which is the beginning of receiving birth and relying upon a physical basis;
this is precisely the sense of the stage where "volitional formations condition consciousness.

This arises because the delusions of past afflictions obscure the fundamental mind, such that one does not comprehend the principle of the *tathatā* (true suchness) of the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm); this is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*). Thus, by means of ignorance...
Various deluded minds arise, and one performs wholesome and unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; therefore, these are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*).

Because these two causes—ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations—give rise to them, afflictions and karma mutually entangle one another, and through the harmony of causes and conditions, the *ālayavijñāna* is caused to enter the mother’s womb.
In a single moment, with craving as the seed, it receives the mental conception and becomes established.
Therefore, it is called "the initial entry of consciousness into the womb. Regarding the growth of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and form-and-mind (*nāmarūpa*):

this refers to the meaning of the stage where consciousness conditions name-and-form. "Name" (*nāma*) is precisely the mind (*citta*), because the mind possesses only a designation and lacks physical substance.
"Form" (*rūpa*) is physical substance; that is, internal and external form. Through the combination of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—it gradually grows and develops.

Regarding the physical form: during the first seven days it is called *kalala* (coagulated mass); the second seven days, *arbuda* (blister); the third seven days, *peśī* (flesh-mass); the fourth seven days, *ghana* (solid flesh);

and the fifth seven days, the stage of *praśākhā* (limb differentiation), wherein the various sense organs, hands, and feet are produced. Thus, the four great elements increase both matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
This is termed the "sixth abiding," which refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). It is so called because it serves as the condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). That is to say, from name...
After the stage of form, reaching six or seven days, it is called the stage of hair, body hair, nails, and teeth.

Reaching the seventh week, it is called the stage of the formation of the sense organs and physical shape; that is to say, the six sense organs unfold and possess the function of engaging with the six objects of perception.

This is the locus where the deluded mind takes its support, and is therefore called the sixth abode (*ṣaṣṭha-vihāra*). Within these sense organs, a real awareness arises, yet one has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure; this is called "contact" (*sparśa*).

"Consciousness" refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), which have the meaning of being the condition for the factor of contact (*sparśāṅga*). This occurs from the time after birth until the age of three or four years;
although the six faculties encounter the six objects and give rise to awareness, one is not yet able to distinguish between suffering and pleasure.
Therefore, it is called "actual awareness. Because awareness arises from the mutual contact of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness, it is called "contact-consciousness" (*sparśavijñāna*).

Furthermore, the consciousness that perceives suffering and pleasure is termed the "three feelings" (*trivedanā*); this refers to the sense in which feeling is conditioned by contact (*sparśapratyaya*).

That is to say, from the age of five or six until the age of twelve or thirteen, due to the objects of the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), one is able to experience [feeling] through the contact of the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*).
When encountering an object of suffering, one immediately perceives it as suffering; this is called the sensation of suffering (*duḥkhā vedanā*).

When encountering an object of pleasure, one immediately knows it as pleasure; this is called the sensation of pleasure (*sukhā vedanā*). When neither suffering nor pleasure is encountered, one perceives that which is neither painful nor pleasant;

this is called the neutral sensation (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*). Although these are said to discern the coarse objects of the six sense-fields, they are not yet capable of giving rise to lustful craving.

This mind is simply called "feeling" (*vedanā*). Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, the discernment of suffering and pleasure is named the three feelings. These five preceding factors constitute the present fruit.
As for the continuous and repeated awakening to and attachment to feeling without end—this is the meaning of the section on "feeling as the condition for craving" (*vedanā-pratyayā tṛṣṇā*).
That is to say, from the ages of fourteen or fifteen until the ages of eighteen or nineteen, one repeatedly gives rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
Regarding objects such as sensual desire, it is said that "one is continuously awakened to and attached to them, experiencing them without end.

As for "desire, the view of self, and attachment to precepts," this refers to the meaning of the stage of "clinging" (upādāna) conditioned by craving (tṛṣṇā). That is to say, from the age of twenty onwards, due to the presence of various desires which stimulate the nature of craving, one engages in various acts of grasping and rejecting;
one clings to a self and clings to a person, giving rise to deep greed and clinging, as well as placing faith in false teachers. And...

They give rise to wrong views and maintain precepts based on wrong views, hoping thereby to attain rebirth in heaven. What is encompassed therein consists of the five dull and five sharp afflictions (*kleśa*), namely the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Therefore, these are termed "desire," "self-view," and "clinging to precepts. Regarding "existence through good and evil": this refers to the meaning of taking [the aggregates] as a condition for the stage of existence (*bhava-aṅga*).

That is to say, due to the six consciousnesses, one rushes about seeking various objects, giving rise to and performing good and evil deeds, which constitute the two types of karma—projecting (*ākṣepaka*) and completing (*paripūraka*).
It accumulates the causes for the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*) and draws forth the *ālaya-vijñāna*; furthermore, it undergoes the retribution of birth within the three realms of existence.
Therefore, it is called "existence" (*bhava*) as good or evil. These three links—craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*)—are the present causes.

Regarding the statement that "consciousness at the initial stage is called birth," this refers to the meaning of the link of birth (*jāti*) conditioned by existence. That is to say, once the causes of good and evil karma have been produced in the present...
One must necessarily undergo the fruits of good and evil karma in future lives; thus, the *ālaya-vijñāna* follows these good and evil karmas to take birth within the six realms.
This consciousness is the very first to enter the womb, and therefore it is said that the "beginning of consciousness" is called birth (*jāti*). The "end of consciousness" is called death (*maraṇa*).

This refers to the meaning of the factors of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) conditioned by birth: from the moment one has taken birth in a future life, the characteristics of the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) mature.
Having returned to dissolution, the span of one lifetime is exhausted. This consciousness is the last to be relinquished; therefore, it is said that the end of consciousness is called death.
Although these two phenomena of birth and death are termed the fruits of future lives, they are spoken of in terms of present causes and actually encompass all three periods of time.
This is the meaning of the arising and ceasing, the going and coming, and the taking up and relinquishing of existence—what is called "passing away."
"Later, one first becomes the lord. This refers to those who possess the ten grades of present causes and conditions for suffering.
This phrase summarizes the preceding text; it means that ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the two causal links of the past.
Due to these past causes, the present fruit is produced. Here, we speak only of the present cause and fruit, and do not mention the two past causes.

Why is this? It is because the effect encompasses the cause. The Buddha wishes for all people present to immediately recognize the present suffering as the effect and the present [defilements] as the cause, so that they do not create further causes of tainted suffering and may forever extinguish future fruits of suffering.
Regarding the statement, "I have long since departed from these modes of activity," it means that although all sentient beings undergo arising and ceasing, and coming and going...
Come! Within the Tathāgatagarbha, one seeks for coming and going, delusion and awakening, and birth and death, yet these are truly unobtainable.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva observes with wisdom and has already entered into the principle within the Dharmadhātu, there is neither birth and death nor coming and going;
thus it is said: "I have long since been detached from them; they possess no intrinsic nature."
