Entering into the supernormal power of radiance, the dhāraṇīs, and eloquence, their every thought-moment practices emptiness. Yet, within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, they manifest kalpas and transformations;
throughout hundreds and thousands of kalpas, they cultivate supernormal powers within those lands, pay homage before the Buddhas, and receive the words of the Dharma.

Furthermore, they manifest bodies in the six realms of existence, and within a single voice, they preach immeasurable categories of Dharma, such that sentient beings each [perceive it according to their own capacity].
They each hear the teachings they desire in their hearts: the sounds of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, non-self, and the single truth.
As their lands differ, their bodies and minds are transformed accordingly.

This explains abiding in the immediate mind (*ānantarya-citta*). Regarding the statement, "I have long since been separated from the ten categories of present suffering, causes, conditions, and fruits," it means that one has now attained entry into the ground of the essence of luminosity (*prabhāsvara-svabhāva-bhūmi*), wherein one is fully endowed with the playful mastery of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*), the gates of *dhāraṇī* and *saṃdhāraṇa*, and the gate of great wisdom consisting of unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*). Although one has attained such [qualities]...

Regarding the spheres of experience, the mind and its activities are empty. Therefore, within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, they can manifest bodies, manifest eons, and manifest transformations;
they undergo successive metamorphoses, and by contracting their stay, they may remain for a hundred eons, or by extending it, they may remain for a thousand eons.
Within the buddha-field, they cultivate supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), pay homage before the Buddha, and receive his teachings.
Furthermore, they are able to manifest bodies within the six realms of existence, employing the method of "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*) to gather and transform sentient beings.

Within a single voice, they expound immeasurable categories of Dharma-gates, such that each sentient being hears according to their own individual capacity the specific Dharma they desire—be it suffering, emptiness, or non-self.
"Permanent," "selfless," and "the sound of the single truth"—this refers to the fact that when the perfect voice is uttered once, beings of different categories understand it equally.
As for "suffering" and so forth, these refer to the four foundations of mindfulness: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. "Suffering" here means the manifold sufferings.
This is the meaning of contemplating that sensation is suffering. Sentient beings are inverted; they take what is suffering to be pleasure.

Therefore, one causes sentient beings to contemplate that sensation is suffering so that they may attain the bliss of quiescence. As for "emptiness," it is the meaning of contemplating that the body is empty.
This means that both internal bodies and external forms are all formed by gathering the impure semen and blood of one's parents and assembling the four great elements. From [the moment of birth...]
From head to foot, everything is entirely impure. Sentient beings, due to their inverted views, grasp it as pure and give rise to craving and attachment;
therefore, they are led to contemplate the body as empty in order to realize the pure Dharma-body. Regarding "impermanence," this refers to the meaning of contemplating the impermanence of the mind.
Here, "mind" refers to the sixth consciousness-mind, which means that the nature of this mind is in flux, arising moment by moment.

They all perish; they are entirely impermanent. Sentient beings are deluded and mistakenly take this for their mind. Therefore, it causes sentient beings to contemplate the impermanence of the mind so that they may realize the eternally abiding true mind.
Regarding "non-self," this refers to the meaning of contemplating the non-substantiality of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
It means that regarding all phenomena—whether wholesome or unwholesome—sentient beings are deluded and falsely claim that there is a self within all these phenomena. Therefore...

It causes sentient beings to contemplate the selflessness of phenomena and to realize the non-arising of a self; therefore, it is said that "suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self" are the sounds of the Single Truth.
Although these are called four dharmas—suffering, emptiness, and so forth—they are actually produced from within the sound of the Single Truth.
This Single Truth alone is without duality or triad. It is because of sentient beings and their lands, as well as the distinction between the primary and secondary [retribution], that...
It is the same. Therefore, this Bodhisattva manifests both body and mind according to the differences in the capacities of sentient beings in order to gather and transform them;
hence it is said that "body and mind transform separately. This refers to what is called: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, universally appearing before all multitudes;
responding to conditions and meeting with needs, there is nowhere it does not reach, yet it ever remains upon this seat of Bodhi. This precisely accords with this.

O Mind, within this Ground of the Radiance of Sublime Flowers, I have briefly opened up a space the size of a single hair-tip. This is as explained in the "Dharma-Section" regarding the gate of contemplative methods,
and as taught in the "Chapter on the Thousand Samādhis."
This is a summary of the merits of this stage; they cannot be fully described, as they clarify the mind of liberation.

Regarding "these wondrous flowers and so forth," it means that all the meritorious practices and vows within the Stage of Wondrous Flower Radiance (*Sudharmaprabhā*)—such as those in the Ocean Treasury (*Sāgaragarbha*) and others—are ineffable.
Here, only one or two have been briefly opened up, resembling [the whole] by no more than the tip of a hair.

If explained in detail, it is as set forth in two passages within the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra]: in the "Chapter on Dharmas" (*Dharmavarga*), in the explanation of the gate of contemplation of dharmas (*dharmavipaśyanāmukha*), and in the "Chapter on a Thousand Samādhis" (*Sahasrasamādhivarga*).
IV. The Ground of Suchness-Flame (*Tathatā-jvālā-bhūmi*) (2) I. Clarifying the meaning of abandonment and realization (*prahāṇa-sākṣātkriyā*). II. Correctly explaining the meaning of the text.
First, the meaning of abandonment and realization is clarified.
The Bodhisattva on this stage abandons one type of subtle obstacle consisting of the active manifestation of afflictions;
this refers specifically to the arising of the subtle delusion of innate ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a portion of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, they abandon...

There are two kinds of deluded attachments: first, the delusion of attachment to meditative attainments (*samāpatti-tṛṣṇā-moha*); second, the delusion of attachment to phenomena (*dharma-tṛṣṇā-moha*).

Only by severing these obstacles of delusion does one ascend to the *Arciṣmatī* (Blazing Wisdom) stage. This means that when this Bodhisattva first enters into realized wisdom, they skillfully cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), thereby being able to give rise to the fire of the wisdom of blazing insight (*arciṣmatī-jñānāgni*) to burn away all root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*) as well as their secondary [afflictions].

The fuel of afflictions can thus be forever severed. Once the obstacles of ignorance are severed, the fire of wisdom is supreme; therefore, it is called the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).
The *tathatā* realized therein is named the "Tathatā Without Appropriation," meaning that this *tathatā* is free from the grasping of self-attachment and the like.
As for the Bodhisattva’s station, he resides as the King of Tuṣita Heaven, provisionally practicing the dharmas of the three vehicles and so forth.
In guiding and transforming sentient beings, among the ten *pāramitās*, the *vīrya-pāramitā* (perfection of diligence) is the most supreme.
2. Correctly explaining the meaning of the text:

If a Bodhisattva, within the ground of the essential nature (*svabhāva-bhūmi*), realizes that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are neither interrupted nor eternal, then...

Arising, abiding, and ceasing occur within a single world, a single time, and a single existence; yet because seeds manifest as various and distinct, the Middle Way of causes and conditions is neither one nor two, neither good nor evil, and neither ordinary nor Buddha.
Therefore, the realm of Buddhas and the realm of ordinary beings—each and every one—is designated as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As for the contemplation of the path of wisdom, there is neither one nor two. This is what is called the "Chapter on the Samādhi of the Mysterious Path. It is thus explained:

The mental activities of the Buddha: first, the causes for awakening—namely, the awakening of faith, the awakening of reflection, the awakening of tranquility, the awakening of excellence, the awakening of mindfulness, the awakening of wisdom, the awakening of investigation, the awakening of pliancy, the awakening of joy, and the awakening of equanimity.
These constitute the path of skillful means for each stage, wherein every moment of mind enters the fruit of meditative concentration.

The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" indicate the names, virtues, and stages [of the bodhisattvas] in order to clarify the meaning of the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).

Because the Bodhisattva, while on the causal stage, cultivates the boundless factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) through the power of great diligence, he, upon reaching the resultant stage, simultaneously illuminates both [aspects], and thus the name and essence of this stage is *Arciṣmatī* (The Radiant).
In other sūtras it is called *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi* (The Stage of Radiant Wisdom), meaning mastery over radiance.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "Thus, the ultimate truth and the conventional are equal," this precisely clarifies the dharma-gate of contemplating essence and function within the stage of *Arciṣmatī* (The Radiant).

It means that in this stage, the wisdom of radiance (*arciḥ-prajñā*) is preeminent and one attains mastery over radiance; thus, one is able to suddenly illuminate and realize the ultimate truth, and illuminate and realize the conventional truth.
Because one illuminates and realizes the ultimate truth, there is no cessation; because one illuminates and realizes the conventional truth, there is no permanence.

That which is called prajñā is signless (animitta). The two truths are eternally thus. Because they are neither interrupted nor permanent, they are simultaneously arising, simultaneously abiding, and simultaneously ceasing.
Because they are simultaneously arising, simultaneously abiding, and simultaneously ceasing, they constitute a single world, a single time, and a single existence.
"One world" means that the three characteristics are equal. "One time" means that the duration of the kalpas is equal. "One existence" means that all phenomena are equal.
Regarding the phrase "because of the difference in seeds and the difference in manifestations," this refers to the equality of true nature (*tathatā*), which is fundamentally without distinction.
That there are distinctions is due to the differences among the perfuming seeds; since the seeds [are different]...

If they differ, then that which is perfumed—the arising of the active manifestation—must also differ. However, the difference between seeds and manifestations exists only through the conjunction of causes and conditions;

it ceases when those causes and conditions separate. Yet the fundamental *tathatā* (suchness) of self-nature does not belong to the existence or non-existence of causes and conditions, nor does it undergo change.
This essence, which is neither transmigrated by nor altered by causes and conditions, is called the Middle Way.
By means of this Middle Way, it is neither one nor two. Why is it not one? Because True Suchness (tathatā) does not change while following conditions;
therefore, it is not one. Why is it not two? Because while following conditions, True Suchness does not change; therefore, it is not two. The *Adornment Sūtra* (*Ābharaṇa-sūtra*) says:
"The Two Truths are eternally thus, and therefore they are not one. Noble wisdom illuminates emptiness, and therefore they are not two. Since this is the True Truth...
Conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) is neither one nor two; it refers to all results, such as good and evil, or ordinary beings and sages, none of which are ultimately real.
Therefore, both the Buddha-realm and the realm of ordinary beings are each termed conventional truth. For what reason is the Buddha-realm also called conventional truth?
This means that "true" is spoken in contrast to the "conventional," "good" in contrast to the "evil," and "sage" in contrast to the "ordinary"; these are all merely matters of relative opposition.
As for the contemplation of the path of wisdom, it is neither one nor two. When a Bodhisattva contemplates it through the path of wisdom, it is neither singular nor dual.
The *Qianbi jing* (Thousand-Armed Sutra) states: "The Bodhisattva contemplates and illuminates in this manner: the Middle Way of quiescent extinction, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
The principle of this is that, from the very beginning, there is neither one nor two. The first part clarifies the meaning of the characteristics of the illuminating function of wisdom;
the latter part clarifies the meaning of the characteristics of quiescence within the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding what is called the practice of the Buddha-mind:
since it is said to be neither one nor two, how can there still be the path and dharmas of Bodhi, as well as the distinctions between the worthy and the sage? It is because...
The profound and wondrous Dharma of the Way, all its categories of meditative concentration, are none other than explanations of the Buddha’s mental activities during the stage of the causal ground.
These mental activities of the Buddha are the wisdom-practices that arise within the wondrous mind of Bodhi.

This is precisely the initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) that all Buddhas of the three periods and all Bodhisattvas first give rise to within their own causal grounds, whereby they awaken to the fundamental wondrous enlightenment; it is the very first entry into the Way.

Regarding the skillful means of the "Initial Awakening" (*ādi-bodhi*): it takes fundamental concentration (*mūla-samādhi*) as its cause. All ordinary beings are collectively deluded regarding this concentration and lack the awakening of wisdom.
Now, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have awakened to this concentration; since initial awakening possesses a fundamental basis, it is called the "fundamental cause of initial awakening.
By virtue of this first awakening, one awakens to the fact that one's own nature is fundamentally concentrated, and is truly identical with the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
They are equal and without distinction. Because one’s faith is singular, eternal, and forever without regression, it is next termed "faith-awakening. Regarding faith, the treatise states:
its nature is that of a pure mind characterized by profound acceptance, delight, and aspiration toward reality, virtue, and capability; it serves as the antidote to lack of faith (*aśraddhā*).
To delight in goodness is one’s practice; it is like the water-clearing jewel that can purify turbid water. Therefore, faith is the very root of entering the Path.
For this reason, among the ten factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyā dhammā*), the factor of enlightenment of faith (*saddhā-sambojjhaṅga*) is the first.

Nevertheless, although the object of faith is fundamentally certain, if one does not engage in reflection and cultivation, it will ultimately result in empty faith. Thus, the next is called the factor of enlightenment of reflection (*vicaya-sambojjhaṅga*). As for "reflection," it means to...

Its nature is mental formation (*cetanā*). Its function is to employ the mind with respect to wholesome categories and so forth; that is, by apprehending the characteristics of objects such as correct causes, it directs the mind to perform various wholesome deeds.
However, even if there is wholesome volition, if it is not sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [it cannot produce its full effect].

Fearing that this might belong to distracted thought, it is therefore followed by "quiescent awareness" (*śamatha-bodhi*). Quiescence is precisely meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Its nature is to focus intently upon the object of observation without distraction;
its function is to serve as the support for wisdom. Now, within this quiescent awareness, one maintains and upholds this power of concentration.
If one lacks the power of diligence (*vīrya*), there is a fear of falling into a state of non-determination (*avyākṛta*); therefore, it is followed by superior awakening (*adhimokṣa*).

Superior awakening is the mind of diligent application; its nature is valor and fortitude regarding the tasks of cultivation and abandonment within the categories of the wholesome and the unwholesome;

its function is to counteract laziness and to bring wholesome qualities to fulfillment. However, while being diligent and untiring, one must further maintain mindfulness and constant attention, so as not to forget.

Because [mindfulness] prevents loss, it is followed by the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Mindfulness has the nature of causing the mind to clearly remember objects previously experienced, and its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

However, although the mind does not forget through mindfulness, one must further apply the mind of wisdom (*prajñā*) to illuminate the object, so that it is perceived with clarity and without confusion;
therefore, it is followed by the awakening factor of wisdom (*prajñā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Wisdom has the nature of discerning the objects under investigation, and its function is to sever doubt.
It functions as an activity. However, although the wisdom-consciousness (*manovijñāna*) cognizes objects without delusion, it remains coarse; therefore, one must further engage in subtle observation.
Thus, it is followed by the mental factor of investigation (*vicāra*). "Investigation" means to illuminate and examine the object of observation, having the nature of thorough scrutiny.

Its function is to enter into reality. Because one enters into reality through the awakening of contemplation (*saṃprajanya*), body and mind become light and pliant; therefore, the awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) follows next.
"Tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*) is precisely lightness and pliancy. Regarding the object of contemplation, it removes coarseness and heaviness, harmonizing and refreshing body and mind.
Its nature is fitness (*karmanyatā*). Its function is to counteract lethargy (*styāna*) and to bring about the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).

Furthermore, it is said that being free from heaviness is called "lightness" (*praśrabdhi*), and being harmonious and supple is called "ease" (*sukha*). Because this lightness and ease are perfectly adapted, they can cause both body and mind to experience joy;

therefore, the perception of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*) follows next. "Pleasure" (*sukha*) is synonymous with delight and gladness. Its nature is such that, through the principle realized, no inversion arises. Correctly...
Its function is to accord with suchness (*tathatā*). Because one attains liberation through this unerring joy and delight, the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*) follows next.

"Equanimity" refers here to equanimity within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), specifically that which causes the mind—through the faculties such as diligence—to abide in a state of evenness, rectitude, and effortlessness;
its nature is to counteract restlessness (*auddhatya*) and its function is to dwell in tranquility. These are the ten awakening factors.

[The term] "branch" (*aṅga*) refers collectively to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). As for their synthesis: the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*) is combined with the factor of intention (*saṃkalpa*); the factor of investigation (*dharma-pravicaya*) is combined with the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*);

and the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) is combined with the factor of concentration (*samādhi*). Although these differ in their respective categories, they all assist within the dharmas that cultivate the path.

In the preliminary stage of the path (*pūrvaprayoga-mārga*), they enable the practitioner to realize and enter the fruit of meditative absorption (*samādhi-phala*) through every thought and moment of mind.

This person abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), vividly perceiving that the activities of phenomena (*dharmas*) are empty. If a thought arises, they enter a state where the mind is born from concentration;
concentration gives rise to love and compliance, and they are transformed by birth through the Path-dharma. This is called "patience in the joy of the Dharma" (*dharmaprīti-kṣānti*).

Abiding in patience, realizing patience, and attaining the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha-kṣānti*), all Buddhas—while [the practitioner] is within the *Prabhāsa-prabhāsa-puṣpa-samādhi*—manifest immeasurable Buddhas who stroke their crown with their hands and preach the Dharma with a single voice.

Though there are hundreds of thousands of arisings [of thought], he does not emerge from concentration; he abides in concentration, relishing the bliss of concentration, clinging to concentration, and craving concentration for one kalpa or a thousand kalpas while remaining in concentration.
He beholds Buddhas seated upon lotus flowers, who preach hundreds of Dharma-gates. This person makes offerings and listens to the Dharma, remaining in concentration for a kalpa.

At that time, the light of all Buddhas touches the crown of his head, awakening the factors of concentration, manifesting the signs of emergence, the signs of progress, and the direction toward which he moves.

Because of these marks, one does not sink, does not regress, does not fall, and does not abide in the *mūrdhan* samādhi. The Dharma-superiority, joy, and patience are forever exhausted without remainder.
This extensively clarifies the meaning of the fruit of entering meditative absorption. Such a person who abides within concentration—such a person shall immediately...
As for the person at this stage: because this person cultivates the factors of the path, they attain abiding in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

By virtue of abiding in concentration, they immediately give rise from within that concentration to the blazing radiance of wisdom. This radiance illuminates the phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas, revealing them to be utterly empty.
That which is called unimpeded, pure wisdom all arises based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

As for "if a thought arises, it enters from concentration and gives birth to the mind," this means that at the moment a thought arises, there is nothing that does not proceed from within the state of concentration, giving rise to a single thought—a mind that illuminates through pure wisdom.

Therefore, it is said that "it enters from concentration and gives birth to the mind. Regarding "concentration gives birth to loving compliance," it is because [loving compliance] is developed from concentration.
Because the arising of wisdom illuminates the mind, one attains the *samādhi* of mastery over the joy of awakening to the Dharma (*dharmaprīti-vaśitā-samādhi*).

Within this meditative concentration, there is the compliance of craving and delight; hence it is said that "concentration gives rise to craving and compliance. Regarding the phrase "transformative birth through the path of Dharma" (*mārgadharmopapatti*):

this refers to cultivating the path of the Dharma of Bodhi, and is thus called transformative birth through the path of Dharma. Within this path of Dharma, one finds conviction in the mind and finds delight in the body.
Therefore, it is called the "patience of the joy of the Dharma. Within this patience, the bodhisattva dwells immovably and deeply realizes the state of non-retrogression.

Because these two forms of attachment—attachment to meditative concentration and attachment to the Dharma—are difficult to eliminate, although this stage realizes quiescence (*śānti*), the bodhisattva has not yet attained the two patiences of the eighth stage and beyond:
the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena and the patience regarding quiescence. For this reason, the Buddhas possess a heart of great compassion.

Recalling the power of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), within the *Prabhāsa-praveśa-samādhi*, he manifested immeasurable Buddhas, each of whom stroked his head with their right hand to comfort and empower him.
They preached the Dharma with a single voice, exhorting and inspiring him through hundreds of thousands of skillful means.

Yet this bodhisattva does not emerge from concentration. Why? Because they dwell in concentration, savor concentration, delight in concentration, become attached to concentration, and crave concentration.
Initially dwelling [in it] is called "dwelling"; once having dwelled, there is a further nourishment, which is called "savoring concentration"; having obtained that savor, one is at ease.
Delighting in concentration is called *samādhi*. Clinging to pleasure as real is called *samādhi*. Clinging and firmly adhering to it is called *greedy samādhi*.
Thus, those with sharp faculties may abide in concentration for one kalpa; those with deep obstructions may abide in concentration for a thousand kalpas.

Taking this concentration as their practice, they emit light from within concentration. Within that light, they see the Buddha sitting upon a precious lotus flower, for the sake of all sentient beings.

Regarding the exposition of the *Cittabhūmi* (Mind-Ground) and other such works, as well as the *Śatadharma-vyākhyāna-mukha* (The Gate of Illumination of the Hundred Dharmas): those who are Bodhisattvas offer various forms of worship and listen to and receive the wondrous Dharma.

Their faith and mindfulness endure for a long time; they abide in meditative concentration for an eon, extensively cultivating merit and wisdom. Day by day these become deeper and more profound, until they attain a realization of the mind and its essential nature that is identical to that of all Buddhas.
They enter and emerge from [samādhi] without difficulty, and at that time they move the Buddhas. Furthermore, amidst the radiant flowers...
Within samādhi, he rubs [the disciple's] head with his hand and exhorts him twice; only then does he initiate the category of samādhi for benefiting sentient beings.
Regarding the Samādhi of Radiant Flowers: by means of two lights, he destroys the two obstacles; by means of flowers of merit, he extinguishes the flowers of sin.
By means of samādhi, one settles the mind; by stroking the crown of the head, one settles the body. Thereupon, body and mind become tranquil and secure.

At that time, the Bodhisattva receives the office of being stroked on the crown and attains great liberation. Immediately, they give rise to the category of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), manifesting their form to benefit sentient beings;
thus, there are the signs of emerging, advancing, and departing. "Emerging" refers to arising from concentration; "advancing" refers to entering concentration; "departing" refers to...

Manifestation and direction refer to specific locations; that is to say, entering meditative absorption in the east and arising in the west, entering absorption in the south and arising in the north, or entering right concentration within the body of a boy and arising from concentration within the body of a girl, and so forth, such as entering through the eye and emerging through the ear.
Therefore, regarding this concentration, one knows emergence without sinking, and knows advancement.
He does not regress. Knowing he goes, he does not fall; knowing he advances, he does not abide.

Therefore, he does not abide even in the Samādhi of the Summit (mūrdhan), nor does he abide in the patience regarding the joy of the Dharma (dharmāgra-kṣānti). Furthermore, he does not abide in such attachment to meditative concentration or attachment to the Dharma.
Because he has abandoned both obstacles, it is said that they are forever exhausted without remainder.
They immediately enter all Buddha-lands and cultivate immeasurable categories of merit. Every practice they perform is luminous;
they enter into skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform and teach all sentient beings, enabling them to perceive the Buddha-nature (*buddhatva*), which is eternal, blissful, self, and pure.

This explains the meaning of abiding in the "unquestioned mind" (*anābhoga-citta*). Following from the above, by virtue of not dwelling in attachment to meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to manifest the body and enter into all Buddha-lands to serve the Buddhas of the ten directions.
With courageous diligence, one further cultivates immeasurable and boundless categories of all meritorious dharmas; every single practice is a great radiance. Practice.

"Radiant Light" refers to the simultaneous union of wisdom and conduct. Because one does not dwell in attachment to dharmas, one enters into various skillful means of the roots of goodness to teach and transform all sentient beings. This enables all to perceive the essential nature of all Buddhas;
it does not stop at mere perception, but also causes them to realize this Tathāgata’s true permanence, true bliss, and true self.
These are the four virtues of True Purity (*bhūtatathatā*).
When a person is born and dwells within this stage, they practice the gates of transformation; these gradually become profound and subtle.

Through the wisdom that contemplates flowers in the sky, they enter the Middle Way of essential nature, wherein all categories of Dharma-gates are fulfilled like a diamond (*vajra*). This is the "Chapter on the Path of the Sun and Moon" from the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*.
The meaning of this has already been clarified.
This bond pertains to the inconceivable merit and wisdom of that stage; it serves to clarify the meaning of liberation of mind.
Regarding the phrase "this person is born and dwells therein," it means that once this Bodhisattva is born in this stage, they also dwell within it.

Within this stage, one realizes the dharma-gates of transformative practices for delivering all sentient beings; from this point onward, they gradually become increasingly profound and subtle, such that they are difficult to fathom.

The wisdom of the "contemplation of empty flowers" realized by the Bodhisattva enters into the Middle Way of the essence-nature of all Buddhas, proceeding as a single unified whole. Therefore, all categories of dharma-gates of the Buddhas attain perfection.
This is fully complete. This has been explained briefly here; within the Great Treatise, it is illustrated by the simile of the vajra.
This meaning has already been further elucidated at length in the "Chapter on the Path of the Sun and Moon" above.
V. The Ground of the Wisdom that Illuminates the Fivefold Nature (2). Part One: Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization; Part Two: Correctly Explaining the Meaning of the Text.
Part One: Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization.
On this stage, one abandons the obstacle to the nirvāṇa of the inferior vehicles (hīnayāna).

This refers specifically to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) that consists of a natural aversion to the suffering of saṃsāra and a tendency toward the bliss of nirvāṇa; it is so named because it arises based upon those [obstructions].

Furthermore, two types of deluded attachments are abandoned: first, the delusion of exclusively directing the mind away from saṃsāra; second, the delusion of exclusively directing the mind toward nirvāṇa.
Foolishness. These three dharmas can obstruct the fifth stage; only by severing these delusive obstructions does one ascend to the stage of "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjayā).

Now, the Bodhisattva cultivates the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), whereby the two wisdoms become perfectly integrated and the ultimate and conventional truths are unimpeded, such that what is difficult to unify is unified.

By means of the path of non-differentiation, one is able to sever [the obstacles] forever. Because the obstacles of delusion have been severed, it is called the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā bhūmiḥ*).

The suchness realized therein is called the "suchness of non-differentiation in categories" (*anānātva-lakṣaṇa-tathatā*); that is to say, this suchness is [identical] with respect to both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

Their nature is equal, for there is no distinction between them. The stage of the Bodhisattva is entrusted to the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations (Nirmāṇarati), where he provisionally practices the dharmas of the three vehicles to transform and guide sentient beings. Among the ten pāramitās, the pāramitā of dhyāna is the most preeminent.
II. Correctly explaining the meaning of the text:

O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, at the stage of the essence-ground illuminated by wisdom (*prajñā-prakṛti-bhūmi*), there are ten kinds of categories of the arising of the powers of dharmas (*dharma-daśabala-utpatti-varga*).

They give rise to all meritorious practices through the skillful means of a single wisdom (*eka-prajñopāya*), knowing the two types of karma—good and evil—within the category of the power of distinguishing the spheres of action (*caryā-viśeṣa-bala-varga*).

The Chapter on the Power of Knowledge of Karma regarding wholesome and unwholesome actions; the Chapter on the Power of Desire regarding all desires, aspirations, and the fruits of birth within the six realms of existence;

the Chapter on the Power of Nature regarding the different classifications of the natures of the six realms of existence; and the Chapter on the Power of Roots regarding the individual differences among all wholesome and unwholesome faculties.
The Chapter on the Faculties and Powers: The state of wrong determination, right determination, and no determination—this is called the Chapter on the Power of Concentration.

All causes and effects: this vehicle is the cause, and this vehicle is the fruit; reaching the place of the fruit by means of the causal path—this is the Chapter on the Power of the Path. The five eyes know all phenomena.

Because he perceives all births, there is the Chapter on the Power of the Divine Eye (*divyacakṣus-bala*). He knows each and every event of a hundred eons; this is the Chapter on the Power of Past Lives (*pūrvanivāsa-bala*).

Regarding all births, there is the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding all sensations; this is the Chapter on the Power of Liberation (*vimukti-bala*).

This is the wisdom of the Chapter on the Ten Powers (*daśabala*), which knows the causes and effects of one’s own cultivation, as well as the distinctions between the causes and effects of all sentient beings.

The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" designate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages [of the Bodhisattva], thereby clarifying the meaning of the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).

Regarding "the wisdom that illuminates the nature and ground": this refers to the power of the profound meditations and great concentrations, which are ineffable, cultivated by this Bodhisattva during the causal stage;
consequently, in the resultant stage, he attains the wisdom corresponding to the various truths (*satya*), which perfectly illuminates the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, it is said that this stage is the "Stage of the Essence Illuminated by Wisdom. In other sutras, it is named the "Difficult to Conquer Stage" (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
Because the two truths are difficult to unify, this stage unifies what is difficult to unify, causing them to correspond; hence it is called the Difficult to Conquer Stage.

Regarding the "ten kinds of powers arising in this stage," this clarifies the dharma that is realized. That is to say, within this stage, there is the great dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) that is realized.

The Chapter on the Arising of the Ten Powers. These are capable of giving rise to all immeasurable meritorious practices of sentient beings, both mundane and supramundane, all of which are produced through the skillful means of a single wisdom. The above clarifies the essence of the ten powers as realized;
below, the functions of the ten powers are explained. First, the power of knowing the distinct spheres of action regarding the two karmas of good and evil.

This refers to the power of knowledge that thoroughly understands the distinctions among all sentient beings regarding their performance of wholesome and unwholesome deeds, as well as the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions thereof.
What is meant by "distinctions" is that some who perform wholesome karma do not obtain a wholesome reward.

Instead, they invite evil retribution. Or, when performing evil deeds, they fail to receive evil retribution and instead invite good rewards. Question: Why is it that those who cultivate goodness instead invite evil retribution?

Answer: It is as described in the *Yinjing* (Printed Scripture): creating images, providing meals for the monastic community (*zhaiseng*), and establishing assemblies are acts of cultivating goodness.
Yet, within these acts, there are those who do not truly establish the Triple Gem (*triratna*), but instead use the public cause to further their private interests and deceive others.

Because one is ignorant of the fruit, one cultivates what is wholesome yet obtains an unwholesome retribution. This is precisely what is meant by "heaven has not yet been established, but hell is already formed.

How could it be that committing evil instead brings about a wholesome reward? For example, to eliminate wicked people, malevolent beasts, and to destroy the cohesion of heretics—even to the point of killing an icchantika—these are acts of evil. Among these, there is nothing that is not [evil].

In reality, although this appears to harm sentient beings, it is actually the killing of one to save many; it eliminates harm and promotes goodness, which is precisely what is enacted by the great compassion of a Bodhisattva.
Because such an act is performed [with pure intent], there is no karmic retribution for evil. This is what is meant by "killing with a compassionate heart";
the more lives one saves, the more merit arises. Such are the various spheres of differentiated practice, each undertaken for the sake of sentient beings.
Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Distinct Spheres of Activity. Second, regarding the "Chapter on the Power of Knowledge of the Performance of Good and Evil Deeds":

this power of knowledge refers to the ability to fully comprehend the various good and evil deeds performed by all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, as well as their resulting causes and effects.
For instance, when one is meant to receive a long life as retribution, it may instead result in a short life; or when one is meant to receive a short life...
Regarding the timing of retribution: why is it that one who was long-lived becomes short-lived, or one who was wealthy becomes poor, or one who was poor becomes wealthy?
This is because the karmic fruits of these actions depend entirely upon the accumulation or depletion of causes, and the accumulation or depletion of merit.

As it is said: "By virtue of merit, life is extended; by the depletion of merit, life is shortened. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "This person has committed evil deeds in previous lives..."

Regarding karma: although other karmic residues remain such that one would fall into the evil realms at the end of this life, through the merit of upholding this sutra now, those sins from previous lives are immediately extinguished.
Not only will one not fall into the evil realms, but one shall attain Bodhi.
This is because the power of the supramundane Dharma is a vast cause; therefore, one must not fail to cultivate mundane and supramundane roots of goodness.
Thus, for each case of certainty and uncertainty, he explains it for the sake of sentient beings; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Knowledge of Karma.
Third is the knowledge of all sentient beings' desires, pursuits, and vows, as well as the fruits of their births throughout the six realms of existence.
Regarding the "Power of Desires," this power of knowledge refers to the ability to fully comprehend everything that sentient beings desire, pursue, and vow within their minds. All [of these].

"Desire" (*chanda*) refers to longing or aspiration. This means either constantly desiring to make offerings to the Triple Gem, Heaven, Earth, the sovereign, parents, teachers, and elders, and to draw near to virtuous friends in order to constantly repay their kindness;
or it means constantly desiring to contemplate wealth, beauty, fame, food, sleep, and so forth—all such things being sought.
"Seeking" (*prārthanā*) refers to the act of begging or requesting. This means either delighting in seeking a good teacher or a good friend, or...

Seeking fame, reputation, and material gain; or seeking merit, glory, wealth, and nobility; even down to seeking the birth of excellent sons and grandsons—these are all "vows," meaning essential aspirations.
This refers to, for example, aspiring to be born in the Western Land to attain Buddhahood and save sentient beings;
or aspiring to be born in the heavens or among humans; or even aspiring to be born in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. These are called "all [vows]."

It is called the "Chapter on the Power of Desire" because it explains for each individual sentient being the various distinctions of their aspirations and the fruits sought in birth after birth throughout the six realms.

The "Chapter on the Power of Nature" refers to this power of wisdom that skillfully understands how the natures and dispositions of all sentient beings differ—whether they are sharp or dull. It discerns these differences in nature.

Regarding the attainment of the fruits, there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior; [the timeframes] range from one birth, two births, or three, four, or five births until the attainment of Bodhi.
Thus, he preaches this individually for each sentient being; therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Nature" (*dhātu-bala*).

Fifth is the knowledge of all roots of goodness and evil, which differ one from another; this is the "Chapter on the Power of the Roots" (*indriya-bala*), meaning that by this power of wisdom, one is able to thoroughly understand them.
Regarding all sentient beings, there are differences in their faculties and elements. How are they differentiated?
It is said that from wholesome seeds, wholesome manifest activities arise; from unwholesome seeds, unwholesome manifest activities arise. These roots of good and evil are either light or heavy.
Those who are light are easily transformed through teaching; those who are heavy are difficult to transform through teaching.

Those easily transformed are such as the bhikṣus who came forth by the "Welcome" (Ehi-bhikṣu) formula, whose saṃghāṭī robes were donned upon their bodies and whose hair and beards fell away spontaneously.

Those difficult to transform are such as the old woman of the eastern city and others. Thus, for each distinction of faculties and elements, he taught for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is said: "Faculties..."

This is the Chapter on Power (*Bala-paṭala*). Regarding the sixth [power], the knowledge of wrong concentration, right concentration, and indeterminate concentration—this is called the Chapter on the Power of Concentration (*Samādhi-bala-paṭala*).

It means that by this power of wisdom, one is well able to thoroughly understand all the wrong concentrations of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), the partial concentrations of the Hīnayāna, the right concentrations of Bodhisattvas, and the indeterminate states of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Having attained penetration into each of these, one explains them for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is said: "This is called the power of concentration."
This is the Chapter on Powers (*Bala-varga*). Seventh, knowing all causes and effects: the vehicle is the cause; the vehicle is the fruit.

Reaching the place of the fruit by means of the causal path—this is the Chapter on the Power of the Path (*Mārga-bala-varga*). This refers to this Chapter on Wisdom (*Jñāna-varga*), which clearly knows the six realms of existence:
riding upon contaminated causes to reach contaminated fruits, and riding upon uncontaminated causes to reach uncontaminated fruits, reaching the place of the fruit by means of the causal path.
To thoroughly comprehend each and every thing and explain it for the sake of sentient beings is called the Chapter on the Power of the Path.

Regarding the Eightfold Knowledge of All Phenomena through the Five Eyes and the Vision of All Rebirths: as for the Chapter on the Power of the Heavenly Eye, that eye has five aspects. Namely: the Heavenly Eye is a supernormal power (*abhijñā*) that is unimpeded;
the Fleshly Eye is impeded and not a supernormal power; the Dharma Eye observes only the conventional (*saṃvṛti*); and the Wisdom Eye takes only emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its object. The Buddha...
"The eye is like a thousand suns; though illuminating diverse forms, they are seen as identical. This refers to the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

It means that through the realization of the divine eye, one perceives clearly all phenomena of the present world—whether the sense faculties or their objects, whether defiled or pure, and all their various distinctions—as well as all sentient beings, seeing them at the moments of birth and death as they receive retributions of beauty or ugliness according to the conditions of their wholesome or unwholesome karma.

First, it is shown to all sentient beings; hence it is called the "Chapter on the Power of the Divine Eye. Ninth, knowing the events of a hundred kalpas, knowing each one individually, is the "Chapter on the Power of Past Lives," which states that by this power of wisdom, one thoroughly understands the various past lives of all sentient beings.

Throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, he explains to sentient beings, exactly as it is, their deaths here and births there, their clans and names, their suffering and joy, and their lifespans;
therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Past Lives. [The phrase] "Knowing all births, afflictions are extinguished;
knowing all sensations, ignorance is extinguished" refers to the "Chapter on the Power of Liberation," which states that by means of this power of wisdom, one thoroughly understands...
All births, which are the cause of afflictions, are extinguished; all sensations, which are the fruit of ignorance, are extinguished.

Afflictions, ignorance, and all habitual tendencies—cause and effect—are utterly extinguished. Because he teaches this according to reality for the sake of sentient beings, it is called the "Chapter on the Power of Liberation."

Such is the wisdom of the Chapter on the Ten Powers. It knows the causes and effects of its own cultivation, and likewise knows the causes and effects cultivated by all sentient beings, discerning them with clarity and without error.

Among these ten kinds of wisdom, the first five thoroughly understand the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of sentient beings, while the latter five thoroughly understand the causes and conditions for their cessation and non-arising.
Furthermore, body, speech, and mind function separately; they take a pure land as an evil land, and an evil land as a land of wondrous bliss.
They can transform good into evil and evil into good; they can transform form into non-form, and non-form into form.
They take a man for a woman, and a woman for a man; they take the six realms of existence as not being the six realms, and that which is not the six realms as being the six realms.
Even regarding earth, water, fire, and wind, they perceive them as not being earth, water, fire, or wind.

At that time, by the power of great skillful means, this person perceives within all sentient beings that which is inconceivable—something that those on lower stages cannot know or perceive. Thus it is raised up.
"Your Excellency’s conduct is exemplary.
This explains that [the Bodhisattva] abides in an uninterrupted state of mind (*anantarya-citta*). This is to reveal that the essence and function of this stage are inconceivable;
it is not merely the attainment of the categories of wisdom of the ten powers (*daśabala*), but that his body, speech, and mind possess further distinct and wondrous functions. Not...

This can be measured. As for the distinct functions of body, mind, and speech: the body is able to manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the mind is able to maintain focused mindfulness, and the mouth is able to preach the Dharma.
These are the powers of the wondrous application of the three wheels. Therefore, it is said that the body, mind, and speech have distinct functions;
because of these powers of the wondrous application of the three wheels, one is able to manifest the Pure Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
In the stage of the mixed habitation of the five destinies, one is able to take a land of mixed habitation of the five destinies and transform it into a Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Since these lands are fundamentally without distinction, they merely manifest individually according to sentient beings; thus it is said:
"One takes a pure land and makes it an evil land; one takes an evil land and makes it a pure and wondrous land. This refers to the three transformations of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The Pure Land is such a place. One who can transform good into evil is like King Ajātaśatru; one who can transform evil into good is like the butcher Pūrṇa-mukha.

That which transforms form into non-form and non-form into form refers to various miraculous transformations, such as emitting light and scattering flowers, surging up in the east and sinking down in the west, or surging up in the west and sinking down in the east. By means of these...
To transform a man into a woman is, for example, as when Śāriputra was turned into the form of a woman by a single finger-point from a celestial maiden.
To transform a woman into a man is, for example, as when the dragon girl in the *Lotus Sūtra* suddenly transformed into a man and attained Buddhahood in the world of Vimala.
To regard the six realms of existence as not being the six realms, and that which is not the six realms as being the six realms—[is likewise so].
The six realms are the ordinary; that which is not the six realms is the noble, such as the Great Being Mahāmati and others.
Even regarding earth, water, fire, and wind—that which is not earth, water, fire, or wind—within this context, one phrase should be supplied:

"That which is not earth, water, fire, or wind, acts as earth, water, fire, and wind. This is like using the eighteen supernatural transformations to turn one's body into water or fire, or to carry [loads].

Carrying dry grass, entering fire without being burned, and so forth—these are examples. As for the aforementioned natures of good, evil, and so on, not one of them can be apprehended as having a fixed nature;
if there were a fixed nature, it could not be transformed. Such various sovereign spiritual powers are all produced by the power of the Bodhisattva’s great skillful means and wisdom.
They are manifested for all sentient beings to behold according to their own dispositions.
Yet they all cause one to enter suddenly into the inconceivable. It is not only the ordinary sentient beings of the lower realms who find it inconceivable upon seeing it;

even the various Bodhisattvas of the preceding lower stages are unable to know or perceive the actions of a Bodhisattva’s lifting and setting down of the feet—namely, that those on the first stage do not know the matters of the second stage.
This person possesses great and clear wisdom. They advance gradually; their wisdom unfolds bit by bit.
Immeasurable, immeasurable gateways of the Dharma—unspeakable and unspeakable—manifest before them.
The merits of this stage are inconceivable, for it clarifies the mind through liberation. To continue from what was stated above:

why is it that those of lower stages cannot know this? It is because this Bodhisattva’s great, luminous wisdom and insight gradually deepen and advance, enabling them to progressively realize and enter into the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience) of all Buddhas; such is their realization.
The light of the wisdom-light is immeasurable and immeasurable, extending to all that is unspeakably unspeakable.

Such various dharma-gates, at one and the same time, each manifest before one in the present. How could these be the objects of deliberation or discourse for the limited consciousness of ordinary beings?
Six: The Ground of Flower-Light (Flower-Luminosity), Part Two. First, clarifying the meaning of abandonment and realization; second, the formal explanation of the textual meaning. First:
Clarifying the meaning of abandonment and realization.
On this stage, one abandons the obstacle consisting of the manifestation of a single type of coarse characteristic.

This is so named because it arises from a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that involves the grasping at the manifestation of coarse characteristics regarding defilement and purity. Furthermore, two types of deluded attachments are abandoned:
first, the delusion regarding the observation of the flow of phenomenal existence; second, the delusion regarding the frequent manifestation of characteristics. This...
These three dharmas can obstruct the Bhūmi of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). Only by severing these delusions and obstructions does one ascend to the Bhūmi of Presence.

Now, knowing that all phenomena are neither defiled nor pure, one dwells in mental attention directed toward the signless (*animitta-manasikāra*), causing True Suchness (*tathatā*) to become perfected.

Thus, one is able to permanently sever the delusions and obstructions; since Prajñā becomes manifest once these are severed, it is called the Bhūmi of Presence. This is the True Suchness that is realized.
It is called the *tathatā* of non-defiled purity; this means that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this *tathatā* is neither defiled nor pure.
The stage of the Bodhisattva is entrusted to the Heavenly King Vaśavartin, who provisionally cultivates the dharmas of the three vehicles and so forth to transform and guide sentient beings.
Among the ten *pāramitās*, the *prajñāpāramitā* is the most supreme.
II. Correct Explanation of the Textual Meaning:

O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas on the stage of *Huaguang* (Flower Radiance), whose essential nature is thus, are able to manifest within all worlds the category of the ten supernormal powers and clear wisdom to all sentient beings, through various transformations. By means of the clear wisdom of the divine eye...
Within the lands of the three periods of time, they know all forms, equal in number to the atoms of dust, as being divided into the bodies of sentient beings of the six realms.
They know each individual body, from its subtle atomic forms up to its great composite forms, part by part.

With the wisdom of the divine ear, they know the sounds of suffering and joy of sentient beings in the six realms throughout the ten directions and three periods of time—sounds that are neither non-sounds nor non-noises, and the sounds of all dharmas.
By means of the wisdom of the celestial body, they know all forms—both form and non-form—and those that are neither male nor female in shape.
In a single thought-moment, they pervade the lands and kalpas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, manifesting bodies as numerous as the atoms within great and small lands.

By means of the celestial knowledge of others' minds, they know the mental activities of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time across the six realms of existence in the ten directions.
Regarding the mental states and mental concomitants— such as suffering and pleasure, good and evil— he uses his celestial and human wisdom to know,

one by one, the past lives, sufferings, pleasures, and lifespans of all sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time, even for those whose lives continue for a hundred kalpas.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" designate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages, thereby clarifying the meaning of the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).

Regarding the "Essential Nature of the Flower-Light Stage": it means that because this Bodhisattva has cultivated immeasurable wisdom during the causal stage, upon reaching the resultant stage, they realize the *prajñāpāramitā* of all Buddhas; thus, the flowers of great wisdom-practice bloom all at once.
Therefore it is said: "The essential nature is the Ground of Flower-Light. In another sutra, it is named the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
This means that all fundamental merits and wisdoms simultaneously become manifest; hence it is called the Ground of Manifestation.
It is capable, within all worlds, of fulfilling a single section of the chapter on the hundred thousand great vows. This explains abiding in the uninterrupted mind. The Bodhisattva dwells...

Within this stage, one is able to exercise ten kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the category of great clear wisdom throughout all worlds in the ten directions, manifesting various transformations for all sentient beings; these are all difficult to fathom.
What are the ten kinds of categories of clear wisdom? First, the clear wisdom of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); that is, the divine eye.

Pervasive: This refers to the category of wisdom that is able to discern the colors of the lands throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, down to the subtle particles and divisions of earth, water, fire, and wind—all the illusory forms of the four great elements.

It knows how these are gathered part by part to form the physical characteristics of sentient beings in the six realms, and within each of those segmented bodies, it knows the precise extent of every pore and color.

First, regarding how minute particles of form constitute the large-scale physical form of a single body: because one understands each and every aspect of these constituent forms without error, [this is the first].
Second, as for the wisdom of the divine ear: this is the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*).

It means that by attaining this wisdom, one is able to hear and know the mental and physical states—whether oppressed or delighted—of sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence across the ten directions and the three periods of time.

The sounds produced by the sensations of suffering and pleasure are neither non-sounds of the sensations of suffering and pleasure, nor are they non-voices of the sensations of suffering and pleasure.
This extends to all rivers, lakes, seas, the sound of flowing water moved by the wind, and the various sounds of bells, gongs, cymbals, and drums;
because each and every such sound is known, this is the third, the knowledge of the celestial body, which is the supernormal power of the form body (*rūpakāya-abhijñā*). That is to say, one attains—

This wisdom is able to cognize all that is form (*rūpa*) and that which is non-form. Regarding "form and form": this refers to all sentient beings; the environmental realm of the land (*bhājanaloka*);
and the physical bodies and sensory faculties (*indriya*) as the primary retribution (*vipākaphala*). Such sensory faculties and objects—these internal and external forms—are called "form and form.
Regarding "non-form": this refers to the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the dharma-nature realm (*dharmatā-bhūmi*) wherein the Buddha dwells.
Furthermore, because the Buddha’s light universally illumines the pure body of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), it is said to be "non-form.
Regarding the statement that it is neither male nor female form: since form is already non-form, all characteristics such as male and female are entirely absent.
Thus, within a single thought-moment, one universally knows all such forms—whether they be forms, non-forms, and so forth—and likewise knows the three [realms] throughout the ten directions.
The world-systems, the magnitude of kalpas— whether vast or small, prolonged or brief— as well as the atoms within those world-systems and their respective bodies;
fourth, the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna), which is the power of knowing others' minds, meaning that by attaining this wisdom,

one is able to fully comprehend the mental activities of sentient beings throughout the three periods of past, present, and future, as well as all [beings] within the six realms of existence across the ten directions.

Regarding sentient beings, whatever they think in their minds and mental factors— whether thoughts of suffering or pleasure, good or evil, and so forth— the fifth [superknowledge] is the knowledge of gods and humans,
which is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). This means that by attaining this knowledge,

one is able to fully comprehend the causes of the wholesome and unwholesome karma of all sentient beings throughout the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time, as well as the present experiences of suffering and pleasure and the duration of their lifespans.
One is able to know each and every karmic retribution, as well as the length of one's lifespan and matters such as its continuity over hundreds of kalpas;

all these are clearly understood and explained for the sake of sentient beings. The five aforementioned wisdoms are used to know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of dependent origination, wherein no defiled characteristic can be found.
The five subsequent wisdoms are used to know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of liberation through the cessation of conditions, wherein even no pure characteristic exists.
The signs are perceivable.

By means of the divine knowledge of liberation, one knows the liberation of sentient beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, whereby they sever all afflictions—whether many or few—from the first stage up to the tenth stage, until every extinction is completely exhausted. This is accomplished by means of the divine mind-knowledge of meditative concentration.

He knows the minds of sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and the three periods of time—whether they are concentrated, unconcentrated, neither concentrated nor unconcentrated—as well as the methods for inducing concentration.
He possesses the samādhis of "that which is grasped" and the "one hundred samādhis.

By means of his celestial awakening-wisdom, he knows all sentient beings, whether they have already attained Buddhahood or have not yet attained it, even down to every single mind of those in the six realms of existence; he likewise knows all things throughout the ten directions.
The Dharma spoken from within the Buddha’s mind, through the wisdom of celestial recollection (*divyasmṛtijñāna*), knows the lifespans and the duration— whether long or short—
of all sentient beings throughout hundreds and thousands of kalpas, as well as the intermediate and great kalpas. Through the wisdom of celestial vows (*divyapraṇidhijñāna*),

he knows the individual practices and vows within the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and thirty minds of the noble ones (*ārya*), whether they seek suffering or happiness, or that which is Dharma and non-Dharma— all of it.
Seeking the fulfillment of the ten vows and the hundred thousand great vows constitutes the explanation of the wisdom of the latter five chapters.
The "sentient beings" mentioned below all refer to noble sages (*ārya*), which differs from the previous usage.
Sixth, regarding the "heavenly knowledge of liberation," this refers to the supernormal power of cessation (*nirodha-abhijñā*); it means that by attaining this wisdom, one fully understands.
Sentient beings of the ten directions and three periods of time attain liberation according to the measure of their wisdom,

severing all afflictions— whether many or few. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage, they sever and realize them in successive order, thereby eliminating a portion of the obscurations of ignorance and delusion,
and attaining realization of a portion of the wondrous principle of *tathatā* (suchness), until finally reaching the ultimate extinction of the diamond-like state (*vajropama*).

They are extinguished, all exhausted without remainder. Because one knows each of these various liberations in this way, [the seventh is] "the knowledge of the minds of others through celestial concentration," which is the supernormal power of the basis of psychic power (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*).

This means that having attained this knowledge, one clearly understands the minds of sentient beings within the lands of the ten directions and three periods of time—whether their minds are concentrated, unconcentrated, neither concentrated nor unconcentrated, or those who have emerged from concentration.
Method: Because one knows each and every thing—the samādhis of inclusion, the hundred samādhis, and all dharmas such as meditative concentrations—[one attains this].

Eighth, by means of the wisdom of celestial awakening, which is the supernatural power of speech and sound, this wisdom thoroughly understands the minds and thoughts of all sentient beings, whether they have already attained Buddhahood or have not yet attained it, even including all persons within the six realms of existence.

Regarding what is contemplated: as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, [the Buddha] knows the various types, characteristics, and essential natures of all sentient beings—what they contemplate, what they think about, and what they cultivate, and so forth.

He not only knows the thoughts and mental states of all sentient beings, but also knows that which is taught according to the faculties and conduct of beings within the minds of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Ninth, by means of the wisdom of celestial recollection (*divyānusmṛti-jñāna*), [he knows] that which has not yet...

Next is the supernormal power of knowing the past. This wisdom thoroughly understands the lifespans of all sentient beings throughout hundreds and thousands of kalpas, as well as the distinctions in the duration of these kalpas—whether great or small.
Yet, in their essential nature, these kalpas have no extension or contraction;

they appear long or short only according to the varying degrees of lightness or heaviness, thickness or thinness of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings. Thus, the measure of a kalpa also possesses length and brevity.

They are not equal. All sentient beings receive their life-span, which varies in duration—some long, some short, some increasing, some decreasing—and these lifespans and kalpas are each known in their entirety;
this is what is meant by "contemplating immeasurable kalpas in a single thought-moment.

Tenth, through the wisdom of celestial vows, which is the unconditioned penetration (*anabhisaṃskāra-abhijñā*), this wisdom thoroughly knows every single thing regarding all worthy ones (*ārya*), sages, and sentient beings.
Regarding the gates of practice: each of the great vows that are generated—whether seeking suffering or seeking happiness—is as follows.

Those who seek suffering are like the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja), who burned his body and set his arms ablaze; they are like the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging (Sadāparibhūta), who endured being struck and pelted with staves and wood.

Ānanda, the vow to enter [the world] first during the five turbidities is of this nature. Those who seek happiness are like Vaidehī, who vowed to be born in a land of bliss, such as the Land of Dharma-Treasury (Dharmākara).
"O Bhikṣu, to vow that all sentient beings shall be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) and so forth—this is [the Dharma].
That which seeks the Dharma consists of the provisional and the ultimate, the exoteric and the esoteric, the teachings of the orthodox doctrine, and so on.

That which is not the Dharma consists of the teachings of celestial Māras, external paths, and heterodox doctrines; even the vow to become King Yama to restrain all transgressors is termed 'not the Dharma.'"
This is so. "All that is sought" summarizes the upward seeking and downward transformation; there is nothing that is not sought.
These ten vows are like the King of Vows of Samantabhadra, together with the ten inexhaustible phrases, and even the immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of great vows of all Buddhas;
the Bodhisattva of this stage fully possesses each one and knows them all completely.

This person abides within the stages and, amidst the ten supernormal powers and clarities (*abhijñā-vidyā*), manifests immeasurable distinct functions of body, mind, and speech to explain the merits of the stages.

Even in hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, these could not be exhausted. Yet, as many Śākyamunis as there may be briefly open up this chapter on the supernormal powers and clarities, as explained in the "Chapter on Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination."

This section concludes the merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) at this stage, clarifying the liberation of the mind. The phrase "this person abides within the ground" refers to the ground named *Padmaprabhā* (Flower-Light), which is the fundamental nature of the ground.
The two middle lines among the ten supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) conclude the ten categories of wisdom, representing the merit of the wondrous function of the distinctions of the three wheels.
The three lines explaining the merits of the ground provide a general conclusion for this section.
The virtues of the earth are profoundly deep, immeasurable, inexhaustible, and endless;
their meaning cannot be fully expressed even in unspeakably many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas. Such is the case for Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
This merely provides a brief opening to the chapter on the "Clarity of Wisdom regarding Supernormal Powers" of this stage.
What is explained here is, within the great compendium, no different from what is taught in the chapter on "Contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination."
VII. The Stage of Fulfillment of Essential Nature (2) I. Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization II. Correctly Explaining the Meaning of the Text I.
Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization
The Bodhisattva on this stage abandons one type of obstacle consisting of the manifestation of subtle marks (*sūkṣma-nimitta-pravṛtti-āvaraṇa*).

This is specifically that portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which arises from the manifestation of subtle marks based on the grasping at arising and ceasing; therefore, it is so named.

Furthermore, two types of deluded attachments are abandoned: first, the delusion regarding the manifestation of subtle marks; second, the attachment to the exclusive mental engagement (*manasikāra*) seeking the signless (*animitta*).
Foolishness. Due to these three factors, one is able to obstruct the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*). Only by severing these delusive obstructions does one ascend to the seventh stage.

Now far removed from the triple world and close to the rank of the Dharma King, one’s practice surpasses that of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), skillfully cultivates the signless (*animitta*), and reaches the limit of the signless.
As its functional effort reaches its ultimate, it is far superior to what preceded it; therefore, it is named the Far-Reaching Stage. Thus, one is able to forever...
Obstruction is severed. Once the obstructions of ignorance are severed, the True Suchness (Tathatā) realized is called the "True Suchness of the Non-differentiation of Dharmas.
This means that this True Suchness can discern that all various teachings are identical to True Suchness, for they are not devoid of characteristics.

The stage of the Bodhisattva is entrusted to the Heavenly King of the First Dhyāna, where he provisionally cultivates the dharmas of the three vehicles and so forth to transform and guide sentient beings regarding the ten pāramitās.
In this [middle stage], the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) is supreme.
2. Correctly explaining the meaning of the text:
"If, O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, having fulfilled the stage of the essential nature (*svabhāva-bhūmi*), enter into these dharmas, there are eighteen types of noble persons (*ārya-pudgala*)."

The Chapter on Wisdom (*Jñāna-varga*). That which is not shared with those in the lower stages consists of: the body being free from untainted transgressions; speech being free from verbal offenses; mindfulness being free from lapses;
being detached from the eight worldly dharmas; equanimity toward all phenomena; and constantly abiding in samādhi. These six qualities are fully perfected upon entering the stages.

Furthermore, from this wisdom, one gives rise to the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Because the habitual tendencies of the fetters within the three realms are ultimately never received again, there is the perfection of desire.
Because all merits and all dharma-gates are fulfilled as sought, the mind of diligence is complete.
Because all matters of dharmas, all matters of kalpas, and all matters of sentient beings are known simultaneously within a single mind, the mind of mindfulness is complete.
Because the six realms of sentient beings are all dharmas characterized by these two truths, wisdom is complete. One who knows the ten destinies of beings is...
Because they have no fetters and no residual habits (*vāsanā*), they possess the "feet of liberation" that reach all Buddhas.

Because they perceive all sentient beings and know others, themselves, and their disciples, being free from outflows and all residual habits of affliction, they possess the "feet of the six supernormal powers" that know the bodies of others through wisdom.
This person enters into the sixfold fulfillment of clear wisdom and thereby gives rise to the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*).
Following the mental activities of sentient beings throughout the six realms, they eloquently expound immeasurable categories of Dharma-doors to manifest them to all sentient beings.

Following the mental activities of all sentient beings, they constantly enter samādhi, causing the great earth of the ten directions to tremble and flowers to manifest in the void, thereby enabling sentient beings to...
Regarding mental activity: through the perfection of great clear wisdom, one perceives the appearance of Buddhas throughout all past kalpas;
this also demonstrates the minds of all sentient beings. Through non-attached wisdom, one perceives all lands within the ten directions of the present.
Through the supernormal knowledge of the path of the mind, one perceives all Buddhas and all sentient beings throughout all kalpas in the future,
seeing how all sentient beings receive the Way and hear the Dharma from these Buddhas as they appear in the world.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" designate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages, thereby clarifying the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*).

Regarding the "stage of the nature-ground of fulfillment": because one cultivates the means of deliverance (*upāya-pāramitā*) during the causal stage, one realizes and attains the Tathāgata’s conduct of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-caryā*) in the resultant stage, which is perfectly complete;
therefore, it is called the stage of the nature-ground of fulfillment. In other sutras, it is named the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*).

This Bodhisattva has emerged from the river of the triple world (*traidhātuka*), transcended the stages of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*), reached the city of *nirvāṇa*, and is close to the station of the Dharma King;
therefore, it is called the "Far-Reaching Stage" (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "entering into this dharma," this indicates the dharma that is realized.

That is to say, one enters into the dharma of the fulfilled essential nature (*svabhāva*); this already constitutes the category of the eighteen noble ones' knowledges (*jñāna*) of a Tathāgata, and is not shared with the two [vehicles].
These are shared by those who possess limited power; they are not merely shared with these [lesser beings], but even the bodhisattvas of the lower stages cannot attain them.

Therefore, they are called the "eighteen unshared [qualities]. What are the eighteen noble wisdoms? First, being free from outflows and faults in the body is also termed "the body being without error.
This means that this bodhisattva, from time immemorial, has constantly cultivated all the precepts.
In his body and mind, all afflictions and other hindrances are purified and exhausted without remainder. Because this physical karma is pure, he attains great supernormal powers;
thus it is said that "the body is free from outflows and faults. Second, "the mouth is free from verbal transgressions" is also called "the mouth is without error.
This means that from immeasurable kalpas ago, this Bodhisattva has constantly employed the five modes of speech in accordance with the needs of sentient beings.
Through skillful means, he preaches various sublime dharmas to enable others to attain the fruits of the Path;
thus, because his verbal karma is pure, it is said that "his mouth commits no verbal transgression. Third, regarding "no loss of mindfulness," this is also called "no lapse of the mind.
This means that from beginningless time, this Bodhisattva has constantly cultivated the various dhyānas, such that his mind is free from attachment and his will is free from negligence. However...
