According to the capacities and needs of sentient beings, he employs skillful means to gather and transform them. Because his mental karma (*manas-karman*) is thus pure, it is said that "his mindfulness is free from loss of mindfulness.
Fourth, regarding being "free from the eight worldly dharmas," this is also called the "mind free from divergent thoughts.

This means that this bodhisattva, having come from the stage of the causal ground, employs skillful means solely to teach and transform sentient beings; he has already transcended both ordinary worldlings and those of the two vehicles.

To cling to existence is to grasp at the mark of existence; to cling to non-existence is to grasp at the mark of non-existence; to cling to permanence is the view of permanence; to cling to annihilation is the view of annihilation.
Because this mind is free from these eight kinds of perversions, it is said that one is "detached from the eight dharmas.

Regarding the equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward all phenomena among the five [mental factors], it is also called the "mind of equanimity through non-ignorance. This means that this Bodhisattva, from time immemorial, has illuminated [all things] with great *prajñā*.
He observes that all phenomena, whether mundane or supramundane, defiled or pure, are in their very essence entirely empty and ultimately ungraspable.
Because his mind is thus free from craving and attachment, it is said that he practices equanimity toward all dharmas.
Sixth is the samādhi of permanence, also called "the absence of an unsettled mind," meaning that this bodhisattva has never been separated from it since beginningless time.
This profound great samādhi merely follows sentient beings, manifesting or remaining hidden as it gathers and transforms them; hence it is said that "he is constantly in samādhi.

The phrase "this is the one who has entered the six stages" concludes the wisdom of the preceding six stages. The phrase "furthermore, from this wisdom... initiates the wisdom of the subsequent six stages.
This means that by virtue of being fully endowed with the essence of the wisdom of the six stages, there further arises from this wisdom the [wisdom of the next] six.
The fulfillment of the function of wisdom. What are the six kinds of wisdom? First, the fulfillment of desire (*chanda*), also called the non-diminution of desire.

This means that although this Bodhisattva manifests birth within the three realms (*tridhātu*) to gather and transform sentient beings, they ultimately do not undergo the fetters, habitual tendencies, or afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms;
therefore, it is called the fulfillment of desire. Second, the fulfillment of the mind of vigor (*vīrya*), also called the non-diminution of diligence...
"Diminution" refers to this bodhisattva’s fulfillment and perfection of all the Tathāgatas’ wisdom, the treasury of all meritorious qualities, and all the skillful means of conversion;
thus it is said that their "mind of progress is fulfilled. Third, the "fulfillment of the mind of mindfulness" is also called "non-diminution of mindfulness.
This means that this bodhisattva is able to thoroughly comprehend both the mundane and the supramundane.
In an instant, one simultaneously and fully understands all matters concerning the establishment of the Dharma, the long and short durations of all kalpas,
the expansion and contraction of time, the causes, conditions, karmic retributions, the length of life, and the experiences of suffering and joy for all sentient beings,
as well as the mental activities and thoughts of all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that the "mind of mindfulness" is perfected.
Regarding the fourth, the perfection of wisdom (*jñānasaṃpad*), it is also called the non-diminution of wisdom.

This means that this bodhisattva is able to thoroughly comprehend the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—as well as the two characteristics of existence and non-existence, the mental activities of sentient beings in the six realms, and all phenomena such as causes and effects.

He explains each one for the sake of sentient beings; therefore, it is called "sufficiency of wisdom. Regarding the fifth, the "limb of liberation" (*vimokṣāṅga*), it is also called "liberation without decrease.

This means that this bodhisattva is able to know that from the ten types of persons who have set out on the path up to all Buddhas, they have severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), ignorance, fetters (*saṃyojana*), and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), exhausting them without remainder; therefore, it is called "liberation."

This is sufficient. Regarding the "sufficiency of the sixfold sixes," it is also called the "unfailing knowledge and vision of liberation. This means that this bodhisattva is fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*):

the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), the power of miraculous transformations (*ṛddhi*), and the power of mastery over the mind (*kāmacāravaśitā*).
Because of these, they clearly perceive all worthy ones and sages, as well as sentient beings in the six realms of existence, and are able to thoroughly understand all other beings.

Because my transformed disciples are free from outflows and all habitual tendencies of affliction (*kleśavāsanā*), they are able, by means of this wisdom, to know the characteristics of others' bodies as well as their own bodies;
hence it is called the "six supernormal powers" (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). The phrase "these persons, etc. below concludes the aforementioned six-footed wisdom.
The phrase "they then give rise to the wisdom-body, etc. refers to the arising of the subsequent six types of wisdom. These are the bodhisattvas.
Not only has he already entered into the six perfections of clear wisdom (*prajñā*), but he further possesses the full application of the six types of wisdom.
What are these six wisdoms? First, the arising of the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*) that accords with the mental activities of sentient beings throughout the six realms of existence;

this is also called "bodily action following the movement of wisdom" (*kāyakarma-jñānānuparivartin*). This means that this Bodhisattva, through skillful means (*upāya*), mobilizes and brings forth the body of wisdom, conforming to that wisdom.

It transforms and manifests miraculous signs for the sake of sentient beings throughout the six realms, taming their various mental activities so that each may perceive these signs, attain understanding, and realize the fruits of the Path. Therefore, it says: "Then he rose from his seat," and so forth.
Second is the chapter on "Expounding Immeasurable Dharma Gates with Eloquence," which is for the purpose of instructing all sentient beings.
That which accords with the mental activities of all sentient beings is also called "verbal karma that accords with the movement of wisdom.
This means that this bodhisattva, by means of pure and subtle verbal karma, operates in accordance with wisdom and accords with the mental activities of all sentient beings through skillful means.
They provide guidance and instruction, enabling others to attain understanding and realization, and to enter the fruits of the Path; hence it is said: "eloquent speech," and so forth.
Third, "constantly entering samādhi in accordance with the mental activities of all sentient beings" is also called "the mental karma following the movement of wisdom.
This means that this bodhisattva, by means of pure mental karma, functions in accordance with wisdom and accords with the mental activities of all sentient beings.

He constantly enters samādhi, observing the faculties of beings to provide teachings suited to them as he preaches the Dharma. He eradicates the darkness of ignorance and delusion within sentient beings;
thus, through the karmic functions of the three wheels, his concentration and wisdom are perfectly luminous.

For this reason, the great earth throughout the ten directions trembles six times, and from within the void, the heavens rain down four kinds of flowers, enabling sentient beings to awaken to their own mental activities. Therefore...

It is said: "In accordance with the mental activities of all sentient beings," and so forth. Fourth, being fully endowed with great clear wisdom, they see the appearance of Buddhas throughout all past kalpas;
this is also that which reveals the minds of all sentient beings, and is called the unimpeded wisdom of the past.
This means that these bodhisattvas, through their great clear wisdom, clearly perceive the times of the past. First.
Throughout all immeasurable and boundless, ineffable eons, every single Buddha who appeared in the world preached the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings;
and all these sentient beings received the Way and heard the Dharma from these Buddhas.

He is able to know them all completely. By means of this, he reveals and manifests the mental activities of all sentient beings present before him, causing each and every one to awaken and enter [the truth].

Fifth, by means of unattached wisdom, he perceives all Buddhas and all sentient beings, along with their respective mental activities, within all lands throughout the ten directions in the present; this is also called "unimpeded wisdom of the present. That is to say:
This Bodhisattva, by means of unattached wisdom, perceives the present age:
within all the lands throughout the ten directions, all Buddhas appear in the world and preach various teachings for the sake of all sentient beings;
these sentient beings listen to the Dharma from the Buddhas and are able to receive and uphold it entirely, and they also manifest all the mental activities and practices of their minds.

First, in order to cause sentient beings to attain awakening; sixth, by means of the supernormal power of knowledge regarding the future, one perceives all kalpas within the future, the appearance of all Buddhas in the world, and all sentient beings who receive the Way and hear the Dharma from these Buddhas.

This is also called the unhindered knowledge of the future. It means that this bodhisattva, by means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of the path, perceives all kalpas and so forth within the future world, as well as the appearance of all Buddhas therein for the sake of all sentient beings, and their preaching of various dharmas.
He also perceives how these sentient beings listen to the Dharma and receive instruction from these Buddhas. Furthermore, he demonstrates...
For the sentient beings present before them, they cause their minds to open through this awakening and entry, whereby they abide among these eighteen noble ones.

With every thought-moment in samādhi, they contemplate the forms of the three realms as being like motes of dust, perceiving them as their own former bodies and all sentient beings as their own parents; thus they now enter this stage, wherein all merits [are perfected].

Because I have already entered all the divine lights, all the dharmas practiced by the Buddhas, and even all the categories of dharma-gates within the eighth and ninth stages, I manifest as a Buddha in all buddha-lands—
attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa— and thus transform others throughout all lands of the past, future, and present.
This clarifies the mind of liberation. "Dwelling among these eighteen noble ones" concludes the preceding section. "Mind-moment after mind in samādhi" introduces what follows.
This Bodhisattva dwells within the wisdom of these eighteen noble ones, constantly maintaining that mind-moment after mind does not depart from the right concentration of samādhi.
Within this samādhi, he further contemplates the forms of the three realms, which are like motes of dust. This is...
When I was formerly an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), I observed that the physical bodies I received were all the parents who provided my physical form throughout immeasurable kalpas.
As the sutra says: "The bones discarded [in this process] would equal Mount Sumeru;
the breast milk drunk would equal the waters of the four great oceans. Such is the vastness of the discarded bones.
The breadth of those for whom I have drunk milk is truly not limited to parents from one or two lifetimes, nor from a hundred or a thousand lifetimes,
but extends even to parents throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of unspeakable eons.
Because I have practiced the path over successive kalpas to repay my parents and to benefit all sentient beings, I have now entered this stage of the Ground of Fulfillment of the Essential Nature.
He is fully endowed with compassion, joy, and equanimity, as well as the six perfections and the myriad practices—the embodiment of the accumulation of all merits.

This body is able to manifest transformation-buddhas and preach the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and other teachings for the sake of the three provisions and the four preparatory practices of all bodhisattvas.
This stage is fully endowed with the gathered radiance of all supernatural powers and wisdom; it is therefore called the "Body of the Gathere Radiance of Wisdom.
This body can manifest as the Reward Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*), preaching the Dharma of the Single Vehicle for the sake of great Bodhisattvas.
This stage is the perfection of the Dharmakāya—the principle and fruit realized and cultivated by all Buddhas. This body serves as the locus for all Buddhas and sentient beings.
The essence of the Correct [Path]—the three bodies (trikāya)—are here fully perfected and complete; therefore it is called the "Stage of the Ground of Perfect Fulfillment.
Now, having entered this stage, all merits, all divine radiances, and all dharmas practiced by the Buddhas [are attained].
Up to the eighth stage, and within the ninth stage, I have already attained realization and entry into all categories of Dharma-gates.
Regarding the phrase "in all lands," etc., this clarifies the meaning of the three bodies (trikāya) realized therein;
by virtue of having partially realized the three bodies, one is able to manifest birth, renunciation, ascetic practice, and the attainment of enlightenment within all lands.

He becomes a Buddha and turns the Great Wheel of Dharma to deliver sentient beings. Having fulfilled his mission for this particular cycle of existence through these appropriate conditions, he then manifests entry into parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he continues to transform and teach other regions; throughout the past, present, and future, he is ever-present within all lands, manifesting in various ways that are inconceivable.
VIII. The Stage of the Buddha’s Lion’s Roar (2): Part One, Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization; Part Two, Correctly Explaining the Meaning of the Text.
Part One: Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization.
The Bodhisattvas on this stage eliminate one type of obstacle to preparatory application (*prayoga-āvaraṇa*).

This is a portion of the innate aspect (*sahaja*) within the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) which prevents the signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*) from arising spontaneously; for this reason, it is so named. Furthermore, they eliminate two types of deluded attachments.
First is the delusion of exerting effort regarding the signless; second is the delusion of lacking mastery over signs.
These three factors can obstruct the eighth stage. Only by severing these delusional obstructions does one ascend to the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

This means that this bodhisattva now enters the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*), attains the illumination of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) which continues spontaneously, and their conduct through the power of maturation (*vipākacaryā*) becomes fully refined.
Abiding in the signless (*animitta*), one contemplates without being moved by the afflictions of any phenomena; thus, one is able to sever them forever.
Because ignorance and obstructions have been severed, it is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). The *tathatā* realized therein is called the *tathatā* that neither increases nor decreases.

This means that this *tathatā*, while abiding in the contemplation of the signless, does not undergo increase or decrease according to defilement or purity. The Bodhisattva’s provisional stationing [in this stage] is twofold.
The Celestial King Dhyāna is the sovereign of a small thousand-world system. He transforms and guides sentient beings through the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna) Dharma;
among the ten pāramitās, the pāramitā of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā) is his most preeminent.
II. Correctly explaining the meaning of the text:

O Sons of the Buddha! Bodhisattvas, abiding in the stage of the Buddha’s Roar (buddha-ghoṣa), enter the Samādhi of the Dharma-King Throne. Their wisdom is like that of a Buddha because of the Buddha-Roar Samādhi.
Thus, the ten grades of the Great Illumination Gate of Emptiness (śūnyatā) are constantly manifest before them, as is the Flower-Light Sound (Puṣpa-prabhā-svara).

Entering the samādhi of the mind. As for the wisdom of emptiness, it refers to the gate of internal emptiness-wisdom, the gate of external emptiness-wisdom, the gate of conditioned emptiness-wisdom, the gate of unconditioned emptiness-wisdom, the gate of essential emptiness-wisdom, the gate of beginningless emptiness-wisdom, the gate of ultimate truth emptiness-wisdom, the gate of emptiness-of-emptiness wisdom, the gate of emptiness-of-emptiness-and-further-emptiness wisdom, and the gate of emptiness-of-emptiness-of-emptiness-and-further-emptiness wisdom. It is as follows:

These are the ten gates of emptiness. Each of the lower stages is unaware of them. In the stage of the equality of empty space, which is unspeakably unspeakable, one employs the supernatural powers and the wisdom of the path;
with the wisdom of a single thought-moment, one knows all phenomena in their distinct and particular differences, yet enters into immeasurable Buddha-lands.
Before each Buddha, one receives and accepts the Dharma, turning the wheel of the Dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
Bestowing the medicine of the Dharma upon all sentient beings, they act as great Dharma masters and great guides;
having destroyed the four māras, their Dharma bodies are fully perfected, and through continuous transformation, they enter the Buddha-realm.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha’s disciple" indicate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages, thereby clarifying the mind of superior progress.
Regarding "the stage of the essence-nature of the Buddha’s roar": this Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma without fear, being equal and without distinction from the roar of the Great Teacher;
therefore, it is called the stage of the essence-nature of the Buddha’s roar. In other sutras, it is named the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*). This Bodhisattva [shares] the Buddha-mind...
The thought of grasping and the thought of nirvana do not arise at all; therefore, it is called the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).
Regarding the phrase "entering the samādhi of the rank of the Dharma King," this reveals the dharma-gate that has been realized. "Entering" means to realize and enter.

The Bodhisattva realizes and enters the unsurpassed noble wisdom of self-awakening (*anuttara-svayambhū-jñāna*) and the precious throne of the Great Bliss Samādhi of the Dharma King among all dharmas.
Having mastery over phenomena, whether emerging from or entering into them, the mind remains constantly in meditative concentration; hence it is called the "Samādhi of the Dharma-King’s Station.
As for "his wisdom is like that of a Buddha": when he enters the Samādhi of the Dharma-King above, this is the unexcelled Nirvāṇa realized, which is the collection of principles of the Dharmakāya.
His wisdom being like that of a Buddha refers to the unexcelled Bodhi realized, which is the Sambhogakāya.
The "mass of wisdom" refers to the Buddha’s Roar Samādhi (*buddhagarjita-samādhi*), wherein the Dharma-body and Reward-body are undivided and the three bodies manifest perfectly.
From this, subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) arises to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings; this is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the mass of merit.

As for the ten stages of the Great Illumination Gate of Emptiness being ever present before one: it means that this Bodhisattva has attained the realization of the Tathāgata’s three bodies in perfect clarity and the four wisdoms (*catur-jñāna*).
Fully manifesting the ten stages, the great illumination of the gate of wisdom of emptiness is constantly present before one, neither identical with nor separate from it.
As for the Samādhi of Entering the Heart through the Flower-Light Sound, this clarifies the meaning of the Buddha’s roar. "Flower" refers to the flower of practice.
The virtue of maturing beings: "Light" refers to the light of wisdom that shatters the obstructions of others; "Sound" refers to the sound of the Dharma that dispels the delusions of others.
"Entering the mind" means that by means of the practice of wisdom and the sound of the Dharma, these enter the minds of sentient beings, whereby they attain perfect enlightenment.

Therefore it is said: "The Flower-Light Sound Enters the Mind Samādhi. As for its "Wisdom of Emptiness," this refers to the meaning that the ten categories of Great Illumination Wisdom of Emptiness are constantly present before one.
What are these ten categories? The first is the Gate of Internal Emptiness Wisdom (*adhyātma-śūnyatā-prajñā-mukha*).

This refers to the emptiness of the internal roots, consciousnesses, and elements of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Sentient beings are deluded regarding this gate of wisdom and falsely identify with the four [great elements].

Conditioned by the provisional conjunction [of causes], one falsely identifies the characteristics of one's own body as the mark of the self, and falsely recognizes the reflected images of the six sense-objects as the mark of one's own mind.

This serves as the gateway to the root of birth-and-death and the gateway to delusive thoughts and afflictions. The Bodhisattva constantly uses wisdom to directly illuminate the five aggregates of body and mind;
seeing that they are entirely empty in their very substance and are all like illusions and dreams, he is thus able to realize and enter the gate of internal emptiness.
Furthermore, there are two aspects. Second is the gate of the wisdom of external emptiness (*bāhya-śūnyatā-prajñā-mukha*).

This refers to external emptiness—the mountains, rivers, lands, and all phenomena such as the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*)—which ordinary beings do not realize are all manifestations of the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*). They grasp at them through deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), being driven and displaced by external conditions;
thus, these become gates of names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*) and gates of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*). Bodhisattvas constantly use wisdom to illuminate and shatter these six [objects].

All dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, one attains entry into the gateway of wisdom regarding external emptiness. Third is the gateway of wisdom regarding conditioned emptiness (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

This refers to the general emptiness of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): all conditioned phenomena—both the internal faculties and consciousnesses and the external world—belong to the conditioned.
Sentient beings, not knowing that these are illusory and unreal, cling to "self" and "what belongs to self."
One cannot attain liberation; it serves as a gateway for the cyclic flow of birth and death. Bodhisattvas constantly use wisdom to illuminate and shatter all internal and external phenomena.
Since they arise through conditions like illusions and possess no inherent nature (*svabhāva*), they are able to realize and enter the gateway of the wisdom of conditioned emptiness.
Fourth is the gateway of the wisdom of unconditioned emptiness, which is the ultimate truth of emptiness. All unconditioned phenomena [are realized by] the two vehicles...
Such people do not realize that form is itself emptiness and existence is itself non-existence;

yet these qualities of form, emptiness, existence, and non-existence all belong to the realm of duality and constitute a narrow and inferior gateway. The Bodhisattva, by means of profound wisdom, clearly perceives the unconditioned Dharma.

These, too, are all empty; thus one attains entry into the gate of the wisdom of unconditioned emptiness (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā-prajñā-mukha*). Fifth is the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā-prajñā-mukha*):
it holds that both natures, conditioned and unconditioned, are entirely empty. This means that while ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) cling to existence, the Tathāgata says they do not exist;
while those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayānika*) sink into emptiness, the Tathāgata says they are not empty. It is by virtue of this non-existence that there is existence.
This is wondrous existence; it is empty while not being empty, and this is true emptiness. It is the gate of conformity.
By means of this profound prajñā-wisdom, the bodhisattva illuminates the dharma-realm, wherein phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused and all are without obstruction.
Since the two natures are empty and quiescent, and are equal and impartial, one attains entry into the gate of the wisdom of essential emptiness. Sixth: from the beginningless...
The Gate of the Wisdom of Emptiness refers to the afflictions of the dwelling-place (āśraya-sthiti-kleśa), which are beginningless ignorance. They originally have no root;
because of this ignorance, non-awakening suddenly arises. The bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds cannot comprehend this, as it constitutes the gate of arising and ceasing.
Bodhisattvas, by means of the illumination of great wisdom, shine light upon all dharmas and give rise to the characteristics of that which is beginningless.

The characteristic of extinction has no end; at the juncture of arising and ceasing, no dharma can be apprehended. Thus, one attains entry into the gate of the wisdom of beginningless emptiness (*anādikāla-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Seventh is the gate of the wisdom of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā-jñāna*), which is the principle of the Middle Way and is named the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
This name is provisionally established in relation to the second meaning as the gate of the supreme truth (*agryārtha*). By means of this suchness (*tathatā*), the Bodhisattva...
When wisdom and discernment illuminate the gate of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), all things are identical with true nature;

no marks can be apprehended. One does not abide in the two extremes, nor does one maintain a middle way. Thus, one attains entry into the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā-prajñā*).

Eighth is the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-prajñā*): this refers to the emptiness of the aforementioned emptiness of the ultimate meaning, serving as the gate of "emptiness of emptiness. The Bodhisattva, [thereby...]

By means of the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-jñāna*), one illuminates this very emptiness so that it, too, does not persist; thus, one attains entry into the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of emptiness.
Ninth is the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness. This refers to the emptiness upon emptiness—the emptiness of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
It constitutes the gate of the "emptiness of the double emptiness. By means of this wisdom of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness, the Bodhisattva illuminates this emptiness.
Emptiness is also empty; thus one attains entry into the gate of wisdom that is the emptiness of emptiness, which is further empty.

Tenth is the gate of the wisdom of the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness, which is further empty. This refers to the emptiness within emptiness, and the emptiness of that which is further emptied.
This is called the ultimate gate of the emptiness of all emptinesses, which is further emptied. This emptiness, too, should be emptied, for by this there is no emptiness.
This emptiness is an emptiness that has nothing to be emptied; it is thus the emptiness of non-apprehension.

Therefore, one attains entry into the wisdom-gate of the emptiness of emptiness, and further, the emptiness of the emptiness of emptiness. These ten wisdom-gates of emptiness are realized only in this eighth stage (*bhūmi*);
they are unknown to the bodhisattvas of the lower stages. As for the phrase "the stage of the equality of empty space," this refers to the level.
This classification serves to manifest their virtues. It refers to that which those on the lower stages are each unable to know:

namely, that these Bodhisattvas have attained the wisdom-ground of the equality of space, which is not limited to the ten voids alone, but further comprises unspeakably unspeakable gateways of the wisdom of supernatural powers and paths; yet even the Bodhisattvas of the lower stages remain unable to know them.
"Shen" (Spirit) means that it is wondrous and difficult to fathom. "Tong" (Pervasion) means that its transformations are unimpeded.
"Dao" (Way) refers to the principle that is difficult to exhaust. "Zhi" (Wisdom) refers to wisdom that is immeasurable. What is called the Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space;
responding to things by manifesting forms, it is like the moon reflected in water. All such various spiritual powers, ways, and wisdoms are entirely equal; therefore, by means of this one...
With mindfulness and wisdom, they fully comprehend all phenomena, both defiled and pure, distinguishing their various differences.
According to the faculties [of beings], they bestow gifts and provide guidance, while further entering immeasurable Buddha-lands to serve the Buddhas before each and every one of them.
They receive and listen to the Dharma with courageous diligence, and further turn the non-retrogressive wheel of Dharma.
They deliver all sentient beings by bestowing the medicine of the Dharma upon them; for this reason, they are great Dharma masters and great guides who destroy the four māras.
Once the four māras are destroyed, the Dharma-body is perfected, and through the perfection of the Dharma-body—
Therefore, they are able to transform one another in succession, entering the realm of the Buddhas.
Among the ranks of these Buddhas and within the stages of the ninth and tenth bhūmis, they nurture the Dharma-body through hundreds of thousands of *dhāraṇī* gates,
hundreds of thousands of samādhi gates, hundreds of thousands of *vajra* gates, hundreds of thousands of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) gates, and hundreds of thousands of liberations.
The Gate of Liberation. Thus, within hundreds of thousands of such gates of equality with empty space, he exercises great mastery.

In a single thought-moment, at one time, he traverses eons as if they were not eons, and what is not an eon he describes as an eon; what is not the Path he describes as the Path, and the Path he describes as not the Path;

those who are not beings of the six realms he describes as beings of the six realms, and beings of the six realms he describes as not beings of the six realms; and what is not a Buddha he describes as... [a Buddha].

The Buddha. The Buddha speaks of non-Buddha. He enters and emerges from the Samādhi of the Essential Nature of all Buddhas, performing retro-reflection, forward-reflection, reverse-reflection, anterior-reflection, posterior-reflection, causal-reflection, resultant-reflection, reflection on emptiness, reflection on existence, and reflection on the ultimate truth of the primary Middle Way.
This wisdom is realized only in the eighth stage; it is beyond the reach of lower stages. It is immovable, unattainable, non-emergent, non-entering, unborn, and unceasing.

This clarifies abiding in the mind of immediate succession (*ānantarya-citta*). Regarding "being of the same number as all Buddhas," it means that this Bodhisattva is reckoned among the ranks of all Buddhas.

Within the ranks of the Ninth and Tenth Stages (*bhūmi*), they nurture the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and thereby attain hundreds of thousands of gates of *dhāraṇī* retention, hundreds of thousands of gates of samādhi and right concentration, and hundreds of thousands of adamantine [powers].
The gate of destruction; the hundreds of thousands of gates of supernatural transformations;

the hundreds of thousands of gates of liberative skillful means—within such hundreds of thousands of diverse Dharma-gates, one attains great mastery within the gate of the equality of space. What is meant by "mastery"?
It is because one is able to practice them all within a single thought-moment and at a single time. As the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "Without moving from Bodhi..."

The King of the Second Dhyāna attains a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) that is eternally sovereign; he is able to manifest in accordance with the various forms of sentient beings across ten million dust-mote lands.
He fully knows the immeasurable kalpas of the three periods of time, yet remains eternally unmoved within the ultimate truth (paramārtha). This is it.
Regarding the statement "kalpas are said to be non-kalpas," etc., this clarifies the meaning of sovereignty; it means that what is called a kalpa is not [truly] a kalpa.

Regarding "kalpa" and "non-kalpa explained as kalpa": in Sanskrit, *kalpa* (劫波羅) means "time-period" (*kāla-bhāga*). It is said that there are large and small kalpas, and long and short kalpas, as their time-periods differ.
For example, the gods have the "stone-removal kalpa," the hells have the "mustard-seed-in-a-city kalpa," and the human realm has the "pulley-wheel kalpa.
When a Bodhisattva’s cultivation reaches its ultimate completion, they pass through three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Only when the kalpas have exhausted ignorance does one finally attain Buddhahood; this is what is called a "kalpa.

Such kalpas as these are fundamentally not substantially existent, and are thus called "non-kalpas. Therefore, it is said: "A kalpa is spoken of as a non-kalpa, and a non-kalpa is spoken of as a kalpa.
Regarding "speaking of the non-path as the path, and speaking of the path as the non-path": because one creates various karmas of evil and false views, it is so called.
It is not the Way. Because one cultivates the ten wholesome practices and the Dharma of the Bodhi-path, it is called the "Way. In contrast to what is not the Way, one speaks of the "Right Way";
because of the Right Way, one speaks of what is not the Way. Yet, when seeking the Right Way and that which is not the Way, neither can be found at all.
Therefore, it is said: "The non-Way speaks of the Way; the Way speaks of the non-Way. The six realms are the mundane; they are not the six realms [of the enlightened].

They are themselves the holy ones. Because of ordinary beings, one speaks of the holy; because of the holy, one speaks of ordinary beings. Thus, in the ultimate sense, the characteristics of ordinary and holy beings cannot be found at all.
Therefore it is said: "Not being beings of the six realms, they are called beings of the six realms; they are beings of the six realms."
It is said that these are not the sentient beings of the six realms. Demons and heterodox teachers are themselves the Buddha; the Buddha is himself demons and heterodox teachers.

Whether in the realm of demons or the realm of Buddhas, if one seeks their distinct essences, they cannot be found. Therefore it is said: "That which is not the Buddha speaks as the Buddha; the Buddha speaks as that which is not the Buddha."
In this manner, within the realm of the empty nature of reality—the sphere of equality—there is no extension or contraction, no good or evil, no sage or ordinary person, and no Māra or Buddha.

At one moment all are affirmed; at another moment all are negated. Whether acting contrary to the way or in accordance with it, whether speaking contrarily or in accordance with it, there is nothing that is not a skillful means and nothing that is not the work of the Buddha. This is what is meant by "either being so, or not being so."
People do not recognize this; whether moving against or with the flow, even the heavens cannot fathom it.

To enter and emerge from the samādhi of the essential nature of all Buddhas refers to this Bodhisattva: whether entering or emerging, whether hidden or manifest, they never depart from the samādhi of the essential nature of all Buddhas, having attained great mastery. This is elucidated through the following ten kinds of wisdom-illumination.
Entering and emerging from the samādhi of the essence-nature of all Buddhas, regarding the meaning of the inconceivable realm:

as for "reflecting back," "reflecting forward," and "reflecting in reverse"—"reflecting back" refers to reflecting upon the primordial state: how is it that one follows the flow of ignorance (*avidyā*), goes against the principle of *tathatā*, and gives rise to all defiled phenomena?
Furthermore, how is it that one follows the principle of *tathatā*, goes against the flow of ignorance, and gives rise to [all pure phenomena]?

All phenomena are pure dharmas; therefore, it is said that they "reflect back," and so forth. Regarding "prior illumination," "subsequent illumination," "illumination as cause," and "illumination as fruit":

"prior illumination" refers to the cause of suffering, which is the non-awakening of beginningless ignorance; "subsequent illumination" refers to the fruit of suffering, which is the bondage of karma through birth after birth in saṃsāra.

Furthermore, "prior illumination" refers to the cause of bliss, which is initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*); "subsequent illumination" refers to fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) in its ultimate state.

This is the fruit of bliss. Therefore, it is said: "The preceding [refers to] illumination and so forth. Illumination of emptiness, illumination of existence, and illumination of the ultimate truth of the primary Middle Way:
"Illumination of emptiness" means illuminating the True [Dharmadhātu] and being free from all marks; "illumination of existence" means illuminating the conventional, which is all phenomena.

Therefore, it illuminates the true as not truly existent, and it illuminates the conventional as not conventionally existent. It does not abide in either of the two extremes, nor is it established as a middle way.
It is free from both identity and difference; thus it is called the "illumination of the ultimate truth of the primary Middle Way. Such are the ten modes of intellectual illumination.
This is realized only in the eighth stage; the bodhisattvas in the lower stages each fail to reach it. Why?
It is because the *tathatā* (suchness) realized by these bodhisattvas is unmoving and unarriving, for they are free from the characteristics of movement and arrival.

They neither emerge nor enter, for they are free from the characteristics of emergence and entry. They are neither born nor extinguished, for they are free from the characteristics of birth and extinction. Regarding this...
This wisdom definitively illuminates both the object of illumination and the illuminator; they are simultaneously quiescent.
This is the section on the Dharma-gate of the Grounds, immeasurable and immeasurable, unspeakable and unspeakable.
Now, I shall briefly open up but a single hair-tip’s worth of the hundreds of thousands of divisions within these Grounds, as was already clarified in the section on the Arhats.
This summary reveals all the qualities realized, thereby clarifying the liberation of the mind.
Regarding the phrase "these dharma-gates of the stage" and so forth: it means that all the dharma-gates realized by this bodhisattva are immeasurable and immeasurable;
they are unspeakable and unspeakable categories of dharmas, without limit, and beyond the reach of verbal expression. Now, they are briefly explained.
Among the hundreds of thousands of millions of merits within the [Buddha] ground, this is merely a matter equivalent to the tip of a single hair;
it is explained briefly here. This meaning has already been clarified within the *Arhat-parivarta* of the Great Treatise (*Mahā-śāstra*).
Section Nine: The Ground of the Flower Ornament’s Essential Nature (2). Part One: Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization; Part Two: Correctly Explaining the Meaning of the Text.
Part One: Clarifying the Meaning of Abandonment and Realization.
The Bodhisattvas on this stage eliminate one type of obstacle to the desire to practice (*anabhirati-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*).

This refers specifically to a portion of the innate clinging to phenomena (*sahaja-dharma-grāha*) within the cognitive obstacles (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*), which arises from a lack of diligence in performing activities for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings; therefore, it is so named.
Furthermore, they eliminate two types of deluded attachments: first, the delusion regarding dhāraṇīs; and second, the lack of mastery over eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Foolishness. These three dharmas can obstruct the ninth stage. Only by severing these delusive obstructions does one ascend to the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (*sādhumatī*).
This means that this bodhisattva now attains ten kinds of unimpeded intellectual application (*jñānaprayoga*) which manifest before them; among all forms of knowledge, these are the most preeminent.
Because these intellectual applications are unimpeded, they are able to sever delusive obstructions forever. Once the obstructions have been severed, one is able to transform the pure...
He purifies the great wheel of the Dharma; thus, because he skillfully employs his wisdom, it is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī*).

The *tathatā* realized therein is named the *tathatā* of mastery over knowledge (*jñāna-vaśitā-tathatā*), meaning that within this *tathatā*, the function of wisdom is sovereign, as it serves as the basis for the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*).
The Bodhisattva, occupying the station of the celestial king of the third dhyāna, acts as the lord of a medium chiliocosm.
Using the Dharma of the One Vehicle, he transforms and guides sentient beings. Among the ten *pāramitās*, the *bala-pāramitā* (perfection of power) is the most supreme.
Second, the correct explanation of the meaning of the text.

If, O sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattvas abide in the stage of the Essential Nature Adorned by the Buddha-flowers, they manifest the majestic deportment of the Buddha and the Sovereign King Samādhi of the Tathāgata.

Entering and emerging from this sovereign concentration at no fixed time, they simultaneously attain Buddhahood and turn the wheel of Dharma throughout the ten directions—in the three thousandfold world systems, across ten billion suns and moons, and ten billion sets of four continents—up until their final parinirvāṇa; such is the nature of all Buddhas.

With a single mind, he simultaneously manifests for all sentient beings all manner of physical bodies, the eighty minor marks and thirty-two major signs, sovereign bliss, and a splendor equal to space, adorned with the marks and signs of immeasurable great compassion.
He is neither deva nor human, nor does he belong to the six realms; yet, transcending all dharmas, he constantly traverses the six realms, manifesting in infinite ways.
With an immeasurable body, immeasurable speech, and immeasurable mind, he expounds immeasurable Dharma-gates. He is able to turn the realm of Māra and enter the realm of the Buddha;
from the realm of the Buddha, he enters the realm of Māra. Furthermore, he turns all views and enters the view of the Buddha;

from the view of the Buddha, he enters all views. The Buddha-nature enters the nature of sentient beings; the nature of sentient beings enters the Buddha-nature. The radiance of that ground shines with light; wisdom shines with wisdom.
Blazing radiance, blazing radiance! Fearlessness, the immeasurables, the ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, liberation, nirvana, and the unconditioned, singular path of purity.
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" indicate the name, virtue, and rank [of the stage], thereby clarifying the mind of superior progress.

Regarding "the Flower Adornment (Avataṃsaka) nature-ground of the Buddha": this refers to the realized realm of this Bodhisattva, which is equal to and without distinction from the adornments of the Buddha.

"Flower" refers to the flowers of the myriad practices; "adornment" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. This means that by cultivating the causal flowers of the myriad practices, one adorns the fruit of Buddhahood of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

In other sutras, this stage is named the "Stage of Excellent Wisdom" (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*). Because this Bodhisattva skillfully enters the lineage of all Buddhas and skillfully employs the Buddhas' equal great wisdom (*samatā-mahājñāna*), it is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom. Regarding the phrase "with the majestic deportment of a Buddha," it is precisely...

This clarifies the function of the excellent wisdom of the *Avataṃsaka*’s essential nature. This Bodhisattva’s physical appearance and demeanor are identical to those of a Buddha, without duality or distinction.

Possessing a majestic presence that inspires awe, he subdues all Māras and restrains all non-Buddhists; this is through the gate of refutation (*pratisedha*), by which he transforms and guides sentient beings.

Possessing a dignified bearing worthy of contemplation, he enlightens devas and humans and leads the multitudes of living beings; this is through the gate of inclusion (*saṃgraha*), by which he transforms [them].
He guides sentient beings by means of the Buddha’s majestic deportment; this is transforming and benefiting sentient beings amidst movement.
By means of the Tathāgata’s Sovereign King Samādhi, he transforms and benefits sentient beings amidst stillness. "Tathā" (Thus) signifies original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*);

"āgata" (Come) signifies initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). Because initial and original enlightenment are non-dual, it is further said that there is nowhere from which he comes, and no place to which he goes.
Wherever he goes, there is no coming and no going; therefore, he is named "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One).

Regarding the term "Sovereign King," since "king" carries the meaning of "sovereignty," the phrase "the king’s entry and exit are certainly without fixed time" clarifies the meaning of the sovereign's essence and function (*tǐyòng*) to manifest the *dharmakāya*, which is able to manifest the realm of the *saṃbhogakāya*. Whether this Bodhisattva moves or remains still, whether he comes or goes...
Whether sitting or reclining, throughout all four modes of deportment, he enters and emerges from the Tathāgata’s Samādhirāja-samādhi at no fixed time.
This is what is meant by "speaking in silence" and "silence while speaking"; the Great Gate of Giving is opened wide without obstruction.

Regarding the phrase "the three thousandfold worlds of the ten directions," this serves to reveal that both the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body) and the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (emanation body) do not depart from the realm of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). Indeed...
The Dharma-body pervades all places, just like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water.

Because this Dharma-body is formless and signless, yet is able to manifest in form, it simultaneously manifests the attainment of Buddhahood throughout the ten directions, within the three thousandfold world systems, amidst the ten billion suns and moons and the ten billion sets of four continents. Simultaneously...
He manifests the turning of the wheel of the True Dharma; at one time he manifests the liberation of sentient beings, and even at one time he manifests entry into *nirvāṇa*.
All such various Buddha-activities are manifested simultaneously before all sentient beings within a single thought-moment, neither before nor after. All the *dharmakāyas* thus manifested...
Possessing the eighty minor marks and the thirty-two major signs, it is sovereign great bliss, identical to empty space.
It is fully endowed with immeasurable great compassion, immeasurable radiance, immeasurable marks and signs, and immeasurable adornments.

It is neither deva nor human, nor does it belong to the six realms of existence. What kind of realm is this? It is precisely all phenomena, beyond the sphere of the two truths, and does not fall [into any category].
As for their number: though they are not devas, they manifest as devas; though they are not humans, they manifest as humans;

and so on, even though they do not possess the bodies of the six realms of existence, they are able to constantly traverse the six paths. They simply manifest infinite bodies, infinite mouths, and infinite minds, preaching infinite categories of Dharma-doors according to the various differences in what sentient beings see and hear, appearing in accordance with their capacities. It is because of this.
Through the wondrous function of the three wheels, one is able to immediately transform the realm of Māra and enter the realm of the Buddha;
or transform the realm of the Buddha and enter the realm of Māra; or transform all views and enter the view of the Buddha; or transform the view of the Buddha and enter all views;
or transform the nature of sentient beings and enter the Buddha-nature; and further, transform the Buddha-nature and enter the nature of sentient beings. It is like this.
These various transformations possess no dual characteristics. Furthermore, they do not cease within these realms.
In that stage, the light of wisdom shines; light illumines light, and wisdom illumines wisdom, mutually examining all phenomena without end.
As for "light illumining light," it means that light and light illuminate one another, because wisdom is able to illuminate objects. As for "wisdom illumining wisdom," it refers to wisdom...

It illuminates in mutual resonance with wisdom, for wisdom is able to comprehend objects. "Brilliantly blazing, brilliantly blazing" refers to the majestic and fierce aspect of wisdom, which destroys all that is knowable because it leaves no trace or sign.
"Fearless" means that this wisdom is without obstruction. "Immeasurable" means that this wisdom is uninterrupted.
Because this light does not belong to the sphere of objective conditions, it is the fundamental radiance of wisdom.
Because these qualities are gathered therein, it is said to be "fearless and immeasurable. Regarding the phrase "the ten powers, etc.," this extends the previous statement;

it means that this Bodhisattva not only attains radiant light, but further attains the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), and so forth, as well as realizing liberation, nirvāṇa, and the pure, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) single path.
This is the principle: what is called the light of wisdom illuminates the immeasurable, and skillful means are inexhaustible.
Thus, one regards all sentient beings as one's own parents and siblings, preaching the Dharma for them until the end of all kalpas so that they may attain the fruits of the Way.
Furthermore, one manifests bodies in all lands, regarding all sentient beings as one would look upon one's own father or mother.
Regarding celestial Māras and followers of external paths, they regard one another as fathers and mothers;

this clarifies abiding in the mind of non-interruption. It manifests the Bodhisattva’s great kindness, great compassion, great vows, and the power of great aspiration, whereby all sentient beings of the ten directions, the four modes of birth, and the six realms are treated as parents, and their debt of gratitude is repaid.

One should conceive the thought of being brothers and supporting one another. Through various skillful means, one preaches the Dharma for them until the end of all kalpas, ensuring that they both attain the fruits of the Path;
only then is the Bodhisattva’s original vow to save sentient beings fully realized.

This is the remote causal condition for the gate of inferior practice, as it accords with the capacities and needs of sentient beings of middling and lower faculties. Furthermore, one manifests in all lands...

Regarding the characteristics of the earthen body: it is intended so that all sentient beings may regard one another as fathers and mothers, and furthermore, so that celestial Māras and followers of external paths may likewise regard one another as fathers and mothers.
This is the proximate cause and condition for the Gate of Honored and Exalted Practice, for it accords with the capacities and needs of sentient beings of superior faculties.
Abiding in this stage, from the limit of birth and death up to the adamantine limit,

one manifests such events within a single thought-moment and is able to enter into the realms of immeasurable sentient beings. Such immeasurability is, briefly stated, like a single drop of water in the ocean.
This clarifies the meaning of the liberated mind. It concludes the merits of this stage by stating that it is inconceivable.
Regarding the phrase "one who dwells in this stage," this cites the person to manifest their virtues.

This Bodhisattva, dwelling in this stage, begins from the limit of the cycle of birth and death arising from the non-awakening of ignorance, and proceeds until reaching the ultimate limit of the diamond wheel of fundamental awakening. Within this...

Within that interval, all phenomena of the mundane and the sagely, of delusion and awakening, of defilement and purity, and of the causes and effects of cultivation and severance—all such diverse dharma-gates—are manifested within a single thought-moment, as briefly as a finger-snap.
Thus, he is able to enter into immeasurable realms of sentient beings to bring them to liberation; such [realms] are infinite and boundless.
The characteristics of his inconceivable merits shall be explained briefly: they are like a single drop of water from a hair-tip compared to the waters of the great ocean.
Part Two: The Ten Essential Natures Entering the Stage of the Buddha-Domain. I. Clarifying the Meaning of Severance and Realization. II. The Direct Explanation of the Text.
Meaning. ○ First, the meaning of abandonment and realization is clarified.
In this stage, the Bodhisattva abandons one type of obstacle to the lack of mastery; this is the portion of the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that is concomitant with the mind.

It gives rise to the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). It is produced by the sovereign power of a portion of the flavor of the Dharma (*dharmarasa*), and it can obstruct the great cloud of wisdom and the activities arising therefrom from manifesting before one; therefore, it is so named. It simultaneously severs two kinds of deluded grasping. The first is:
First is the delusion regarding the manifestation of great supernatural powers; second is the delusion regarding the subtle and secret. These three factors can obstruct the ten stages (*bhūmi*).

Only by severing these delusional obstructions can one ascend to the Stage of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), where the Bodhisattva’s *dharmakāya* is perfected, their innate wisdom is purified, both emptiness and existence are forgotten, and they fully realize the principle of the Middle Way. Once these delusional obstructions have been severed, [all afflictions are exhausted].
Therefore, the clouds of wisdom pervade the entire Dharma-realm and rain down the great rain of the Dharma, fully satisfying all withered sentient beings;
hence it is named the "Dharma-Cloud" stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*). The *tathatā* realized therein is called the "Tathatā of Sovereignty over Karma.
Because all karmic afflictions have attained complete liberation and are in accord with the principle of *tathatā*, the Bodhisattva takes the four *dhyānas* as their provisional station.
O Heavenly King, as the sovereign of the great trichiliocosm, you expound the Dharma of the One Vehicle to transform and guide sentient beings.
Among the ten pāramitās, the pāramitā of wisdom is the most supreme; all other pāramitās and all merits reach complete fulfillment and perfection upon arriving here.
II. Correct Explanation of the Textual Meaning (2): A. First, Clarifying the Virtues of Realization; B. Second, Concluding Praise of the Dharma Gate.
A. First, Clarifying the Virtues of Realization:
O Sons of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva enters the stage of the fundamental nature of the Buddha-realm, their great wisdom is empty, empty, and again empty.
Emptiness is further emptiness, like the nature of empty space. It is the wisdom of equality; it possesses the Tathāgata-nature, fully endowed with the ten qualities of merit.

Emptiness has a single characteristic; its essence is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Its spirit is void and its substance is one; phenomena are identical to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is called the Tathāgata.

One should accord with the Four Truths and the Two Truths, exhausting the limits of the wheel of birth and death. Since the Dharma-sustenance and the Dharma-body are non-dual, this is called "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

Because one possesses right knowledge and noble liberating wisdom that pervades all worlds and all phenomena, knowing the existence and non-existence of all dharmas and the faculties of all sentient beings, this is "Perfectly Complete Knowledge" (Samyaksaṃbuddha). This is the clear and luminous cultivation at the stage of Buddhahood.

Because he is endowed with these, he is the One Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct (vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna). The Sugata’s teachings on the three times are the same as those of the Buddhas of former times.
A Buddha is "Sugata" because he goes well and comes well; thus he is named Sugata. This person, practicing such supreme virtue, enters into the world.
He transforms and educates sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from all fetters and bonds; therefore, he is called the "Liberator of the World.
This person, standing above all dharmas, enters the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha; his physical demeanor is like that of a Buddha.

As a Great Being who dwells in the sphere of practice, he acts as the Liberator of the World, taming and harmonizing all sentient beings; thus he is named a "Great Man" (Puruṣa). Among devas and humans, he transforms and educates them all.
Because sentient beings consult and receive his words of Dharma, he is the Teacher of Gods and Humans. His wondrous fundamental nature is non-dual;
the Buddha-nature is profound awakening, eternally and fully perfected. Because all sentient beings prostrate to him and revere him, he is the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Because all people in the world consult him, receive his teachings, and honor them, this is the Buddha-ground—the place entered by all sages within that ground.
Therefore, it is called the Stage of the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu-bhūmi*).
The three phrases beginning with "If a Buddha-son" designate and manifest the names, virtues, and stages, thereby clarifying the mind of supreme progress.

Regarding "entering the essential nature-ground of the Buddha-realm": this refers to all the treasuries of merit consisting of the principles, wisdom, practices, and vows realized by this Bodhisattva.

This is identical and without distinction from the realm realized by the Buddhas of the ten directions; therefore, it is called the Ground of Entering the Essential Nature of the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dhātu-svabhāva-bhūmi*).

In another sutra, it is named the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (*dharma-meghā-bhūmi*). Because the Bodhisattva manifests clouds of boundless bodies and pours down the rain of boundless teachings, it is called the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud.
The phrase "that great wisdom, emptiness, and so forth" clarifies the entry into the Buddha-realm.
This is to manifest abiding in the uninterrupted mind. That which is the Great Wisdom of Emptiness is precisely the emptiness above;

it is the gate of wisdom wherein emptiness is further emptied by emptiness. Since that emptiness is already empty, even emptiness itself is again empty. Such emptiness is like the nature of space, equal and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
This is the Great Perfect and Stainless, the ultimate perfection of the accumulation of principle; it is precisely the realm of the Dharmakāya.
The Dharma-body is without marks and is equal throughout the ten directions; therefore it is said: "Its great wisdom is empty;

emptiness is also empty; emptiness is also empty. This is precisely the nature of empty space. As for the Wisdom of Equality, that which possesses the Tathāgata-nature is the Wisdom of Equality itself.
When the accumulation of wisdom is perfectly luminous, this is the realm of the Saṃbhogakāya (Reward Body). By means of this Reward Body...

One realizes the Dharma-body; hence it is said that there is the Tathāgata-nature. That which is "endowed with the ten merits" is precisely the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
When the accumulation of merits is fully perfected, this is the realm of the Nirmāṇakāya (Emanation Body). And as for this Nirmāṇakāya:
It is accomplished through the cultivation of the various *pāramitās*. Therefore, it is said: "The ten qualities (*daśaguṇa*) are fully perfected.

Regarding the phrase "emptiness is identical to the same characteristic" (*śūnyatā-samatā-lakṣaṇa*), this explains the aforementioned "Chapter on the Ten Qualities" in order to clarify that the three bodies (*trikāya*) of the Bodhisattva are perfectly manifested and the ten titles (*daśanāmadheya*) are simultaneously revealed, according to the principle of being neither identical nor separate. What is meant by the "Chapter on the Ten Qualities"? The first is the Tathāgata, who is emptiness.
"Of identical character; its essential nature is unconditioned. These two phrases reveal the fundamental Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Since the Tathāgata of the fundamental Dharma-body comes from nowhere and goes nowhere, he is like space, which lacks any material characteristics such that they can be seen in relation to one another.
Because this essential nature is fundamentally unconditioned and free from volitional activity, it is said to be "identical to emptiness."
The "one mark" refers to this very state of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in its essential nature. "The spirit is void and the substance is one; phenomena are identical to the dharma-nature.
These two phrases reveal the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Response Body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Because the Reward and Response Buddhas possess a spiritual subtlety that is unfathomable, a voidness that is penetrating and numinous, and a responsiveness that pervades the realms of all sands, their essence is no different. Furthermore, the manifested bodies are themselves the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*). This is so.
Because the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are equal and identical, it is said that their spiritual essence is one and their dharmas are the same as the *dharmatā*;
therefore, they are called *Tathāgata*. Second is "Worthy of Offerings" (*Arhat*): this means being worthy of and conforming to the offerings made to the Four Truths and the Two Truths.
Regarding the Four Truths, there are four types of Four Truths: first, for those who are *śrāvakas*, there are the Four Truths of arising and ceasing; second, for those who are *pratyekabuddhas*.
First, those who correspond to the four truths of non-action; second, the three types of bodhisattvas, who correspond to the four truths of non-arising;
third, the Tathāgatas, who correspond to the four truths of the immeasurable. Regarding the two truths, they are the ultimate truth and the conventional truth.

Because the Tathāgata has exhausted the five stages of dwelling, eternally extinguished the two deaths, perfected the myriad practices, and is fully endowed with merit and wisdom, he perfectly corresponds to the four truths.

With offerings of the two truths, until the very end of the wheel of birth and death, one nourishes the Dharma-body through the teachings of the four truths and the two truths within the reality-limit of *tathatā*.
Free from dualistic characteristics, one universally manifests throughout the *dharmadhātu* to benefit all sentient beings.
This is the title "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat). Third is "Perfectly Complete Knower" (Samyaksaṃbuddha). Its meaning has two aspects. First is "complete knowledge":

by means of the correct wisdom that realizes [enlightenment], as well as the wisdom of all noble liberations originally realized, one universally and pervasively covers all realms, thoroughly knowing all phenomena—whether defiled or pure, whether existent or non-existent. All...
The distinctions in the faculties and natures of the noble ones and ordinary beings, as well as the phenomena of dependent origination, are all clearly understood;
this is called "universal knowledge" (*parijñā*). Second is "correct knowledge" (*saṃjñā*), which means knowing that all dharmas are, in their true nature, non-dual.

This is called "right knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*). When these two meanings are combined, it is called "right universal knowledge" (*samyag-saṃbodhi*). Fourth is "the one perfected in knowledge and conduct" (*vidyā-caraṇa-saṃpanna*).

"Knowledge" refers to the three types of supernormal knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*); "conduct" refers to the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*). This means that from the time of first generating the bodhicitta on the causal ground, one awakens through wisdom and practices with increasing clarity.

The myriad practices serve as the flowers of the cause, and the radiance of wisdom serves as the fruit; thus, upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, one possesses the twofold adornment of merit and wisdom.

He is perfectly endowed [with these qualities], which is why he is called the "Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings" (*dvipadottama*). Therefore, it is said: "One Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct" (*vidyācaraṇasampanna*).

Fifth is "Well-Gone" (*sugata*), meaning that he skillfully traverses the three realms, manifesting birth, renunciation, entering the mountains for practice, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and transforming sentient beings, finally manifesting parinirvāṇa. This is the path and dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods of time. The Buddha...
The Buddha-way is identical [to that of the Buddhas of antiquity]. The ritual protocols of the ancient Buddhas are the same as the Dharma of the previous Buddhas.

Regarding the Buddha: when he departs, it is "good and good" (*śaṃ-śaṃ*). He comes in accordance with conditions; he manifests coming by attaining perfect enlightenment, yet in reality, there is no place from which he comes.

His coming and going are auspicious; this is what is meant by "good and good. Sixth is the "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*); this refers to one who, being a person of this stage, is able to practice the supreme "good and good" of all Buddhas.

Virtue. By manifesting this body, he enters into the world and extensively establishes the vehicles of teaching to transform and enlighten sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from the bonds of afflictions, habitual tendencies, and karmic fetters; this is called "liberation in the world.
Seventh is the "Unsurpassed One," meaning a sage who is able, regarding all phenomena, to enter the majestic spiritual power of a Buddha, with a physical demeanor such as [that of a Buddha].
The Buddha is thus the sphere of practice for Great Beings; because he is liberated within all worlds and none can surpass him, he is named the Unsurpassed One (*Anuttara*).
Eighth is the Tamer of Men (*Puruṣadamyasārathi*): "Taming" (*damya*) means to regulate, just as a skilled physician skillfully treats all manner of illnesses;
"taming" (*sārathi*) means to drive or control, just as a skilled charioteer skillfully manages elephants and horses. The World-Honored One is...

He is the King of Physicians for the three realms and the compassionate father of the four modes of birth. He is well able to eliminate the two types of illness—physical and mental—for all sentient beings, causing them to leave suffering behind and attain happiness.
Because he skillfully disciplines and guides them while always acting in accordance with their needs, he is called the "Tamer of Men" (Puruṣadamyasārathi).
Ninth, he is the Teacher of Gods and Humans; that is to say, among the heavens and the human world, he teaches the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of supernatural beings.
In the midst [of the world], he teaches and transforms all sentient beings, enabling each and every one to receive and accept his words of Dharma, to understand them deeply, and to obtain benefit;
thus he is named the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). Tenth is the Buddha, the World-Honored One (*bhagavān*). This refers to the wondrous fundamental non-duality:

that is, the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening (*prakṛti-bodhi*) and the luminous wondrousness of the original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). Because this wondrous fundamental nature-awakening is without duality and without marks, it is the profound Buddha-nature.
Awakening fills the Dharma-realm; it is neither identical with nor separate from it, neither following it nor changing.
It is eternally and immensely full. Within it, the wondrous source is non-dual; this is the Dharmakāya. Buddha-nature and profound awakening are the Sambhogakāya.

Being eternally and immensely full, they are the Nirmāṇakāya. It is also called self-awakening and awakening others. With the perfection of the practice of awakening, the three bodies are fully realized.

When the three types of awakening have reached fulfillment, one is called a Buddha (*buddha*). Because he enables all sentient beings to prostrate and revere him, he is called the World-Honored One (*bhagavat*).
When these two meanings are combined, he is termed the Buddha-World-Honored One. The above clarifies the meaning of the ten titles;
below, the meaning of entering the stage of the Buddha-realm is clarified. "Entering" means to advance into. This refers to, by means of all...

Worldly people consult, receive, and respectfully follow its teachings, single-mindedly taking refuge in it; because there is a path of awakening to which they have returned, this is called the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*).
It is said that this Buddha-ground can increase the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom for all sentient beings, as well as the sprouts of the crop of Bodhi;
therefore, it is named the Buddha-ground. Within this ground is the place entered by all sages; therefore, it is called "Buddha" (*buddha*).
The terms "realm" (*dhātu*) and "ground" (*bhūmi*) are spoken here as a compound of two meanings; thus, it is said at the outset: "entering the Buddha-realm and ground.
The *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "In the dharma-realms of the ten directions, all Tathāgatas rely upon this gate to attain Buddhahood.
If one says that Buddhahood can be attained by transcending this, such is the teaching of the various Māras, not the teaching of the Buddha. Therefore, it says: "All..."
This is the place where the Sages enter and dwell.

○ Second, the concluding praise of the Dharma-gate (in two parts): First, the praise of the principal figures and their retinue from the native land; second, the praise of the principal figures and their retinue from other lands.
Section One: Praise of the Original Land’s Principal and Retinue (in two parts). Part One: The Buddha of the Original Land Bestows Prophecy; Part Two: Praise by the Retinue of the Original Land.
Section One: The Buddha of the Original Land Bestows Prophecy.
At that time, he sat upon a precious lotus flower. All were filled with joy as they received their prophecy of enlightenment. The Dharma-body hand stroked his crown;
this signifies the ultimate perfection and entry into the ocean of the fruit of wondrous awakening, thereby manifesting the mind of liberation.
It is said that "at that time he sat upon a precious lotus flower" refers to Vairocana Buddha and the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas upon the thousand petals of the flower.
The thousands of billions of Śākyamuni Buddhas, as well as all other Buddhas, bestow upon these Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-Cloud Stage the prophecy that they shall attain Buddhahood.
Regarding matters such as the adornments of their future kalpas and lands, they rejoice and leap for joy;
with the hands of the Dharma-body’s pure light-net marks, they all simultaneously stroke the crown of the Bodhisattvas' heads, exhorting them to turn the wheel of the Dharma.
Second, the companions from his own land offer praise.
These bodhisattvas, who share the same vision and the same practice, with one voice and in unison, offer non-dual praise.

They possess the same vision and the same understanding; that is to say, they share the same vision of the *dharmakāya* of *tathatā*, which is the principle of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). They are identical.
"Training" means training under the same teacher; that is, training together in the bodhisattva path and being equally conferred the office of empowerment.
Because they are fellow students in the bodhisattva path, they all, with one voice and in unison, offer praise without duality.
II. Praise by the Lords and Retinues of Other Directions (2): First, the Request to Turn the Wheel of Dharma; Second, the Praise of Supreme Merits. ○ First:
The Request to Turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, from hundreds of thousands of billions of worlds, all Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas gathered like clouds at once,
requesting that the ineffable Dharma-wheel— the Dharma-gate of the transformative guidance of Ākāśagarbha— be turned.
The preceding passage speaks of bestowing predictions (*vyākaraṇa*). This current passage refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas simultaneously requesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
This is precisely because they desire to widely propagate and circulate this Way, so that its transformation may continue unceasingly throughout the heavens and the human realm.
The "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattvas of this stage, by the power of their own vows, give rise to clouds of great compassion and manifest various bodies."
Moving back and forth in a single instant, they pervade the hundreds of billions of nayutas of worlds and lands as numerous as atoms throughout the ten directions,
expounding the Great Dharma and requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, thereby mutually illuminating this meaning.
II. Praising the Supreme Merits:
This stage contains unspeakably many wondrous and marvelous dharma-gate chapters, extraordinary triple-knowledge (*traividya*), doors of samādhi, and doors of dhāraṇī.
These are not known by the mind-consciousness of ordinary beings in lower stages; they are known only by the immeasurable body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas.

One may exhaustively trace its source. As explained in the "Chapter on the Light-Sound Heaven" (*Ābhāsvara-deva-parivarta*), the ten kinds of fearlessness (*daśa-vaiśāradya*) are identical to those of the Buddha-way.
This serves as a summary to manifest the merits of this stage; they are subtle and wondrous, difficult to fathom, extraordinary, and preeminent.
It means that it is not merely that one is fully endowed with the *Gaganagañja* dharma-gate of transformation and guidance, but there is furthermore that which is inconceivable and inexpressible.

The Chapter on Discoursing upon the Wondrous and Vast Dharma Gates: the wondrous gate of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*), the wondrous gate of the power of concentration in samādhi, and the wondrous gate of dhāraṇī-retention.

These various dharma gates cannot be known by the mental consciousnesses of bodhisattvas of the lower stages or of ordinary beings; they are manifested only by Buddhas and Buddhas through immeasurable bodies and speech.
Only with a focused mind can one fully explain its source; that is to say, it can only be known through personal realization and is difficult to fathom.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can exhaustively investigate the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).

The meaning of this passage is the same as what is taught in the "Chapter on the Heaven of Light-Sound" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, regarding the ten fearlessnesses being identical to the Buddha-way. Furthermore—
There is no distinction. This Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground is the realm of experience enjoyed by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the great Bodhisattvas while abiding in their own samādhi.

For us ordinary people of the mundane world, to rely on the texts to explain the meaning and investigate the source of the mind within the ocean of teachings—this is called "arising of concentration through precepts" and "arousing of wisdom through concentration."
Practicing according to the Dharma, they equally realize that within the *samādhi* of the Tathāgata there is no duality of characteristics.
