○ First, the initial formulation explains the Mind-Ground.
At that time, Vairocana Buddha, for the sake of this great assembly, briefly opened up within the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground—
a teaching as vast as the sands of hundreds of thousands of Ganges Rivers— just a space the size of a hair-tip.

This passage introduces the speaker in order to reveal the Dharma being taught. The two characters "at that time" (爾時) signify the moment when the previously explained thirty minds and ten stages have been completed.
Vairocana Buddha is the *vipākakāya* (retribution body), the speaker; he is called "retribution" because he is the result realized through the cultivation of causes.
Furthermore, this *vipākakāya* is both self-referential and other-referential. The self-referential retribution is the principle (*li*).
The wisdom-body of suchness is the body of recompense for others; that is, the inexhaustible body of marks and signs.
This is the saṃbhogakāya, named Rocana Buddha. The Vairocana Buddha described in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra is precisely this Rocana Buddha.

In Sanskrit it is called Vairocana; in the language of China, it means "Pure and Perfect. "Pure" refers to the exhaustion of the five stages of dwelling and the eternal cessation of the two types of death, as all afflictions have been purified and exhausted.
"Perfect" refers to the perfection of the fruit of the three awakenings and the completion of the causes of the ten thousand practices, as merit and wisdom are fully endowed.
This is that which cannot be known by any śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or others; it belongs only to the Buddha and...
This refers to the Buddha’s ability to exhaustively investigate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Thus, in the *Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta* of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Cittarāja asks the Buddha: "What is meant by 'asaṃkhyeya' (incalculable), up to 'unspeakably unspeakable'?
The Buddha then explains for him the infinite, inexhaustible, and immeasurable dharma-gates of calculation, which accumulate to form ten kinds.

It transcends all numerical calculations and shatters all systems of reckoning. Now, within the ground of the mind—the Dharma-gate of the ineffable—I shall briefly explain and reveal it, as a mere fragment of a hair-tip of a phenomenon.
II. Manifesting and Explaining the Mind-Ground (2) A. Citing Others to Validate Oneself B. Citing Oneself to Inspire Faith A.
Citing Others to Validate Oneself:
This has been taught by all Buddhas of the past, will be taught by the Buddhas of the future, and is being taught now by the Buddhas of the present throughout the three periods of time.
"Bodhisattvas have studied, shall study, and are now studying"—this refers to those who have attained the fruit [of the path] in the past;
by citing them as having realized and taught this in common, it encourages faith. "Equal throughout the three periods of time" refers to those who are on the path;
by citing them as having practiced and studied together, it encourages acceptance. As for the phrase "the aforementioned ground of the mind":
Regarding this Dharma gate: although it may be a dharma as minute and subtle as a single hair-tip, its power is exceedingly great.

It is that which the Buddhas of the three periods have realized in their realization and taught in their teachings; it is that which the Bodhisattvas of the three periods have cultivated in their cultivation.

That which is studied is this very thing. Thus, a Great Sūtra says: "Suppose there were a great sūtra scroll, equal in size to the three-thousandfold world system, contained within a single mote of dust.
If there were a person of wisdom who could break open the mote and bring forth the scroll, thereby benefiting all people."
Therefore, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas perform great Buddha-works within the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground, which is as small as a single mote of dust.
Thus, the Lotus Sutra says: "All Buddhas of the past who appeared in the world did so for the sake of one great causal matter;
they appeared in the world to reveal, teach, awaken, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that all..."
Because sentient beings awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,
future Buddhas who appear in the world likewise appear for the sake of this one great causal event, in order to reveal, cause awakening to,

and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that all sentient beings may awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. [The same applies to] those of the present...
The appearance of all Buddhas in the world is likewise for the sake of one great causal matter;

they appear in the world to reveal, cause to awaken to, and lead others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, so that all sentient beings may awaken to the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and enter the path of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
This Buddha’s knowledge and vision is precisely the Dharma-gate of the mind-ground. Therefore, all [Buddhas] of the past...
The Buddhas have already taught it; all future Buddhas shall teach it; and all present Buddhas are teaching it now.
All Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time—those who have passed away have already studied and cultivated it; those yet to come shall study and cultivate it;
and those currently living are studying and cultivating it now. From Buddha to Buddha, from patriarch to patriarch, there are none who do not rely upon this Mind-Ground.
This Dharma gate is the radiant Vajra Jewel Precept. It transmits mind-to-mind through the seal of the mind, continuing from lamp to lamp without end.
(O) Second, [the section on] personal realization and faith.
"I have cultivated this mind-ground for a hundred kalpas; I am named Rocana.
To say "I have cultivated this mind-ground for a hundred kalpas" is to cite the cause to clarify the fruit.
To say "I am named Rocana" is to cite the fruit to clarify the cause. Following the preceding text, it says: "All..."

Since that which all Buddhas have realized, spoken, cultivated, and studied throughout the three periods of time is neither different nor false, how could what I myself now cultivate, study, realize, and speak be false? Therefore it is said: "I have cultivated this for a hundred kalpas," and so forth.
It can be seen that the fruit of realization is fundamentally not caused by anything else; it lies solely within this mind-ground.
II. Entrusting and Exhorting to Turn [the Wheel] (2). A. General Exhortation to Turn and Transform. B. Specific Exhortation to Turn and Transform.
A. General Exhortation to Turn and Transform:
"O sons of the Buddha, you must turn what I have taught and open the path of the bodhisattva for all sentient beings."
This is the meaning of Vairocana, the World-Honored One of Great Compassion, exhorting the thousand Buddhas to turn the Dharma wheel and transform sentient beings.
As for my statement that I have cultivated this "Mind-Ground" for a hundred kalpas, it may be called the profundity of the cause.
My being titled "Vairocana" represents the ultimate fruition. Because of this profundity of cause and ultimacy of fruition—the foremost path—I now transmit it to you.
"You should propagate this 'Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground' which I have taught to you, and explain it to all sentient beings, thereby opening the path of the mind-ground for them.

Since all sentient beings are each fully endowed with this path of the mind-ground and are no different from the Buddhas, the subsequent text states: 'This is the source of all Buddhas, the [source] of all Bodhisattvas...'"
The source of the Bodhisattva, the seed of Buddha-nature; all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature because there is always, at every moment, the ever-present cause.

This is the eternally abiding Dharmakāya. As for what is called "opening the path of the mind-ground," this mind-ground is, from the beginning, free from defilement and stain, without obstruction or hindrance, vast and empty, numinous and wondrous, pure and sovereign.

What is meant by "opening"? That which is called "opening" is spoken in contrast to being "sealed. Because all sentient beings are obstructed by their conscious emotions (*vijñāna*), they are deluded and turn their backs on reality, remaining unaware.
Were it not for a wise person pointing out and revealing [the truth], they would ultimately never be able to perceive the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the Buddhas.
It is like one who is blind: unless a golden probe (*suvarṇa-śalākā*) is used to shift the pupil, one will ultimately never regain sight.

One beholds the myriad phenomena of the universe. It is said that a dark chamber of a thousand years can be dispelled by relying on a lamp; likewise, the afflictions accumulated over kalpas are only eliminated upon attaining wisdom.
II. Specific Exhortation to Convert Others (in two parts): A. Bestowing the Exhortation to Convert Others B. The Order of Bestowing the Exhortation [End of section]
First, regarding the bestowal of the exhortation to turn [the wheel] for the sake of transformation:
At that time, within the Lotus Flower Treasury World, upon the majestic lion throne of celestial light, Vairocana Buddha emitted rays of light.

These lights addressed the Buddhas upon the thousand petals, saying: "Take this 'Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground' and depart. Thereupon, they were further transmitted to the thousands [of Buddhas].
"Billion Śākyamunis and all sentient beings" refers to the environment and its support (*niśraya-vipāka*).
"The brilliant celestial light, etc. refers to the primary retribution (*mūla-vipāka*). "Vairocana emits light" reveals the excellence of the one who proclaims;
"the light proclaims, etc. reveals the excellence of that which is proclaimed. "Sustain us, etc. [refers to the result].
This clearly explains the words addressed [to him]. As for the "lion throne" (*siṃhāsana*): the lion is the king among beasts;

when it roars, all other animals hear it and their brains are split asunder. This symbolizes that the seat upon which the World-Honored One, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, sits is the "seat of fearlessness," and the Dharma he proclaims is the "Dharma of fearlessness. [It is] against the celestial Māras and non-Buddhist paths...
Whether they see or hear it, all lose their composure and are struck with terror. Regarding the statement that "light is emitted" and "the light proclaims," there are two meanings.
First, it refers to the Buddha emitting light and summoning a proclamation from within that light. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One emitted from the crown of his head a hundred-jeweled light of fearlessness. From within the light, there emerged a thousand-petaled jeweled lotus. Therein...
The Buddha’s transformation body sits in the full lotus posture and proclaims a divine mantra; this is the meaning of summoning and addressing from within these rays of light.
Second, it refers to the very light emitted, for the light itself is also capable of addressing others.

This means that not only does the primary retribution body (the physical form) excel at preaching the Dharma, but even the light of the secondary retribution—the lotus flower—is likewise fully capable of preaching the Dharma. As for what is called "secondary retribution":

This is the primary retribution. Constantly proclaiming the wondrous Dharma, the precious nets within the numinous mind-palace—where water flows and wind moves—all expound the meaning of the sounds of the Dharma.
"To uphold my ground of the mind" and so forth means that one desires for the thousand Buddhas to successively transmit it to all sentient beings.

When the thousand Śākyamunis have finished entrusting [the teaching] and exhorting [others] to turn the wheel, they further transform into a thousand times ten million billion Śākyamunis to entrust [the teaching] and exhort [others] to turn the wheel, thereby opening the path of the noble stages for all sentient beings. Therefore, it is said:
"They further transform into a thousand times ten million billion Śākyamunis, as well as for all sentient beings."
Second, the sequential exhortation to bestow [the teaching]:
I shall now explain in order the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Superior Ground of the Mind. You should receive, uphold, read, and recite it, practicing with single-minded devotion.

The phrase "in sequence" (*cibì*) clarifies that this is not an instantaneous teaching. The phrase "you all receive the lower [vehicle]" clarifies that within the gradual approach there is also the instantaneous.

The underlying intent is that while the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cixin*) consists of forty stages, the natures of sentient beings possess varying degrees of capacity—whether great or small, sharp or dull—and the forty-two grades of ignorance (*avidyā*), characterized by arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing, likewise differ in their degree of gravity. Therefore, it is necessary...

I shall now explain in sequence the chapter on the Dharma-gate of the Superior Ground-Mind (Cittabhūmi). As for this sequence: first, the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*) are taught, which are the wondrous principle of true emptiness;

next, the Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*) are taught, which are the wondrous conduct of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); next, the Ten Transferences (*daśapariṇāmanā*) are taught, which are the single truth of the Middle Way;

and finally, the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are taught, which are the *tathatā* realized therein. Within this perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), the sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) is explained; it is not as [if they were separate].
This is the discourse of the True Suchness of the Unobstructed. You all should receive it below.
This is the entrustment from Śākyamuni Buddha to the thousand Buddhas and the hundreds of billions of Śākyamuni Buddhas, so that they may further entrust it to all sentient beings.

To accept and take in is called "receiving" (shou); to firmly maintain is called "upholding" (chi); to read against the original text is called "reading" (du); to recite apart from the original text is called "reciting" (song). As for the term "single-mindedness," there is...
Five. Within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, one attains awakening and understanding by provisionally employing the principle of the Four Noble Truths to explain the One Mind.
In the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s first turning of the wheel), one understands through the eighth consciousness that all dependently originated phenomena are empty;

each lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet they receive the fruits of karmic maturation (*vipāka*). In the Final Teaching, it is said that all the eternally vast, pure, and virtuous qualities are [inherent].

The Tathāgatagarbha-citta is endowed with the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), which, within the mind of a single thought-moment that does not arise, suddenly reveals the principle of nature (li-xing) as being neither defiled nor pure.
The Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao) features the perfect fusion of principal and satellites, wherein all phenomena are unimpeded; one is all, and all is one.

All is one; it is sovereign in both contraction and expansion, encompassing all phenomena. These five, in their totality, do not transcend the mind that initiates and perfects, which is also called the Samādhi of One Practice.
That is to say: to collect the mind in a single place is the site of enlightenment for all Buddhas;
to be distracted for even a moment is the realm of sentient beings. To receive, uphold, read, and recite [the teachings]... one...

They act with their minds. Within this sequential progression (*pannatti*), the teaching of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*) is expounded; it is not like the mere differentiation of names and characteristics.
III. Having Received [the Teaching], They Transform Others (2): 1. After Receiving, the Teacher Passes Away; 2. Each Returns to Their Own Realm.

Once the initial reception was concluded and the teachers had departed, at that time, the Buddhas upon the thousand-petaled lotuses—the hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis—arose from their majestic lion thrones within the Lotus Treasury World.
Each took leave and withdrew, emitting inconceivable light from every part of their bodies; each ray of light transformed into countless...
The Buddhas of the Ten Directions, at one time, offered immeasurable flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white to Vairocana Buddha.
Having completed the reception and upholding of the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Ground of the Mind" as explained above.
The phrase "at that time" refers to the moment when Vairocana exhorted and transmitted the teaching for the sake of transformation.

Once Vairocana had completed the entrustment, the Buddhas who were present according to the needs of the occasion received his intent and each returned to their own original and manifested worlds to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings, departing in accordance with conditions.
The mention of "the entire body" and so forth signifies the manifestation of the light of the mind-ground precepts, giving rise to that which is immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha of Wisdom. All these Buddhas—the fundamental Buddha, the manifested Buddha, and the manifested-of-manifested Buddhas—flow forth from the light of the precepts of the mind-ground.
This light cannot be conceived by the mind or discussed in words; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
As for "light upon light," this refers to the inconceivable light emitted by the thousand Śākyamunis, as well as the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Śākyamunis. Furthermore...

Within each radiance, there are manifested immeasurable and inconceivable Buddhas. Thus, through this Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground, the light of the precepts is inexhaustible, and because it gives birth to the various Buddhas, it is likewise inexhaustible. "Simultaneously" means that the path of practice and the fruit are identical.
The flowers symbolize causal practice; without the flowers, there would be no fruit. Without the myriad practices of the cause, there can be no fruit.
The Buddha is the world’s flower and fruit; worldly flowers and fruits grow from the soil, while supramundane flowers and fruits grow from the mind-ground.

Therefore, with exquisite flowers one adorns exquisite fruits: blue flowers represent the ten abodes (*bhūmi*), red flowers represent the ten practices (*caryā*), yellow flowers represent the ten transferences (*pariṇāmanā*), and white flowers represent the ten stages (*bhūmi*). This is explained extensively in the *Qianbi jing* (Sūtra of the Thousand Arms).
This clarifies [the preceding]. Thus, using the flower of the mind-ground as the cause, one returns to making offerings to the Buddha of the fruit of the mind-ground. As it is said:

"Among all forms of offering, the offering of Dharma is the most supreme. Regarding the phrase "upholding," etc., this serves as a concluding summary from within the section on offerings to introduce the following text;
hence it says: "The Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground is completed."
II. Each Returns to Their Own Realm (2): 1. Entering Samādhi and Returning to the Source; 2. Emerging from Samādhi to Preach the Dharma.
1. Entering Samādhi and Returning to the Source:
Each of them vanishes from this Lotus Treasury World. Having vanished, they enter the Flower-Light of Essential Nature Emptiness (*tattva-śūnyatā-kusuma-prabhā*).

Samādhi. Returning to the original source world, beneath the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa, "each and every one being equal" reveals that they have become hidden from the world upon which they originally relied. The initial concealment is called "disappearance"; the final concealment refers to having already disappeared.
Entering into the fundamental nature below, this correctly clarifies the place where the traces of concealment enter, namely, entering the Dharma-nature Samādhi of the fundamental essence.

This refers to the Samādhi of the Body-Nature of Empty Space and Flower-Light. This is an alternative name for the fundamental samādhi of the Dharma-body. It is said that this Dharma-body eternally abides in its fundamental samādhi;
its essential nature does not increase when in the state of a Sage, nor does it decrease when among ordinary beings.

Thus, one knows that the Buddha-mind and all sentient beings are non-different in three ways—equal and perfectly equal. (Note: The term "昧定" (mèi dìng) likely refers to a specific samādhi, possibly a scribal variant or archaic transcription; "體性" (tǐxìng) here functions as "essential nature" or "intrinsic substance.")

This means that within the minds of all Buddhas, sentient beings attain enlightenment from time to time; and within the minds of sentient beings, all Buddhas realize the Truth in every thought-moment.
Sentient beings are deluded and do not awaken, failing to enjoy this for themselves;

whereas the Buddhas, having realized this, appear and disappear, manifesting and concealing themselves with sovereign ease and without hindrance, just like empty space. Its essence is fundamentally not a form or appearance, yet it manifests through forms and appearances.

It reveals the essential nature of the *dharmakāya*, which fundamentally neither comes nor goes, being formless and signless. Yet, by means of the flower of practice and the light of wisdom, it is spontaneously adorned;
function does not depart from essence, and illumination does not depart from stillness. Illumination and stillness are equal, and principle and practice are non-dual.
Therefore, it is called the "Samādhi of the Essential Nature of Space, Flower, and Light. Question: How does this samādhi differ from the aforementioned *samantabhadra*?

What is the difference between the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the fundamental source of the nature of space as the attainment of Buddhahood, and the Samādhi-light of the eternally abiding Dharmakāya?
Answer: That samādhi is for the purpose of illuminating the mind of the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) in order to cultivate the awakening of the resultant stage (*phala-bhūmi*);
therefore, it is called "attaining Buddhahood and the Samādhi of the eternally abiding Dharmakāya. This [present] samādhi, however, is precisely for the purpose of illuminating the resultant stage.
This is the awakening that manifests in form to benefit sentient beings; hence it is called the "Flower-Light of Space Samādhi. These two concentrations differ in name but are identical in essence.
As for returning to the world of the source, this refers to the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas and the thousands of billions of Śākyamuni Buddhas.

Each one emitted light from their respective original lands to manifest to the assembly, each receiving those beings who harbored doubts, so that they might all go together to the presence of their original teacher, Vairocana Buddha, to hear the Dharma of the precepts.
Once the reception of the precepts was completed, they each returned to the fundamental world upon which their manifested traces depend.
Because they were seen to appear and disappear without ever departing from their proper place, it is said: "Returning to the source."
As for the world: Jambudvīpa refers to the southern continent of Aparagoyānī within the four continents of the Sahā world-system.

Bodhi is the Chinese term for the "Path of Enlightenment" (Awakening); it is also called the "Tree of the Path," because all Buddhas manifest the attainment of supreme enlightenment beneath this very tree.
II. Emerging from Samādhi to Preach the Dharma (2): 1. Explaining the Horizontal Teaching; 2. Explaining the Vertical Teaching. I.
Explaining the Horizontal Teaching (2): 1. Manifesting the Characteristics of Emerging from Samādhi; 2. Properly Expounding the Dharma Gates.
First, the signs of emerging from meditative absorption are shown.
He emerges from the Samādhi of the Flower-Light of the Voidness of Essential Nature.

Having emerged—since there was previously entry, there must necessarily be emergence—the initial manifestation is called "emerging," and the completion of that manifestation is called "having emerged. Question:

The Dharma-body of all Buddhas fills the ten directions; in the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting All Form-Bodies, how could there be any characteristics of entering or emerging from meditative concentration?
Answer: Briefly, there are three meanings. First, the meaning of contemplating the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*):
it is fundamentally free from the characteristics of names, speech, and so forth. That which is called the quiescent mark of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words, except by a Buddha.

It is taught through skillful means that there are thus the characteristics of entering and exiting. Second, when contemplating the time of preaching the Dharma, there is the distinction between the appropriate time for preaching and the inappropriate time for preaching;
that is to say, one who wishes to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature should contemplate the timing and causal conditions.
Therefore, there are these characteristics of entering and exiting. Third, [the Buddha] observes the faculties of sentient beings; according to which faculty he teaches which dharma.

This is what is meant by "expounding the teaching according to their capacities" and "administering medicine according to the illness. Therefore, there are these characteristics of entering and exiting. As the Sūtra says:
First, he spoke the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* and again entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Meanings;

even until emerging from samādhi to proclaim his virtues, he caused those of various capacities to become fully matured and to look up with deep devotion, and only then did he preach to them—this precisely accords with this principle.
II. The Correct Exposition of the Dharma-gate (3): First, that which is taught according to the gradual sequence; second, that which is taught according to the perfect and sudden;
third, the concluding summary.
Regarding the first, that which is taught according to the gradual sequence:
He sat upon the Vajra-Thousand-Rays King Throne and in the Hall of Sublime Light, where he expounded the ocean of dharma-gates of the ten worlds.
Rising again from his seat, he went to the palace of Śakra and expounded the ten abodes (*bhūmi*). Rising again from his seat, he went among the Yāma devas and expounded the ten practices (*caryā*).
Rising again from his seat, he went among the Tuṣita devas and expounded the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Rising again from his seat, he went to the Nirmāṇarati...
In the Tuṣita Heaven, he taught the ten dhyānas. Rising again from his seat, he went to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven and taught the ten stages (bhūmis).

Returning once more to the first dhyāna, he taught the ten vajras. Returning to the second dhyāna, he taught the ten patiences (kṣāntis). Returning to the third dhyāna, he taught the ten vows (praṇidhānas).
This explains the meaning of emerging from meditative concentration to preach the Dharma and manifest traces.

Regarding the phrase "just as he sat upon the vajra," this refers to the first assembly where the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths was preached. "Just as" (fang) means correctly. "Vajra" takes the sense of being most firm and most sharp.
"Thousand Lights" (Sahasraraśmi) takes the sense of ultimate clarity and ultimate illumination. "King" (Rāja) takes the sense of supreme sovereignty beyond compare.
These terms manifest that this seat is what has been transmitted by the thousand Buddhas—immovable, indestructible, without darkness, without obscuration, and without peer.

This is the Great Jewel Flower King Throne. A Bodhisattva of the First Ground, through the accumulation of merit and the resonance of their practice, relying on the power of their original vow, takes a provisional station within the human vehicle as a Golden Wheel-Turning King.
They cultivate the ten wholesome actions to transform sentient beings and practice the dharma of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) to adorn the wondrous fruit.
Governing all the lands of the four continents, it is for this reason that the Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment.
Awakening. It was here that the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, and it is here that the Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths is taught.
As for what is called the "Ocean of Dharma-gates of the Ten Worlds," this refers to the ten world-oceans of the Flower Treasury Adornment (*Kusumatalagarbha-vyuha*).
This single mind of True Suchness (*tathatā-citta*) is the realm of enjoyment for the noble wisdom of self-awakening of all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. All Buddhas...
Riding upon this Dharma-gate, one turns the vessel of compassion in reverse. All Bodhisattvas cultivate this gate until they reach the ultimate ocean of fruition.
All sentient beings, however, because they are deluded regarding this mind, wander through the ten directions, their cycle of birth and death never-ending.

Therefore it is said: "The ocean of the dharma-gates of the ten worlds. This further reveals that the worlds of the ten directions are inexhaustible, the Buddhas are inexhaustible, and sentient beings are inexhaustible; thus, the dharma-gates of the Buddhas are likewise inexhaustible.

The metaphor of the ocean signifies depth, vastness, and expansiveness, containing all things without exception and possessing no characteristic of exhaustion. This is the ocean of the dharma-gates of the ten worlds.

The meaning is profoundly deep; words cannot exhaust its expression. Its general intent is to cause sentient beings to immediately enter into perfect faith, thereby giving rise to perfect understanding, so as to attain the meaning of perfect realization.

If one wishes to explain this extensively, one should consult the "Ten Worlds" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, as well as the chapters concerning the names of Vairocana Tathāgata and the manifestations of the Tathāgata, each of which elucidates this point.
Regarding this meaning: "He rose from his seat again and went to the palace of Śakra, etc. refers to this second location.

It concerns the meaning of the Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*) as explained in sequence. Question: Why does Vairocana teach only the thirty mental states (*triṃśaccitta*) and the Dharma-gate of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*)?
Question: For what reason are the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) taught first, followed by the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*)? Answer:
Because Śākyamuni Buddha spoke to the thousand Buddhas, he taught the "Chapter on the Ground of Mind" (*Cittabhūmi-parivarta*) all at once.

Since the Ten Abidings fully encompass the Ten Faiths—and since there can be no abiding without faith—what was previously stated regarding the "Ten Minds of Aspiration" (*daśa-prasthāna-citta*) within the stage of Firm Faith-Patience (*kṣānti*) refers to their orientation toward the fruit; here, we clarify their sequential order.
For this reason, the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) are explained first, followed by the ten abodes (*vihāra*).

he again went to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara within the Fourth Dhyāna and taught the Lotus Treasury World, the source of my own origin.
The *Dharmadhātu*. The "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" taught by Vairocana Buddha.

Joy. The bliss of the third dhyāna is such that the mind is free from hatred and attachment; in a single thought, it is equanimous, pure, and unadulterated.

the remaining thousands of millions of Śākyamunis are likewise thus, without duality or distinction, as explained in the "Chapter on the Worthy Eon" (Bhadrakalpika-parivarta).

First, the manifestation of signs and the attainment of enlightenment:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha, having first appeared in the Lotus Treasury World and entered the celestial palace from the east, preached the *Sūtra on the Conversion of Māra*.

The above clarifies the Thousand Śākyamunis and the hundred billion Śākyamunis, all of whom expound the "Chapter on the Dharma-Gate of the Mind-Ground" throughout the worlds of the ten directions.

"Immortals practice the Way here. Furthermore, all Buddhas of antiquity who appeared in the world manifested their births in this very place;

The term "etc. indicates the names and virtues of his birth parents. In the Sanskrit language, *Māyā* means "Great Illusion" (*Mahāmāyā*), for by means of great illusory arts she manifested all Buddhas;
thus, she is the mother of all Buddhas throughout the ten directions who manifest their births.
As for the father's name, "Pure White" (*Śuddhodana*), this is the translation used in this region; in the Sanskrit language, it is *Uttaradatta*. The world... [text continues].
When the World-Honored One was about to undergo birth, he observed that King Śuddhodana was pure and his nature and conduct were benevolent and virtuous;
furthermore, Lady Māyā had served as the mother of a Bodhisattva for five hundred lifetimes. He thought, "I should go there to take conception.
This refers to the second and third signs: namely, manifesting entry into the mother’s womb and abiding therein. As for my name, Siddhārtha, it signifies "manifesting birth."
This is his renowned virtue. In the Sanskrit language it is *Siddhārtha*; here it is translated as "Sudden Auspiciousness" (*Dunji*).
Because at the time of the Prince’s initial birth, the precious treasuries were all emptied, yet having been empty, they became full once more, he was thus named "Sudden Auspiciousness.

He is also named "Accomplisher of All Meanings" (*Sarvārthasiddha*), because he accomplished the meaning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane. Thus, at that time, the Prince [descended] from Mā...

He emerged from his mother’s right side and stood upon a lotus flower. With one hand pointing toward heaven and the other pointing toward the earth, he gazed in the four directions and took seven steps, declaring:
“In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am most honored; among all that is mundane and supramundane, this Dharma is supreme.
This is what is called the manifestation of birth from the womb, the fourth sign. It is said that at the age of seven, he departed.

"Family" (kula) indicates the meaning of departing from the secular world, returning from delusion to the True, and reverting to the Real. When the World-Honored One was first a crown prince, he possessed great wisdom and achieved a mind of renunciation.
Observing the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, he grew weary of the five desires of the world and abandoned the rank of a universal monarch as if discarding nasal mucus or saliva.
His mind longed for the life of a renunciant, so he went to inform his royal father; however, his royal father did not permit it. Therefore—
On the third day of the second month, his body emitted a radiance that illuminated the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings and extended as far as the palaces of the Śuddhāvāsa gods.
When the devas beheld this, they went to the Prince’s presence, prostrated at his feet, and said: "Bodhisattva, after immeasurable kalpas, your cultivation of the path has reached fulfillment;
it is now precisely ripe for you to transcend the city walls at midnight and go forth into homelessness to practice austerities."
In the forest, he shaved off his hair and beard; this is what is meant by manifesting the departure from the city and the practice of asceticism in the woods—the fifth sign.
As for the statement that at thirty he attained the Way and was titled Śākyamuni Buddha: "Way" refers to the fruit of the Way.
The World-Honored One’s meritorious practices were fulfilled; the Way was perfected and virtue complete, such that the three bodies manifested in full and the four māras were subdued.
It is subtly extinguished. The name of the perfect fruit of realization he attained is also clearly revealed by the Buddha Pradyota’s prophecy that it would not be in vain;
therefore, he is named Śākyamuni Buddha. This refers to the sixth mark: the manifestation of attaining enlightenment and subduing Māra upon seeing the morning star.
This sutra states that he left home at seven years of age and attained enlightenment at thirty; other accounts do not [agree].

First: Some say it is an error in transcription; some say it is one out of eight thousand repetitions; some say it signifies that in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there is no regression from the seventh stage of faith (shixin) upward;

some say the number seven represents the seven factors of enlightenment (bodhyanga); and thirty represents the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga)—thus possessing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma). This applies to all Buddhas.
Those who transcend the world, preach the Dharma, and deliver sentient beings all rely upon this. Now, however, it is not so. At seven years of age one leaves home;

this is what is meant by "seven years since leaving home. It refers to the time when, having first left home, one first studies the *ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of nothingness) and attains its realization before long.

Knowing that this is not the ultimate goal, one next studies the *naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi* (the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception) and attains its realization before long, knowing that this too is not [the ultimate].
Having reached the ultimate goal, he subsequently traveled through various kingdoms for a full year.
He then practiced further asceticism for six years until he was thirty, at which point he attained perfect enlightenment; this is according to the explanations found in the Vinaya-piṭaka.
II. Attaining Enlightenment and Preaching the Dharma:

From sitting upon the Vajra-flower-light-king throne at the site of the tranquil and extinguished Way-place (śānta-mārga-maṇḍala), up to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, he preached throughout these successive stages and locations.
"Regarding the site of the tranquil place of enlightenment (śānta-maṇḍala)": this indicates the appearance of attaining the Way and turning the wheel of Dharma.
In terms of phenomena (*dharma*), it refers to true *araṇya* (forest hermitage), the proper locus for spiritual practice.

In terms of principle (*tattva*), it refers to the realized *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), signless (*animitta*), pure, and tranquil principle—namely, the so-called "returning to the fulfillment of *bodhi*."
There is nothing to be attained. Therefore, the Buddhas realize equal and perfect enlightenment within the principle of non-attainment and quiescent extinction;

they sit upon the Great Seat of Enlightenment and turn the Great Wheel of Dharma within that principle of non-attainment and quiescent extinction. Thus it is said: "In the Seat of Quiescent Extinction.
The phrase "sitting beneath the Vajra" clarifies the place where the Dharma is turned. Having already realized the Way, one should then turn [the wheel].
The Wheel of Dharma. To deliver all sentient beings. At that time, the World-Honored One reflected to himself:
"I have attained wisdom, yet none are able to believe and accept it. If I remain in the world, it will be of no benefit to the world;

it would be better for me to enter parinirvāṇa. Then Brahmā addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, today the ocean of Dharma is full and the turning of the Dharma has been established. It moistens..."
"To provide guidance and lead them across, now is precisely the right time. Why do you wish to abandon all sentient beings, entering nirvana without preaching the Dharma?
At that time, having accepted the invitation of the Brahma King, although the Tathāgata knew their faculties were dull, he nonetheless acceded to his original intention;
therefore, he manifested two forms simultaneously: one remained at the Deer Park for the sake of Kauṇḍinya.
The five bhikṣus and others turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths and taught the various doctrines of the Hīnayāna.
At one time, in the Bodhimaṇḍa, he expounded the Great Avataṃsaka Sūtra; furthermore, within the Hall of Universal Radiance, he preached this very sūtra together with a thousand Buddhas.
All that these Buddhas spoke was from the initial sitting upon the Vajra Thousand-Radiant King Throne until the conclusion at the Śūla [Hall].
Regarding the celestial palaces, the abodes described therein in sequence total ten.
Whether taught by many Buddhas or by a single Buddha, whether taught all at once or gradually, as well as the various abodes, they are all non-dual and without distinction.

The *Avataṃsaka* was spoken across seven locations and nine assemblies; this sutra was spoken across ten locations and ten assemblies. These two scriptures are largely the same with minor differences.
That which is called "manifesting the attainment of enlightenment and turning the Great Dharma Wheel" constitutes the seventh phase.
Why is there no eighth? It is because [the Buddha] has not yet entered parinirvāṇa.
Third, the account of the scripture’s origin:
At that time, the Buddha observed the Great Brahma Kings and their causes—the net-like banners—and for their sake he spoke of the infinite worlds, which are like the meshes of a net;

This explains the meaning of the introductory narrative for the "Chapter on the Precepts of the Mind-Ground" (*Cittabhūmi-śīla-paṭala*), as well as the occasion upon which the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* received its name.
Regarding the "time": it refers to the time when this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground was taught within this Brahma-heaven. At that time, the World-Honored One...

Within the palace of Mahābrahmā, he took the banner of the net-lattice as a metaphor to explain the immeasurable worlds, the mental activities of sentient beings, and the distinctions between the environment and its inhabitants.
Just as the individual meshes of a net are each different and infinitely diverse, so too are the gates of the Buddha's teaching established according to the capacities of beings; it is likewise thus.
The meaning of both has already been explained in the preface; I shall not elaborate further here.

"I have now come to this world eight thousand times. For the sake of this Sahā world, I sit upon the Vajra-flower Radiance [throne]."
From the royal throne up to the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara, he has finished briefly opening the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground for all the great assemblies therein.

Again. It is said that the Buddha’s compassion is inexhaustible and sentient beings are inexhaustible.

Although he has come eight thousand times, if one compares this with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, specifically the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" and the "Chapter on Names and Epithets," his names, epithets, teachings, and eras cannot be exhausted by any numerical count. How lamentable it is that we remain mired in ignorance until now!

the Vajra throne is that upon which all Buddhas of the three periods of time sit to attain enlightenment, remaining without the slightest change or decay.
"Thus, 'up to' (乃至) refers to the fact that this site for preaching the Dharma consists of ten locations; having transcended eight of them, it is said 'up to.

The Differentiated Explanation of the Precepts.

Furthermore, descending from the palace of the Heavenly King to the Bodhi tree beneath the Jambudvīpa, for the sake of all sentient beings upon this earth—those ordinary people shrouded in the darkness of ignorance—I shall expound the single precept that I, as the original Buddha Vairocana, have constantly recited since first awakening the mind within the heart-ground.
This is the Radiant Vajra Jewel Precept, the source of all Buddhas. One...
The fundamental source of all Bodhisattvas and the seed of Buddha-nature: all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

All mental faculties, consciousnesses, form, and mind—whether emotional or cognitive—all enter into the precepts of Buddha-nature because they always possess the causal conditions for each and every moment, and thus they eternally abide in the Dharma-body.
These ten Pratimokṣas emerge from the world; they are the Precepts of the Dharma.

All sentient beings of the three periods of time receive and uphold this upon the crowns of their heads. I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly, again expound the Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries of Precepts, which is the source of the precepts for all sentient beings and is pure by its very nature.

The preceding section, from "From the earth, ascending to the great [heavens]" through the contemplation of the Brahma-net pores as the cause, has detailed the thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*) within the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).

Having concluded the chapter on the Dharma-gates for Cultivation and Severance (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa-dharma-paryāya*), the text now proceeds from the celestial realms back down to the human world to provide a detailed enumeration of the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts of the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*). Therefore, it says: "Again, from the Palace of the Heavenly King," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "this ground and above," it correctly clarifies the meaning of extending downward to Jambudvīpa. "All sentient beings" refers collectively to all beings within the realm of Jambudvīpa.
As for "ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) in the darkness of delusion," those who have not yet emerged from the three realms are all termed ordinary persons;
because the afflictions (*kleśa*) of ordinary persons shroud the mind, the eye of wisdom does not open, and thus they are called "those in the darkness of delusion."
Such a person must rely upon what dharma to break through obstructions and open their wisdom, thereby entering the ranks of the sages and transcending the mundane?
If one does not use the dharma of precepts to restrain the mind, one will ultimately remain within the ocean of afflictions and birth-and-death, never attaining liberation.
Therefore, for the sake of this assembly, I have descended once more from the celestial palace to expound the causal stage of the Mind-Ground of my original teacher, Vairocana Buddha.
In the initial arousal of the bodhicitta, there is one precept that is constantly recited. What is the name of this precept? It is the "Luminous Vajra Jewel Precept.
When it says, "I, the Buddha Vairocana," it indicates that the Dharma has a teacher from whom it originates.

That which is "constantly recited as the one precept" reveals the essential substance of the precept; this essence of the precept is what the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* calls the "One True Dharma Realm. Great!

The essence of the dharma-gate of universal characteristics is as stated in the *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra*: "the treasury of great radiant light of supernormal powers. As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*:
"it is the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature. And as stated in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "the real mark of the One Vehicle, known and seen by the Buddhas.
Herein, it is termed the "Radiant Vajra Jewel Precept. Regarding the phrase "radiant vajra jewel":
"Precepts" refers to the manifestation of the characteristics and virtues of the precepts. "Radiance" is wisdom. "Vajra" is firmness and sharpness.
"Precious Precepts" means being fully endowed with the wealth of all wholesome dharmas. [One maintains them] because one wishes to shatter the darkness of the afflictions.
Without the light of great wisdom, it cannot be achieved. To shatter fundamental ignorance, nothing but the firm and sharp wisdom of the vajra can suffice.
To adorn the resultant marks of the Dharmakāya, nothing but the jewel-like precepts of manifold virtues can suffice.
Indeed, this one precept is that which all Buddhas and sentient beings equally and fully possess; it is of a non-dual nature.

For both Buddhas and sentient beings, there has fundamentally been neither increase nor decrease. Therefore, by means of this one precept, it serves as the fundamental source of the ocean of all Buddha-fruit, and as the fundamental source of the causal ground for all Bodhisattvas—not only for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, but because...
This precept is the fundamental source. This single precept is precisely the seed of the Buddha-nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings.
Since all possess the Buddha-nature, why do they not attain the path of Buddhahood?

The reason they fail to attain the path of Buddhahood is that they employ their various consciousnesses, forms, and minds to become deluded and turn their backs upon the precept-body of the Buddha-nature. As for the meaning [of this]:
"Intentional reflection" (*manas*) refers to the seventh consciousness, the *kliṣṭa-manas* (defiled mind); it is also termed the "basis for both defilement and purification.

"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to that which discriminates; by grasping at names and characteristics, it gives rise to delusions and creates karma—this refers to the preceding six types of evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
"Form" (*rūpa*) refers to that which is perceived as an object; this refers to the five sense organs and the six sense objects. "Mind" (*citta*)...
The term "mind" (*citta*) refers to that which accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena]; it is the eighth consciousness, named *ālaya*. It subsumes the preceding seven types of consciousness.

This mental consciousness possesses the threefold meaning of "storehouse" (*ālaya*), as it gathers all mundane and supramundane phenomena, both defiled and pure. First, it is the "capable storehouse" (*nirbhāga-ālaya*).

That which is stored [within]—the storehouse of my self-attachment—is the essence of this consciousness. Its fundamental nature is the seed of Buddhahood; it is inherently without change or alteration.

When spoken of in relation to the realm of sentient beings, it is called "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*); when spoken of in relation to the realm of non-sentient beings, it is called "Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
Because it currently exists as a cause, it is termed "Buddha-nature. If one can possess great wisdom and awaken to this essential nature...
This very substance, this emotion, and this mind all enter into the Buddha-nature precepts.
Since it is said that they all enter into the Buddha-nature precepts, one should give rise to the mind of the original, eternally possessed, correct cause (*samyak-hetu*).

Once this mind of the correct cause has been aroused, one should practice in accordance with this correct cause and not fall into false causes. Since one does not fall into false causes, in the future one will certainly...
One definitively realizes the eternally abiding, pure Dharmakāya, the fruit that is neither born nor extinguished, and is thus not defiled by the illusory body.
Therefore it is said: "Because there is always a cause at every moment, there is the eternally abiding Dharmakāya at every moment.
Such [teachings] as the ten *prātimokṣa* rules represent the function of the precepts. Now, when observing sentient beings, all possess...

The cause of precepts brings about the fruit of precepts; this is what the Buddhas have realized and what ordinary beings are deluded regarding. To exhaustively fulfill this single precept is the realization of all Buddhas.
Seeing that sentient beings are deluded and fail to awaken to these inherently present supreme causes and fruits, the Buddhas cannot bear it.
Therefore, if one does not rely upon these various categories of precepts to maintain them one by one, how could one possibly attain [realization]?
This causes the six sense faculties to turn back from delusion and return to the truth. For this reason, this single precept is further skillfully expanded into ten.
Thus, these ten *prātimokṣa* emerge in the world to instruct all people. All Buddhas have attained Buddhahood by taking these ten precepts as their fundamental rule.
If a person relies upon these precepts, they will realize and cultivate the essence of the Dharma.
By practicing this, one will certainly attain Buddhahood; it is precisely the precept that serves as the standard for the Buddhadharma of all sentient beings.

Therefore, it is called the "Dharma-precept. As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*: "First is the Greatness of Essence (*tathatā*): because True Suchness is equal and neither increases nor decreases, this very single precept is it.
Second is the Greatness of Characteristics: namely, the Tathāgatagarbha, which is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits."
Therefore, this is precisely that light of the Vajra Jewel Precepts. Third is the greatness of function, for it can produce the causes and effects of both mundane and supramundane goodness;
this is precisely these ten *pratimokṣa*. In the Sanskrit language, *pratimokṣa* is translated here as "protective liberation" (*baohuajietuo*).
This means that those who uphold these precepts protect the three karmas and the six sense faculties, thereby attaining...
This is the Great Liberation. Regarding the phrase "all those of the three periods of time," this is an exhortation to all beings to receive and uphold [these precepts].

It is said that these ten precepts, being the very standard of the Dharma and the great function for attaining Buddhahood, should be venerated and worn upon the head by all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
They must never be treated with disrespect; rather, they should be received and maintained, and embodied at every moment.
One must not neglect or forget this; therefore, it is said that one should "receive and uphold it upon the crown of the head.

Regarding the phrase "I shall now, for the sake of... and so forth, this concludes and clarifies the Dharma of the precepts. Although they are inexhaustible, they do not depart from the meaning of their fundamental essence.

The statement "for this great assembly" refers specifically to the fourfold assembly currently receiving the precepts and the great assembly of the eight classes of beings. Regarding the phrase "repeatedly speaking," it means this...
The essence of the precepts is one; yet because the mental intentions of sentient beings are inexhaustible, this dharma of the precepts is likewise inexhaustible.
Therefore, by means of this single precept, it is expanded into ten, and these ten precepts are further opened up into forty-eight.
Extending even to thirty-eight thousand [precepts], they are inexhaustible and endless. There is not a single category of precept that is not subsumed within these ten *prātimokṣa*.
Therefore, it is said: "I shall now, for the sake of this great assembly, once again proclaim the ten inexhaustible treasury precepts.
These are the source of the precepts for all sentient beings; their self-nature is pure. This...
These two lines specifically point to the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*). Originally, they are of a single flavor and equal.
Because the mental activities of sentient beings are inexhaustible, the various categories of precepts taught by the Buddhas are likewise inexhaustible.

Fearing that sentient beings might cling to these external marks of the precepts (*nimitta*) and fail to realize the nature of the precepts (*dharmatā*), it is further stated: "These inexhaustible precepts are, in fact, all..."
The fundamental source of sentient beings is the essence of precepts, which is intrinsically pure. Originally, there are no precepts to be observed, nor are there any precepts to be spoken of.
That there are now those who speak of them and those who receive them is entirely due to skillful means.
2. Verses recapitulating the preceding and introducing what follows:
"I, now Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal; surrounding me on a thousand petals, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis."
Upon a single flower are ten billion lands; in each land is a Śākyamuni, each sitting beneath a bodhi tree, all attaining the Way of Buddhahood at once.

Thus, these thousands, tens of thousands, and hundreds of millions are the original body of Rocana. These thousands, tens of thousands, and hundreds of millions of Śākyamunis each receive and guide beings as numerous as motes of dust.
They all came to where I was and listened as I recited the Buddha’s precepts; the gate of ambrosia immediately opened.

At that time, the hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis returned to their original places of enlightenment and each sat beneath a Bodhi tree, reciting the precepts of my original teacher: the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts.
The precepts are like the sun and the moon, and they are also like jeweled necklaces. By means of them, the multitude of subtle-dust Bodhisattvas attain perfect enlightenment.
This is what Rocana recites; I likewise recite it in this way. You who are newly trained Bodhisattvas, receive and uphold these precepts upon the crown of your head.
Having received and upheld these precepts, transmit them to all sentient beings. Listen attentively as I correctly recite the treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma, the Prātimokṣa.
With sincere faith in your hearts, O Great Assembly: you are those who shall become Buddhas; I am one who has already become a Buddha.
Always maintain such faith. Having fully perfected the precepts, all sentient beings with a mind should receive the Buddha’s precepts.

When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of the Buddhas. Once their rank is equal to that of Great Enlightenment, they are truly the children of the Buddhas.

The great assembly all paid homage and listened with a sincere heart as I recited this section, which serves as a general summary of the preceding and following parts. It opens the exposition of the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts, concluding what precedes and initiating what follows;

it is a broad outline praising [the teaching] and exhorting its reception and practice. "I, now Vairocana," indicates the Buddha in terms of his original essence (*honji*) and manifested traces (*suijaku*). This is the Sage.
When people preach the Dharma, they all use "non-self" to shatter every form of self. Yet, what is here called "self" is not the self of the mark of selfhood held by ordinary beings;
nor is it the self of the *puruṣa* (divine soul) held by non-Buddhists; nor even is it the provisional self of the expedient vehicles.
This is the self within non-self, the self of the eight masteries, the self of non-arising. Now, [regarding this...]
At the time of this teaching, Rocana Buddha is the primary Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), while Vairocana is the primary Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*).
Yet, regarding the Buddha’s Dharma Body, there are distinctions such as one body, two bodies, three bodies, ten bodies, and so forth.
Because this Buddha perfectly encompasses all of these, it says: "I, Rocana, now... As for "sitting upon the lotus pedestal," this...
This clarifies the fundamental and manifested aspects of the dependent retribution of the land. "Square" (fang) means correct; "sitting" (zuo) means peaceful dwelling.

By means of the Dharma-precepts of the correct mind-ground, one peacefully dwells within one's own body and brings peace to the bodies of all sentient beings. The lotus flower possesses two general meanings: first, it remains eternally pure even while in the mud;
second, it emerges from the water fragrant and clean. These serve as metaphors to reveal the essence of the precepts within the mind-ground, even when in the state of an ordinary person.
The Middle Way is fundamentally devoid of any characteristic of defilement; within the state of the sages, it is fundamentally devoid of any characteristic of purity. This is what is meant by:

while dwelling within the stream of birth and death, the black pearl shines alone amidst the vast blue sea; while perched upon the shore of nirvana, the crescent moon is solitary and radiant in the azure sky.

Furthermore, the lotus possesses the meaning of opening and closing, which symbolizes the Tathāgata’s revelation of the provisional to manifest the real, and his convergence of the provisional back into the real.
This refers to revealing the reality of the One Vehicle’s mind-ground precept-dharma; expounding the provisional teachings of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts;
and further returning to the reality of the mind-ground precept-essence, which is fundamentally and inherently pure.
Furthermore, it symbolizes that the single body of Śākyamuni transforms into a thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas, and further manifests as a hundred billion Śākyamuni Buddhas. And this—
The thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas and the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Śākyamuni Buddhas are all subsumed within the fundamental essence of Vairocana Buddha.
Furthermore, regarding the principle of the simultaneous manifestation of cause and effect: the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause.
The "platform" (*tai*) signifies height and prominence; it symbolizes the essence of the *śamatha* (calm-abiding) mind-ground precepts, which is unsurpassed and beyond compare.
That is to say, among all the various codes of discipline, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* (Precept Scripture) is supreme and foremost.

Furthermore, the platform is situated in the center, for through the center, the ten directions are encompassed; this symbolizes that the Tathāgata *Samantabhadra* is the lord of the thousand Buddhas and the ground of the mind.

The wondrous precepts are the root of all precepts. That which "surrounds the thousand petals" clarifies the manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*) and their dependent retribution lands (*niśraya-vipākabhūmi*), manifesting the meaning of the pervasive interpenetration between the fundamental reality (*mūla*) and its manifestations, as well as between the dependent and the retributive.

Furthermore, that which "again manifests the thousand Śākyamunis" clarifies the manifested traces and their primary retribution bodies (*adhipati-vipākadeha*), manifesting the meaning of the pervasive interpenetration between the fundamental reality and its manifestations, as well as between the primary and the retributive. This refers to [the manifestation] upon the thousand petals.
Within each flower, there is further a manifested Buddha-body seated upon it;
this immediately reveals that from the single radiance of the Vajra Jewel Precepts, the wondrous precepts of the ten *pratimokṣas* are brought forth.

"One flower contains ten billion lands" clarifies that each trace [of manifestation] relies upon a land of retributive support (*niśraya-vipāka-kṣetra*), manifesting the land of retributive support for the Buddha of Traces, which is all-pervasive and perfect.
The meaning of "fusion" (rong) refers to each of the thousand flower-blossoms having ten billion petals;
each petal represents a Buddha-land, and within each land there is an emanation-Buddha preaching the Dharma for the assembly.

This serves to symbolize the forty-eight minor precepts, as well as the infinite categories of training rules, all of which are manifested from within the ten precepts. Each sits [in its respective place].

The Bodhi tree represents those who attain the Way of Buddhahood at one and the same time, clarifying that the response and transformation [of the Buddha] occur simultaneously and that essence and function are non-dual.
This symbolizes the precepts of the mind-ground; although their categories are numerous, they share the same essence of the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*).

The eight preceding phrases clarify the arising of function from essence. The subsequent passage beginning with "In this manner, thousands of millions... clarifies the returning of function to essence. As for the word "thousand":
The ten billion Śākyamunis take the thousand Śākyamunis as their basis, and those thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas, in turn, take Vairocana Buddha as their basis.

The three preceding sections above summarize the entire great scripture. The text of the first nine chapters specifically elucidates the meaning of the causal origination (*nidāna*) of the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts.
This is explained in the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground Precepts" within the *Qianbi jing* (Sūtra of a Thousand Arms).
First, we shall take up this meaning; subsequently, the Dharma-gates of the Three Sages and Ten Stages will be explained.

The text and its meaning are interwoven, for within the current upper fascicle there is also the principle of "arising from the fundamental to manifest the traces" and "subsuming the traces to return to the fundamental.
This appears to use the latter as an illustration of the former, serving as the point of departure. Below, the verse formally expounds the causes and conditions for the initiation of this chapter.
The five phrases beginning with "The billions of Śākyamunis" are a verse summarizing the preceding section.

From the moment the Buddha Śākyamuni emitted rays of wisdom from his body which illuminated all, the gods and humans were moved to doubt. The Lord of Mysteries gathered the assembly and inquired about the characteristics of the light.
Śākyamuni leads the assembly to the abode of Vairocana, where they listen to and receive the meaning of a major section of the scripture concerning the Treasury of Mind-Ground Precepts.
Question: Why is it stated here that only the thousand-billion Śākyamunis go to the abode of Vairocana, rather than the thousand Śākyamunis?

Why is this? Answer: Since each of the thousand-billion Śākyamunis individually receives as many beings as there are motes of dust to come to the presence of Vairocana to hear and receive the precepts, it goes without saying that each of these thousand Śākyamunis also individually receives as many beings as there are motes of dust to come and hear and receive the precepts.
Question: Regarding the statement that each receives as many beings as there are motes of dust, from where do these beings come? Answer: They are the beings of the thousand Śākyamunis.
Kāśyapa, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of Śākyamunis who, from their original source-worlds, extend their hands to guide and receive beings beyond the limit of expression.
Yet, those who harbor doubts and give rise to such thoughts—beings of great capacity—come to the presence of their own Original Teacher to hear and receive the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts;
it is clearly not for those of small capacity. All those who have come to my place are [of this latter sort].

This means that those beings whom the Buddha has taken under his care are able to join him; thus they arrive together at the Flower Treasury World (Kusumatalagarbha), which is why it is said they "come together.

"Listen as I recite the Buddha’s precepts" means to listen to the Great Precepts of all Buddhas recited by Śākyamuni, thereby manifesting that these Great Precepts of the Mind-Ground are collectively realized by all Buddhas.
"The gate of ambrosia opens immediately" is a praise of the virtue of the precepts; this means that...
The Dharma of the precepts is like the ambrosia of the world; if one obtains it to consume, one immediately attains purity and coolness, becoming neither subject to aging nor death.

If a person can receive the pure precepts, they will immediately transcend the heat and affliction of birth and death within the triple world—this is a metaphor for the opening of the gate of ambrosia.
At this time, the four lines beginning with "thousands of billions" eulogize the thousand Śākyamuni Buddhas and their [attendants].
One billion Śākyamunis led their assemblies to the abode of Vairocana; having finished hearing and receiving the precepts, they each immediately returned to their original source-worlds.
There, they manifested birth, left the household life, attained enlightenment, ascended to celestial palaces, and completed the teaching of the Dharma in ten locations to transform the devas.
Having finished these tasks, they again descended from the palaces of the heavenly kings to the realm of Jambudvīpa to preach the fundamental teachings of Vairocana.

The Buddha, from the moment he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], constantly recited a single precept, up to the passage of scripture beginning with "the fundamental source and self-nature are pure.
At that time, the "thousand times ten million" refers to Śākyamuni as Vairocana;
this was the occasion when he transmitted and received the Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts. "Returning to the original site of enlightenment" refers to the thousand Śākyamunis and—

The thousands of billions of Śākyamunis, having finished hearing the precepts, returned once more to their original places of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings.
This is to manifest that all Buddhas—whether emerging from or entering meditative absorption, departing, arriving, sitting, or standing—never depart from their fundamental essence.

Thus, the statement that they "sat beneath the Bodhi tree" manifests that the Buddhas’ attainment of enlightenment and turning of the Dharma are identical to original awakening (*mūlajñāna*); there is no second path.
Furthermore, "reciting my original teacher’s precepts" reveals that the conferral of the precepts has a teacher, because one does not forget the fundamental mind.

The above verses praise what has preceded; the following verses praise what follows. "The ten grave [precepts] and forty-eight [minor ones]" refers to the manifestation of the characteristics of the precepts.
"The precepts are like the sun and moon, and also like jeweled necklaces" praises the merit of the precepts; it means that if a person can receive and uphold them...
This precept can extinguish the dark obstruction of ignorance, just as the sun and moon can dispel darkness.
Furthermore, one who upholds the precepts purifies the six sense faculties and constantly attains liberation regarding all phenomena;

this is also like the sun and moon, which shine brightly throughout the ten directions, moving freely and without hindrance through space. Moreover, the upholder of the precepts eradicates the defilement of transgressions. Thus...
It is like the bright sun, which can melt frost and snow; likewise, one who upholds the precepts can extinguish the heat and affliction of body and mind, just as the bright moon can bring coolness.
It is also like a jeweled necklace: for a person who upholds the precepts, concentration arises from the precepts, and wisdom is generated from concentration;
thus, all meritorious virtues, wisdom, and the Dharma-body are all accomplished through the perfection of ethical discipline.
Because it is like a jeweled necklace that adorns the physical form, making it perfectly beautiful;
because the multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust who attain perfect enlightenment thereby manifest that those who uphold the precepts bring about true benefit that is not in vain.
The term "multitude of motes of dust" indicates that those who uphold the precepts obtain manifold benefits, such as these immeasurable and boundless motes of dust.
"O assembly! By upholding the ten grave precepts and the forty-eight light precepts, one attains Buddhahood.
Those who aspire to the fruit of Buddhahood must certainly receive and uphold these precepts. This is what Rocana recited; I, too, recite it in this same way."

Continuing from above: it is said that these various precepts were recited by my own Teacher, and I have likewise recited them accordingly; it is not that I failed to recite them myself and thus taught others to recite them.
The four lines beginning with "You new learners, bodhisattvas, etc. exhort you to receive [the precepts] for yourself in order to bestow them upon others.
As for the aforementioned multitude of bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust, since they have already attained Buddhahood by means of these precepts, you [should likewise do so].
A newly initiated bodhisattva should single-mindedly receive, uphold, and honor these precepts.
Having received and upheld these precepts, one should further transmit them to all sentient beings. Because they benefit both themselves and others, they are called Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
If one does not transmit them to sentient beings, one will be indistinguishable from the Śrāvakas. Listen attentively as I recite them correctly.
These three phrases constitute an exhortation to listen. "Attentively" (*di*) means to examine with scrutiny; "listen" (*ting*) means to receive and comprehend.
"I am now reciting" distinguishes this from the biased and deviant precepts recited by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Non-Buddhists falsely speculate that they have come from among chickens or dogs in their previous lives, and thus they observe the precepts of chickens and dogs, isolating themselves, consuming filth, and practicing asceticism in the hope [of liberation].
To be born in the heavens is called "perverse precepts," which is itself "perverse recitation. The Two Vehicles maintain and recite the precepts of quiescent emptiness;
this is called "partial precepts," which is itself "partial recitation. Now, one recites the wondrous precepts of the mind-ground, the true reality of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, it is called "correct recitation. Since this Dharma is correct, if one does not listen with careful discernment, one will ultimately fail to enter the One Vehicle.
This is the wondrous precept of the mind-ground of the true mark; therefore, you must listen with careful scrutiny.

Regarding the treasury of precepts within the Buddha-dharma, there are three treasuries of the Dharma taught by the Buddha, and this is the treasury of precepts among those three. The treasury of precepts is the *vinaya*. In the Sanskrit language it is called *vinaya*;
in the Chinese language it means "inherent goodness," because its nature is fundamentally good from the beginning. It is also called "abiding well."
Because it enables the Buddha-dharma to abide long in the world, it is also called "Virtuous Longevity" (*sujīvita*).
This means that if the *vinaya* abides in the world, then the Buddha-dharma abides in the world; if the *vinaya* should perish, then the Buddha-dharma will quickly perish.

Since the *vinaya* is the life-force within the Buddha-dharma, it is said to be the "Treasury of Precepts" (*śīlapiṭaka*) within the Buddha-dharma. *Prātimokṣa* refers to the meaning of the fruit of the precepts.
Observing the precepts is the cause; liberation is the fruit. Therefore, if a person can maintain pure precepts, they will be able to protect themselves and attain great liberation.
The four lines following [the previous verse] are for the great assembly to believe with a sincere heart; they are an exhortation to believe with sincerity.
This means that if one listens without believing, it is merely empty listening and of no benefit; therefore, one must sincerely believe these precepts as the direct cause for attaining Buddhahood.
If you can uphold [this teaching] in such a manner, you will certainly attain Buddhahood in the future without doubt.
Furthermore, I am already a Buddha, yet it was by my faith and upholding of these precepts of the Mind-Ground that I have already attained the perfection of merit and wisdom.
Moreover, as one who has already become a Buddha, I still constantly maintain such faith; how much more so for you, who have not yet attained Buddhahood? For this reason, I exhort you.
"One should believe with earnest sincerity. These six phrases beginning with "All who possess a mind" are an exhortation to accept [the teaching].

This means that having believed, one should accept it; to believe without accepting is not true belief. When it says "all who possess a mind," it distinguishes them from wood or stone, which lack a mind.
It means that all who possess a mind shall become Buddhas; how could this be a matter of minor causes and minor fruits? Therefore...
It says: "All who possess a mind should all embrace the Buddha-precepts. Question: The previous statement said that both emotion and mind all enter into the Buddha-nature precepts;
this current statement says that all who possess a mind should embrace the Buddha-precepts.
What is the difference between these two meanings? Answer: The former proceeds from the outside inward, and thus it says they all "enter" the Buddha-nature precepts. This [latter]...

This is because they are received based on the internal [mind]; therefore it says, "All should be subsumed within the Buddha's precepts. Furthermore, the preceding [passage] refers to the meaning of returning from delusion to the True;
thus it says, "all enter. Now, this refers to uniting with awakening and turning away from the dust of sensory objects; hence it is called "subsuming" (*she*).

When it says, "When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas," this precisely clarifies the meaning that all should be subsumed within the Buddha's precepts. For outside of the mind...
There is no Buddha apart from the mind. Outside of the ground [of the mind], there is no ground of the Buddhas.

Now that sentient beings have received the Dharma-precepts of the Buddhas’ mind-ground, do they not immediately enter the rank of the Buddhas? To say, "Their rank is identical to that of Great Enlightenment;

they are truly the children of the Buddhas," is to praise and encourage them by citing their attained rank. Question: Since it was stated above that they "immediately enter the rank of the Buddhas," this...
Furthermore, it is said: "If one's rank is equal to that of the Great Awakening, one should already be a Buddha. Why, then, is one merely called a 'Son of the Buddha'? Answer:
Although their rank is equal to the Great Awakening, this does not mean they have actually realized the fruit of the path of Great Awakening.

Because their causal practices are not yet perfected, they must necessarily pass through three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, extensively cultivating all the myriad practices of the six *pāramitās*, and serving [the Buddhas].
The Buddhas of the ten directions have all practiced the path and Dharma of the Buddhas;
with their vows fulfilled, they have first succeeded to the rank of Buddha, just as a consecrated prince, while still serving as the crown prince, is merely called a "prince.

Now, by receiving the Buddha-precepts and cultivating the conduct of a Buddha, one is named a "Son of the Buddha. Regarding those who are truly Sons of the Buddhas, there are three kinds of such sons.
First, the outsider sons of the Buddha: this refers to all ordinary beings who have never entered the Path and have never succeeded to and flourish the lineage of the Buddhas;

therefore, they are called outsiders.
