Nothing obstructs the bodhicitta, nothing obstructs the bodhisattva vow, nor indeed anything else, more than anger. Therefore, one must restrain it.
The passage beginning with "If a Buddha’s disciple... clarifies the nature of anger. Regarding the phrase "one's own anger," it refers to the resentment arising from within oneself.
Regarding the act of becoming angry oneself or teaching others to become angry, there are three meanings: first, borrowing another's anger toward a third party to vent one's own resentment;
second, teaching others to be angry with someone else in order to gain profit therein; and third, [teaching anger] toward someone who is already hated by others.
It causes the two parties to harbor mutual hatred and inflict harm upon one another, finding pleasure therein, so that neither family may attain liberation.

As for the cause of hatred (*dveṣa-hetu*), it refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of resentment accumulated since beginningless time. As for the condition (*pratyaya*) of hatred, it refers to the presence before one of the person or object toward whom one feels hatred.
As for the phenomenon of hatred (*dharma*), it refers to the mind itself giving rise to calculations and schemes, causing the other to suffer humiliation.

Regarding the karma of hatred (*dveṣa-karman*): through the conjunction of these three factors, one performs the action of hatred, which results in the experience of the bitter retributions of the three miserable realms (*apāya*) in the future.
As the Sūtra says: "If one does not sever the mind of hatred, even if they possess merit, great wisdom, and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they will receive the retribution of an asura;
just like a person who lacks merit, wisdom, and concentration, they will instead receive the retribution of a tiger or a wolf."
The retribution of snakes, scorpions, and the like. That which has been prohibited above is the severing of all evils; that which follows, "the Bodhisattva," is the cultivation of all virtues.

One who practices the path of a Bodhisattva should give rise to roots of goodness that are impartial toward the minds of all sentient beings, free from any cause for contention, and should constantly maintain a single mind of compassion.
One should regard all sentient beings as one's own children and so forth, and should nurture them; it is for this reason that one cannot bear to feel anger toward them.
Furthermore, one should constantly give rise to a heart of filial piety, regarding sentient beings as one's own parents and so forth, and should serve them;
for this reason, one does not dare to feel anger. One who possesses such a mind is a true child of the Buddha.
Regarding the gate of equal contemplation: if one is unable to do so, one has already failed to employ the impartial expedient means of a son of the Buddha;

how much more so if, furthermore, among all sentient beings—even toward those who are not sentient beings—one reviles them with harsh speech, strikes them with the hand, or attacks them with knives and staves, and yet the mind still finds no rest? Those who are "not sentient beings" are none other than the Buddhas.
This extends even to noble sages or transformed beings (*nirmāṇa-puruṣa*). To revile and insult them with harsh speech constitutes unwholesome verbal karma (*vāg-karma*).
To further strike them with the hand constitutes unwholesome bodily karma (*kāya-karma*). If the mind still does not cease, it constitutes unwholesome mental karma (*manas-karma*).
Through these three karmas being committed simultaneously, the offense is considered self-inflicted; or, [it may be directed] toward the one previously resented.
When someone comes to seek repentance for their transgressions, one should respond with kind words to apologize and humble oneself to dissolve their anger.

If, despite this, they continue to knit their brows and glare with eyes of rage, such that their hatred remains unresolved, this is not the mental conduct of a Bodhisattva; therefore, it constitutes a fault.
This is a *pārājika* offense for a Bodhisattva. As for those who do not commit such an offense, they are like King Anala and others, who possessed these three poisons yet [remained steadfast].
This is the true practice of a Bodhisattva.
○ Tenth: The Precept Against Slandering the Triple Gem.

If a disciple of the Buddha slanders the Triple Gem themselves, or teaches others to slander the Triple Gem—whether through the causes of slander, the conditions of slander, the dharma of slander, or the karma of slander.
When a bodhisattva hears even a single word of slander against the Buddha from a non-Buddhist or an evil person, it is as if three hundred spears pierce his heart;

how much more so when they slander him with their own mouths? If he fails to give rise to a mind of faith or a mind of filial obedience, and instead assists those evil people and those of wrong views who slander, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for the bodhisattva.
This explains the tenth precept concerning the slander of the Triple Gem. "Slander" refers to being ignorant of the principle and lacking true insight, thereby falsely leveling criticisms.
The Triple Gem is the field of merit and source of protection for all sentient beings;

to slander it is to lose one's own sprout of bodhisattva virtue and likewise to lose the sprouts of virtue in those sentient beings. Therefore, the transgression is no small matter. Thus [it is said].
This is to warn against it. Those who slander the Triple Gem do so because they themselves have not yet attained right view, nor have they understood the profound Dharma;
or because they see the scriptures of non-Buddhists, or hear the words of non-Buddhists, or comply with the wishes of those in positions of power.

That is, one speaks it oneself and likewise follows along without objection. "Teaching others to slander" means causing another person to revile and disparage [the teaching], desiring to join their faction.
"The cause of slander" refers to the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) for fondness toward heterodox discourse since beginningless time.
"The conditions for slander" refers to encountering an opportunity and joining together with such words as the condition. "Slandering the Dharma" means that—

Using clever words and false sophistry to cause the ignorant and those with wrong views to take them as the Dharma and believe in them—this act of slandering is the conjunction of these three factors, which constitutes the karma of slander.

This causes one, in future lives within the three evil realms, to neither see nor hear the Triple Gem, thereby undergoing the fruits of suffering. All that has been cautioned against above is to be severed entirely.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva encounters those who practice evil, he exhorts them toward their conduct, which is the cultivation of all that is wholesome.

For one who follows the path of a bodhisattva, if they see a non-Buddhist or an evil person uttering even a single malicious word to slander the voice of the Buddha, and it enters their ears, it is as if three hundred spears and pikes were thrust into their heart; the pain is unbearable and equal [to any other suffering].
There is a difference. Why is this? Because it cuts off the Buddha-seed of all sentient beings. This is true of even a single word; how much more so for many words?
It is true even when merely heard by the ear; how much more so when one personally utters words of slander? The Buddha is the Great Teacher of gods and humans;
he has cleared away the clouds of my delusion and guided me out of the three realms. One ought to give rise to faith and reverence, yet instead you do not give rise to faith.
With a heart of reverence: the Buddha is the Great Compassionate Father who can uproot my suffering and bestow upon me happiness;
it is precisely right that I be filial toward him, yet instead of giving rise to a filial heart, I have already ceased to be a child of the Buddha and have gone so far as to assist evil people.
Those with wrong views who slander and revile the Triple Gem, taking perverse pleasure in such discourse, are like worms within a lion’s body that eat the lion’s own flesh;
this constitutes a *pārājika* offense for a bodhisattva.
II. Summary of the Ten Grave Precepts:
O virtuous practitioners who study well, these are the ten *prātimokṣa* precepts of a bodhisattva; you should train yourselves in them.

Within these, one must not commit even a single transgression so minute as a speck of dust, let alone commit all ten precepts in their entirety. If there is anyone who commits such a transgression, they shall not...
Though they may manifest in this body and give rise to the bodhicitta, they will lose their status as a king, as well as their status as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).

They will also lose their status as a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī, and they will lose the ten stages of departure, the ten stages of nourishment, the ten adamantine stages, the ten bhūmis, and the wondrous fruit of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature.
Having lost all these, they fall into the three evil realms for two or three kalpas, where they shall not hear the names of their parents.
Regarding the names of the Three Jewels, one must not transgress each of these individually.

You all, O Bodhisattvas—those who are now learning, those who shall learn, and those who have already learned—should train yourselves in these ten precepts in this manner. Respectfully uphold them; the eighty thousand categories of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) shall be explained in detail.
This section summarizes the characteristics of gain and loss regarding the ten precepts, and offers an exhortation to firmly uphold these disciplinary laws.
"Those who learn well" and below cite individuals to praise their virtues. "These bodhisattvas" and below cite the Dharma itself to clarify that the disciplinary laws ought to be maintained.
One should not disparage it. If there are those who violate even the minor precepts, [the text] clarifies the faults of breaking the precepts.

"You all," and so forth, is an exhortation to study and uphold them throughout every lifetime; you must not forget this. "The eighty thousand," and so forth, cites the extensive to clarify the concise.
"O virtuous ones who study well" is a term of praise from the Buddha, meaning that such a person is fully capable of receiving and upholding these precepts.
He possesses the virtues of compassion, kindness, and filial piety; therefore, he is called a "virtuous learner.
Since he is called virtuous, he ought to diligently study these ten *prātimokṣa* precepts, the category of pure morality.
Within them, he must not transgress even so much as a speck of dust; if one cannot transgress even by a speck of dust, how much less so otherwise?
Is it possible to fully violate the ten precepts? This is a definitive statement that they must not be violated.

If one were to violate them, [the following] assumes and determines the characteristics of the gain and loss regarding the violation of the precepts: namely, if among the ten grave precepts (*daśa-śīla*) one does not violate even as much as a mote of dust, such a person can give rise to the bodhicitta and may preserve the position of a king or the precious throne of a *cakravartin* wheel-turning monarch, O Bhikṣu.
The stage of a bhikṣuṇī may also be permitted to enter the causal stages of the thirty minds and the ten bhūmis;
it may be hoped for that she will attain the fruit-stage of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature and wondrous enlightenment.
Were it otherwise, even if there were only a slight transgression, she would be unable to give rise to the bodhicitta in her present body. Why is this? Because as for the bodhicitta—
This is precisely the pure, luminous, adamantine jewel-precept of the wondrous enlightened mind.

Now, having turned one's back on enlightenment and conformed to the defilements, one pollutes the holy life and thereby loses this mind; hence it is said: "One cannot manifest the arousal of the bodhicitta in this present body."
This mind is the very root of both merit and wisdom. Now that the root has been lost, from what shall the flowers and fruits of the Buddha arise?
Therefore, the status of a king and the status of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) are also lost; the status of a bhikṣu and a bhikṣuṇī are likewise lost.
For the status of a king and the status of a golden-wheel-turning monarch constitute the most supreme positions of merit in the world.
The rank of bhikṣu, the rank of bhikṣuṇī, and the rank of the supramundane wisdom of the noble ones—
now that these ranks of mundane and supramundane merit and wisdom have already been lost, [one loses] the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing, and the ten adamantine stages.
The causal stages of the ten bhūmis are likewise lost. If the causal stages are lost, how can the resultant stage of wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) be attained?
Therefore, the Buddha-nature that abides eternally and the resultant stage of wondrous enlightenment are both lost. Precepts are like the great earth from which all myriad virtues arise;
now that this ground is absent, there is no place for the seeds of the Buddhas and sages to be established. The seeds of the Buddhas...
If the sprouts of Buddhahood have not been planted, how can they arise? Therefore it is said: "Everything is lost. Question:

Since all blessings, wisdom, causes, and fruits, as well as all precious positions, are lost, in what state does this person reside? Answer: They fall into the most agonizing places within the three evil realms.
The mention of "two kalpas" or "three kalpas" indicates the vast duration of time spent in those places of extreme suffering.
Those who do not hear the names of their parents or the Three Jewels are shown to have deep and heavy karmic obstructions and offenses from the three miserable realms of hell and so forth;
they are unlike those born in the human realm who possess the retribution of merit, nor are they like those who have attained the opportunity to receive the Buddha-dharma.
For this reason, they do not hear the names of their parents or the Three Jewels at all. By this one should know that one must not transgress each and every one of these precepts.
Below, I shall provide an exhortation regarding the meaning of what should be upheld and what should not be violated.

If one violates the precepts, one loses great benefit and incurs great suffering. Since one must not transgress even so much as a speck of dust from among these ten grave precepts, you who are all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time should therefore reverently uphold these ten precepts with a respectful heart. Thus...

This must not be forgotten for as long as one lives. This is a brief explanation; if explained in detail, it is contained within the eighty thousand sections on dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) in the Great Canon.
Regarding the ten grave precepts mentioned above, if one violates any single precept, one shall be punished according to the original offense.
If one commits one of the seven heinous transgressions (*ānantarya*), the retribution belongs to the Avīci Hell. If one commits other minor offenses...
This encompasses the latter forty-eight precepts. Such categories of offenses exist solely because they enter into the realms of gravity or lightness according to where a person’s thoughts arise.
Alas! Even a thought as slight as a hair’s breadth becomes a karmic cause for the three miserable realms; can one not be cautious?
II. Explaining the Characteristics of the Minor Precepts (2). First, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one; second, the detailed explanation of the textual meaning.
Regarding the first—concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent:
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying: "The ten *pratimokṣa* have already been explained. Now, as for the forty-eight minor [offenses]..."
It shall now be explained.
This is the proclamation of our Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed to the Bodhisattvas present in the assembly, including those of the Three Grades of Sages and the Ten Stages of Holiness.
"Having already explained" and below refers to the conclusion of the ten preceding sections; the explanation is finished. [The forty-eight minor precepts now begin.]
Next are the minor precepts; these shall now be explained.
Part Two: Detailed Explanation of the Textual Meaning (48).
First: The Precept Against Showing Disrespect to Teachers and Friends.

If, O sons of the Buddha, you wish to receive the rank of a king, the rank of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*), or when officials receive their positions, you should first receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
Then all ghosts and spirits will protect the person of the king and the persons of the officials, and all Buddhas will rejoice.
Once you have received the precepts, you should give rise to a heart of filial piety and obedience, and a heart of reverence. Upon seeing seniors, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), or ācāryas...
"Venerable Upāsaka, those who are fellow students, share the same views, and practice the same path should rise to welcome them, pay homage, and inquire after their well-being.

Yet, this Bodhisattva instead gives rise to arrogance, conceit, delusion, and anger; he does not rise to welcome them or pay homage, nor does he provide each of them with offerings according to the Dharma.
Rather than doing so, he sells himself, his kingdom, his cities, his sons, his daughters, the seven treasures, and all manner of goods to provide for them."
If one does not act thus, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
This explains the first precept: not revering teachers and friends. Teachers provide guidance and instruction, while friends provide mutual refinement;

the attainment of the Dharma-vessel for both worldly and world-transcending goals depends entirely upon teachers and friends, and they must therefore be revered and honored. Should one harbor arrogance or pride, throughout one's entire life...
Because merit and wisdom are thereby extinguished, one must observe the precepts. The passage beginning with "If a disciple of the Buddha" introduces the person to clarify their status.

The passage beginning with "One should first receive" clarifies the foundation of the two positions of merit and wisdom. The passage beginning with "Having already received the precepts" clarifies the recipient of the precepts.

Those who have benefited from the Dharma of purification should repay that kindness. The passage beginning with "The Bodhisattva" below clarifies that those who turn their backs on kindness and forget their origins are to be charged with an offense.
As for "kings," these are the benevolent rulers of various states; there are four types of wheel-turning kings (cakravartin): those of gold, silver, copper, and iron.
The four types of Wheel-Turning Kings are the sovereigns who rule over the four, three, two, or one world-systems. The hundred officials are the civil and military ministers.
Why must such holy rulers and worthy ministers, when desiring to receive their royal or official positions, necessarily first receive the Bodhisattva precepts?
It is because those who receive the Bodhisattva precepts must, by means of compassion, bring benefit and salvation to others.
With filial piety and obedience as their guiding principle: if a ruler receives the Bodhisattva precepts, he becomes a benevolent and virtuous sage-king;
if a minister receives the Bodhisattva precepts, he becomes a loyal and excellent official.

They will move all ghosts and spirits to protect the king’s person and ensure his throne is forever preserved. They will protect the persons of the hundred officials and cause their ranks to advance. Not only the ghosts...
The deities provide protection alone; they also move the Buddhas of the ten directions to rejoice, protect, and mindfully remember them.

Why is this? The defense of the Dharma relies entirely upon them. As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states: "If a king receives the bodhisattva precepts, extensively practices the ten wholesome dharmas, and teaches and transforms sentient beings, his body and mind will experience happiness, the three calamities will never occur, and he will remain far removed from the eight [difficulties]."
It is difficult [to describe]. The realm is peaceful and secure; the people sing with joy, and so forth.

Therefore, by first receiving the Bodhisattva’s wisdom-precepts and subsequently attaining the positions of kings and ministers, one obtains the protection of spirits and deities and brings joy to all Buddhas. Such are the benefits.

If it were not for the instructions and admonitions of teachers and friends, by what means could this be attained? Therefore, one should recognize their kindness and repay their virtue, giving rise to a mind of filial piety and obedience.
One should revere the precept teacher as one reveres one's own parents, not daring to transgress even slightly, and should cultivate a heart of profound respect.
One should revere virtuous friends as one would revere an elder brother, not daring to harbor any arrogance.

Only those who possess such a mind may be called practitioners who recollect the precepts and enter the Path. This passage, from "seeing elders" downward, clearly elucidates the meaning of filial piety, obedience, and reverence.
The term "Elder" (*sthavira*) is used in contrast to those of middle and lower status, as there is no one superior to them.
The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are three types of Elders: first, the Elder by birth, which refers to venerable seniors of advanced age;
second, the worldly Elder, which refers to those possessing great wealth, high rank, noble lineage, great power, and a large retinue.
Third, the *dharmatā-sthavira* (Elder of the Dharma-nature) refers to one who has attained the stage of Arhatship.
The *upādhyāya*—translated into Chinese as "Power-Born" (*lìshēng*)—is the preceptor who originally confers the precepts.

The *ācārya*—translated into Chinese as "Model Teacher" (*guǐfàn shī*)—refers to the various masters such as the *karmācārya*, the *śikṣācārya*, the *niśrayācārya*, and the *sākṣyācārya*. The term "Virtuous One" (*bhadanta*) is used to address these various masters.

Because those of long standing and superior virtue are preeminent, they also encompass the meanings explained below. "Fellow students" refers to those who study the supramundane path under the same teacher.

"Shared views" means having the same perspective, as they have likewise understood the principles within the Middle Way. "Shared practice" means following the same gateway to the pure and white *brahmacarya*.
When such teachers or friends arrive, regardless of whether they are far or near, one should rise to welcome them and pay due respect.
One should pay homage and further inquire after their well-being; this is what is meant by a mind of filial piety and reverence.
One who is a bodhisattva ought to give rise to a mind of filial piety, yet instead gives rise to a mind of anger and envy;

ought to give rise to a mind of reverence, yet instead gives rise to a mind of irreverence, arrogance, and self-exaltation regarding name and status, becoming haughty and self-important. Therefore, it is so named.
The mind of arrogance; the mind of pride; looking down upon others and being haughty toward those with virtue—therefore it is called the mind of pride. The mind of delusion;
seeing the worthy yet not associating with them, seeing the sages yet not revering them, and lacking wisdom—therefore it is called the mind of delusion.

The mind of anger; resenting the strict admonitions of one's teachers and friends—therefore it is called the mind of anger. Because these four kinds of minds exist, when one sees teachers and friends approaching...
He does not go out to meet him; when the other arrives, he does not offer salutation, nor does he inquire after his well-being or daily activities.

The four factors beginning with pride belong to the mental action (*manas-karman*). Not rising to welcome or prostrating belongs to the bodily action (*kāya-karman*). Nor does he inquire after his well-being or daily activities.

This pertains to verbal karma. Because these three types of karma are unwholesome, even such things as food, clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions are each offered in a manner that does not accord with the Dharma.
From the phrase "selling oneself" onwards, it follows directly from the explanation of what accords with the Dharma;
it says that since one has become a child of the Buddha, one ought to value the Dharma above one’s own body, life, and wealth, seeking transcendence from the world.

The Way consists of one’s own person internally, and the state and its cities externally; it includes beloved men and women, the seven precious treasures, and all manner of manifold objects—all of these may be sold, and in this way one should make offerings.

As for what is called "selling one's body," it is like Sadāprarudita, who sold his heart and liver to study the Prajñāpāramitā; or as the World-Honored One did while on the path of practice, when he relinquished his body for half a verse.
The entire body, even to the point of lighting a thousand lamps upon it—this is the sacrifice of the body as a model for the Dharma. To cite just one or two such examples:
this constitutes the magnificent observance of repaying the debt of gratitude for those who hold high rank and position. It is not like merely receiving them with formal welcome and prostration.

To fail to make offerings to one's teachers and friends constitutes a minor secondary offense for a bodhisattva. This offense, compared to the ten major grave offenses mentioned previously, is reduced by only one degree;
it is not to be called a trivial or insignificant matter.
The second precept against drinking alcohol:
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally drinks alcohol, the faults arising from such drinking are immeasurable. If one passes a vessel of alcohol through one's own hands, [one commits an offense].
One who provides alcohol to others shall be without hands for five hundred lifetimes; how much more so for drinking it oneself?
Furthermore, one must not teach any person to drink, nor allow any sentient being to drink alcohol; how much more so for drinking it oneself? No form of alcohol whatsoever may be drunk.
If one intentionally drinks it oneself or teaches others to drink, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
This explains the second precept concerning the consumption of intoxicants. Regarding the term "drinking alcohol," it does not refer to the brewing of wine.

While those who brew and sell wine cause harm on a vast scale, those who drink it only bring harm upon themselves; thus, there is a slight distinction between the gravity of their respective offenses.
The Vinaya states: A person who drinks alcohol falls into the Burning and Boiling Hell for five periods of five hundred years each.
For the first five hundred years, they are in the Hell of Salty Dregs; for the second five hundred years, in the Hell of Boiling Excrement;
for the third five hundred years, in the Hell of Curved Worms; for the fourth five hundred years, in the Hell of Flies and Gnats; and for the fifth...
For five hundred lifetimes, one falls into the hell of delusion, fever, and ignorance; such is the retribution for karma, and therefore one is cautioned against it.
Thus, regarding those who drink alcohol, the Vinaya permits its use in cases of serious illness when a physician says it will cure the ailment by using wine to facilitate the medicine.
If one drinks without cause, or drinks under the pretext of illness, this constitutes intentional drinking.
Since the faults arising from alcohol are immeasurable, the principle that one must not drink alcohol is clarified as follows: Alcohol is a fermented rice broth;
for what reason is it forbidden to drink? It is because those who drink alcohol become deluded in mind and disordered in nature, leading to immeasurable transgressions.
Loss arises from drinking alcohol; therefore, one must not drink.

Not only does one who drinks alcohol themselves incur immeasurable faults, but even one who passes a vessel of alcohol with their own hand to another for them to drink will likewise incur the retribution of being without hands and feet for five hundred lifetimes, let alone drinking it oneself without cause. Self-...
If one may not even drink it oneself, how could one teach others to drink?
For this reason, one must not teach any person to drink wine, nor teach any sentient being to drink wine. If teaching them is not permitted, how much less so drinking it oneself?
Therefore, no kind of wine whatsoever is to be drunk. Regarding the term "all kinds of wine": there are many varieties of wine. [Yáng...]
Plum, jujube, sugarcane, grape, and other such wines, even if they only cause intoxication and possess the aroma and flavor of alcohol, must not be drunk under any circumstances.
The above clarifies the precept; hereafter follows the determination of the offense. If one intentionally drinks them oneself, [it constitutes a violation].
If a Bodhisattva teaches others to drink [alcohol], they commit a minor offense.
The third is the precept against eating meat:
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally eats meat, no meat whatsoever may be eaten. Indeed, those who eat meat sever great compassion.
The seed of Buddha-nature exists within all sentient beings, yet they see it and abandon it.
For this reason, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being. To eat meat incurs immeasurable sin; if one eats it intentionally, they commit a minor offense.
This explains the third precept against eating meat. All sentient beings possess the nature of spiritual awareness;
they all share the desire for life and the dread of death, and they all harbor thoughts of affection and consciousness that are no different from my own.
It is said that all things belonging to the realm of blood and breath must possess consciousness; and all that possesses consciousness must share a common essence.

Yet, how can there be a class of people whose minds are shrouded by false views, who for the sake of their own mouths and bellies eat the flesh of those sentient beings, and yet speak with such audacity:
As long as one has clearly realized the Great Matter, there is no hindrance to eating meat.
If the Great Matter is already realized, then one is utterly detached from the faculty of the tongue and the object of taste; thus one may say there is no hindrance to eating meat.

If it has not been realized, how could there be no hindrance to eating meat? I then mock him, saying: "If, as you claim, there is no hindrance to eating meat once the Great Matter is realized, then..."
Molten copper and red-hot iron should likewise present no obstacle. One who can swallow molten copper and red-hot iron may certainly eat meat.
For example, when Ji Dian of the Song dynasty solicited funds to gild a Buddha statue, he spent all the proceeds on wine and meat;

subsequently, gold was vomited from his mouth, with which he was able to complete the gilding of the Buddha’s image. This is truly "unobstructed. As for Master Zhi eating a pigeon, one day [he... from...
The mouth spat out all the live pigeons, which flew away together. This is truly unimpeded.

If one cannot yet reach this level, then as for those who claim to have clarified the Great Matter (the ultimate truth), why do they alone feel intimacy toward flesh and take pleasure in its proximity to the mouth, while feeling estrangement toward molten copper and hot iron, and fearing their proximity to the body?
Furthermore, how could such a person rightfully claim to be "unimpeded"? — *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*
It says: "The sheep dies and becomes a human; the human dies and becomes a sheep. You owe me my life, and I shall repay your debt.

Because of this, they devour one another without end; therefore, it is forbidden. When it says, "If a Buddha's disciple intentionally eats meat," the word "intentionally" (hù) is used as a provisional device.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a year of famine and no vegetables grew.
By the spiritual power of the Buddha, he manifested five kinds of pure meat from the tips of his five fingers;
these were not actually flesh or blood, but were temporarily manifested as a skillful means. How could there be any real flesh from the bodies of sentient beings for a son of the Buddha to eat?
Therefore, the flesh of the bodies of all sentient beings must not be eaten. Indeed, those who eat meat sever the great compassion of the Buddha.
Regarding the phrase "severing the seeds of the Buddha-nature of great compassion," there are two meanings.
First, it refers to severing the seeds of the Buddha-nature of a bodhisattva’s great compassionate mind. Why is this so?

Because when a bodhisattva gives rise to the bodhicitta, they vow to cause all sentient beings to leave suffering behind and attain happiness; this constitutes the sole cause for attaining Buddhahood.
[This is] practicing [wrongly]. Now, to eat the flesh of sentient beings without a compassionate heart is to sever the causal seed for one’s own attainment of Buddhahood.
Once the causal seed is severed, how can the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood be hoped for? Second, it is to sever the seed of the Buddha-nature in sentient beings.
This means that although all sentient beings have been wandering through the six realms since beginningless time, changing their heads and faces, [their Buddha-nature remains].
Furthermore, that nature of theirs which fears birth and dreads death is precisely the seed of my own awakened compassion and Buddha-nature.
If I now wish to eat their flesh to cause them terror so that they will see me and depart, I would lose the causal conditions for transforming them;
this would be to sever the seed of the great compassion of Buddha-nature. As the *Pratideśanā-parivarta* (Chapter on Vows) says: "All sentient beings are like trees."

The roots are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who act as the flowers and fruits; through the water of great compassion, they benefit sentient beings and are thus able to bring to fruition the flowers and fruits of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Now that the roots of the Buddha-tree have been lost, from where shall the flowers and fruits of the Buddhas arise?
As for those sentient beings who see [this] and abandon it, their mutual breath is filled with the air of slaughter.
To welcome poison from the Rong and Di tribes is like the seagull losing its trust with the fisherman, or the pigeon disturbing the shadow of an Arhat.
Therefore, no Bodhisattva may eat the flesh of any sentient being; if one eats it intentionally, they incur immeasurable sin.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that for immeasurable causes and conditions, one should not eat meat, for the sake of all...
Sentient beings have, from the very beginning, always been [bound] by their six kin;

because they are produced and grow from impure physical elements, when sentient beings smell this fragrance, they all give rise to terror, just as dogs bark in alarm upon seeing Caṇḍālas, Taṃbas, and the like.
Now, because practitioners of the path do not give rise to compassion, it is foul, filthy, and impure, and lacks a good reputation.
Therefore, it causes all incantations and arts to fail; one is abandoned by the devas; one's breath becomes foul;
and one has many evil dreams at night. Even in a secluded forest, tigers and wolves will scent the odor.
For these reasons, one should not eat the flesh of sentient beings. If one eats it intentionally, one commits a minor offense of defilement.
The fourth is the precept against eating the five pungent roots.
O Disciples of the Buddha, one must not eat the five pungent roots: garlic, leeks, scallions, onions, and asafoetida.
These five kinds are forbidden among all foods; if one intentionally eats them, one commits a minor offense.

This explains the fourth precept regarding the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*). The "five pungent roots" refers to the five *huǎn* (garlic-like vegetables), not the five *xīng* (meat-based pungents).
As for the five pungent roots: first is garlic, also called *hú*; this refers to the *húcōng* (leek). Second is *gècōng*, which other sutras call *gécōng*;
this refers to the *xiècài* (shallot). Third is *cícōng*, which is simply the common onion. Fourth is *láncōng*, which is the small... [text fragment ends].
Garlic; fifth, *xingqu* (i.e., *jiji*). Regarding what is said about not eating these: because these five kinds, when eaten cooked, arouse lust, and when eaten raw, increase anger.
Furthermore, there are five [conditions] under which one should not eat: first, when life has passed its prime; second, when heaven is far away; third, when ghosts are near;
fourth, when merit is exhausted; and fifth, when Māra gathers. The *Xiyuji* states: "If there is a person in the household who raises pungent plants, [one must] drive them away..."

He was ordered to leave the city walls. For this reason, it is not permissible to eat alone or in isolation. Generally speaking, among all types of food, one must not consume anything that has been mixed with or used as an accompaniment [to the forbidden items].
If one claims there was no killing involved and yet deliberately consumes the five pungent roots (pañca-gandhaka), one commits a minor offense (laghu-pāpaka).
Fifth, the precept against failing to instruct others to repent for their offenses.

If a disciple of the Buddha sees any sentient being who has violated the eight precepts, the five precepts, or the ten precepts; who has transgressed prohibitions, committed the seven heinous acts, or fallen into the eight difficulties;

or who has committed any offense against the precepts—they should instruct them to perform repentance. Yet, if a Bodhisattva does not instruct them to repent, but instead dwells with them as equals...

If one partakes in the communal *poṣadha* ceremony with the Sangha’s offerings and dwells within the same assembly for the recitation of the precepts, yet fails to expose their transgressions or instruct them to repent,
one commits a minor offense of defilement.
This explains the fifth precept: not instructing others to repent for their transgressions. "Instruct" (jiao) means to provide admonition; "repent" (hui) means to regret one's errors;

and "transgression" (zui) refers to guilt or fault. This means that one who acts as a teacher to bodhisattvas must, whenever they see someone commit a fault, be able to instruct them to perform confession and repentance.

If one does not instruct them, one incurs transgression. Why is this? Long ago, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a bhikṣu who served as many as three masters and ordained many disciples, yet he failed to instruct or admonish them. Because his disciples did not maintain the precepts, after death they fell among the dragons.
According to the laws of the dragons, they undergo punishment by being burned against a fire once every seven days until their flesh is consumed.

The bones remained; after they were searched for and returned, he burned them again. Unable to endure the suffering, the dragon—possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā)—reflected upon what transgression had caused this.
He perceived through his vision that it was due to his former teacher’s failure to instruct him, leading him to commit many unrighteous acts.
Consequently, he harbored resentment toward his teacher and intended to inflict harm upon him. Later, five hundred merchants entered the sea to gather treasures, and their teacher was among them.
The dragon emerged from the water and seized the boat. The crowd was greatly terrified and questioned the reason for the dragon’s action.
The dragon said, "The bhikṣu inside this boat is my former teacher. Because he failed to instruct me, I am now suffering this pain;
therefore, I have seized the boat. If you take the bhikṣu down into the water, I shall release the boat."
When the crowd saw that the matter did not cease, they wished to seize the bhikṣu; however, the bhikṣu then threw himself into the water and died.
The Buddha said, "Judging by this instance, when one ordains a disciple, one must certainly provide instruction and admonition.

From the words "If a son of the Buddha" onwards, the text cites a person to clarify the characteristics of transgression. "Seeing all sentient beings" refers collectively to both householders and those who have left the home life.
The seven groups of followers, both great and small, are those who receive and uphold the precepts. "To transgress" means to violate them.
The eight precepts and the five precepts are the characteristics of the two groups: the *upāsaka* (laymen) and the *upāsikā* (laywomen).

The eight precepts are received for only one day and one night, unlike the five precepts, which are maintained for the duration of one's life. There are two types of ten precepts: first, those of the *śrāmaṇera* (novice monks)...

The Ten Precepts for Laypeople (*śrāvaka-daśa-śīla*), the Two Sets of Ten Grave Precepts for Bodhisattvas—those who violate these are said to "destroy" them; those that prohibit are said to "restrain and extinguish.

These were established by the Tathāgata: the two hundred and fifty precepts for *bhikṣus* and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts for *bhikṣuṇīs*, which are termed "prohibitory precepts" (*vinaya-śīla*).
If one receives them but does not uphold them, or upholds them but does not recite them, one transgresses against the Sage.

It is said that to transgress what has been prescribed is called "violating the prohibitions" (*huìjìn*). The seven heinous offenses (*qīnì*) are: killing one's father; killing one's mother; killing one's *upādhyāya*; killing one's *ācārya*;
causing a schism in the *saṃgha* engaged in the performance of the *karmavācanā* or turning the wheel of the Dharma; shedding the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind; and killing an *arhat*.
When the Buddha was in the world, [the offense of] shedding the Buddha's blood occurred; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [the offense of] selling the Buddha’s bodhi...
To sell images of the Buddha, as well as the Buddha’s sutras and vinaya, is called shedding the blood of the Buddha’s body.
To kill a bhikṣu-saṃgha is equivalent to killing an arhat. The "eight difficulties" (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa) refer to the eight unfavorable conditions for practice mentioned below.
When a bodhisattva sees any such person who has violated the precepts, they should give rise to a heart of compassion and instruct them to repent for their prior transgressions.

After having repented, do not commit [the offense] again; this is what constitutes benefiting oneself and others. If one does not instruct another to repent, one has already failed to fulfill the duty of instructing them to repent for their transgressions;
how much more so when one dwells in the same place, shares in the same monastic provisions, and furthermore performs the *poṣadha* together with them?
While dwelling within a single, pure, and harmonious Saṃgha, he preaches the Buddha’s precepts yet fails to bring forth the transgressions of those who have broken them so that they may repent.
Thus, failing to instruct them in the rectification of their errors,
such a person is a Bodhisattva teacher who commits a minor defiling offense.
Sixth, the precept on providing offerings and making requests for the Dharma:
If a disciple of the Buddha sees a Mahāyāna Dharma Master, a fellow student of the Mahāyāna, or those who share the same views and the same practice, entering the monastic quarters.
Whether they come from within a hundred li or a thousand li, he rises to welcome them and sees them off;

he pays homage and makes offerings to them, providing sustenance three times each day. He consumes three *liang* of gold daily for food and drink of a hundred flavors, as well as beds, seats, and medicine.

One should serve the Dharma Master by providing all that is required. One should constantly invite the Dharma Master to preach the Dharma during the three periods of the day, prostrating at each of the three times daily, without giving rise to anger or a mind of affliction. One should be willing to sacrifice one's own body for the sake of the Dharma and request the teachings without weariness.
If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense.
This explains the sixth precept concerning failing to provide for those who request the Dharma.

A practitioner of the Bodhisattva path, whenever they see a Dharma teacher of the Mahāyāna, should prepare incense, flowers, and all manner of offerings, no different from how one would make offerings to the Buddhas themselves.
Please turn the Wheel of Dharma so that the Way and its teachings may circulate and the life-force of wisdom may not be severed.
If those who are Bodhisattvas do not provide for those who request the teaching of the Dharma, they will fall into the streams of stinginess and greed, arrogance, scorched sprouts, and ruined seeds.

One would lose a great benefit; therefore, this serves as a warning. The section beginning with "If a disciple of the Buddha" identifies and clarifies the teachers and friends who are worthy of veneration.

Regarding the term "Dharma Master of the Mahāyāna," this distinguishes them from those of the Hīnayāna who seek only their own salvation; rather, it refers to one who possesses great faith and understanding.

Having resolved upon the mind of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-citta*) and hastening toward the fruit of the Great Vehicle, they are masters who practice the union of wisdom and compassion for the benefit of both self and others;

thus they are called "Dharma Masters of the Mahāyāna. Regarding the phrase "fellow students of the Mahāyāna" below, this indicates that the friends mentioned are likewise practitioners of the Mahāyāna.

"Fellow students" (*sahādhyāyin*) refers to those who have received the Mahāyāna *citta-bhūmi-śīla* (mind-ground precepts) from the same teacher. "Same view" (*samadṛṣṭi*) means having identical philosophical perspectives.
Regarding the ultimate reality of the mind-ground precepts and views, they practice together in the same Bodhisattva mind-ground precept-dharma, which is the pure and white Brahma-conduct.
If one encounters such teachers and friends who practice unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-maitrī*) and enter a monastic dwelling or a private residence, [one should receive them].
In cities and other locations, whether far or near, if anyone comes from even a hundred or a thousand *li* away, the presiding Bodhisattva should rise to show respect.

When they arrive, one should welcome them; when they depart, one should see them off. Regarding all matters of prostration and making offerings within this context, one must attend to each detail exactly according to the Dharma and not give rise to indolence. As for those who provide the offerings, they should likewise...
On each day, one must not lack offerings during the three periods. These three periods are the beginning, middle, and end of the day.
As for what constitutes the offering: every day, one should use three *liang* of gold to prepare food and drink of a hundred flavors as an offering.
Furthermore, it does not stop at this alone. One should additionally prepare seats and bedding for him to rest upon, and provide a full range of medicines for his care.
Using these four matters, one should serve the Dharma Master. Whatever this Dharma Master requires, all should be provided to him.
One should exert one's heart to honor and make offerings as is fitting; one should not be stingy or parsimonious. By doing so, one cultivates merit and fulfills [one's vow].
The *dānapāramitā* (perfection of giving) consists of constantly inviting [the Dharma teacher] and so forth; this is precisely the cultivation of wisdom, which is the *prajñāpāramitā*.

Regarding "constantly inviting and so forth," this refers back to what was stated above: those who respectfully prostrate to and make offerings [to the teacher] three times each day do not do so merely for the sake of seeking the minor fruits of merit and retribution of the human or celestial realms. It is truly for the purpose of constantly inviting the Dharma master. Day by day...
To preach the sublime Dharma three times each day is for the purpose of sustaining the life-force of wisdom of all sentient beings;

this signifies the meaning of the donor’s devotion through the vocal action (*vākkarman*). To prostrate three times each day is the formal etiquette for requesting the Dharma, signifying the meaning of devotion through the physical action (*kāyakarman*). The statement "not giving rise to a mind of anger" explains the request.

Within the exposition of the Dharma, "not feeling anger toward teachers and friends" and "regarding strict instructions as honorable and high" mean that one does not give rise to a mind of resentment or affliction;

within the explanation of making offerings, "not resenting the expense and abundance of one's offerings" refers to these two states of mind, which collectively express the meaning of devotion in the mental faculty (*manas-karman*).
The phrase "for the sake of the Dharma, even if it means being lowly" summarizes the preceding meanings to exhort [the practitioner] toward Bodhi.
Regarding the term "sat" (true person): one should thus sacrifice the body for the sake of the Dharma. This has two meanings.
First, those who truly seek the Dharma do not spare even this body or life; how much less would they fail to provide offerings of material requisites?
Second, those who truly seek the path to liberation should abandon this non-solid body to exchange it for a vajra-like indestructible body, abandoning that which is unreal.
The life of the world is real, yet it can be exchanged for the life of wisdom of the Dharma-body. Just as the Buddha, while in the causal stage,
sought the Great Dharma and used his own body as a seat, spread his hair over the mud, lit lamps for half-verses, and performed various ascetic practices—

all of which serve as models for sacrificing one's body for the sake of the Dharma— those who practice the path of the Bodhisattva should likewise request the Dharma in this manner and must not be indolent.
If it were not so, there would be a slight degree of indolence; this phrase is definitive. If one does not thus cultivate a mind of making offerings, one commits a minor offense of defilement.
○ Seventh, the precept against laziness and failing to listen to the Dharma:

If a disciple of the Buddha, wherever there is the preaching of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the Sūtras, or the Śāstras—such as in a great house or at a place where the Dharma is being taught—[fails to attend].
A newly initiated bodhisattva should carry the scrolls of the sutras and vinaya to the place where the Dharma Master resides to listen, receive, and inquire about them.
Whether it be in mountain forests, under trees, on monastic grounds, in rooms, or at any place where the Dharma is preached, they must go to all such places to listen and receive the teachings.
If one fails to go there to listen and receive them, one commits a minor offense.
This explains the seventh precept against laziness regarding the non-hearing of the Dharma. This precept follows from what was stated previously:

it is not only when a teacher comes to one’s own place that one should provide offerings and listen to the Dharma; rather, wherever there is a place where the Dharma is being taught, one should go there to hear and receive it.
One must not be indolent and fail to listen. Indolence is one of the eight major secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); because of this...
Laziness gives rise to heedlessness; heedlessness leads to loss of mindfulness; loss of mindfulness results in great distraction;
distraction leads to lack of clear comprehension; and lack of clear comprehension gives rise to delusion, whereby one commits various evil deeds.
Thus, beginning with laziness and failing to listen, one ultimately commits every kind of evil. Therefore, wherever the Dharma is being preached, one should—
One should go there to listen and receive [the teachings]. If one does not go to listen, this is precisely arrogance toward the Dharma.

Because of such arrogance toward the Dharma, merit and wisdom are extinguished, while evil and transgression increase. That is to say, if the flavor of the Dharma does not nourish the spirit, there will ultimately be no liberation;

therefore, it is forbidden. It is said that as a child of the Buddha, one must seek the higher and transform those below; this is the fundamental causal mind, through which one extensively studies and learns much.
Hearing is the supreme skillful means. If one does not extensively study and possess great learning, how could one be capable of upholding the Triple Gem?
Therefore, wherever there is a place for the preaching of the Dharma, one should go to listen and receive it.

As for the term *vinaya*, which refers to the Sūtras and Vinaya, it specifically clarifies the Dharma-treasure that extinguishes evil and gives rise to goodness. In the Sanskrit language, *vinaya* is translated here as "subduing" (*tiáofú*). This means to subdue the three [poisons].
It is karma that subdues the six sense faculties, extinguishes all evil, and gives rise to all goodness.
It is also called "virtuous longevity" (*śubhāyu*), because when this *vinaya* abides in the world, the Buddha-dharma abides; if the *vinaya* perishes, the Buddha-dharma perishes.

Furthermore, since the sūtras encompass the *vinaya*, and the *vinaya* encompasses the sūtras—and because the sūtras elucidate the principles of nature and characteristics while the *vinaya* restrains [transgressions]—[the two are inseparable].
The terms *vinaya* (毗尼) and *sūtra* (經律) both encompass the two meanings of *prakṛti-sāvadya* (性罪, natural offenses) and *prajñapti-sāvadya* (遮罪, prohibited offenses).

Regarding the phrase "within a great house," this specifically clarifies the location for preaching the Dharma. During the Buddha’s lifetime, various bhikṣus frequently accepted invitations from kings, ministers, and great donors (*dānapati*) to enter their homes for the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) and preach the Dharma; this constitutes preaching within a great house.
This concerns the locus of the Dharma. For those who are newly trained and of inferior capacity, it is a precept that they should listen.

That is to say, wherever there is any teaching of the Dharma, the Vinaya, or the Sūtras and Śāstras, any novice Bodhisattva observing the precepts should hold the scrolls of the Sūtras and Vinaya in their hands and go before the Dharma Master.
There, with a sincere mind, they should listen and receive the teachings. If they do not understand the meaning, they must consult and inquire about each point one by one. And...
This is to resolve doubts. Regarding the phrase "in mountain forests and the like," this uses the distant to illustrate the near;

it means that one should not only constantly follow and listen while at the homes of laypeople (*gṛhapati*), but should likewise go to listen wherever the Dharma is taught—even in mountain forests, in monastic quarters, or even in any remote location where the teaching is given.
In ancient times, the youth [Śāriputra] traveled south to seek instruction across a hundred districts.

Patch-robed monks have traveled across a thousand mountains; even Touzi went there three times and Dongshan ascended nine times, all for the sake of this Great Matter and not sparing themselves of toil.
How could one not go to listen to the Dharma? The Vinaya permits those who are ill, elderly, or whose physical strength makes travel difficult.
Furthermore, it may be that what is being taught is something they have heard before, or that they themselves possess great wisdom and great eloquence.
If one is cultivating profound dhyāna or great samādhi, or if one knows that what is being taught is the dharma of non-Buddhists and thus does not go to listen,

in both cases there is no offense. Apart from these circumstances, if a newly initiated bodhisattva does not go within a distance of forty *li* to listen to and receive the Dharma, they commit a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*).
The eighth is the precept against turning one’s back on the Great Vehicle and turning toward the Small Vehicle.

If a disciple of the Buddha, in their heart, turns their back on the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya that abide eternally, claiming they were not spoken by the Buddha, yet instead accepts and upholds the teachings of the two vehicles of the śrāvakas,
the evil views of external paths, or any precepts, heterodox views, sūtras, or vinayas— this constitutes a minor offense of defilement.
This explains the eighth precept: turning one's back on the Great Vehicle and inclining toward the Small.

It means that while one should everywhere seek to listen to and receive the teachings, one must only fear that the mind turns its back on the principle of the Middle Way and the Great Vehicle, instead inclining toward partial, small, heterodox, or external paths.
This path is precisely that which severs the Buddha-nature and obstructs the causes and conditions for the path to Bodhi; therefore, it is forbidden.

The passage beginning with "If a Buddha’s disciple" clarifies the turning away from the Great Meaning. The passage beginning with "To say it is not the Buddha's" clarifies the leaning toward the Small Meaning.
As for the statement "the mind turns its back on the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas of the eternal abiding," this refers to the Dharma of the Mahāyāna path taught by the Buddha, and within that...
The precepts of the Dharmakāya’s essence and form elucidate the mind-ground of the eternally abiding true reality, which is neither born nor extinguished.
These are the teachers of all Buddhas and the mothers of Bodhisattvas; therefore, they are called the "Eternally Abiding Sūtras and Vinaya.

To harbor doubts regarding this and, conversely, to claim that these were not spoken by the Buddha, while instead upholding the provisional and inferior teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle of the Two Vehicles—this is, on the contrary,...
To accept the evil views of non-Buddhists and all their prohibitions, heterodox views, sutras, and vinayas is therefore called "turning toward the Small Vehicle.

Because one thus turns one's back on the Great Vehicle and turns toward the Small Vehicle, one commits a minor offense (light impurity). Formerly, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu composed five hundred treatises.
He praised the Lesser Vehicle and disparaged the Great Vehicle. Later, upon encountering Asaṅga, he repented of his errors and wished to cut out his own tongue.

Asaṅga Bodhisattva instructed him to use that very tongue to praise the Mahāyāna once more. Vasubandhu followed this instruction; he disciplined his mind toward the Great Vehicle, propagated and expounded it widely, and ultimately attained the fruit of sainthood.
To reform one’s faults without regret—this is what constitutes a bodhisattva.
○ Ninth Precept: Not Neglecting the Sick.
If a disciple of the Buddha sees anyone who is ill, they should always provide for them with offerings as if they were no different from the Buddha himself.

Among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit of nursing the sick is the foremost field of merit. This applies whether it be one’s parents, teachers, monks, or disciples who are ill, or when their faculties are impaired.
If one encounters those afflicted by the hundred kinds of physical ailments and suffering, and fails to provide offerings to cure them;
or if, out of a heart of resentment, one does not look after them— even when seeing the sick in monasteries, cities, towns, wildernesses, mountain forests, or on the roads—
one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

This explains the ninth precept concerning the failure to tend to the sick. The bodies and lives of sentient beings, composed of the five aggregates, all depend upon the four conditions and the six sense objects;
they are but a provisional union of deluded thoughts and cannot escape the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, and death.

The Tathāgata, the Physician-King of the triple world and the Compassionate Father of the four modes of birth, constantly employs a heart of great compassion to skillfully regulate the physical and mental ailments and distresses of sentient beings.

Once one has become a bodhisattva, if upon seeing anyone afflicted by illness one does not give rise to the thoughts of great kindness and great compassion, nor attend to those suffering sentient beings, this is to lose for oneself the very root of attaining Buddhahood; therefore, one is cautioned against such negligence.

Regarding the statement "seeing all those who are ill": from parents and teachers above, down to children and disciples below, through brothers and the six types of relatives in the middle, to enemies outside—regardless of who they may be—one should always provide for them.
Question: If one does not actually provide relief, why speak of "providing for" (offering sustenance)? Answer: It is because one possesses this mental intention of providing for them.

Naturally attending to the sick is the cultivation of the mind-field; thus one attains permanence. To say that it is no different from serving the Buddha is to clarify the meaning of making offerings.
This means that the Buddha takes the bodies of sentient beings as his own body and the illnesses of sentient beings as his own illness;

therefore, whenever one sees those who are ill, one should regard them as the Buddha. Formerly, the Elder Yan personally resided in a leper ward, suckling and washing the patients without any sense of aversion.
Master Kuan carried the sick back home; he made no distinction between monastics and laypeople, which can truly be called making offerings as if to a Buddha.
Furthermore, the reason for making offerings as if to a Buddha is that, among the eight fields of merit, the field of merit consisting of caring for the sick is the foremost.

The eight fields of merit are: first, the Buddhas; second, the sages; third, one’s father; fourth, one’s mother; fifth, the upādhyāya; sixth, the ācārya; [seventh, the *saṃgha*; eighth, those who cultivate the path].
There are eight types of individuals: the seven groups of the Sangha and the sick person. Among these eight, the sick alone are subject to affliction.
Because one who can rescue others from the cause of suffering and affliction will themselves receive the fruit of peace and happiness, the caregiver is the foremost field of merit.
Whether it be parents, teachers, monastics, or disciples, when anyone among the superior or inferior becomes ill, one should care for them all with an impartial mind. Thus it is said.

"Those with impaired faculties" refers to those whose six sense organs are deficient. "The affliction of a hundred kinds of diseases" refers to wind, cold, heat, and dampness—the four hundred and four diseases;
this is mentioned briefly to encompass the extensive range. Such residual sufferings should all be met with compassionate offerings to bring about their recovery.
How could there be any reason for one who is a bodhisattva to harbor anger or resentment and fail to look after them? Thus it is said:

Regarding those who refuse to look out of anger and resentment: this may occur when one has been disciplined or instructed by parents or teachers during ordinary times, or when one has been disrespectful or arrogant toward them as a disciple;
or it may occur during times of illness, such as when they are vexed by trivial requests and the like. Consequently, resentment arises in the heart and one refuses to look after them.
The phrase "and so forth" (etc. indicates that this extends from the distant to the intimate; it applies not only to parents and teachers.

If one does not even look after one's own disciples when they are ill, how much more so should one rescue and aid all sick persons—whether in monastic quarters, cities and towns, wildernesses, mountain forests, or on the roads—with every effort of one's heart; this is especially true for one's parents.
"Does the master-monk not look after his disciples when they are ill? The *Five Hundred Questions* states:
"If, while traveling on a road, one sees a sick person and does not go to visit them, nor employs skillful means to entrust them to someone else before departing, one incurs an offense.
Therefore, if one sees a sick person and departs without providing relief, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti-dukkaṭa*)."
○ Tenth, the precept against possessing instruments of killing.
O disciples of the Buddha, you must not possess any swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, axes, or implements for combat; nor may you possess evil nets or any devices for killing living beings.
You must not possess any of these at all. Even if it were a matter of killing one’s own father or mother, a bodhisattva [should still not do so].

One does not retaliate; how much less so in killing all sentient beings? One must not keep implements for killing sentient beings. If one intentionally keeps them, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
This explains the tenth precept regarding the possession of implements for killing. There are two kinds of such implements: first, instruments of war; second, [implements for hunting].
One should take up the instruments for slaying all things; these are all means of taking life and wounding compassion. Since the murderous mind arises easily, one must therefore observe this precept.

As a disciple of the Buddha, one should practice the conduct of the Buddha. One should maintain the great sword of wisdom that cuts through Māra and severs craving, the staff of valor, the bow of great power, the arrows of diligence, the armor of patience, the axe of meditative concentration, and the spread of the Great Dharma-net.
A net: one may possess it to ensnare sentient beings within the three realms and pull them out from the river of craving; such a person may indeed do so.
Furthermore, De Shan’s staff for protecting life and Shi Gong’s bow for saving those facing death—these are precisely what may be kept.
However, one must not keep any swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, axes, or instruments of combat and murderous violence. It is not only these items that are forbidden.

[These are] livestock. As for evil nets and instruments for killing living beings, because they are all instruments of cruelty that easily arouse the impulse to kill, they are not appropriate for a son of the Buddha to possess;
therefore, none of these may be kept. The passage beginning with "And the Bodhisattva" clarifies the meaning of why they must not be kept:
it means that once one has become a Bodhisattva, even if someone were to murder one's own parents, one still must not [retaliate].
[The Buddha] replied: "This refers to the ultimate instruments of killing; they must absolutely not be kept. For instance, it was like the intention of the minister Ning You-dao.

Furthermore, if one does not take revenge for such an enemy, sentient beings, receiving his compassionate guidance, turn their hearts toward transformation and are thereby enabled to attain liberation.
This is precisely the great expedient (mahopāya) manifested by a Bodhisattva. Even regarding those who appear to deserve execution, there are still cases where one does not kill."
This being so, how much more so for one who, without cause, kills all sentient beings with whom one shares life and destiny—beings who harbor no enmity and have committed no offense?
If a Bodhisattva intentionally keeps such implements for fighting and harming sentient beings, they commit a minor transgression.
"These ten precepts should be studied; they should be respectfully upheld.
This single phrase summarizes the preceding ten precepts. The two phrases "should be" and "respectfully upheld" collectively exhort one to practice and study these precepts.
One should wear them upon the crown of one's head and respectfully uphold them, never forgetting or losing them.
○ The eleventh precept concerning serving as a state envoy.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, you must not, out of a mind for gain or evil intent, serve as a state envoy during military mobilizations or the gathering of armies."
When armies are raised to wage war against one another, killing immeasurable sentient beings, even a bodhisattva is not permitted to enter the midst of the army to come and go;
how much less so for one who intentionally acts as a traitor to the state? If one does so intentionally, they commit a minor offense.
This explains the eleventh precept concerning national envoys. The previous statement said that one should not possess instruments of killing;
this present statement says that one must not travel back and forth within military forces. These are established collectively to prevent difficulties for the beginner bodhisattva.

As for the term "national envoy," it refers to one who acts as a messenger for life-and-death matters between two hostile nations. It is said that as a son of the Buddha, one ought to act [in accordance with these principles].
As an envoy of the Buddha, you transmit the Buddha’s seal of mind; as a teacher of wisdom, you lead valiant generals to slay the thieves of affliction.
You should engage in battle against all demons, just as Deng Yinfeng flew his monk’s staff to resolve a conflict, or as the Venerable Chen cast away his shoe to break the siege.
If you can truly act in this manner, you will be able to repel enemies for the sake of sentient beings, cease strife and contention, and lay down weapons of war.
To propagate the holy Way is precisely what a Bodhisattva does when appearing in the world; it is the practice of great compassion.

If one acts as an envoy between two nations for the sake of profit or fame, thereby harming sentient beings, it is for this reason that it is prohibited. The Buddha said: "A son of the Buddha must not do such a thing.

This clearly indicates that seeking merit and receiving rewards is not the purpose of transmitting the Dharma or guiding others through transformation. The term "evil mind" serves to distinguish [this from a compassionate motive].
It is not that a wholesome mind resolves a conflict; rather, it is because one is the master who raises troops to kill people.
Regarding "throughout the country" and so forth, this explains the intention behind seeking profit and sustenance. "Throughout" (*tong*) means transmitting matters between this and that.

As for the term "missionary" (*shimingshi*), it refers to setting dates for reporting on battles and establishing treaties with other states. Regarding "military arrays" and so forth: "military" (*jun*) refers to approximately twelve thousand [soldiers].

A thousand men constitute an army (*jun*). When divisions (*shi*) and hosts (*lü*) form ranks, it is called an array (*chen*). "To join" (*he*) means to unite for battle; "to assemble" (*hui*) means to gather the troops.
"Raising armies to strike one another" and so forth serves to clarify the intent of their malevolence. "To raise" (*xing*) means to mobilize.
"Shi" (師) means "a multitude. Two thousand five hundred people constitute a *shi*. When these two sides engage in military campaigns against one another, it is termed "mutual assault.

As for the phrase "killing immeasurable sentient beings," this refers to the fact that when these two nations contend with each other, there is a great deal of slaughter; [to refrain from such acts] constitutes being a Bodhisattva.
One may not even enter the military to come and go; how could one be permitted to act as a state envoy?

What is meant by "not permitted" is precisely using the physical traces to illustrate the mind: it means that such places of violent killing are not fit for the bodies of the Buddha’s disciples to personally visit, let alone intentionally acting as a traitor to the state for the sake of profit and sustenance, killing sentient beings. Therefore, it is not permitted.

To do so [is an offense]. If one intentionally causes it to be done, one commits a minor secondary offense (*āpatti*). Question: If one causes it to be done but does not kill oneself, why is there an offense? Answer:
Although it is not the case that one kills with one's own hand, all people are incited by me to carry out the killing; therefore, one incurs the offense.
○ The Twelfth Precept on Buying and Selling:
If a disciple of the Buddha intentionally buys and sells free persons, male or female slaves, or the six types of domestic animals;

or trades in coffins, planks, and other materials used for containing the dead—he should not do this himself, much less teach others to do so. If he intentionally does it himself or teaches others to do so, he commits an offense.
This is a light offense.
This explains the twelfth precept concerning buying and selling. Buying and selling is not the occupation of a Buddha’s disciple.
It is said that, having become a Buddha’s disciple, one should take compassion as one’s livelihood and filial piety as one’s virtuous enterprise. One should contemplate...
All sentient beings are like one’s own parents, children, and other close kin; how could one not possess a heart of compassion?
To trade in humans or animals, causing them to be separated from one another and made to suffer, is therefore forbidden. The passage beginning with "If a Buddha-son" explains the matter of trading.
To treat the base as noble is called "trading" (*pan*); to take goods out and obtain wealth is called "selling" (*mai*). [This refers to] free persons (*liangren*)... of good [quality].
The children of others, as well as the six domestic animals—namely oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, chickens, and dogs—and the wooden planks for coffins used to contain the dead;
to trade in these is likewise a lack of benevolence. It greatly contravenes and damages the mind of compassion;
therefore, they must not be sold. The phrase "it should not even be equated with" is intended to prevent further schemes.
Furthermore, if one says, "I cannot do it myself; let someone else sell it for me," this may perhaps not be an offense.

However, if one does not realize that acting improperly oneself harms only oneself, while instructing others to act so harms others as well, then to intentionally act in such a way oneself or to instruct others to do so constitutes a minor transgression (light defilement).
○ Thirteenth: Slandering and Defaming the Precepts.

If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, groundlessly slanders a virtuous person, a good person, a Dharma Master, a preceptor, a king, or a noble official, saying they have committed the seven reversals or the ten grave offenses—yet among parents, siblings, and the six kinds of relatives, one ought to give rise to filial piety and obedience.
If one harbors a mind of compassion yet instead commits further acts of hostility and harm, thereby falling into an undesirable state, one incurs a minor offense (light defilement).
This explains the thirteenth precept, that against slander. To speak groundlessly with calumny is called "slander"; it refers to destroying a person's reputation and virtue.
It says, "Slander. This refers to the fault of slandering others' transgressions; because one receives an unwholesome retribution for this, it is prohibited.

The phrase "If a Buddha-son" identifies the person concerned. "Because of an evil mind" clarifies the root of the slander. This means that although the slander issues from the mouth, [its origin lies in the mind].
This is brought about by the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*). Thus, whether it be jealousy, greed, or anger, all are termed "evil minds.
To slander others without cause is precisely an evil mind. Since there is no basis for the accusation, one falsely hears with the ears and speaks falsely with the mouth;
this is entirely termed "slander. Therefore, it is called "without cause. Regarding "good people" and so forth, this clarifies that one ought not to slander them.
These are individuals who ought to be respected: the "excellent person" (*liangren*) refers to one who is gentle and kind; the "virtuous person" (*shanren*) refers to one who is good and mild;
the "Dharma Master" (*fashi*) refers to one who takes the teachings as their own teacher and serves as a teacher for others. Regarding teachers, there are three teachers and seven teachers.
The Sangha refers to the Sangha endowed with the five virtues and the six harmonies. Kings and nobles are those who possess fame and rank.
Such holy sovereigns and worthy ministers, as well as excellent teachers and good friends, are not only revered by worldly people.

Furthermore, the Three Jewels rely upon [the state] as their golden fortress; yet you, on the contrary, engage in such slanderous speech for no reason, claiming that [these people] have committed the seven heinous offenses and the ten grave transgressions.
Now, teachers and monks stand in the relation of parents to [the ruler]; commoners and virtuous men stand in the relation of brothers;
and those of noble rank stand in the relation of the six kin. As for those in superior positions, they ought to give rise to a heart of filial piety and obedience. As for...

Those who are inferior should give rise to a mind of compassion. Through filial piety and compassion, they will surely achieve fame and virtue for the other, while also attaining fame and virtue for themselves in this present life, leading to inexhaustible enjoyment in future lives. Thus, both parties will have their every wish fulfilled.
Yet, instead, they act contrary to these sentiments and harbor harmful intentions, causing the other’s reputation and virtue to be ruined and falling into what is undesirable.
Regarding the "abode" (or situation): for this reason, one incurs a transgression and commits a minor offense (*āpatti*).
○ The Fourteenth Precept: Against Burning with Fire.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind, sets a great fire to burn mountains, forests, wildernesses, or open lands—whether for four months or even up to nine [months]...

The Moon emits fire. If one burns the houses and dwellings of others, cities and towns, monastic quarters, fields and trees, as well as the property of spirits, deities, or officials—any property belonging to another—one must not burn it intentionally. If one burns it intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
This explains the fourteenth precept concerning the burning of fire. The causes and conditions for setting fire are manifold, yet the offense invariably results in harming people and damaging things;
therefore, it is prohibited. Regarding the phrase "because of an evil mind" and so forth, this precisely clarifies the mental state of one who sets fire.
Whether it stems from resentment and anger or from indulging one's own whims, such a person fails to give rise to a heart of benevolence and compassion for all beings.
Therefore, it is called an "evil mind. As for "emitting a great fire," this refers to burning mountain forests and wildernesses; hence it is called a "great fire.
