Because of these great fires, many classes of insects are harmed. For this reason, from the fourth month until the ninth month, one must not intentionally set fires.
The statement that one must not burn [the forest] at this time refers to the period between summer and autumn, when many types of insects are present;

therefore, burning is prohibited. The internal allowance for burning after the ninth month means that the Buddha prescribed that when setting fire in the twelfth month, one must lead the assembly to recite mantras while circumambulating the mountain to announce the intent, thereby causing the insects to flee to a distance before the fire is released. If one fails to give such notice, [it is a transgression].
This is because one fears harming various classes of insects and creatures. As for the phrase "if it burns others" and so forth, this uses a proximate case to illustrate a distant one;
that is to say, even if one sets fire to ward off wild beasts, if it unexpectedly spreads to cities and towns, such an act must not be undertaken, even though no lives are lost.

How much more so regarding the taking of life? Therefore, one must not burn houses, cities, monasteries, fields, trees, objects belonging to spirits, government property, or indeed any object that has an owner—regardless of whether it causes harm to living beings or not.
If one intentionally burns such things, one commits a minor offense (light impurity).
○ The Fifteenth Precept on Deviant Teachings:

If a disciple of the Buddha—whether toward fellow disciples, non-Buddhist practitioners, wicked people, the six types of relatives, or all spiritual friends—should not teach them one by one to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, nor teach them to understand their meanings and principles, thereby causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta; this constitutes the first of the ten transgressions.
The mind of inclination; the ten minds of nurturing; and the ten adamantine minds. Within these thirty minds, one must understand the sequential application of their methods.

If a Bodhisattva, out of an evil mind or a mind of anger, arbitrarily teaches the sūtras and vinaya of the two vehicles—śrāvakas—as well as the heterodox treatises of external paths and false views, they commit a minor offense (light impurity).
This explains the fifteenth precept concerning heterodox teachings. "Heterodox" (pì) means partial or biased.

It refers to not teaching people by means of the Mahāyāna’s perfect and sudden True Dharma, thereby causing them to lose their Mahāyāna spiritual capacity. Since the fault is no small matter, this precept is established to guard against it.

"Those who are disciples of the Buddha are the inner assembly of the Triple Gem. As for those who are non-Buddhists and evil persons, they are individuals with false views whose minds wander outside the Way;
because such people can cause sentient beings to fall into the pit of nihilism and eternalism, they are called 'evil persons.
'Six relations' refers to parents, brothers, and children. 'All virtuous friends' refers to—"
Among those with whom one knows and is acquainted, there are close friends who possess the potential for the Mahāyāna.
Toward all such relatives and friends, whether internal or external, one should individually instruct them to receive and uphold the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya.
Not only should one instruct them to receive and uphold them, but one should further cause them to understand their profound meanings and principles.
Not only does he cause them to understand and comprehend this, but he also causes them to give rise to the bodhicitta from within what they have been taught.

From that bodhicitta, they proceed to the ten *prasthāna-cittas* (minds of setting forth), initiate practice and cultivation, enter the ten *paripuṣṭi-cittas* (nurturing minds), and dedicate themselves toward the ten *vajra-cittas* (adamantine minds).
Within these thirty minds, he causes them to understand the sequential order of each one.
Regarding the application of the dharma-practice: as previously practiced in the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), one attains certainty through faith and does not deviate from the principle.
Next, one practices the ten abodes (*vihāra*) of true understanding; having perfected this faith-understanding, one becomes capable of non-retrogression within the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, next one practices the ten kinds of wondrous conduct (*caryā*), dedicating them toward the Middle Way. Through these three stages of the Three Sages—faith, understanding, and practice—the myriad [dharmas] are fulfilled.
Their practice becomes complete and they immediately ascend to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), realizing the fruit of the Buddha-way; therefore, this is called the sequential application of the Dharma.
Such instruction is termed the "correct teaching" of a bodhisattva. It benefits oneself and others, leading both equally to the ultimate Way; this is what constitutes a bodhisattva.
If, however, one harbors an evil mind of jealousy, looks down upon others, and does not aspire to the path and Dharma of the Mahāyāna—[this is not].

Either out of a mind of anger harboring resentment, or because they were instructed but did not comply and thus gave up on them, or by perversely teaching them the sūtras and vinaya of the two vehicles and śrāvakas, as well as the heterodox treatises of all external paths; in these ways, they acted arbitrarily and at whim.
They do not employ systematic principles. Thus, they should not teach what is trivial yet they teach the trivial; they should not teach what is heterodox yet they teach the heterodox.
This is what is meant by "fine timber without a craftsman" or "a beautiful vessel left unused. It leads students astray and severs the life-force of the Buddha's wisdom.
Such perverse teaching is truly not the practice of the Mahāyāna mind; due to the fault of severing the bonds of affliction, one commits a minor defilement offense.
Offense.
○ Sixteenth, teaching the precepts perversely for the sake of profit:
If a disciple of the Buddha, with a sincere heart, should first study the Mahāyāna Vinaya-sūtras of dignified conduct and extensively explain their meanings and nuances, yet—
Later, there may be newly initiated bodhisattvas who come from a hundred or a thousand *li* away to seek the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinayas.
You should, in accordance with the Dharma, explain to them all forms of ascetic practice, such as burning the body, burning the arms, or burning the fingers.

If one does not burn the body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, they are not a renunciant bodhisattva—even [if they do not offer themselves] to hungry tigers, wolves, lions, or any hungry ghosts. All...

One should offer one's own body, flesh, hands, and feet as an offering; thereafter, one should explain the True Dharma to each person in successive order, causing their minds to open and their intentions to be liberated.
Yet, for the sake of gain and for the sake of fame, a bodhisattva may fail to answer when they ought to answer.
To explain the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya in a distorted manner—without proper sequence—and to slander those who preach the Triple Gem, constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
This explains the sixteenth precept: preaching for the sake of profit in a distorted way. The Tathāgata does not permit preaching the Dharma for the sake of personal gain.
How much more so regarding those who preach perversely? The *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: The Buddha said, "I do not permit the preaching of the Dharma for the sake of profit.
I permit monks who maintain pure precepts to preach from a high seat.

Therefore, when preaching the Dharma to a newly initiated bodhisattva, one must first strengthen their aspiration and only then exhaustively explain the essential principles. This constitutes the sequence of before and after.
This is the sequential order. To teach according to the Dharma in its entirety is called "speaking as it is.

If one does otherwise, it constitutes inverted speech, slanderous speech, or speaking for the sake of gain and sustenance; the resulting offense is not slight, and therefore one is cautioned against it.

As for the phrase "with a good heart," it means having as one's intention the Mahāyāna’s correct teaching and pure practice of the Dharma for the benefit of both oneself and others; thus, it is called a "good heart. First...
Regarding "studying [the precepts] first," this clarifies that one must first accomplish self-benefit before being capable of benefiting others.

The *Mahāyāna-Ārya-Vinaya-Sūtra* distinguishes itself from the disciplinary teachings (*vinaya*) of the Hīnayāna; it is the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the method for strictly regulating body and mind.
Therefore, one should first study these teachings. "Studying first" refers to practice (*caryā*). "Extensively opening [them]" refers to understanding (*prajñā*).
Possessing both practice and understanding, he is fit to serve as a teacher and model for future generations.
This indicates that his own virtuous intent is for self-benefit; seeing those who are new students in the future clarifies his altruistic intent. He says:

"Since I am a senior practitioner, those who come from a hundred or a thousand *li*—whether far or near—to seek the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya should know that I ought to first [assist them] according to the Dharma."
For such persons, one should explain the various ascetic practices of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas.

As for these ascetic practices, they may involve burning the body, burning the arms, or burning the fingers as an offering to the Buddhas—just as was done by the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana in burning his body, the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja in burning his arms, and even by the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara when he sought a verse; all of these cases can be cited as proof. If one does not burn [the body],...
Those who offer their bodies, arms, and fingers as an act of worship to the Buddhas are merely ordinary persons who have fallen into karma and attachment to signs;
their physical characteristics are not yet empty, and the notions of self and other remain vividly present. This is not the practice of the path to liberation for an ordained Bodhisattva.

Furthermore, it is not only the burning of the body and such that should be performed with all one's strength as an offering to the Buddhas; even upon seeing a starving tiger, wolf, or lion, one [should act accordingly].
"All hungry ghosts should even give up their own bodies, flesh, hands, and feet to make offerings to them; how much more so should they do so when making offerings to the Buddhas?
Furthermore, how could they still cling to the characteristics of a self-body? By this, one must examine whether the seeker of the Dharma is earnest or not.
Only if they are able to receive it according to the teaching may the Way be transmitted. Thereafter, one shall explain it to them one by one in proper sequence."
The sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna and its profound principles are taught in such a way that they cause the mind to open without obstruction and the intellect to understand without bondage;
this is called "right teaching" and is called "teaching with a virtuous mind in proper sequence."

Thus, one does not betray the original aspiration of former scholars. Yet, if a bodhisattva, for the sake of gain and offerings, for the sake of fame and reputation, or because they have failed to obtain such fame and profit, fails to answer what should be answered regarding those who seek instruction;
or even if they do answer, speaks contrary to reason by inverting the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya; or teaches the Mahāyāna [inappropriately]—and so forth.
Furthermore, not to speak of ascetic practices is to lack what precedes; to misinterpret the words of the Sūtras and Vinaya so that their meaning has no point of reference is to lack what follows.
One who speaks in such a manner violates the Buddha’s compassion above and loses the faithful yearning below.
To conceal one's good intentions within is to contend with the Buddha, contend with the Dharma, and contend with the Sangha.
This is called slandering the teachings of the Triple Gem; such a person commits a minor offense.
○ The seventeenth precept against begging by relying on one’s power:
If a disciple of the Buddha, for the sake of food, drink, wealth, profit, or reputation, associates with kings or princes.
If high ministers or officials rely on their positions of power to beg, extort, beat, or drag others about, taking wealth by force or seeking profit in every way—
this is called "evil seeking," "excessive seeking," or "seeking through the conversion of others. To do so without a heart of compassion or a heart of filial obedience constitutes a minor offense.
This explains the seventeenth precept concerning begging by relying on one's power. Regarding the phrase "for oneself," there are two meanings.
First, it distinguishes this from acting for the sake of the community; thus it says, "for one's own food, drink, money, and material gains.
Second, it distinguishes this from seeking to protect the Dharma; thus it says, "for one's own reputation. Regarding the phrase "associating with," it refers to [associating] within the kingdom...
The king, princes, ministers, and officials regarded him as an intimate friend;
relying on this position of influence and leaning upon the power of those who were strong, they used it to intimidate those who were weak. Whatever wealth or silk they required was easily obtained.

If, however, they could not obtain what they begged for, they would resort to beating and flogging. If they could not get it through beating and flogging, they would then drag, pull, and haul them about.
To forcibly extort money and property from others through intimidation—such as all forms of seeking in this manner—are collectively termed unwholesome.

This is called seeking through evil means; this is called seeking with excessive greed. Not only does one fail to obtain anything for oneself, but if one instructs others to seek it, [the same fault applies].
Furthermore, they possess neither a heart of compassion nor a heart of filial piety. Regarding the absence of a heart of compassion:

it means that those who claim to be bodhisattvas should single-mindedly regard all sentient beings as their own brothers, six types of relatives, or family members, ensuring that each one has an abundance of food and clothing and is peaceful, secure, and free from fear; yet instead, they seek [gain] through power and through fame.

They take profit for themselves, while leaving deficiency and meanness to others; hence it is said, "They utterly lack a heart of compassion. Regarding the phrase "they utterly lack a heart of filial piety":
one should regard all sentient beings as one's own parents and all teachers as those to be served and supported.
Yet, instead, they use their power to beg and extort, causing others to suffer in poverty and resentment without end; hence it is said.
They possess no heart of filial piety whatsoever. This character [“no”] is definitive: lacking compassion and deficient in filiality, they commit a minor offense.
○ The Eighteenth Precept: Not Teaching as a Master Without Understanding.
O sons of the Buddha, you should study the twelve divisions of the sutras and recite the precepts.
Six times every day, you should uphold the Bodhisattva precepts and understand their underlying principles and the nature of the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).

If a Bodhisattva does not understand even a single sentence or a single verse, nor the causes and conditions of the Vinaya, yet falsely claims to understand them, they are deceiving themselves and deceiving others; they do not understand any of it at all.
To act as a teacher for others and bestow precepts while being ignorant of all dharmas constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).

This explains the eighteenth precept: "Acting as a Teacher Without Understanding. It means that anyone who can serve as a teacher must necessarily possess wisdom themselves and be unimpeded in their conduct in the world;
only then are they fit to be a model for others. How could one who is themselves muddled and ignorant [qualify]?

And how can one cause others to attain clear illumination? It is like an ordinary physician who does not recognize the origin of a disease and is unacquainted with prescriptions and pulses, yet rashly treats a person's illness;
it is also like a blind man leading the way, where both are subject to the danger of falling or drowning. Therefore, this is cautioned against.

Having become a child of the Buddha, one must first rely upon the understanding derived from the study of Prajñā to propagate the Dharma above and transform those below, while internally possessing...
One whose wisdom-mind externally perceives the conditions of sentient beings—such a teacher is what the Tathāgata permits to serve as a model for future generations.
There are three ways of practicing and studying Prajñāpāramitā: first, the Prajñā of Words and Letters, which refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
Second is contemplative prajñā, which is precisely the upholding of the bodhisattva precepts. Third is the prajñā of the true mark, which is the understanding of the nature of buddha-nature.
Within these few phrases, the entirety of the doctrinal meanings of the Great Canon taught by the Tathāgata is subsumed.
According to the various holy masters, there are four classifications of the gates: first, teaching; second, principle; third, practice; and fourth, fruit. This...

The twelve divisions of the scriptures within the middle [turning of the wheel] constitute the teaching; upholding the bodhisattva precepts constitutes the practice; and the nature of the Buddha-nature constitutes the principle.
Thus, based on the principle of the true mark (dharmatā), one establishes the teaching of written words; from the teaching of written words, one gives rise to the gate of contemplative practice;
and through the practice of contemplation, one enters the fruit of the principle of the true mark. Therefore, if one is not clearly enlightened...
The *prajñā* of words refers to the sacred teachings. How can one attain the correspondence between contemplative insight (*vipaśyanā*) and practice-and-understanding (*caryā-pratipatti*)?
If one does not correspond with the practice and understanding of the Mahāyāna, how can one enter the fruit of the principle of the true mark (*tathatā*)?

Therefore, a Bodhisattva who is a beginner in *prajñā* must first study the twelve divisions of the scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-buddhavacana*) to give rise to the wisdom of understanding (*adhimukti-jñāna*). Although the wisdom of understanding has arisen, if...
Without the provisions for practice, one merely achieves deluded understanding; it is like picking up another’s promissory note—what does it have to do with oneself?
Therefore, one ought to recite the precepts to stabilize the foundation of fixed wisdom. Regarding the precepts to be recited, do not recite those of the Hīnayāna;
rather, one must daily recite the Bodhisattva Mahā-śīla during the six periods of the day to cultivate the bodhisattva conduct. As for the word "daily":
Regarding the "six periods of the day": this is because one fears that those who uphold the precepts might become slightly indolent and thereby lose their bodhicitta.

As for the phrase "to understand the meaning and principle of the nature of Buddha-nature," it means that although a person who has received the precepts may recite the Mahāyāna disciplinary codes, if they do not clarify where the precepts ultimately point, they will still be unable to reach the ultimate, unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, one ought to...

To understand its meaning and principle: to understand its meaning is to understand the nature of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*). What is called "Buddha-nature" is the nature of awakening (*bodhi-svabhāva*);
it is the fundamental awakened nature (*mūla-bodhi-svabhāva*) of all sentient beings. This nature does not increase in the sages.
Abiding among ordinary beings, it is not extinguished; dwelling among the sages, it is not pure. Residing among the common, it is not defiled.

To clearly realize this nature is to see that fundamentally there is no defilement, purity, increase, or decrease. Thus, though one reads the sutras all day long, there are no sutras to read; though one observes the precepts all day long, there are no precepts to observe;
though one engages in Chan meditation and investigates the mind all day long, there is no mind to investigate. Such is reading the sutras; such is observing the precepts.
Only through such Zen practice can a person become a teacher and model for humans and devas. Those below the level of a Bodhisattva lack clear understanding and are unfit to serve as teachers.

To say that one does not understand a single phrase or a single verse means that one does not know the meaning within the twelve divisions of the scriptures, nor the causes and conditions of the precepts; this is to be ignorant of upholding the Bodhi-mind.

Regarding the meaning within the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla*, since the interpretation has already failed to penetrate the principles and the meaning of the precepts remains unclear, and the fundamental nature of reality (*dharmatā*) has not been thoroughly realized, one cannot yet achieve self-benefit.
One ought to feel shame and remorse; how much more so for those who, out of ignorance, falsely claim to understand.
Is this not precisely using oneself to deceive oneself? Having already deceived and deluded oneself, one further deceives others.
To deceive others may be called being audacious and shameless. "Not understanding each [point]" concludes the two preceding phrases regarding not understanding the Buddha-nature.
"Not knowing all dharmas" concludes the two preceding phrases regarding not knowing the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
To falsely act as a teacher for others and bestow precepts because of such lack of understanding and knowledge constitutes an offense.
A light offense of defilement.
○ The nineteenth precept against double-tongued speech:
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, sees a precept-observing bhikṣu holding an incense burner and practicing the bodhisattva path.
To incite strife between two parties, to slander and deceive the worthy, and to commit every kind of evil—this constitutes a transgression of the minor defilement offense.
This explains the nineteenth precept against double-tongued speech. Regarding "double-tongued speech," it means speaking of this person to that person, and speaking of that person to this person;
turning back and forth between both sides to instigate trouble in their midst. Therefore, when the Tathāgata was on the path of practice, he spoke of sincerity.

Speaking the truth truly evokes the mark of the broad and long tongue. This unwholesome practice of double-tongued speech will inevitably bring about retribution such as having one's tongue torn out in the future;
therefore, it is forbidden. There are two reasons for this being due to an evil mind: first, because of a mind of jealousy and envy.

First, seeing those who uphold the precepts as being different from oneself; second, because of obstructing the mind, or because of seeing others praise and make offerings [to them], one sees the bhikṣus who uphold the precepts and instigates discord between both sides, causing them mutual unease.
A bhikṣu who upholds the precepts is distinguished from a śramaṇa in name only; he is a virtuous and practiced member of the Saṅgha-ratna, a noble and holy one.
One who holds a censer while practicing the path of the bodhisattva clearly illustrates the noble and holy Saṅgha.
The censer is one among the eighteen types of ritual implements, and its significance is twofold. First, it symbolizes the faculty of faith, penetrating deeply.
The Dharma-realm. Because faith is primary, these two represent pure conduct. The five-part body is perfected entirely through practice;
thus, when it says "practicing the bodhisattva path," it distinguishes this from the practices of the Lesser Vehicle. Since one is already practicing the bodhisattva path...
If one aligns oneself with the conduct of others to become a bodhisattva, it is precisely appropriate to perfect the excellence of others and together turn the wheel of Dharma transformation.
How could one instead incite discord between two parties to find pleasure therein or seek personal gain? This is nothing other than destroying the Dharma gate for oneself.
"Inciting discord" (*dòu*) means to give rise to mutual malice; "instigating" (*gòu*) means to provoke disputes over right and wrong.
"Two heads" refers to speaking from two sides; it means inciting this person to fight that person and that person to fight this person, thereby instigating both parties to commit evil.
Regarding the phrase "slandering and deceiving the worthy," this specifically refers to the meaning of "two-headed speech":
it means that although monks are originally all virtuous and noble, one nevertheless gives rise to groundless slander out of a heart of jealousy, conversely claiming that they possess no faults.
One must not do so, for it causes both parties to remain unsettled. To thus slander a worthy person is to commit a minor offense.
○ The twentieth precept: Not practicing liberation and rescue.
O disciples of the Buddha, out of a heart of compassion, you should engage in the practice of releasing living beings and reflect in this way:
"All men have been my fathers; all women have been my mothers. In every lifetime, there has never been one from whom I did not receive birth.
Therefore, the sentient beings of the six realms have all been my parents. To kill and eat them is to kill my own parents. It is also to kill...
My former bodies were all the earth and water; my original essence was all the fire and wind. Therefore, one should practice the karma of releasing living beings.

In every birth and throughout successive lifetimes, if one sees people of the world killing animals, one should employ skillful means to protect them and liberate them from their suffering and distress.
One should constantly teach and preach the Bodhisattva precepts to save and deliver sentient beings. If [one's] father...
On the day a mother’s brother dies, one should invite a Dharma Master to lecture on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra and Vinaya.
This merit shall support the deceased, enabling them to behold the Buddhas and be reborn among humans or in the heavens. If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense.
This is the commentary on the twentieth precept, the precept against failing to release and rescue. "Release" means to set free; "rescue" means to protect and save.
To fail to release and rescue is to lose the practice of a bodhisattva’s compassionate mind; therefore, one is cautioned against it.

Regarding the phrase "by means of a compassionate mind," this means that when cultivating the myriad practices of a bodhisattva, the compassionate mind is taken as the foundation. For this reason, one constantly employs it.
The mind brings happiness to sentient beings. Desiring to grant them happiness, one must first extract their suffering; for it is only by being free from suffering that one can experience happiness.
Therefore, one should constantly practice releasing living beings as one's primary vocation. Regarding the phrase "one should form this thought," etc.:
following what has been stated above, since one practices the release of living beings as one's vocation, one should cultivate contemplation to strengthen the resolve to release them.
What kind of mindfulness should one cultivate? One should contemplate all men as being one’s father and all women as being one’s mother.
Why is this known to be so? Because in every successive birth, there is no one from whom I have not received birth.
Since all living beings receive their births from such sources, how could all men and women not have been my parents throughout many lifetimes and many kalpas?
If one extends this reasoning further, then all sentient beings of the six realms have all been my parents.
Therefore, if one were now to kill and eat them, it would be no different from killing my own parents throughout many lifetimes and many kalpas.
"O Mother! As for your statement that you killed my former body: [the sequence] above proceeded from the distant to the near; this [sequence] proceeds from the near to the most intimate.

Yet nothing is more intimate than one's own body, which is likewise the 'former body' that you killed. This makes it even clearer that the mind intent on liberation and rescue should be as urgent as possible.
Furthermore, it shows that I and all sentient beings are identical in this single body, without distinction."
It is distinct. Regarding the statement, "All earth and water were my former bodies," this explains the meaning of the body that was killed by me above.
It means that at the very beginning of entering the womb, first the two kinds of water and earth—the father’s semen and the mother’s blood—coalesce and congeal into one.
By means of this deluded consciousness, a deluded vision arises; one perceives the parents, and their emotional attachment becomes insatiable. That is to say...
It is cast into that [womb]. Therefore, it is called the "prior body. As for the statement that all fire and wind are one's own fundamental substance:

fire is warmth, and wind is breath. Thus, these three—consciousness, breath, and warmth—constitute its substance. Were it not for these three—consciousness, breath, and warmth—[the body would perish].
Holding together the red and the white, this physical body immediately falls into decay; therefore, it is called the "original substance" (*mūla-tattva*).

Since it is the original substance of one's former body, it remains deeply indebted to one's parents; thus, one should form this thought: to constantly practice the release of living beings as one's vocation.
Not only should one practice the karma of releasing life in this present birth, but one shall do so throughout every successive rebirth. If one sees people of the world...
When killing an animal, one should always employ skillful means to rescue and protect it, relieving it of its suffering and distress.

Whether by using wealth and treasures or by speaking kind words, one should employ various methods to turn the mind of the killer away from the act, thereby alleviating the suffering of the victim being killed.
Regarding the phrase "always teaches," the preceding section clarified rescuing sentient beings through material means; this section clarifies [rescuing them] through...
The skillful means of the Dharma rescue and deliver sentient beings. The skillful means of material wealth are limited; they can only alleviate the suffering of the present life.
The skillful means of the Dharma are infinite, for they enable those who are living and those who have died to forever escape the suffering of saṃsāra throughout many lifetimes.
The passage beginning with "If one's parents... correctly clarifies the deliverance [of beings] after death.
When sentient beings' breath ceases and their spirits depart, it is called "death. To have no further connection with the world is called "passing away.

Regarding the day and time when one's parents, brothers, or sisters pass away, if one wishes to be a filial son or a virtuous brother, one should invite a Dharma Master who has received the Great Precepts.
I lecture on the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtras and Vinaya, dedicating this merit to the deceased so that they may behold the Buddhas and be reborn among humans or in the heavens.
How is this known? Because the Mahāyāna Vinaya possesses the power to produce goodness and extinguish evil, and the virtue of eliminating transgressions and attaining blessings;
by dedicating this to the deceased, their obstructions are cleared and wisdom is awakened, enabling them to behold the Buddhas.
Sins are extinguished and merit arises; one is liberated from the three evil realms and attains rebirth among gods and humans for this reason.
To protect and deliver sentient beings in this manner is called a bodhisattva repaying the kindness of the Buddhas. If one does not do so, one commits a minor offense.
These ten precepts should be studied and upheld with a reverent heart. As explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Extinction of Sin," each individual aspect of the precepts is clarified;
this is a general summary of the exhortation. The phrase "in this manner" below concludes the discussion of the Dharma; the phrase "should [be practiced]" below exhorts one to cultivation.
As stated below "Extinction" (*nirodha*), this is a citation from the *Vaipulya* [sūtras]. It says: "O sons of the Buddha, these ten precepts should be practiced and studied one by one.
You should uphold them with a reverent heart, cherishing them at every moment, so as not to forget or become indolent.
Only then will you be a true child within the dharma-gate of the virtuous precepts. Thus, the above ten grave and twenty light precepts are extracted [from the scriptures].
For a lay bodhisattva, there is both permission and prohibition; for a monastic bodhisattva, it is entirely prohibited. One who acts as a teacher should investigate this deeply.
The same applies to the following twenty-eight minor offenses.
Direct Commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll II, Part One;
Direct Commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll II, Part Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
A Direct Explanation of the "Bodhisattva’s Mind-Ground Chapter," Part Two, by the Śramaṇa Jik-kō, a later student who received the precepts in Guangling.
The Twenty-first Precept: Against Anger, Assault, and Vengeance.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, one must not repay anger with anger, nor strike back in retaliation for being struck.
Even if one's parents, brothers, or six types of kinsmen are killed, one must not seek retribution. If a sovereign ruler is killed by another, one likewise must not seek retribution.

To kill in order to retaliate for a killing does not accord with the Way of Filial Piety. One should not even keep slaves to beat, whip, or insult them; rather, one should rise three times every day..."
The karmic retribution for verbal offenses is immeasurable; how much more so for intentionally committing the seven grave transgressions.
If a renunciant bodhisattva, lacking a heart of compassion, intentionally seeks revenge even against their own six kinds of relatives, they commit a secondary offense of defilement.
This explains the precept against anger, striking, and seeking revenge. This precept arises from the practice of releasing living beings out of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
According to that text, one contemplates that all men are one's fathers and all women are one's mothers;
thus, even those who now provoke my anger or strike me have all been my parents. Having made this contemplation, [one refrains from retaliation].
How could one have a son who, out of anger, strikes back at his own parents? Furthermore, anger is one of the heaviest among the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
This dharma has the nature of increasing resentment and the function of fostering evil; it stands in opposition to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion (*karuṇā*).
To deviate from the path of Bodhi while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, one must give rise to great vows to deliver sentient beings;

therefore, one should take a compassionate mind as the foundation. If one gives rise to even a single thought of anger, it violates the original vow, whereby one abandons sentient beings and loses the fundamental compassion.
For this reason, it is forbidden. When the Buddha says, "O Son of the Buddha," he uses this title to exhort [the practitioner]. It is not...

One must not retaliate against anger with anger, nor strike back in response to being struck. A Bodhisattva should maintain a mind of emptiness and a state of stillness, where both self and other are forgotten;

one must not harbor a heart of non-benevolence to seek revenge through anger or blows. As for the mention of killing one's parents and so forth, this is intended to illustrate by means of the heavy that which is light:
it means that one must not harbor a desire for retaliation even when others have harmed one’s own person, let alone when they have committed such grave acts as killing one’s parents.
Suppose someone were to kill my parents, brothers, or other close relatives; even so, I would not be permitted to seek retribution.
Furthermore, even if the sovereign of a state were killed by another, he likewise would not be permitted to seek retribution.

Now, according to the principle that one must avenge a crime against one's parents—a debt that cannot be borne under heaven—it is right to retaliate; yet all Buddhas prohibit seeking retribution. What is the meaning of this?

It is because the Bodhisattva seeks to transform and guide sentient beings, severing their afflictions and fetters, leading them out of the saṃsāra of the three realms, and causing them to forever cut off birth and death so that they may attain great liberation.
How could one kill one life and receive retribution for one life, thereby causing all sentient beings to kill one another incessantly from lifetime to lifetime? As it was said above: "All men..."
"Women are my parents. If one now kills living beings to repay those who gave birth to them, one is killing many parents from past lives to repay the parents of this life;
how could this be the way of filial piety? Therefore, killing living beings to repay those who gave birth to one does not accord with the path of filiality.
Furthermore, it is not only this: even a practitioner of the Way must not keep slaves or beat them."
Insults arise day after day; there are the physical karma of striking, the verbal karma of insulting, and the mental karma of anger.
Among these three types of karma, the transgression of verbal karma alone is already immeasurable.

How much more so for the seven heinous crimes, such as intentionally killing one's father or mother to retaliate against them, which violates the way of filial piety? Therefore, one must not respond with anger or blows.
This is an enemy. Yet, the text states that those who have left the household life must not seek revenge. To clarify the meaning of "not seeking revenge":
this refers specifically to the renunciant bodhisattva, for whom enemies and kin are equal and both self and others are forgotten.

How could such a person harbor a desire for retribution, as if they were an ordinary worldly person whose grievances and harms follow one another? Question: If I do not retaliate, would I not be condoning [the offense]?
"Did he commit murder? He replied, "I reflected that since I did not retaliate, the other person likewise did not give rise to a harmful intent.
Thus, both of us attained liberation. If a lay bodhisattva has a position where they may exercise skillful means, it might be permissible to retaliate;
however, for an ordained bodhisattva, there is no such thing as a compassionate mind that would lead one to strike back in anger or seek revenge—even for the sake of one's own six kin."
Therefore, to seek revenge in this manner constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).

**The Twenty-second Precept: The Prohibition Against Arrogance and Refusing to Request the Dharma.** If a disciple of the Buddha, having first left the household life, has not yet attained any understanding, yet relies on his own cleverness and intelligence, or relies on—

There may be those of noble age and seniority who, relying on their prestigious lineage and high social standing, or their great learning and vast wealth—abounding in the seven treasures—become arrogant and refuse to consult or receive the teachings of the Dharma masters regarding the sūtras and vinaya.

These Dharma masters may be of humble lineage, young, from lowly families, poor, or of inferior station, and may even lack some of their physical faculties; yet they truly possess virtue and have mastered all the sūtras and vinaya.

Explanation: If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not inquire of or receive instruction from a Dharma Master regarding the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) because they judge the Dharma Master’s lineage or social standing, they commit a minor offense of defilement.
This explains the precept against arrogance and refusing to request the Dharma. "Arrogance" (māna) refers to the deep arising of defiled attachment toward one's own prosperity;
its essential nature is intoxication and haughtiness. Its function is to obstruct non-arrogance and to serve as a basis for defilement.

This is because those who are intoxicated by arrogance give rise to all manner of defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*); thus, it is subsumed under the category of craving (*rāga*). That which is non-arrogant is precisely non-attachment (*alobha*). Thus...
One of the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). *Mada* (intoxication/arrogance) is defined as relying on oneself in relation to others, characterized by haughtiness.

Its function is to obstruct non-arrogance and to give rise to suffering. As for its nature as a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), it causes one to be conceited toward those with virtue and prevents the mind from being humble;
because of this, one revolves endlessly in the cycle of birth and death and undergoes various sufferings. It is [one of] the six fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).
First: These two afflictions can obstruct all practitioners from accomplishing any of their merits;
therefore, they are prohibited. From the words "If a Buddha-son" onwards, the root of arrogance is identified.

It states that when this Buddha-son first resolved his mind to leave the household life and depart from the dust of the world, at the outset his knowledge and vision were not yet extensive, and his power of study—
They have not yet deeply penetrated the profound principles within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Having attained not even a hair’s breadth of understanding, they rely on their own cleverness and intelligence; unaware that such cleverness pertains only to what can be known and seen within conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and is not the correct knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*) of the supramundane Dharma. Or, they rely on the high status and nobility of their names and positions.
Some rely on their physical appearance, youth, or seniority; some rely on their family being of great lineage or high standing;
others rely on their extensive learning and profound understanding, or their vast assets and great wealth, including the seven treasures.

All such things as these are the most highly esteemed in the mundane world, yet none constitute the honored path that transcends the world. Thus, when a son of the Buddha has first left the household life, he may rely upon these [worldly attributes].
Because of arrogance, they do not inquire with an open mind nor receive the sūtras and vinaya taught by the learned Dharma masters.
This is like having already drunk poison; even if a genuine medicine appears before them, they cannot swallow it.
All the above describes those who rely on a heart of arrogance. The following section clarifies the objects upon which that arrogance relies. As for that Dharma...
Regarding the teacher: if they are of a minor clan or young in years, yet in the presence of someone of noble lineage or advanced age, they rely on their own high birth and seniority;

or if they are from a lowly family, poor, or of humble station, yet in the presence of someone of exalted lineage, noble status, or great wealth, they rely on their own high origins and aristocratic rank;

or if they have impaired faculties, yet in the presence of someone who is clever and wise, they rely on their own supposed intelligence—yet in reality they are inferior. This precisely clarifies that one must not act in such a manner.
To judge by outward traces is to rely on the person rather than the virtue; it is said that one should rely on the Dharma, not on the individual.
Although such a Dharma master may be inferior in every respect regarding worldly matters, he is truly possessed of virtue in terms of the supramundane stages.
Furthermore, his learning is vast and profound; he is fully capable of understanding all the sutras and vinayas, serving as a model for future generations. Yet, these...
A newly initiated bodhisattva must not observe whether the Dharma Master’s lineage is superior or inferior, thereby giving rise to false arrogance.
They should seek what they have not heard and request the explanation of what they do not understand.

If, instead, they rely on their own origins to judge themselves as high or low and harbor pride in their hearts, ultimately failing to come to consult and receive the First Noble Truth expounded by the Dharma Master, they commit a minor offense.
Offense. ○ Twenty-third: Preaching the *śīla* with Arrogance and Bias.
If, O Sons of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts with a sincere heart, [one should do so] before a Buddha or a Bodhisattva...
Before an image, one should take the precepts through a self-vow. One must perform repentance before the Buddha for seven days until a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*) is seen;

once this is attained, one obtains the precepts. If a favorable sign is not obtained within seven days, one should continue for two weeks, three weeks, and so on, up to a year, until a favorable sign is definitely attained.
Once one has obtained a good sign (*lakṣaṇa*), one may then receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.
If one does not obtain a good sign, even if one receives the precepts before an image of the Buddha, one does not obtain the precepts.

However, when receiving the Bodhisattva precepts in the presence of a Dharma Master who has previously received them, it is not necessary to see a good sign. Why is this? It is because this Dharma Master has received the transmission through the succession of masters. Therefore, [the sign is not required].

One must await a good omen (*lakṣaṇa*). For this reason, when a Dharma Master receives the precepts before [an image], one immediately obtains the precepts; because a mind of supreme reverence has arisen, one thereby obtains the precepts.

If there is no master capable of conferring the precepts within a thousand *li*, one may receive the precepts through a self-vow before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, provided that one seeks to see a good omen.
If a Dharma Master relies on his own understanding of the Sūtras and Vinaya and teaches the Mahāyāna precepts...

If a king, a crown prince, or a high official regards [the Bodhisattva] as a virtuous friend, yet when a newly initiated Bodhisattva comes to inquire about the meaning of the Sutras or the Vinaya with a frivolous mind,
an evil mind, or an arrogant mind, and does not answer each question well, they commit a secondary offense (light defilement).

This explains the perverse teaching regarding arrogance (*māna*). The meaning of "arrogance" has been explained previously. As for "perverse" (*pì*), it refers to partiality, which is [wrong] view (*dṛṣṭi*).

Because such views are incorrect, one will inevitably fall into the ranks of external paths (*tīrthika*) and malevolent spirits; therefore, one is cautioned against them. Examining the force of this passage:

This meaning has two parts. First, from "If a Buddha’s disciple... down to "...shall immediately obtain the precepts," this section clarifies the meaning of the disciple having no pride or deviance in receiving [the teachings], and the teacher having no pride or deviance in explaining them. Second, from "If a Dharma master...
down to "...does not answer questions well one by one," this section correctly clarifies how a teacher relies on pride and explains [the teachings] perversely.
A disciple must not receive [the precepts] with arrogance or partiality. There are three ritual procedures for receiving the precepts:

first, when the Buddha was in the world, those who received them directly in his presence obtained the superior grade of precepts; second, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who received them according to the Dharma before a Dharma Master who has previously received the Bodhisattva precepts obtained the middle grade of precepts;
third, [those who receive them from a Dharma Master who has not yet received the Bodhisattva precepts obtain the inferior grade].

If, within a distance of a thousand li, there is no Dharma master capable of bestowing the precepts, one may personally make a vow before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva to receive the Buddha-precepts;
in such a case, one must certainly see a favorable sign (*lakṣaṇa*). If a favorable sign is seen, [the precepts are received].

One attains the lower grade of precepts. As for the phrase "the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa," this distinguishes the period when the Buddha was in the world from the present time after his parinirvāṇa.

When the Buddha was alive, one took the Buddha as one's teacher; now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, one takes the Dharma of the precepts as one's teacher, regarding the Precept Master as the Buddha.

Regarding the phrase "wishing with a sincere mind" and so forth, this precisely clarifies the meaning of receiving [the precepts] without arrogance or deviation. With respect to the forms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
As in the former case, this refers specifically to when the Buddha is not present in the world and no teacher is before one.
When one wishes to uphold the Bodhisattva precepts with a sincere mind, one may only receive the precepts by making independent vows before an image of the Buddha or a Bodhisattva.
The vow says: "I, [Name], and others, shall give rise to the fourteen kinds of great vows, and further establish the thirteen..."
Having made these various vows and generated the aspiration, you should further perform diligent repentance before the Buddha for seven days to eliminate all karmic obstacles.
Once the obstacles have been extinguished and you perceive an auspicious sign, you may know for yourself that you have attained the precepts.
Should you fail to obtain an auspicious sign within the first seven days, you ought to continue for two weeks, three weeks, and so on, up to a year.

One must wait for this duration and necessarily obtain a good omen (*lakṣaṇa*). Once a good omen has indeed been obtained, one may then permit that person to personally vow to receive the precepts before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva;
only then does one truly realize the superior conditions for attaining the precepts.
If a good omen is not obtained, although one receives the precepts before a Buddha image, it is not called "attaining the precepts"; there is merely the name of having received them.
Yet it lacks its reality; it is a single lifetime of falsehood, its essence being that of a layperson (*avadātavasana*).

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there is a Dharma master who has previously received the Bodhisattva precepts, one should immediately seek the precepts before such a teacher with sincere devotion.
It is not necessary to behold auspicious signs (*lakṣaṇa*). Why is this? Because both the speaker and the receiver [of the precepts] are...
"Present before one" means that it is not received remotely or through a proxy, nor is it sought before an image.

Regarding the phrase "previously received," this distinguishes [the candidate] from those who are newly ordained, lack virtue, or have few years of seniority (*kalpa*), as such individuals cannot serve as preceptors.

As for the term "Dharma Master of Bodhisattva Precepts," this refers to a master in whom wisdom and conduct are practiced in tandem; such a master is worthy to serve as a model and guide. It is precisely such a master [who is required].
Previously, when receiving the precepts, it was not necessary to see auspicious signs. Why is this? There are two reasons.
First, the Dharma Master’s attainment of the precepts fundamentally comes from a lineage of successive masters.
This Preceptor who possesses the full precepts is identical to the Buddhas of the past while they were dwelling in the world. Therefore, when the Dharma Master previously received the precepts...

This is because one immediately attains full ordination (*upasampadā*). Second, when a candidate for ordination conceives a mind of supreme reverence before their original preceptor who recites the precepts (*śīla-uddeśaka*), and perceives that preceptor as being the Buddhas, they receive the precepts from that teacher and thereby immediately attain them.
Thus, there is neither arrogance nor deviant reception on the part of the candidate, nor is there arrogance or deviant exposition on the part of the teacher; in every respect, it is thus.
This is in accordance with the Dharma. However, it is very easy to seek and receive [the precepts] before a living teacher, whereas it is very difficult to seek and receive them before an image.

For what reason do you not follow a teacher, but instead receive them before an image? This would only be the case if, within a thousand li, there were no one capable of acting as a preceptor to bestow the precepts.
One may first receive the precepts by making a personal vow before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva.

If one seeks the precepts before such an image, it is absolutely necessary to see an auspicious sign (*lakṣaṇa*) in order to establish the conviction that the precepts have been attained. This applies even if [the image] is within a thousand li.
If there is a preceptor capable of bestowing the precepts, yet one does not receive them in the presence of that master, but instead receives the precepts before an image,
this person not only fails to obtain the precepts, but moreover incurs the sin of receiving them through arrogance and deviance.
If a Dharma master, inwardly relies on his own ability to explain the sutras and vinaya and his adherence to the Mahayana precepts,
and outwardly relies on the kings, crown princes, and officials with whom he associates as virtuous friends,
then when he sees a newly initiated bodhisattva come from afar to inquire about the meaning of the sutras and the meaning of the vinaya, he will instead rely on those associations.
If one relies on such [conditions] as to give rise to a sense of superiority, to look down upon others with contempt, to harbor malice and jealousy, or to treat them with arrogance and negligence,

failing to provide proper and respectful answers to those who come seeking instruction in the Dharma, this Dharma teacher incurs the fault of arrogant and deviant preaching and commits a secondary offense of defilement.
24. Not Practicing the Buddha’s Precepts.

O Disciples of the Buddha, if there are the Buddha’s sutras and vinaya, the Mahayana teachings, right view, right nature, and the true Dharma-body, yet one cannot diligently study and practice them, but instead abandons the seven treasures to study the false views of the two vehicles, the heterodox paths, and secular classics—this is [the twenty-fourth offense]. The Abhidharma...

The *Tanzalun* (Discourse on Miscellaneous Matters) states: "All written records that sever the Buddha-nature and serve as causes and conditions for obstructing the Way are not the practice of those who follow the Bodhisattva path.
If one intentionally creates such works, one commits a minor offense."

This explanation concerns the failure to practice and study the Buddha’s precepts. It means that the various sūtras and vinaya-piṭakas of the Buddhas are the precious raft for transcending birth and death and crossing the ocean of suffering.
Without this raft, one will never be able to emerge from the river of craving within the triple world.

Thus, although the Buddha-dharma exists, those who do not practice and study it willingly remain submerged; therefore, they are cautioned against such negligence. This refers to the existence of the Buddhist sūtras.
Regarding the Vinaya: having become a son of the Buddha, there is a Buddha to whom one may turn; he is my original teacher. There is a Dharma to be revered; it is my original Dharma.
Since these are the original teacher and the original Dharma, one should at all times draw near to them and study them.

"Sūtra" refers to the *sūtra*; "Vinaya" refers to the *vinaya*. Regarding what is called the Mahāyāna within the Sūtras and Vinayas, this means that among the sūtras and vinayas spoken by the Buddha, there is the Bodhisattva Piṭaka and the Śrāvaka Piṭaka; because this belongs to the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, it is called the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Since its fundamental source is the Mahāyāna Dharma-piṭaka, the principles and tenets it elucidates are therefore the correct [teachings].
It is right knowledge, right view, the right nature, and the right Dharma-body. To be neither partial nor deviant is called "right.
From this right knowledge and right view, one clearly realizes that which is neither born nor extinguished, neither shifting nor changing—the right cause of Buddha-nature.

Taking this as the mind of the causal stage, one immediately realizes the fruit of the right Dharma, which is inherently present, neither born nor extinguished, neither shifting nor changing. Indeed, it exists.
The Buddha is worthy of refuge; there is the Dharma worthy of veneration. Yet, one cannot single-mindedly take refuge in and venerate them, nor diligently apply oneself to study.

Instead, one abandons the Buddha’s path to enlightenment and the seven kinds of supreme, ultimate treasures, turning instead to study false views, the two vehicles, non-Buddhist doctrines, secular classics, and all miscellaneous treatises such as the Abhidharma and various records. This severs the Buddha-nature and acts as a cause for obstructing the Path.
"Conditions. As for "those who do not practice the bodhisattva path," since this is not the path of a bodhisattva, how could one study it?
Regarding "false views" and so forth, the explanation is as given above. As for "secular texts," these refer to the four Vedas, the scriptures of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

"Abhidharma" means "fearlessness" in this language; it is also called "discriminating wisdom" (*prajñā-vibhaṅga*). "Miscellaneous treatises" refers to whatever treatises exist among ordinary [non-Buddhist] works.

"Treatises on Non-existence" refers to the treatises of the Hinayana and non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), as well as all written records, including poetry, lyrics, songs, and prose compositions, medicine, divination, yin-yang theory, and the arts of calculation.
To say that these "sever the Buddha-nature" points out the faults of what they have studied.
Based on such false views as described above, those of the Two Vehicles and others should not associate with them; yet they do so instead. This refers to the non-Buddhists.
The teachings of secular classics and the like should not be studied at all; yet you instead study them, thereby deluding yourself and others.

What is called the "aridity and stillness" of the Two Vehicles parches the sprouts of Bodhi; the "extremes of annihilation and permanence" of the non-Buddhists gouge out the seeds of Perfect Enlightenment—this is the severing of Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, these dharmas of false views internally confuse correct understanding and insight, while externally they disrupt the gates of correct practice.
These are truly obstructive evil dharmas that hinder the causes and conditions for the path to Bodhi; they are not the true Dharma for practicing the Mahāyāna of a Bodhisattva.
If one intentionally turns away from what should be studied and instead practices what should not be studied, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). Question:
Since worldly speech and livelihood-generating occupations are all in accord with the True Dharma, why does studying secular classics and the like constitute an offense?

Question: Why is there fault? Answer: Because for those who are newly learning, their wisdom is weak while their consciousness is strong; fearing they might abandon the root to pursue the branches, [the teaching is restricted].
However, if it were a great Bodhisattva on the grounds (bhūmi), they would practice and study without obstruction for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
○ Twenty-fifth: Not Skillfully Knowing the Precepts for the Assembly.

If a disciple of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, acts as a master of preaching the Dharma, a master of the monastic quarters, a master of instruction, a master of seated meditation, or a master of administrative affairs, he should give rise to a heart of compassion.
He should skillfully reconcile disputes and skillfully guard the property of the Triple Gem; he must not fail to do so.

To use [the property of the Sangha] as if it were one's own, and instead of doing so, to cause disorder within the assembly, engage in strife, and recklessly use the property of the Triple Gem—this constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
This explains the precept regarding not knowing the affairs of the assembly well; that is to say, a disciple of the Buddha is one who sustains and upholds the Triple Gem and propagates its teachings.

One who possesses the knowledge of the Dharma should know how to recognize people. If they cause disorder among the assembly and engage in strife, or fail to properly guard even the property of the Triple Gem, they are not disciples of the Buddha;
therefore, they are cautioned against such conduct. As for the phrase "after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa":
This refers to the final age. When the Buddha was in the world, he was the Lord of lords among all the great assemblies;
among his disciples, there was naturally no wanton disorder. Now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, the various disciples each act as their own masters;
hence the phrase "after the Buddha’s extinction. Regarding the expression "acting as the master of the Dharma," it concerns what was taught by the Buddha.

One who is well able to preside over and maintain the teachings of the Tripitaka so that they circulate widely and do not fall into discontinuity is called a Master of Monastic Quarters (*vihārasvāmin*);

this refers to one who skillfully oversees the matters of the upper, middle, and lower seats, as well as the *Kṣudraka-vastu* on the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) and other such affairs for the monastic community.
One who is a Master of Instruction (*śikṣāsvāmin*) is one who can skillfully preside over the sequence of causes and conditions for expedient means of conversion and guidance.

Regarding such matters as these, one ensures that no errors or omissions occur. The "Master of Seated Meditation" refers to one capable of presiding over matters such as the manifestation of demonic realms during the practice of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), and subduing them through skillful means (*upāya*).

The "Master of Movement" refers to one who skillfully presides over matters such as the etiquette for welcoming and seeing off guests from near and far, ensuring that no negligence or disrespect occurs. Since [the monastery] is conducted in this manner...

As the leader of the assembly, you should give rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), skillfully reconcile disputes, and properly guard the wealth and property of the Triple Gem (*triratna*);
do not use them recklessly. The instruction to "give rise to a mind of loving-kindness" is a word of exhortation, meaning that one should cultivate such a mind of compassion.

Because they are able to bestow peace and happiness upon all sentient beings; because they skillfully reconcile those engaged in strife, meaning they cause disputes that have not yet arisen not to arise, and cause those already arisen to be extinguished; and because they skillfully guard the property of the Triple Gem.
This means that regarding the permanent assets of the Three Jewels, one must not allow them to be interchanged, encroached upon, damaged, or lost; thus, there must be no reckless expenditure.
This correctly clarifies the meaning of "properly guarding. Regarding the assets of the Three Jewels, their use must be moderate, and this principle has three aspects:
first, property belonging to the Buddha must originally be used for the affairs of the Buddha; likewise, property belonging to the Dharma must be used for the affairs of the Dharma.
First, regarding the property of the Saṃgha: it is to be used for the affairs of the Saṃgha; when it is required, it may be used, but one must not use it recklessly or with a lack of restraint.
Second, these are the assets of the Triple Gem and should be well-guarded; do not treat them as your own private property and use them according to your own whims.
Third, those who guard the property of the Triple Gem should regard it as they would their own spiritual wealth (dharmadhana), and must not—
If one allows delusions and karma to invade, defile, and destroy [the Sangha], it is said that one must not act without restraint.

Thus, harmonizing with the assembly through a compassionate mind and maintaining virtue is precisely the practice-gate of a Buddha’s disciple. If, however, one cannot harmonize well but instead causes disorder and strife within the assembly;
or if, while being duty-bound to guard [the property] well, one instead indulges the heart in the miscellaneous use of the Three Jewels’ assets—one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
The twenty-sixth precept on receiving offerings alone:
If a disciple of the Buddha is already residing in a monastic dwelling and sees a visiting Bodhisattva Bhikṣu entering that monastery, [he should not receive offerings alone].

Whether it be in houses, cities, or within the residences of kings, even in places where the summer retreat (*varṣā*) is observed or in great assemblies, the resident monks should welcome them upon arrival and see them off upon departure.
They should provide offerings of food and drink, as well as dwellings, bedding, rope-seated chairs, and wooden beds, providing for every necessity.
If they possess no material goods, they should sell their own bodies, or the bodies of their sons and daughters; indeed, they should cut from their own flesh.

If one sells meat and provides whatever is required, giving it all away, yet when a donor invites the assembly of monks and there is a portion of offerings for visiting monks, the master of the monastery should assign visiting monks in turn to receive the invitation.
If the resident monks alone accept the invitation without assigning visiting monks, the master of the monastery incurs immeasurable sin; he is no different from a beast. This is not [the way].
"O Śramaṇa, you are not of the Śākya clan; you have committed a minor offense.

This refers to the precept that the Śākyas alone receive offerings and sustenance. The Saṃgha possesses the virtue of the six points of harmony, namely, harmony in precepts through collective practice."
There is harmony in views and shared understanding; harmony in body through dwelling together; harmony in speech through freedom from contention;

harmony in mind through freedom from anger; and harmony in material benefits through equal distribution. If even one internal form of harmony is deficient, the sixfold harmony will be entirely impaired;

therefore, one must be cautious regarding this. As for those who have previously resided in the monastery, they are naturally the masters. Having already become masters, they must fulfill their duties as such. If they see a guest...
When a bodhisattva bhikṣu enters a monastery dwelling, or enters the residence of a layperson,
or enters a city or town, or enters the palace of a king, or even a place for the summer rains retreat (varṣā),
or a great assembly— whichever such dwelling it may be— the resident monks who have already been living there must yield the primary path to him.
This is extraordinary. When they arrive, one must perform every courtesy of welcoming; when they depart, one must perform every courtesy of seeing them off.

From beginning to end, one should remain consistent and never lose the proper measure. Regarding the offerings made between these times—such as food and drink, dwellings, bedding, rope beds, wooden beds, and all other types of requisites—one must provide for every need and must not begrudge the giving of even a single item.
What does it mean for both to make offerings in accordance with the Dharma? It means first to show reverence for the gateway of the Dharma and to fulfill fully the duty of a master.
Question: Suppose I personally have nothing; how should I make offerings? Answer:

If you are truly seeking the Bodhisattva path, you should sell your own body, as well as the bodies of your sons and daughters, to make the offering. Furthermore, it is not only these that you should sell.
It is merely the body. One should cut one's own flesh and sell it to provide for what is needed, giving it all away.
If this is true when applied to the body itself, how much more so regarding external possessions—how could one instead be stingy and fail to provide?
If there is a donor [who says], "No," [it means] to clarify that one must not accept an invitation alone. Since it is said that the host has no goods, yet...
One has even sold one's own body and cut one's own flesh to make offerings;
how could there be a donor who invites the Sangha for a meal and yet fails to assign the guest monks to receive the invitation in due order? Such a thing is impossible.

Therefore, if a donor comes to invite the assembly of monks for a meal, the guest monks must all share in the portion of the offerings, and the master of the monastery should [assign them] one by one.
Only when guest monks are invited in successive order does one truly possess the six qualities of harmony of a śramaṇa.
If the resident monks alone accept an invitation without yielding it to guest monks, the abbot of the monastery incurs immeasurable sin. The *Wubai wen* (Five Hundred Questions) states:
"If the food for the community of monks has already been distributed and exhausted, and one eats another's portion until full, one commits a pārājika offense. It is not otherwise.
Having committed these offenses repeatedly, one incurs immeasurable guilt; this may be understood by analogy.

Thus, a bhikṣu who acts below the level of human sentiment is no longer a human being, being no different from an animal. One who acts contrary to the etiquette of the Saṃgha lacks the six points of harmony entirely.
Therefore, such a person is not a śramaṇa; they do not accord with the Buddha’s mind above, and by failing to recognize the gravity of the Way, they are not of the Śākya lineage.
While [the teachings] should be received equally, to instead take them into one's own possession alone constitutes a minor offense (āpatti).
○ The twenty-seventh precept: Against Accepting Private Invitations for Personal Gain.
If a disciple of the Buddha, he must not under any circumstances accept private invitations for offerings and take them for himself. Such offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions;
yet by accepting a private invitation, one takes the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself. Among the eight fields of merit, [the foremost are] the Buddhas...
If a sage uses the belongings of individual teachers, monks, parents, or the sick for his own personal use, he commits a minor offense (light defilement).

This explains the precept against accepting special invitations. Following from the preceding [precepts], as a disciple of the Buddha, one must not only refrain from receiving offerings and sustenance alone, but furthermore, under no circumstances may one accept the offerings and sustenance resulting from special invitations from others.
Furthermore, if one accepts invitations for offerings and sustenance individually without sharing them with the community, such a person is not a śramaṇa and is not a seed of the Buddha;
therefore, this is forbidden. No one at all—whether monastic or lay—is permitted to accept individual invitations for offerings and sustain them for personal use.
This means that when any donor, whether monastic or lay, invites the Saṃgha for a meal, they should accept the invitation together with the community.

One must not privately accept invitations from individuals, for one should share the gains equally within the assembly. This section on "gains" explains the meaning of why one may not accept separate invitations.
Question: One should accept the offerings from a separate invitation and take them into one's own possession; why is this not permitted?
Answer: It is said that these offerings belong to the Sangha of the ten directions; all have an equal share in them.

If one were to accept a private invitation, one would be taking the property of the Sangha of the ten directions and privately incorporating it into oneself. For this reason, one must not accept private invitations.

Regarding the "eight blessings" and so forth, this explains the aforementioned meaning: it means that one must not only refrain from privately taking the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself.
Furthermore, among the eight fields of merit, one must not privately appropriate any of the material goods for one's own personal use.
To take them for private use is likewise to misappropriate the communal property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself. The eight fields of merit are: first, the Buddhas;

second, the noble ones (āryas); third, the preceptors (upādhyāya); fourth, the instructors (ācārya); fifth, the assembly of monks (saṃgha); sixth, the father; seventh, the mother; and eighth, [the sick].
The "sick person" refers to oneself. Those called "Buddhas" are the persons of fruition (*phala-pudgala*). Those called "sages" (*ārya*) are the persons of cause (*hetu-pudgala*).
Each "teacher" refers to one's original *upādhyāya*, *ācārya*, and the ten teachers who provide authoritative testimony.
"Sangha" refers to the great assembly. "Parents" refers to the two biological parents. The "sick person" generally refers to all such relatives.
Among one's enemies and kinsmen, there may be those who are suffering and afflicted.

From the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas above down to the seven classes of ancestors, including parents, these are called the Field of Reverence (*gurut-kṣetra*). The category of the sick person is called the Field of Compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*).
These eight together constitute excellent fields for planting merit and cultivating wisdom. If all these goods are used for the public good, one will obtain blessings.

To use [the property] for one’s own private purposes constitutes an offense. Now, if one separately accepts an invitation and takes items from among the "Eight Fields of Merit" solely for one's own use, and does not distribute them to the assembly, one commits a minor secondary offense (light defilement).
The twenty-eighth precept on separately inviting monks:

If, O Sons of the Buddha, there are ordained bodhisattvas, lay bodhisattvas, or any donors who wish to invite the Sangha as a field of merit to seek the fulfillment of their vows, they should enter the monastery and inquire of the administrative official (karmadāna), saying: "I now wish to invite the Sangha to seek the fulfillment of my vows. The official should...
The attendant replied: "To invite according to the sequence of the assembly is to obtain the holy Sangha of the ten directions.

For worldly people to separately invite five hundred Arhats or Bodhisattvas is not equal to inviting even one ordinary monk from the sequential assembly. To separately invite monks is the law of the non-Buddhists;
the Seven Buddhas had no such practice of separate invitations. It does not accord with the way of filial piety. If one intentionally invites monks separately, one commits an offense."
This is a light offense.
This explains the precept regarding the separate invitation of monks. This precept also derives from the aforementioned [precept on] receiving separate invitations.
That is to say, since one who accepts an invitation does not accept it separately, the one who invites the monks likewise should not invite them separately. *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
It says: "If one practices giving without dwelling on signs, that merit is equal to empty space; if one dwells on signs while practicing giving, the resulting merit is limited.
Thus, it serves as a warning. From "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the text identifies those who seek vows and plant the seeds of merit.
The renunciant bodhisattva is one who has shaved their hair, donned dyed robes, and received the full precepts (*mahāśramaṇa*).
The lay bodhisattva is a person who has received the *upāsaka* precepts consisting of the six grave and twenty-eight light offenses.
Furthermore, "all donors" (*dānapati*) refers, as mentioned above, not only to these two types of bodhisattvas but also to all ordinary donors who perform meritorious deeds. (In Sanskrit: *dānapati*.
*Dāna*. This is translated as "excellent giving. Because one practices the Dharma of the *dānapāramitā* excellently, such a person transcends those of the world who are greedy and stingy;

thus, they receive this honorable title. When such a community of donors with right faith invites the Sangha—the field of merit—to seek their aspirations, some may vow to deliver sentient beings, some may offer prayers according to common worldly sentiments, or [others may do so] for...
Upon hearing the Dharma, one may aspire to be born as a deva or a human, or even aspire to be born in the Western Pure Land.
Whatever the Tathāgata seeks or aspires for must be sought within the Triple Gem. The Triple Gem is the excellent field of merit for all sentient beings to plant their blessings.
That the Triple Gem remains in the world depends entirely upon the Saṃgha. Therefore, one should invite the Saṃgha—the field of merit—to seek the fulfillment of one's aspirations.
At that time, one should enter the monastic quarters and ask the administrator, saying: "I, [Name], now wish to invite the Saṃgha to fulfill my aspirations.
That administrator should reply: "If you wish to invite the Saṃgha, you must follow the proper protocol for sequential invitations."
Why is this? Because it is difficult to distinguish between the noble and the ordinary, and one cannot make such a selection.

Therefore, by inviting [the Sangha] in successive order, one obtains the assembly of worthy and noble monks from the ten directions. If one were to use a discriminating mind and specifically invite five hundred Arhats, Bodhisattvas, or noble monks—thus singling out names and making individual invitations—it would not be as good as following the sequence within the general assembly of monks.
The merit of inviting even a single ordinary monk is such because [the donor] possesses a mind that dwells upon signs.
To invite monks individually is merely the practice of non-Buddhists; within my Buddha-dharma, there is no mind of discrimination.
