This is because they seek without attachment to signs. Furthermore, tracing back from the aforementioned seven Buddhas, there has likewise been no separate rite for invitation.
As for the seven Buddhas: Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, and Viśvabhū Buddha—these three Tathāgatas.
These are the four Tathāgatas who have already attained perfect enlightenment during the past *Kṛta-yuga* (Adornment) aeon:

Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, Kāśyapa Buddha, and Śākyamuni Buddha. These seven Buddhas—including these four and the three yet to appear—are the witnesses for this present *Bhadrakalpa* (Auspicious) aeon, during which one has now attained perfect enlightenment. Therefore, one should not separately invite the Saṃgha for the *Pratimokṣa* ceremony.
Indeed, to specifically request [a particular monk] for one's own prayers is precisely to fail to practice the Way of Filial Piety. Why is this?

It is because, above, it violates the path of the Buddha’s sevenfold admonitions; in the middle, it contravenes the Bodhisattva’s mind of equanimity; and below, it forfeits the virtue of benefiting sentient beings.
Therefore, if one intentionally requests monks individually, one incurs the offense of a minor secondary transgression (*āpatti*).
○ The twenty-ninth precept: Against Wrong Livelihood.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind and for the sake of profit and sustenance, sells the charms of men or women; prepares food with one’s own hands; grinds or husks grain oneself;

practices physiognomy on men and women; interprets the good or bad omens of dreams; predicts whether a child will be male or female; or employs incantations, arts, or crafts—[these are all forbidden].

The Method of the Hawk: To compound a hundred kinds of poisonous drugs, a thousand kinds of poisonous drugs, snake venom, the poison of raw gold and silver, or *gū* (sorcery) poisons, entirely devoid of a heart of compassion or a heart of filial piety—if one does so intentionally, one commits a minor offense (*āpatti*).

This explains the precept against wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). "Wrong livelihood" distinguishes it from right livelihood (*samyagājīva*); "livelihood for oneself" distinguishes it from acting on behalf of others.
Having become a son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva bhikṣu should maintain his life by means of the practice of begging for food.
Soliciting the Dharma means soliciting the Dharma of the single vehicle (ekayāna) of true reality, which one must cherish and protect in order to realize the Dharmakāya.
Soliciting food means soliciting a single meal from a donor to maintain oneself in purity, thereby sustaining the physical body.

In this way, benefiting both oneself and others constitutes one’s virtuous practice. Regarding benefiting oneself: it is so that one does not fall [into the state of] being no longer a child of the Buddha. Regarding benefiting others...

This is for the purpose of continuing those roots of goodness. If one seeks through wrong livelihood or improper means, not only is such an act forbidden for the sons of the Śākya, but it is also unsuitable for a pure lay devotee;
therefore, it is prohibited. Regarding the phrase "because of an evil mind," this distinguishes [this practice] from performing the Way with a virtuous mind.
As for "for the sake of gain and offerings," it is also not for the purpose of seeking to rescue and relieve the suffering of sentient beings.

Therefore, regarding the matters of wrong livelihood, they are opened up in immeasurable detail; yet, in summary, there are eight types of practices. The first is the trafficking of men and women for sexual purposes.
This matter involves separating others from their own flesh and blood, defiling the family reputation, and disregarding shame; it is proscribed by both the monastic and the lay communities alike.

Second: preparing food with one's own hands, grinding it and pounding it oneself. Regarding the Buddha’s regulations for the eating of bhikṣus, even when receiving food from lay attendants (*kappiya-kāraka*), they must first have it formally offered before eating;
how could he ever permit śramaṇas to engage in such worldly livelihoods? This would not only cause them to lose their dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) but also foster greed.
This matter is strictly prohibited for those who have left the household life. Third: divining the fortunes of men and women. To "divine" means to predict human calamities.
1. Fortune-telling: This involves judging whether a person’s circumstances will be in decline or prosperity; it is not the work of a śramaṇa. 2. Interpreting dreams:

This involves interpreting the events seen in a person's dreams to determine their auspiciousness or inauspiciousness. 3. Determining gender: This involves determining whether [an unborn child] will be male or female.

This refers to the false determination of whether a child will be male or female based on the six *jiā* (trigrams). Regarding the "six": *zhòu* (incantation), *shù* (craft), *gōng* (skill), *qiáo* (ingenuity), *zhòu* (incantation), and *zhòu* (incantation).
*Zhòu* refers to various incantations; through incantation, one drives away spirits and dispatches generals, and seizes the souls and spirits of people.

*Shù* refers to illusionary arts (*māyā*); it consists of various illusory phenomena used to delude and bewilder people. *Gōng* refers to refined craftsmanship; *qiáo* refers to skillful artistry. These are all the works of worldly people.
The above points are all things that a son of the Śākya [a Buddhist monk] ought not to do. Seventh: the method for training hawks.

"Training" refers to skillfully taming hawks and dogs so that they may act with speed to seize the lives of living beings; this is a precept observed by both the clergy and the laity. Eighth: compounding a hundred kinds of poisonous drugs.
There are hundreds, thousands, and even hundreds of thousands of kinds of poisonous drugs; here, one or two are briefly mentioned. First...
First, because they compound snake venom to harm people and take the lives of living beings;

second, because they compound raw gold and silver into poison—meaning that raw gold and raw silver are by nature most toxic—and use this poison to harm people and creatures, as well as compound various insects and *gū* poisons to poison people and living souls.
These matters have been jointly regulated by both the clergy and the laity; whoever violates them shall [be punished].

They possess no heart of compassion whatsoever; they possess no heart of filial piety whatsoever. To have no heart of compassion whatsoever means that they lack even a single thought of regarding others as their own children.
To have no heart of filial piety whatsoever means that they lack even a single thought of regarding others as their own parents.
Such wrong livelihood, practiced intentionally for the sake of profit, constitutes a minor offense (light defilement).
○ The thirtieth precept: Not honoring the auspicious time.
If a disciple of the Buddha, out of an evil mind, slanders the Triple Gem himself, feigns intimacy and attachment, and speaks of emptiness with his mouth;

To engage in worldly affairs for the sake of laypeople, acting as an intermediary to facilitate sexual union between men and women, thereby creating various bonds and attachments; or to commit acts of killing, robbery,
or theft on the six days of fasting or during the three months of the long fast, thereby breaking the fast and violating the precepts— these constitute minor offenses.

This commentary explains the precept against disrespecting auspicious times (*kāla*). Regarding "disrespecting auspicious times," it refers to failing to cultivate merit and wisdom during the months, years, dates, and periods when a Heavenly King conducts his tour of inspection;
because one lacks a heart of reverence and awe, one loses great benefit, and thus this is prohibited.
From the passage beginning with "If a disciple of the Buddha" down to the four phrases on "intimacy," it clarifies the mental state of disrespecting auspicious times through speech.

He then spoke of emptiness, arriving at the section concerning those who violate the precepts. He explained in detail the matter of disrespecting auspicious times, stating that it is "due to an evil mind" in order to distinguish this from the cultivation of supramundane wholesome states of mind.
Regarding the phrase "one’s own self slanders the Triple Gem," this distinguishes it from merely slandering the Triple Gem with one's mouth;
for if the mind is not upright, then the body itself will not be correct. If the body is not...
Because when things are superficial, all matters are unreal. "Falsely appearing to be intimate" explains the meaning of unreality;

it means that although one is not originally close with others, one manifests an appearance of intimacy in order to seek dependence. "Speaking of emptiness with the mouth" refers to seeing the deception in their mind;
"acting within existence" refers to seeing the slander in their conduct; and "acting as laypeople and the like" refers to [their outward appearance].
This clarifies that one who slanders the Triple Gem and acts according to the principles of worldly existence is a layperson (*avadātavasana*);

such a person merely manages affairs for those within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Regarding the phrase "mediating between men and women": "mediating" (*tong*) means to facilitate communication; "to bring about" (*zhi*) means to convey one's intent.
It refers to conveying a woman’s intentions to a man and a man’s intentions to a woman—namely, all instances of illicit liaison or marriage arrangements.
Matters. These create various fetters and attachments, from which one is not liberated at all. Now, I shall cite one instance to represent the rest.
Regarding the phrase "on the six fast days of the month," etc., this sentence specifically clarifies the precept against disregarding auspicious times.
The six fast days of the month and the three months of fasting in the year are both times when ghosts and spirits gain power; they are also occasions when celestial deities conduct inspections.

For human beings, this is the time for the reckoning of good and evil. On these specific days and months, practicing the precepts and performing meritorious deeds brings merit superior to that of other times.
Regarding the six monthly fast days (*upoṣadha*): the eighth and the twenty-third are the days when Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King, presides over the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa).
The fourteenth and the twenty-ninth—or the twenty-eighth in a short month—are likewise [the days of the Heavenly King].

The Crown Prince was fifteen years old when he was joined by thirty others; these were the very deities of the heavenly kings themselves. Regarding the three months of the "Long Fasting" (Cāturmāsya):

they are the first, fifth, and ninth months of each year. These three months are called the "Three Auspicious Months. They are the months during which Śakra Devānām Indra conducts his tours of inspection.
Within this celestial palace there is a great precious mirror; from the first month of the year, it reflects the continent of Jambudvīpa in the south.

In the second month, it illuminates the western continent of Aparagoyānī; in the third month, it illuminates the northern continent of Uttarakuru; in the fourth month, it illuminates the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha;
and in the fifth month, it again illuminates the southern continent of Jambudvīpa. In these three cycles, it observes the good and evil of human beings.
Whenever an ordinary person raises a thought or stirs a念 (mind), it is naturally and clearly manifested within the mirror.
Therefore, as a disciple of the Buddha, on this day and month, one ought to exhort others to observe the fast and refrain from killing, and to perform various meritorious deeds;
yet, instead, during this very time, one might commit the acts of killing and plundering, breaking the fast and violating the precepts.
To diminish another's merit, to destroy another's Dharma-wealth, and thus to harm oneself and others, constitutes a minor offense of transgression.
These ten precepts should be studied; one should respectfully uphold them. They are explained in detail within the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts."
This single phrase summarizes the preceding ten precepts; it should now be followed by the next two phrases as an exhortation to practice:
at all times and in every moment, with every thought and mindfulness, one must study and train in these precepts, never losing their meaning from one's mind.
One sentence from the "Chapter on the Formulation of Precepts" (*Śīla-vinaya-varga*) cites a separate chapter from the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] to explain this meaning in detail.
○ The thirty-first precept: The Prohibition Against Not Providing Redemption.
The Buddha said: "O Son of the Buddha, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, in the midst of the evil age, if you see non-Buddhists or any wicked people..."
If there are bandits who sell images of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, or their parents, or who sell the sutras and the Vinaya; or those who trade in monks and nuns,
or even sell bodhisattvas who have resolved for enlightenment and practitioners of the Way, making them servants or slaves for all manner of people under the service of officials—
when a bodhisattva sees such things, they should give rise to a heart of compassion and provide protection through skillful means, teaching them everywhere.
If one uses wealth obtained through transformation to ransom images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as Bhikṣus, Bhikṣuṇīs, and all the Sūtras and Vinayas,
yet fails to ransom them, one commits a minor offense.
This explains the precept against redeeming [sentient beings]. "Jiù" (救) means to rescue and protect; "shú" (贖) means to ransom.

A Bodhisattva upholds the Three Jewels through both principle (*lǐ*) and phenomena (*shì*). By using principle to uphold phenomena, and by using phenomena to uphold principle, they mutually illuminate and manifest one another.
If one sees the Three Jewels being destroyed and does not urgently seek to redeem them, the Three Jewels will from this point on be severed and extinguished;

there will then be no ground for the field of merit that sustains the life of wisdom among humanity. Therefore, he warns against such negligence. The passage beginning with "The Buddha said: O Son of the Buddha" indicates the temporal context.
The intent is that during the time when the Buddha was in the world, such matters did not exist; it is only after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, within this degenerate age, that they occur.
There may indeed be such things. "The evil world" refers to the time of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
During this period, there are many non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and wicked people. As for those called "non-Buddhists," they do not realize their own minds and cling mostly to divergent views;
because they stand outside the Right Path, they are named "non-Buddhists. Because they sever the life-force of the Buddha's wisdom, they are named "wicked people. Such persons constantly...

They contend with the Buddha-dharma; they contend with the Sangha; they plunder the wealth of the Triple Gem; they steal and sell images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or even sell the likenesses of their own parents.
Now, the Buddha is the Great Compassionate Father and the Bodhisattvas are the Great Compassionate Mothers;

they are able to bestow happiness upon sentient beings and able to uproot their suffering. By taking refuge, honoring, and making offerings to them, one obtains immeasurable merit. How could one possibly—
To sell them is to destroy the Buddha-treasure, for which one incurs immeasurable sin. This includes selling the Sūtras and Vinaya:

the Sūtras open the mind and reveal its nature, leading to the realization of the true and eternal; the Vinaya restrains the three karmas and the six sense faculties, resulting in purity and liberation.

How could one possibly sell them? To sell them is to destroy the Jewel of the Dharma. To "sell" bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs means that the Saṃgha of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs is the field of merit for humanity and the Jewel of the Saṃgha dwelling in the world; to sell them is to destroy the Jewel of the Saṃgha.
Among the Three Jewels, such offenses are all immeasurable. Furthermore, there are those who sell bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds for enlightenment;

this refers broadly to both monastics and laypeople of the fourfold assembly. That is to say, anyone who has given rise to the Mahāyāna mind and practices the Mahāyāna path is a person of the Way (*dàorén*).
Thus, monks and other persons of the Way may be plundered, kidnapped, or stolen from.

If they are sold into government service or made into slaves for all manner of people, the Bodhisattva, having seen such sufferings and hardships, should give rise to the mind that seeks to uproot suffering and bestow happiness.
Employing various skillful means and establishing numerous gates of expedient methods, he should provide urgent rescue and protection.
He should teach and transform donors everywhere to obtain their wealth and property to redeem the Buddha [statue].
One should provide offerings according to the Dharma to images of Bodhisattvas so that those who behold them may take refuge, thereby attaining merit and extinguishing transgressions;

furthermore, one should ransom Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs to enable them to leave suffering and hardship behind and practice the Way in peace and security; and one should also ransom all the Sūtras and Vinayas.

One should cause the Wheel of Dharma to turn constantly in order to open the way for those lost in delusion; this is called a Son of the Buddha maintaining the Triple Gem and practicing the Bodhisattva path.
If one sees such a matter and fails to provide rescue, remaining indifferent and looking on, one commits a minor offense.
○ The thirty-second precept against harming sentient beings:
If a Buddha’s disciple, they must not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows; nor may they engage in trade using light scales or small measures, nor exploit their official authority or influence.

To seize the property of others; to harbor malice, bind others, or destroy their accomplishments; or to raise cats, wildcats, pigs, and dogs—if one intentionally raises them, one commits a minor offense.

This explains the precept against harming sentient beings. One who is a bodhisattva should take loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) as the fundamental mind, and the six perfections and myriad practices as the gateway of skillful means. If one harms living things and injures loving-kindness, it is not the mental conduct of a Great Being;
therefore, it is prohibited. From the words "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the matters of harming sentient beings are summarized and indicated. It says:
"One must not keep swords, staves, bows, or arrows" means that these evil instruments harm the bodies and lives of sentient beings, and because evil intent arises easily, they must not be kept.
The two characters "must not" (bùdé) govern the following clauses.

One must not engage in trade using light scales or small measures, nor employ deceitful methods to defraud others and harm sentient beings in their transactions. One must not exploit official authority...

By relying on power and influence to seize the wealth and property of others, seeking through unwholesome means and harming sentient beings, one fails to obtain fame or profit and does not achieve one's goals.
Furthermore, by feigning official authority, one harms sentient beings with a malicious intent, binding them and damaging their physical forms;
thus, one’s pursuit of wealth remains unfulfilled, and one coerces others into selling off their children and assets, destroying their established successes.
Regarding one's own kin: one must not raise cats, wildcats, pigs, or dogs to catch mice or harm other creatures, nor sell them for profit, thereby binding oneself in enmity through acts of kindness.
Regarding all the precepts above, one must not commit such acts. Should one violate them below, if one intentionally raises such animals, [one incurs a transgression].

This constitutes a transgression of a minor defilement offense (*āpatti*). Question: Regarding the statement in the text that one "must not keep, sell, harm, or nourish" various things, why does the concluding summary state only, "if one intentionally nourishes them, it is an offense"? Answer: If even keeping them is prohibited, [how much more so the other acts].
How could one permit keeping or selling [such things]? Therefore, one precept is all precepts.
○ The thirty-third: The Precept Against Wrongful Deeds and Discursive Thought.
If a Buddha’s disciple, out of an evil mind, observes the fighting of men and women, or military arrays, soldiers, generals, and bandits—

They shall not engage in fighting. Furthermore, they must not listen to the sounds of conchs, drums, horns, lutes, *saras*, *kṣetra-paṇava*, flutes, *vīṇā*, singing, shouting, or the music of courtesans.

They must not play at *chūpuru*, *go-ṣṭhika*, *bala-vāhana*, *caturaṅga*, *ṣaḍ-yūta*, ball-games, stone-throwing, *tūṇa-hasta*, *śakaṭa*, *aṣṭāpada*, *ratha-yuddha*, *nakṣatra-darśana*, *akṣa-vidyā*, *śalākā-vidyā*, *pātra-vidyā*, or *kapāla-vidyā*. Nor shall they perform these [divinatory] acts.

Regarding divination and sorcery: one must not act as a messenger for thieves or bandits; one must not do so in any instance whatsoever. If one intentionally does so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

This explains the precept against wrong actions, discursive thought, and contemplation (*vitarka-vicāra*). "Wrong action" excludes what is not a right action. "Discursive thought" (*vitarka*) refers to initial mental application or illumination; "contemplation" (*vicāra*)... [refers to sustained mental application].
One should immediately observe that the essence of awakening is fundamentally neither deviant nor correct; it resides entirely in illuminating observation.

If one is turned by external objects, it is called deviant activity of awakening and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*); if one can turn objects, it is called correct activity of awakening and observation.

This is a warning for beginner Bodhisattvas whose mental focus is not yet settled and whose contemplative observation is not yet matured. The section beginning with "If a Buddha’s disciple... provides a general heading.

Regarding the meaning of the fundamental nature of vitarka and vicāra as unwholesome karma: the phrase "because of an evil mind" serves to distinguish this from the wholesome thoughts involved in the hidden and manifest manifestations of skillful means within the course of practice;
it clarifies that these [unwholesome thoughts] involve wandering according to worldly passions, and are therefore termed an "evil mind."
"Observing all men and women engaged in fighting" clearly elucidates the characteristics of the mental states of right and wrong karma.
"Observation" refers to the observing mind; "all and so forth" refers to the objects of observation. These consist of two matters.
First, it refers to all matters of men and women engaging in play and dancing. Second, it refers to matters of mutual contention, strife, and physical combat arising from anger;

thus it is said, "all men and women, etc., fighting. Regarding "fighting in military arrays with generals and soldiers," this refers to the mutual slaughter of two hostile nations, each seeking territory and protection. Regarding "fighting among bandits and the like," this refers to...
Regarding matters such as robbery, plundering, and fighting and killing—these various instances of conflict are all due to the eyes seeing things and causing the mind to wander and stray.
This precept regarding what the eyes see is itself the precept of the mind; one must by no means allow oneself to be swayed by the objects of contention.
One wishes to cause the eye-faculty to attain purity, and the mind likewise to be pure; that is to say, by purifying a single faculty, many faculties are purified.
Therefore, one should emulate the great Bodhisattvas and constantly engage in battle with the Māras, such as the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

Furthermore, regarding the prohibition against listening to the blowing [of wind-instruments] and so forth: this implies that it is not only the case for the eye-faculty that one must refrain from such things.
Regarding perverse observation: the faculty of hearing must likewise not engage in perverse listening; this constitutes the purity of the auditory faculty, which is not usurped by external objects.
This is because it revolves the mechanism of hearing. "Conch" refers to the spiral shell; the people of the Southern Barbarians blow it to keep time for music. "Drum."
The *zhànggǔ* (staff drum) is made by carving wood for the frame and covering both sides with leather so that it may be struck. The *jiǎo* (horn) refers to rhinoceros horn;
the Qiang and Hu peoples blow it to startle the horses of the Central Kingdom. The *qín* (lute) refers to the *yáqín* (elegant lute); its ancient construction consisted of five strings.
The present standard for the seven-stringed instrument is as follows: the *se* has fifty strings; it was created by Pao-xi (Fuxi), though Yu Shun later changed it to twenty-five strings.
The *zheng* has thirteen strings; it was created by Meng Tian. The *di* flute has seven holes; it is made of bamboo.
The *konghou* has twenty-four strings; it was created by Shi Yan. All the above are types of musical instruments.
As for the sounds of singing, shouting, and the music of courtesans, these are the sounds of human music.

Although there are differences among these human musics, once they enter the faculty of the ear, they cause the mind to drift and dissipate; therefore, one must not listen to them. One must also not play *chupuo* (dice) and other such games.
These also cause the faculty of the body to be purified. *Chupubo* (chess/checkers) refers to gambling. *Weiqi* (Go) refers to the game of *yi-qi*.
*Pulosexi* (the elephant game) refers to the game of elephants. *Danchi* (stone-tossing) refers to the *zhuang-lan* game of the Han dynasty.
*Liubuo* (six-sided dice) refers to *shuanglu*. *Paiju* (ball-bouncing) refers to kicking a ball. *Zhishe* (stone-throwing) refers to the modern game of *tou-hu*; in antiquity, one threw stones.
Now, "throwing arrows" (*jishi*) refers to pulling a cord; "running horses" (*jiemai*) refers to such things as selling weapons;

and "walking the city walls" (*xingcheng*) refers to walking upon the battlements of a city wall, or perhaps pulling a cord along the eight paths of the city wall chessboard. Although these activities differ from one another, they all belong to the category of gambling.
As for the "claw-mirror" (*zhaojing*), one applies medicinal ointment to the fingertips and recites incantations over them, whereby they emit a radiance like that of a mirror.

It illuminates people and determines their fortune or misfortune. The *shichao* grass grows from the tomb of King Wen; it emerges in clusters of one hundred stalks per clump, with blue clouds covering it above and numinous tortoises resting upon its qi below.
One must cut it when it has grown large to use it for divination, thereby determining a person's auspiciousness or calamity.
The *yángzhī* (willow branch) is the deity Zhāngliǔ; it clings to the side of a person's ear to report their misfortunes and blessings.

The *bōyú* (alms bowl) is what is now called a water-reflecting bowl; one pours water into the bowl and uses a blade and incantations to stir it until it becomes still, in order to determine a person’s right and wrong.
The *dúlóu* (skull) is taken from a fresh corpse and consecrated through incantations so that it becomes spiritually efficacious, capable of speaking of a person’s misfortunes and blessings.
Therefore, regarding those who practice divination and geomancy—this refers collectively to the several types mentioned above—one must not serve as a messenger for thieves.
This means that even if one were captured by bandits and faced with death, one must under no circumstances act as a messenger for them.
The phrase "not to do any of these" is the concluding summary; it is the Buddha’s earnest exhortation.
These words of admonition mean that the aforementioned various improper activities are none of them to be performed by a child of the Buddha; therefore, one must not engage in any of them.
If one intentionally does so, one commits a minor offense (light defilement). Among the items mentioned in the sutras, such as musical instruments and divination tools—
Most cases are similar to this; therefore, I shall cite and explain them (the preceding text contains two interpretations of *pārasika-krīḍā* and *yanqi*; one suspects these may be scribal errors.
It is likely that *pārasika-krīḍā* refers to the *zhuanglian* game, while *yanqi* refers to the *xiangqi* [elephant chess] game).
○ Thirty-fourth: Briefly Contemplating the Śrāvaka Precepts.

If a disciple of the Buddha upholds the prohibitive precepts, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, during the six periods of day and night, they shall read and recite these precepts as if they were a vajra.
They shall be like one carrying a life-preserving float intending to cross the great ocean, or like the bhikṣu bound by grass, constantly generating a great [mind of resolve].
Riding upon wholesome faith, one should know for oneself: "I am a Buddha-to-be who has not yet attained completion; the Buddhas are Buddhas who have already attained completion.

One must resolve to attain Bodhicitta, never allowing it to depart from the mind even for a single thought-moment. If one gives rise to a single thought of the Two Vehicles or of external paths, one commits a minor offense.
This explains the temporary mindfulness of the precepts of the Hīnayāna. "Temporary" (*zan*) means a brief moment; "mindfulness" (*nian*) means mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Regarding the phrase "precepts of the Hīnayāna," this distinguishes them from those of the Mahāyāna. Formerly, when Śāriputra was practicing the bodhisattva path, he encountered a brāhmaṇa who begged for his eyes.
Śāriputra said, "My eyes are of use to my own body; what will you do with them? The brāhmaṇa—
He said, "You who practice the bodhisattva path, give whatever is asked for, regardless of whether it is useful or not. At that time, Śāriputra immediately took out his eye and gave it to him.
Once the man had it in his hand, he sniffed it with his nose and said, "This is a foul-smelling thing, rank and putrid."
"What use is he? [The Master] spat upon him, stepped over him, and departed. Śāriputra said: "The practice of a Bodhisattva is difficult;

if one abandons the precepts for even a single thought-moment, one falls back to the level of a Śrāvaka for twenty minor kalpas. Therefore, one must guard the precepts. [The text continues with: "If you are a Buddha's disciple... and so forth.

This serves as a general indication of the period during which one practices the bodhisattva path. Regarding the phrase "guarding and upholding the prohibitive precepts" (*śīla*): "Guarding" (*ārakṣa*) means protection, so that Māra cannot cause invasion.
"Upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) means firm adherence, so that the mind does not regress. "Prohibiting" (*saṃvara*) means restraining the five sense faculties so they do not move.
"Precepts" (*śīla*) mean the cessation and extinction of unwholesome states within the mental ground so that they do not arise. This is what is meant by "vigorously upholding."

Pure precepts are like guarding a bright pearl. Throughout the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—and during the twelve periods of day and night (six periods by day and six by night), one maintains the Buddha’s precepts at these times so as not to be dissipated by the winds of external objects.
Thus, through firm precepts, concentration is attained; through the clarity of concentration, wisdom is aroused; and the three trainings are fully perfected.

This is the perfection of the three bodies. To recite this precept is to clarify the skillful means of its protection and maintenance. Regarding the statement that one must protect and maintain these precepts: how does one do so?
One should thoroughly read these precepts, consulting the original text to examine the wording and understand the gravity of the offenses, as well as what is permitted and what is prohibited.
By reciting them apart from the text, one investigates the mind to clarify their ultimate purpose and intent, thereby preserving these precepts. It is just like...

Vajra. By means of vajra-wisdom, one can shatter all deluded thoughts and inversions. To strictly guard the categories of precepts is also like wearing and carrying a life-preserving float to cross the ocean of suffering.
A life-preserving float is an instrument for crossing the sea. Long ago, there was a merchant who carried a float across the sea.
A rākṣasa in the sea begged him for the float; the man would not give it to him, so he then begged for only one [corner].
Even half [of the bag] was not permitted; even when he asked for a single thread, his wish was not granted. Why? Because his life depended on the bag.
If the floating bag were to break, he would never be able to reach the shore. This serves as a metaphor for a person who upholds the precepts and wishes to cross the bitter sea of birth and death:
even if they encounter a rākṣasa of craving and affection and falsely seek a single boon, it will ultimately not be granted.
Why is this? Because life depends upon the precepts. If the precepts are broken, one will sink into the ocean of suffering in birth and death with no hope of escape for a long time.
Therefore, one must protect the precepts in this manner. As for the simile of the "grass-tied bhikṣu," this illustrates the compassionate mind of upholding the precepts.
Because he did not harm living beings: In the past, there was a bhikṣu who was plundered by bandits. Fearing that they would pursue him, the bandits bound the bhikṣu with grass.
Upholding the prohibitions and precepts of the Buddha, the bhikṣu did not pluck the living grass and did not dare to move.
At that time, encountering the king’s passing, one was able to be released and set free. How can this teaching of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) serve as an analogy for the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna)?

The intention is that even those of the Lesser Vehicle, who have no hope of attaining Buddhahood, still maintain these precepts with such firm persistence; how much more so, then, should those of the Great Vehicle?
Benefiting both oneself and others—how could one possibly give rise to negligence regarding this precept? Therefore, a Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts should also be like this.
Those who constantly give rise to wholesome faith in the Mahāyāna refer precisely to those of the Hīnayāna who do not believe that their own minds are Buddha.
As for these new students of the Mahāyāna, although they have given rise to such faith, I fear they may encounter two kinds of objects [of distraction].
Therefore, one should withdraw [from distraction] and exert oneself in this. In the Mahāyāna, one should constantly give rise to wholesome faith that is ever-continuous and uninterrupted.

One should believe that one’s own mind is the Buddha and that one’s own mind creates the Buddha. With resolute faith, one should believe that one is a venerable Buddha within the causal stage who has not yet attained completion;
however, one has not yet attained the adornments of the resultant stage because one’s practice and vows are not yet perfected, and because of delusions.

This is because the obstacles have not yet been emptied. Regarding the statement that "the Buddhas are those who have already attained Buddhahood," the meaning is that the Buddhas have already perfected the three bodies (*trikāya*), are fully endowed with all virtues, have reached the ultimate limit of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*), and have eternally extinguished the two types of death (*dvividha-maraṇa*).
Therefore, as I cultivate such causes, I will necessarily realize such fruits. If there were even the slightest negligence, one would immediately lose what is appropriate.

The arrival of the Buddha is the fruit of adornment. "Diligently upholding the prohibitive precepts" refers to practice (*caryā*). "Constantly giving rise to wholesome faith" refers to faith (*śraddhā*).
"Knowing for oneself that one is a Buddha-to-be while all Buddhas are those who have already attained completion" refers to understanding (*avabodha*).
Regarding the arousal of the bodhicitta: this mind is the essence of the primordially awakened wisdom (*pratyavekṣa-jñāna*) within the stages of faith, understanding, and practice.

Although these three—faith, understanding, and practice—are fully present, when one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood, one must remain focused upon the correctly aroused Mahāyāna bodhicitta, keeping it ever-present and never forgetting it.
Because it is thus maintained in every thought-moment without departing from the mind, one is truly a Bodhisattva.
When one’s practice of the precepts is fully matured, the fruit of Buddhahood may be expected.

However, if within that which is believed, understood, practiced, or resolved, one gives rise to even a single thought of the mind of a follower of the Two Vehicles or a non-Buddhist (tīrthika), one commits a minor offense. Question:

How can a mere single thought be said to constitute a transgression? Answer: Although it is but a fleeting thought, it injures the seed of Buddhahood; it is the loss of the bodhicitta. Thus, [it is an offense].
This constitutes an act of Māra. Will it not lead to a fall and regression for twenty minor kalpas? Therefore, one incurs this offense.
○ The thirty-fifth precept: Not making vows.
If you are a disciple of the Buddha, you should always resolve to make all vows: to be filial toward your parents and respectful toward your teachers and the Sangha;

to pray for an excellent teacher and virtuous companions in study who will constantly instruct you in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, and in the ten stages of setting forth, the ten stages of nurturing growth, and the ten adamantine stages.
The Ten Grounds. May I attain understanding and realization, practice according to the Dharma, and firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts.
Even at the cost of my body and life, may these not depart from my mind for even a single thought-moment. If any Bodhisattvas do not make this vow, they commit a minor offense.

This commentary explains the precept of making vows. Following the preceding discussion on upholding the precepts and generating the resolve for enlightenment, one who has already given rise to Mahāyāna faith and understanding must further make vows to diligently seek teachers and friends in order to clarify the underlying principles.

Fearing that if these principles are not clearly understood, one might harbor erroneous thoughts and indiscriminately conflate the Mahāyāna with the Hīnayāna or non-Buddhist paths, the text therefore enjoins this precept. From the words "If a Buddha’s disciple... onwards, the text provides a general summary of the vow.
These are the great vows. Regarding the phrase "constantly responding," it means that the difficulty lies not in making the vow, but rather in fearing that one will not be constant.
Therefore, one must constantly respond by making vows. Because these great vows are inexhaustible, they are all brought forth.

Since sentient beings are inexhaustible, and their affliction-obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), karma-obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), and retribution-obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*) are all inexhaustible, the bodhisattva’s aspirational mind is likewise inexhaustible.

Because there is exhaustion [of worldly merit], it is said: "One should constantly bring forth all vows. Regarding "filial piety toward parents, teachers, monks, and so forth," this specifically opens up the mind of aspiration.
Although vows are immeasurable, they are subsumed within ten general vows: first, the vow to be filial toward parents;
second, the vow to seek a good teacher; third, the vow to seek fellow students; fourth, the vow to seek the Great Dharma; fifth, the vow to seek...

1. The ten stages of setting forth; 2. the six vows of seeking; 3. the ten stages of nurturing; 4. the seven vows of seeking; 5. the ten adamantine stages; 6. the eight vows of seeking; 7. the ten stages; 8.
the vow of seeking to open understanding of the Buddha-vehicle; 9. the vow of firmly upholding the Buddha-precepts; 10. the vow of being filial toward one’s parents. Question:
Parents have the grace of giving birth and raising one; teachers and monks have the virtue of instructing and admonishing one. From [the perspective of] self...
Nevertheless, one dares not oppose or disobey them. Why, then, need one rely on making vows for filial piety?

It is said that within the precepts of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), if a *bhikṣu* is practicing the Path and his parents cannot provide even thread or needle, and the *bhikṣu* gives half of his alms-food to them, although he is filial, it is not considered great.
Now, within the precepts of the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), one regards all sentient beings as one's own parents; if one does not make a vow [to this effect], [the practice is incomplete].
Regarding filial piety and obedience: I fear these might be views similar to those of the Hīnayāna, wherein the mind is neither universal nor constant; therefore, one should make a vow as follows.

Second, regarding the wish to find a good teacher: this refers to the distinctions among teachers—whether they belong to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, hold right view or wrong view, possess understanding but lack practice, or possess practice but lack understanding. That which is sought now is the wish to find one who possesses both correct knowledge and correct view.
Question: Above, it was stated that one should "make a vow to be filial toward one's teachers and monks," yet here there is a further selection, wishing for a "good teacher.
Why is this? Answer: The former was spoken in the context of making offerings and serving; the latter is spoken in the context of seeking the Way.
Therefore, one should wish to seek a good teacher; this is not the same as a mind of self-conceit (*māna*). Third, the vow for fellow students.
As for a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra): although one may encounter a holy master who provides direct instruction, one must further rely on the support and assistance of a worthy companion.
This is just as Linji was inspired by the Head Seat, or as Changli attained awakening through Sanping; therefore, seeking such a teacher is paramount.
This is the first section on visiting friends. Therefore, those who seek fellow students must seek true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Regarding the fourth vow, "to always instruct me in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya," this means selecting those whose teachings are not of the Hīnayāna dharma.

Building upon the preceding points regarding seeking teachers and choosing friends, this is because one desires that they constantly instruct me in the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, so that I may suddenly and perfectly realize the Buddha-wisdom. As for... [text ends]
Because the five natures differ according to whether one encounters a teacher or the teachings, one consequently aspires to seek the Mahāyāna Dharma.

The fifth vow is to cultivate the ten stages of "setting forth" (*daśa-prasthāna*), which corresponds to the stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*); this is because one awakens to the true source and cultivates the principle of the contemplation of emptiness.

The sixth vow is to cultivate the ten stages of "nurturing" (*daśa-poṣaṇa*), which corresponds to the stage of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*); this is for the purpose of nurturing bodhi and cultivating...

7. "By means of the practice of the provisional (conventional) contemplation" refers to the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), wherein one practices the Middle Way Contemplation through the simultaneous operation of wisdom and compassion.
8. "By means of the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)" refers to the stage of the Ten Sages (*daśārya*).

This is because one perfectly cultivates the three contemplations and perfectly realizes the three bodies (*trikāya*). 9. "May I attain awakening and understanding" refers to being taught the Mahāyāna as described above.
The sutras and vinayas do not merely instruct one to read them thoroughly;

rather, they further desire that within the Mahayana sutras and vinayas, I may understand in detail every dharma-gate of practice and all the methods for cultivating and realizing the path to Bodhi—namely, the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood—so that I may practice according to the Dharma and swiftly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. I firmly uphold these ten vows before the Buddha.

Regarding the precepts: although one may seek the Mahāyāna and practice the union of wisdom and compassion, if one does not firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts, the path and fruits of the sages and saints will all be lost.
That is to say, if one violates them even to the extent of a speck of dust, one will not be able to give rise to the bodhicitta in this very life;
furthermore, everything up to the wondrous fruit of the eternally abiding buddha-nature will be lost. And so forth. Therefore:

One should make a vow to firmly uphold the Buddha’s precepts. Even if one encounters adverse conditions, one must rather sacrifice body and life than ever dare to abandon the mind that firmly upholds the Buddha’s precepts from moment to moment.
One who makes such a vow and maintains the precepts in this way is a true child of the Buddha.
One will certainly attain Buddhahood without doubt. If any bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
○ The thirty-sixth precept: Not making a vow.
If a disciple of the Buddha, having made the ten great vows, upholds the prohibitive precepts of the Buddha and makes this vow, saying:

"I would rather cast this body into a pit of blazing, fierce fire or onto a mountain of knives than ever violate the sutras and vinaya of the Buddhas of the three periods of time by engaging in impure conduct with any woman.
Furthermore, they make this vow: "I would rather [be pierced] by a thousand layers of hot iron mesh..."
They shall wrap themselves all around with these [garments], yet they shall never, with this body of broken precepts, accept any clothing from faithful donors (*dānapati*).

Furthermore, they shall make this vow: "I would rather swallow glowing iron balls and great torrents of fierce fire for hundreds of thousands of kalpas with this mouth, than ever, with this mouth of broken precepts, consume the hundred-flavored drinks of faithful donors."

Having eaten, he further made this vow: "I would rather lie upon a floor of glowing iron within a net of fierce flames with this body than ever accept a hundred kinds of seats from a faithful donor with this body of broken precepts. He further made this vow:
"I would rather have three hundred spears pierce my body with this body for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever [accept...]"
With a body that has broken the precepts, one receives the hundred flavors of food and medicine from a faithful donor; yet one makes this vow:

"I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas than, with this body of broken precepts, receive from a faithful donor a thousand kinds of dwellings, houses, groves, or fields. Furthermore, one makes this vow: "I would rather..."
May an iron hammer crush this body from head to foot until it is reduced to fine dust;
I would never, with this body of broken precepts, accept the respectful prostrations and offerings of faithful donors. Furthermore, he makes this vow:
"I would rather have my two eyes gouged out by hundreds of thousands of hot iron blades and spears than ever, with this mind of broken precepts, gaze upon the beautiful forms of others."

He further made this vow: "I would rather have my faculty of hearing pierced by a hundred thousand iron awls for one kalpa or two kalpas than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, listen to pleasant sounds. He further made this vow:
"I would rather have my nose cut off by a hundred thousand sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily smell various fragrances. He further made...
I make this vow: I would rather have my tongue cut off by hundreds of thousands of sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, consume the hundred-flavored pure food of others.

Again, I make this vow: I would rather have my body hacked and mangled with a sharp axe than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, crave pleasant tactile sensations. Again, I make this vow: May all sentient beings attain Buddhahood.
If a bodhisattva does not make this vow, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
This explains the precept against failing to make a vow. The previous section concerned making a vow; this concerns making a pledge.

To have the vow first and the pledge second is like a horse that, although already equipped with a bridle and reins, is further spurred by a whip to ensure its arrival at the destination. It is because one desires to reach the Great [Enlightenment].
[The result: If one lacks the power of a resolute and great vow, there is fear that upon encountering favorable conditions, one will be unable to transcend them;

thus, what has been vowed will surely become empty. Therefore, he warns against this. Having "aroused the ten great vows" reiterates what preceded; "maintaining the Buddha’s prohibitive precepts" introduces what follows.

Regarding the phrase "firmly maintaining the Buddha’s precepts," it refers to the previous statement: "I would rather sacrifice my body and life, never allowing [the precepts] to depart from my every thought."
Mind. Having made this vow, I further establish a solemn oath to strengthen it. There are four sections to this oath: first, the vow not to engage in non-celibate conduct;
second, the vow not to accept offerings in vain; third, the vow not to defile the six sense faculties;
fourth, the vow to transform sentient beings from the outset. The first clarifies the abstention from non-celibate conduct.
Furthermore, if unwholesome thoughts should arise within us, we shall vow: "I would rather cast this body into a blazing, fierce fire and endure the suffering of being scorched and consumed;
fall into a great pit or trench and endure the suffering of being trapped and falling; or ascend a mountain of blades and endure the suffering of being sliced and severed.
I would rather endure such extreme states of suffering throughout this present life than [give way to them]."

This would be a source of affliction; therefore, I shall never, under any circumstances, dare to violate the pure and definitive prohibitions of the sutras and vinaya spoken by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, nor engage in impure conduct with any woman.
Second, the vow not to receive offerings in vain. This statement further opens into six types. First, the vow not to receive clothing in vain. Furthermore, he makes this vow:

I vow that, were I to encounter a time of cold, I would rather have my body encircled on all sides by a thousand layers of glowing iron mesh, until my skin is scorched and my flesh is consumed, than consider it a hardship;
yet I shall never, with this body of broken precepts, accept any clothing from a faithful donor. Second, I vow not to receive food or drink in vain, and I further make this vow:
If one encounters hunger, it would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball with this mouth;

if one encounters thirst, it would be better to drink a great torrent of fierce fire, enduring the agony of scorched intestines and rotted lungs, than ever to use this mouth of broken precepts to consume the food of a hundred flavors offered by faithful donors.
Third, I vow not to receive bedding and requisites in vain; furthermore, I make this vow:

Vow: Just as when the body is weary, one would rather lie upon a floor of glowing iron mesh amidst a great, fierce fire, enduring the suffering of flesh being consumed and bones being scorched, than ever use this body of broken precepts to accept the hundreds of kinds of couches and seats offered by faithful donors out of their confidence.
Fourth, the vow not to receive medical provisions in vain; furthermore, he made [this vow].

Vow: Just as when one is ill, it would be better to endure the pain of three hundred spears piercing this body—even for the duration of one or two kalpas—than ever to use this body of broken precepts to receive the medicinal offerings of a hundred flavors from faithful donors.
Fifth, not to vainly accept the offerings of village dwellers; furthermore, he made this vow: "Just as..."

While dwelling [in this world], I would rather cast this body into a cauldron of molten iron for hundreds of thousands of kalpas and vow to endure it, than ever receive with a body of broken precepts the thousand kinds of dwellings, houses, gardens, and fields offered by faithful donors out of their confidence.
Sixth, the vow not to receive prostrations in vain: he further makes this vow, as follows: "As for myself..."
When honoring oneself, one would rather have this body smashed with an iron hammer from head to foot until it is reduced to fine dust;
one would never, with this body of broken precepts, accept the respectful prostrations and offerings of faithful donors.
Third is the vow not to defile the six sense faculties. This vow is further divided into five types. First is the vow to purify the faculty of the eye.

One makes this vow: "When the eye encounters forms, I would rather have my two eyes gouged out with a red-hot iron blade or spear and destroy this physical eye than ever look upon the beautiful forms of others with a mind that violates the precepts."
It destroys the pure Dharma-eye. Question: How can the faculty of the pure eye be destroyed? Answer: What is called "destruction" here is not a destruction in the sense of physical decay;
rather, it means that the pure faculty of the eye is rendered unable to penetrate things with unimpeded clarity.
Second is the vow to purify the faculty of hearing. One further makes this vow:

"When the ear encounters sounds, even if I must endure the constant and ultimate suffering of having my ears pierced by hundreds of thousands of iron awls for one or two kalpas, I shall rather endure it than ever listen to pleasant sounds with a mind that breaks the precepts."
Third, the vow to purify the faculty of the nose: He further makes this vow:

"When the nose encounters various fragrances, I would rather endure having my nose cut off by hundreds of thousands of sharp blades than ever, with a mind of broken precepts, greedily inhale those fragrances and thereby destroy the purity of the faculty of the nose. Fourth, the purification of the tongue...

Fourth is the vow regarding the tongue-faculty (*jihvendriya*). He further makes this vow: "Just as when the tongue takes up food and drink, even if one were to cut off that tongue with hundreds of thousands of sharp blades, I would still accept it;
I shall never, with a mind of broken precepts, consume the hundred flavors of human food and thereby ruin my pure tongue-faculty.
Fifth is the vow regarding the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). He further makes this vow: "Just as..."

When the body encounters pleasant tactile sensations, one should rather endure having one's body hacked and severed with a sharp axe than, out of a mind that violates the precepts, become greedily attached to those pleasant sensations and thereby destroy the pure Dharma-body.
The above three sections comprising twelve vows constitute the practice for one's own benefit; the following single vow constitutes the practice for the benefit of others. Fourth:

This was originally a vow to transform sentient beings. Furthermore, he made this aspiration, saying: "I now make this vow and establish this pledge not merely for my own personal purification and liberation;
it is fundamentally for the sake of universally transforming all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm."
This is because all shall attain Buddhahood. To establish such vows and aspirations in this manner is what defines a Bodhisattva.
If one does not make these four categories of thirteen kinds of vows, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).
○ The thirty-seventh precept: Regarding wandering while disregarding hardships.
If a disciple of the Buddha, they should always practice *dhūta* during the two seasons, sit in meditation during winter and summer, and observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*).

They should constantly carry a willow branch, cleansing powder, the three robes, a water flask, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, a mendicant’s staff, an incense burner, a sprinkler bag, a hand towel, and a small knife.
Fire-sticks, tweezers, a corded bed, sūtras, vinaya texts, images of the Buddha, and images of bodhisattvas—
when a bodhisattva practices the dhūta austerities or travels abroad, journeying hundreds or thousands of *li*, these eighteen kinds of items shall always accompany his person.

Regarding the dhūta practitioner: from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month—during these two periods—the eighteen items must always accompany the body like the two wings of a bird.
On the uposatha days, the novice bodhisattva observes the uposatha every half-month and recites the ten grave precepts and the four [intermediate precepts].
The Eighteen Minor Precepts: When reciting the precepts, one should do so before images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If there is only one person performing the *poṣadha*, that single person shall recite them. Whether there are two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand people, only one person shall recite them.

The reciter shall sit upon a high seat while the listeners remain on lower seats. Each participant shall don the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya* robe. This applies during the summer retreat (*varṣā*).
In each case, act in accordance with the Dharma. When practicing *dhūta* austerities, do not enter dangerous places. Whether it be national turmoil or a wicked king;
terrain that is uneven; dense vegetation; lions, tigers, and wolves; water, fire, or wind; bandits on the road; or venomous snakes—do not enter any such perilous locations.
This applies whether one is practicing the *dhūta* path or even during the summer retreat (*varṣā*). These are all dangers.
One must not enter such places; if one enters them intentionally, one commits a minor offense (light defilement).

This explains the precept against traveling while disregarding dangers. As for the previous statement regarding the vow to deliver sentient beings, although one's compassion may be vast and great, [one must still exercise caution].
It is feared that bodhisattvas at the initial stage of their resolve have not yet fully perfected the power of the Way and cannot be entirely unimpeded.

Therefore, when encountering difficult places, one must not travel lightly; thus, they are cautioned. The passage beginning with "If a disciple of the Buddha" clarifies the time for a bodhisattva’s travels.
"One should always [travel] during two seasons" refers to the two seasons of spring and autumn each year; these are times of temperate weather.
When all things are in the process of growing and maturing, it is fit for travel; therefore, one should always transform sentient beings during this time.
*Dhūta* means "to shake off. It refers to shaking away adventitious afflictions (*kleśa*) in order to seek the unsurpassed Dharma.
As for sitting in meditation during winter and summer, and observing the summer retreat (*varṣā*), it is because winter is intensely cold and summer...

At that time, during the intense heat of summer, one should practice *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight meditation) to distance oneself from the states of dullness and distraction, thereby clearing away the afflictions of cold and heat;

for this reason, the winter and summer retreats (*varṣā*) are established so that one may apply oneself diligently to the Buddha-way. The frequent use of *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks) and other items explains the matters concerning the *anagga* (rainy-season retreat).
This means that whenever one enters the winter retreat or rests during the summer, one must always employ eighteen kinds of items as ritual implements (*dharmapātra*).
Among these, the *yāñzhi* (tooth-stick) is used constantly; it provides five benefits: first, it strengthens the teeth;

second, it clarifies the eyes; third, it purifies the mind; fourth, it dispels wind; and fifth, it removes impurities. Therefore, after every meal, it is appropriate to use the *yāñzhi*. As it is said:
Alternatively, it may not be used. The *Five Hundred Questions* states that this constitutes an offense of transgression (*pāyattika*). "Soap powder" refers to soapberries (*sābja*).

Once one has finished using the toilet, with hands and body purified, one may then prostrate to the Buddha, recite mantras, or chant sutras. The "three robes" refer to the five-piece robe (*pañcaka-cīvara*) and the seven-piece robe (*saptaka-cīvara*).
The *saṃghāṭī* (great robe) is also included. Within this *saṃghāṭī*, there are likewise three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—which together comprise nine grades.

All are intended to cover the body, eliminate greed, and serve as attire for transcending worldly life. As for the *pātra* (alms bowl): the Sanskrit term is *pātra*, which here is translated as "vessel of appropriate measure.
The large size is five *dou*; the medium is seven *sheng*; and the small is according to one's capacity. This is the rule for a *bhikṣu* regarding eating.
One carries a single alms bowl to sustain the body, in order to sever wrong livelihood and improper seeking. The "flask" (ping) is the *kundikā*;

it is used to pour forth the water of the Dharma to nourish sentient beings and wash away the dust and defilements of the world. Regarding bedding: the Sanskrit term is *niṣīdana*, which here means "seating mat.
It is also called the "sufficient clothing. One spreads it for sitting in meditation to establish the fivefold Dharma-body, just like a stupa.

Because there is a foundation, there is the *khakkhara* (Sanskrit: *khikkhira*; here translated as "staff with rings"). It is also called the "Staff of Wisdom" (*jñāna-daṇḍa*) or the "Staff of Virtue" (*guṇa-daṇḍa*).

It symbolizes the planting of the banner of the Dharma and manifests the wisdom of the Sage. The incense burner symbolizes faith; it severs doubt regarding the Dharma-realm and leads one into the Buddha-way.
As for the water-strainer, it is made of fine silk; by straining water, one protects living beings, thereby manifesting compassion.
Because of the mind, there is a hand-towel; one wipes the face and then bathes to cleanse away impurities. As for the knife: in antiquity, the precept-knife was used to subdue Māra;
today it is used to shave off beard and hair to sever the root of craving and distinguish oneself from worldly appearances. As for the fire-starter:
one takes fire to provide light and dispel darkness, signifying the possession of wisdom. As for the tweezers: in antiquity, the dhūta practitioners walked barefoot, fearing...

[The staff] pricks the foot; it is used for pulling [out thorns], symbolizing the complete eradication of the poisonous thorns of all afflictions (*kleśa*). The *rajjuparyaṅka* (rope bed) is constructed by stringing together ropes;
it symbolizes the shedding of arrogance and the non-arising of negligence, as well as not being affected by the dampness of the earth. As for what are called the *sūtra* and the *vinaya*:
the *sūtra* is for opening the mind and realizing one's nature (*prakṛti*) so as to attain the fruit of Buddhahood; the *vinaya* is for strictly guarding the body, speech, and mind.
It is for the sake of bringing about liberation. Regarding the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas: the Buddha is the original teacher and the excellent guide;

the Bodhisattva is the fellow student and the virtuous friend. As it is said, "Those who give birth to me are my parents; those who bring me to fulfillment are my teachers and friends. How could I dare to forget them for even a moment?
Furthermore, the Buddha is one who has attained the fruit, while the Bodhisattva is one on the path of cause. Those who have not yet become Buddhas should contemplate this.
"I shall certainly realize Buddhahood in this way. Contemplating that "I have not yet attained Buddhahood," one thinks, "I must certainly practice in this way.
This is precisely the model for practicing the Way during the summer retreat; therefore, one should offer worship to these sublime images.

As for the Bodhisattva’s practice of *dhūta* and so forth, this explains the aforementioned constant practice of *dhūta* and wandering during the two periods [of the day]; one must not be separated from it even for a moment. That is to say, do not...
These are to be used specifically during the winter and summer retreats (*varṣā*).

That is, when a Bodhisattva practices the ascetic dhūta-precepts or travels abroad—whether traveling a hundred or a thousand *li*, whether far or near—these eighteen kinds of items must always accompany him;
they must never be separated from him. The above summarizes the matters concerning the common ritual implements used during both the retreat and travel.

[The preceding section] concludes. Below, the timing of the *cārikā* (wandering) and the meaning of the customary ritual implements are explained. Regarding the statement "the two periods of *dhūta*," at what time do they occur?
It refers to the period from the fifteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the third month, which is the time of the spring equinox;
and from the fifteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the tenth month, which is...
At the time of the autumnal equinox, among these two periods, why do these eighteen kinds of items always accompany the body?
It is because they are like the two wings of a bird; if a wing is lost, the bird finds it difficult to soar. If the requisites of a Dharma-vessel are lacking, the Saṃgha finds it difficult to travel.
Therefore, they must always be carried with one. As for "on days such as the Poṣadha," this clarifies traveling.
The method for performing repentance: in Sanskrit, *poṣadha*; here translated as "performing the ritual to accomplish the task.
It is also called "confessing before me," or "confessing sins face-to-face. Because one possesses transgressions, one confesses and repents those faults while facing the Buddha image.

Regarding "newly initiated bodhisattvas" and so forth: this distinguishes them from those who have long cultivated the stages (*bhūmi*) of the nature (*prakṛti*). "Newly initiated" [refers to those at the beginning].
Because wisdom is inferior and consciousness is strong, one must exert effort to maintain the precepts.
Fearing that one might fall into negligence if body and mind are not strictly restrained, the *poṣadha* rite is performed every half-month.

From this point, one must carefully examine whether there have been transgressions or not regarding the characteristics of these ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, and perform repentance for each accordingly. Regarding all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...
Regarding those who recite before an image of the Buddha: when the Buddha was in the world, they would recite in his presence;
after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they may recite before an image with it serving as a witness, not daring to act on their own authority. Among these eighteen kinds of items:
This is because there are the Sūtras and Vinayas, as well as the images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the phrase "one person for the Poṣadha, etc.," this clarifies the ritual for reciting the precepts. When reciting the precepts, if it is a Poṣadha for one person, then that single person recites them.
Whether it is a Poṣadha for two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand people, it is likewise a single person who recites the precepts; it is not permissible for everyone to recite together.
Recite [the precepts] so as to avoid confusion. Regarding the ritual for reciting the precepts: the reciter shall sit on a high seat while the listeners remain on lower seats.
Both the reciter and the listeners must each wear the nine-strip, seven-strip, or five-strip *kāṣāya* robes;
they must not wear secular clothing, lest it contravene the physical integrity of the Sangha. This ritual protocol for the *poṣadha* is not only for when practicing the *dhūta* austerities.

However, whenever one enters the summer retreat (*varṣā*), every detail must follow these rules; they must not be transgressed. The above concludes the general explanation of the ritual procedures for the summer retreat and wandering.
Below is the explanation regarding those places of difficulty where neither the summer retreat nor wandering is permitted.
First, it is explained that when practicing the *dhūta* (ascetic) practices while wandering, one must not enter places of difficulty. What constitutes a place of difficulty? It is as follows:

Regarding "if there is national hardship": an alternative version reads "an evil land. This refers to times when the practice of killing is widespread within the country, or during calamities such as famine;
it is not appropriate to travel at such times, and therefore one should not go.

As for an "evil king," this refers to the ruler of the country who does not believe in the Triple Gem and does not cultivate merit or wisdom—such a person is an evil king. Regarding the terrain being "high and low," "high" refers to...
There are pits; below, there is dampness. One must travel through perilous and narrow passes where the vegetation is dense and deep, abounding in many predatory beasts.
There is the hardship of being terrified while entering and exiting or traveling back and forth. Disasters of water, fire, and wind are all such that one cannot go there;
for fear there may be the hardships of being swept away, burned, tossed about, or broken. On roads and locations frequented by bandits, there is fear of being left behind, erring, or suffering harm.
Regarding these hardships: on the roads below, there are places where venomous snakes lie across the path;
fearing the danger of being bitten by such creatures along the way, one must not go where such perils exist.

As for "all such perilous places," this refers not only to these specific dangers but to all locations of difficulty whatsoever; one must not enter any such place. If one practices the dhūta austerities...
Regarding "the paths and so forth": do not enter dangerous places. It is not only while wandering for *dhūta* practice that one must avoid dangerous places;
even during the summer retreat (*varṣā*), these dangerous places must not be entered. This is a general admonition to exercise caution regarding both the summer retreat and wandering.
If, however, one relies on one's own perceived virtue and disregards all fears, one violates the words of the Buddha.
Instruction: To forcibly enter and travel through dangerous places constitutes a minor offense of defilement.
○ The Thirty-eighth Precept: Regarding the Violation of the Order of Seniority.

If a disciple of the Buddha, one should sit according to the Dharma in proper sequence; those who received the precepts first shall sit in front, and those who received the precepts later [shall sit behind].
When sitting in the assembly, regardless of whether one is old or young— whether a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a person of noble rank,
a king, a prince, even a eunuch, a slave, or a servant— one who received the precepts earlier should sit in front,
and those who received them later should sit in order behind. Do not be like the foolish outsiders, who sit without regard for seniority or juniority, lacking any proper sequence.
Regarding the regulations for military slaves: within our Buddha-dharma, those who arrive first sit first, and those who arrive later sit later.
If a Bodhisattva fails to sit according to this sequential order of the Dharma, they commit a minor offense.
This explanation violates the order of honor established by the precepts. This precept originates from the procedure for the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts.
Specifically, it means that the one who recites the precepts occupies a high seat, while those who listen occupy lower seats.

Since the assembly of listeners also possesses a hierarchy of high and low, and because the seating of all members of the assembly must not be disordered—lest it contravene the Buddha’s regulations—it is therefore prescribed as a precept.
"O disciples of the Buddha," and so forth, serves as a general heading that clarifies the ritual procedure for sitting. "First receive," and so forth, is the detailed explanation.

This means that when disciples of the Buddha sit according to the Dharma, they should sit in the proper sequence. To say "according to the Dharma" means to sit in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions.
That is to say, those who have received the precepts earlier should sit in front, while those who have received the precepts later should sit behind.
As for seating, one does not inquire as to age or year of birth; rather, one sits according to the order of ordination.
Those who are bhikṣus sit together as one group; bhikṣuṇīs sit together as one group; nobles sit together as one group; and kings [sit together as one group].
The king constitutes one category; the prince another; and so on down to the eunuchs and the slaves, each forming their own category and thus distinguished by precedence.
It is not the case that one sits in a mixed order of precedence regardless of whether one is monastic or lay, noble or lowly.
If it were so, it would not only contravene worldly conventions, but would also fail to accord with the Buddha-dharma. For...
Within the Buddha-dharma, even a bhikṣuṇī of one hundred years must prostrate at the feet of a śrāmaṇera of three years.

These "one hundred" and "three" refer to the number of years since receiving the precepts, not the secular age of birth. This is because the one hundred-year-old has seniority (*vassa*) based on the length of her observance of the precepts, while the three-year-old has juniority due to the brevity of his time with the precepts.
If one were to judge the priority of ordination in a general sense, it should be as follows: [the text here implies that the seniority of the precepts takes precedence].
A three-year-old śrāmaṇera bows at the feet of a hundred-year-old bhikṣuṇī. Why should a hundred-year-old bhikṣuṇī bow at the feet of a three-year-old?
This demonstrates that when discussing precepts, each category stands as its own class, arranged according to seniority; furthermore, it shows that the bhikṣu is the presiding master.
As for the phrase "not like the non-Buddhists," it means that non-Buddhists possess no wisdom and do not distinguish between old and young.
If there are few, they sit without priority or sequence, like the manner of soldiers or slaves.
However, within the True Dharma of our Buddha, one must sit first according to who arrived first, and sit last according to who arrived last;

this is called practicing the Bodhisattva path, establishing the gateway of the Dharma, and embodying the meaning of humility, respect, and yielding. Thus, below the section on Bodhisattvas, it is concluded.

Violating the precepts incurs guilt. Regarding those who claim to be bodhisattvas: if they do not sit according to the proper sequence in accordance with the Dharma, they commit a minor offense (light impurity).
As for this offense, if one does not commit it, it is as stated in the *Samantaprabhā-samādhi*:
"King Ajātaśatru invited Mañjuśrī for a meal. Mañjuśrī respectfully yielded precedence to Mahākāśyapa, saying: 'Mahākāśyapa has long..."*
"To become a śramaṇa, all the arhats in the world follow behind the virtuous; you, O Virtuous One, should go before.
Kāśyapa replied, "According to the Dharma and Vinaya, seniority by years is not the basis for honor. What is recorded in the Dharma and Vinaya is that wisdom is the basis for honor.
It is one who possesses divine wisdom and saintly penetration who is truly honorable; it is one who is widely learned and eloquent who is truly honorable. [The same applies to] the faculties..."
"Only one who is clearly penetrating may be honored; Mañjuśrī is the one who goes before. Question:
"According to this, does it not contradict the proper order of seniority? Answer: "King Ajātaśatru’s invitation was intended for Mañjuśrī, not for Kāśyapa.
It is analogous to how Śakra, Lord of the Devas, invited the teacher of the *Avataṃsaka* and placed his seat above those of the five hundred arhats. Mañjuśrī...
Mañjuśrī first yielded to Kāśyapa, not daring to contravene the constant rule of the ancient Buddhas;
Kāśyapa ultimately deferred to Mañjuśrī, thereby acceding to the original intention of the host. These two Great Beings were precisely subverting the malady of pride and arrogance.
○ Thirty-ninth: The Precept Against Not Cultivating Merit and Wisdom.

If a Buddha’s disciple, they should constantly teach and transform all sentient beings, establishing monastic dwellings, mountain forests, gardens, and fields, constructing Buddha-stūpas, and providing places for winter and summer retreats and for seated meditation. They should establish all such sites for the practice of the Way.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya for the sake of all sentient beings. In times of illness, national calamity, or the threat of bandits;
on the days of the passing of one's parents, brothers, preceptors (upādhyāya), or teachers (ācārya);

and during the third, fourth, or fifth week, up to the seventh week—on these occasions, one should likewise expound the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya at all ritual assemblies (poṣadha) for the purpose of seeking [merit].

Merit. Whether traveling for business or livelihood, one may encounter great fires or floods that burn or sweep away; or a ship blown by black winds; or the perils of rākṣasas upon rivers, streams, and the great ocean.

Furthermore, even if one has committed all manner of karmic offenses, the three evil realms, the eight difficulties, the seven heinous crimes, or is bound by cangues, shackles, and pillories, or is characterized by excessive lust, excessive anger, or excessive ignorance—if they read, recite, explain, and preach this sutra and vinaya... [they shall be liberated].
There will be many illnesses; all should expound this sutra and its vinaya. If a newly initiated bodhisattva does not do so, they commit a minor offense (light defilement).
