O Sons of the Buddha, you should receive and uphold these forty-eight minor precepts; the Bodhisattvas of the past have already recited them.
The future Bodhisattvas shall recite it; the present Bodhisattvas are now reciting it.
"O sons of the Buddha," this single phrase is addressed to the person concerned. These forty-eight single phrases raise up the Dharma to encourage its reception and retention.
The subsequent phrases beginning with "In the past" and so forth cite parallels to encourage the practitioner to recite. [Recite the forty...]
Regarding the eight minor precepts: it is not that I alone am exhorting you beginners to recite them;
rather, they have been recited by all bodhisattvas of the past, shall be recited by all bodhisattvas of the future, and are being recited now by all you bodhisattvas of the present.
This concludes the textual meaning of the section on the True Doctrine (Zhengzongfen).
III. The Section on the Circulation (in three parts): 1. The circulation of the fundamental precepts; 2. A general summary of this chapter;
3. A general praise of the circulation. I.
The circulation of the fundamental precepts.

"Listen, all you sons of the Buddha! These ten grave and forty-eight light precepts have been recited by the Buddhas of the three periods of time—those who have already recited them, those who shall recite them, and those who are now reciting them.
I now likewise recite them. You, the entire great assembly—including kings, princes, and the hundred officials—"

Bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, faithful men, and faithful women who have received and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts should receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe this scroll of the eternally abiding Buddha-nature precepts.
They should circulate it among all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, so that its transformative influence continues without end.

By doing so, they shall behold a thousand Buddhas, with each Buddha extending a hand to them; in every lifetime, they shall never fall into the evil realms or the eight difficulties, and shall always be born [in favorable conditions].
Among humans and devas, I am now here beneath this tree briefly expounding the seven dharmas of the Buddha’s precepts.

You, the great assembly, should single-mindedly study the Prātimokṣa and joyfully practice it, as explained in detail for each point in the "Exhortation to Study" within the *Nirnimitta-devaputra-parivarta*.
At that time, the three thousand scholars seated there listening heard the Buddha recite these words himself, and their hearts were filled with [faith].
I receive this upon my head with joy and shall uphold it.
This is the root precepts for the circulation and dissemination of the teachings. From "O Sons of the Buddha" onwards is the instruction to listen to the method for receiving the root precepts;
from "The Buddhas of the three periods of time" onwards is the citation of evidence to encourage recitation. It says: "O Sons of the Buddha, you all listen to what I [say]..."
I shall now proclaim the ten grave precepts and the forty-eight light precepts. These have been transmitted and recited by all Buddhas of the three periods of time:
the Buddhas of the past have already recited them, the Buddhas of the future shall recite them, and the Buddhas of the present are now reciting them.
I, too, now follow these Buddhas and recite them in this manner. Therefore, you entire assembly—including kings, ministers, and all others—should likewise do so.

The benevolent ruler who is a prince; the virtuous ministers among the civil and military officials—these are all disciples of the Buddha who dwell in the defilements yet remain unstained, honoring the Buddha-Dharma.
The bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs are disciples who have left the household life to receive the Dharma;
the faithful men and faithful women are the lay disciples of pure faith. Since they all uphold the Bodhisattva [precepts]...
Regarding the precepts: one should thoroughly receive, uphold, recite, explain, and transcribe this scroll of the Buddha-nature and the eternal nature-precepts.

To circulate it among all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time, causing it to be transmitted from one to another so that its transformative influence never ceases, is a matter of urgent priority.
The phrase "those who attain the vision of a thousand Buddhas" correctly clarifies the benefits of circulating the dharma of the precepts. As for the term "transmitting,"...

As for the phrase "it circulates and spreads, with transformations following transformations without ceasing," what benefit does this entail? It refers to the opportunity to behold a thousand Buddhas, with each Buddha transmitting the teaching to the next.

Because of this successive transmission from Buddha to Buddha, one shall, in birth after birth and life after life, never fall into the evil realms, the eight difficult conditions, or places of suffering.
This is the benefit of extinguishing transgressions mentioned above; as for the benefit of acquiring merit mentioned below: [Question: Since it is already...
Falling into various states of hardship, where will they be reborn? Answer: They shall always be born among humans and devas, practicing the Way by virtue of their power of aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Regarding the phrase "I now," etc.: from here below, the Dharma is cited to provide a concluding exhortation.

This means that I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, am now here beneath this Bodhi tree, manifesting the attainment of enlightenment and manifesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma. First, the *pāramitā*... [is concluded].
The *Prātimokṣa* consists of ten grave precepts and forty-eight light precepts;

these are a concise exposition of the Dharma-precepts of the Mind-ground, which all sentient beings cultivate as causes and realize as fruits, as taught by the seven Buddhas of the past. You, the great assembly, should [uphold them].
"You should single-mindedly study these ten grave *pratimokṣa* precepts. For this reason, I exhort you to joyfully practice them;

do not be negligent. This is a brief statement; as for the detailed explanation of each point, it is found in the section on Exhorting Study within the 'Chapter on the King of Formlessness' (*Nirnimitta-devaputra-parivarta*) in the Great Section [of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*]. The three thousand scholars are those present in this assembly."

Regarding the Bodhisattvas—encompassing the eight classes of beings such as devas and nāgas, as well as those of the secular and monastic orders, both noble and humble—those present who were sitting and listening heard the Buddha personally recite the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts; they all received these words upon their heads with every thought.
They received and upheld it with joyful exultation, not daring to forget even for a moment the seed of the Buddha-nature.
II. Summary of this Chapter:
At that time, Śākyamuni Buddha spoke of the mind of Vairocana Buddha in the Lotus-Treasury World above.
In the "Chapter on the Dharmas of the Grounds," the "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts" concludes. The thousand billion Śākyamunis likewise speak thus.

From the palace of the Heavenly King Maheśvara down to this dwelling place beneath the Bodhi tree, in this "Chapter on Teaching the Dharma," for the sake of all bodhisattvas and the inexpressibly vast assembly, they cause [this teaching] to be received, upheld, recited, and its meaning explained; it is also thus.
In worlds numbering in the hundreds of thousands of millions, in the Lotus Treasury World, in worlds as numerous as motes of dust—

in all these, the heart-treasury of all Buddhas, the earth-treasury, the precept-treasury, the treasury of immeasurable practices and vows, and the eternally abiding treasury of the Buddha-nature of cause and effect—
thus have all Buddhas expounded the entirety of the immeasurable treasuries of all dharmas. Within these hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds, all sentient beings receive and uphold them.

Rejoicing, they shall practice accordingly. If one wishes to extensively open the characteristics and marks of the mind-ground (*cittabhūmi*), it is as explained in the "Seven Practices Chapter" of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-rāja-sūtra*.
This summary reveals the Dharma of the mind-ground precepts taught by one Buddha, many Buddhas, the primordial Buddha (*mūlabuddha*), and the manifested Buddhas (*nirmāṇabuddha*).

Regarding the general meaning of the exhortation for circulation: from the time when Śākyamuni reaches the conclusion of the "Dharma Chapter" section, he thereby concludes this section on the Dharma taught by a single Buddha within this world-system.

As for the phrase "at that time," it refers to the auspicious occasion when the Great Assembly was entrusted with the *cittabhūmi* (mind-ground) precepts and teachings. Śākyamuni Buddha is [the teacher] of our Sahā world.

The Transformation Tathāgata of the Founder of the Teaching spoke this "Chapter on the Ten Inexhaustible Precepts" within the "Chapter on the Mind-Ground Dharma Gate" transmitted by Vairocana Buddha in the World of the Superior Lotus Flower Treasury. Thus, it is both sequential and perfectly integrated.
Each and every matter and principle has already been explained to its ultimate conclusion. Furthermore, the thousand billion Śākyamunis are all exactly like this;

what is taught by the Teacher of this Sahā world is no different. All have come from the palace of King Maheśvara to this foot of the Bodhi tree and other dwelling places, and the dharma chapters they teach are likewise without difference, forming a single [unity].
All Bodhisattvas and the unspeakably vast assembly—such a great assembly as this—each upholds, recites, copies, and explains its meaning.
Furthermore, they uphold non-duality just as the assembly of Vairocana does. It is not only this;
it is likewise for all the Buddhas throughout worlds numbering in the hundreds of thousands of billions, even down to the Buddhas within worlds as small as a single atom. These are one.
Within all worlds, there are the primordial Buddhas, the manifested Buddhas, and the manifested-of-the-manifested Buddhas.

Regarding all that these Buddhas have taught—the thirty minds, the Treasury of Minds; the ten stages, the Treasury of Stages; the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts, the Vajra Jewel Precepts of Radiance;
the Treasury of Precepts; and the immeasurable, wondrous practices arising from the three levels of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood—these constitute the [Treasury of] Practice.

The Treasury of Vows, which comprises the immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of great vows that have been made; the Treasury of Causes, which consists of the superior causes cultivated through practice over a hundred kalpas;
the Treasury of the Fruit, which is the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood, equal and perfect enlightenment;

and the Treasury of the Ever-Abiding Buddha-nature, the original awakening inherent in all sentient beings—these seven aspects of the mind-ground, comprising precepts, practices, vows, causes, and fruits, are distinct, yet the Buddha-nature is one.
The term "seed" (*gotra*) is the general designation. The two characters "permanently abiding" (*nitya-sthita*) are words of praise;

they praise this Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), which, although it receives names according to conditions, its nature undergoes no change or alteration. As it exists in the mind, it is called the "unborn and undying pure fundamental mind";
as it exists in the earth, it is called the "ground of the principle of true suchness" (*tathatā-samatā-bhūmi*); and as it exists in the precepts, it is called the "luminous vajra."
As a precious precept in practice, it is called the myriad practices of Samantabhadra; as a vow, it is called the king of all great vows;
as a cause, it is called the profound cause of the original source and intrinsic nature; as a fruit, it is called ultimate, unsurpassed Bodhi.
Because it is the wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa*, it is said that the Buddha-nature is eternally abiding.

As for the term "treasury" (*garbha*) used in both cases, it refers to these eight kinds [of consciousness], which are vast and inclusive, perfectly integrated and all-encompassing, fully possessing everything without end.
Thus, as stated above, all Buddhas have taught that this "Mind-Ground" and so forth constitute the ultimate culmination of the immeasurable treasury of all dharmas.
Within thousands of billions of worlds, all sentient beings receive, uphold, and rejoice in [the teachings], practicing them one by one;

they are exactly like the sentient beings of this world, without any difference. Such is the general outline of how the Original Buddha, the Traces Buddha, and the Buddhas of successive traces preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
As for the extensive opening of the mind-ground and the meaning of its various characteristics—

Furthermore, this is contained within the Great Collection (Mahāsaṃnipāta). As explained in detail in the "Chapter on the Seven Practices of the Buddha Flower-Light King," it repeatedly speaks of "marks and marks" (*lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa*), extensively unfolding immeasurable marks based upon the marks of the stage of the one mind.
III. General Praise for the Propagation (3): 1. Praising the Benefits of Upholding the Precepts; 2. Exhorting Contemplation of the Essence of the Precepts;
3. Exhorting Protection and Dedication. I.
Praising the Benefits of Upholding the Precepts.
The person of wisdom possesses strong patience and insight; they are able to uphold such a Dharma as this. Before attaining the path of Buddhahood, they will securely obtain five kinds of benefits:
first, the Buddhas of the ten directions will compassionately regard and constantly protect them; second, at the time of death, they will possess right view and their hearts will be filled with joy.
Third, they are born in places where they become friends to all bodhisattvas. Fourth, they are a mass of merit, having fully accomplished the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
Fifth, in this and future lives, their natural morality, merit, and wisdom are complete. These are the children of the Buddhas; let the wise contemplate them well.
This is the meaning of praising and extolling the benefits of upholding the precepts. The term "wise person" (*vidvān*) refers to one who has transcended the class of foolish beings.
The two characters "patience" (*kṣānti*) and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) clearly manifest that a wise person is capable of guarding the essence and function of the precepts.
That is to say, this wise person possesses the dual virtues of the two powers of patience and wisdom; because they possess the power of patience...
Therefore, one is not turned by external objects. Because of the power of wisdom, one is able to turn objects [according to one's will].
Such a person is able to uphold the precepts of the mind-ground; this person will certainly attain Buddhahood in the future, without doubt.
Furthermore, even before attaining the Buddha-way, one will first securely obtain five kinds of extraordinary benefits. What are these five benefits?

First is the benefit of the Buddhas' protection. This means that for a person who upholds the precepts, the Buddhas of the ten directions will immediately manifest before them, looking down with compassionate mindfulness and constantly providing guardianship, so that they may advance on the path without demonic interference and succeed in propagating and flourishing the Dharma.
First, because of the seed of the Buddha. Second, the benefit of a virtuous death: because this person upholds the Buddha’s precepts, at the time of their passing they attain right view;
their mind gives rise to joy, and they remain far removed from inverted dreams and delusions, as no evil objects appear before them.

Third is the benefit of excellent companions: throughout successive lives and in every place where this person is born, they will travel and dwell together with fellow Bodhisattvas as spiritual friends, because they are not mixed with or associated with evil factions. Fourth is the benefit of the perfection of virtues:
this person’s immeasurable accumulation of meritorious qualities arises from upholding the ten grave precepts and the forty-eight light precepts of the *Vajra-prabhāsa*.
The perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*): one is able to fully accomplish it, for there is not a single dharma that is lacking. Fifth is the benefit of the accomplishment of the Path:

from this point forward, this person’s intrinsic nature of the precept-body (*śīla-svabhāva*) will be perfected in merit and wisdom, and shall be named the "Two-Legged Honored One" (*dvipada-damya-sārathi*).
The first four kinds of benefit are the cause; the final one kind of benefit is the fruit.

These five kinds of profit are obtained by the sons of the Buddhas who uphold the precepts. Wise people should contemplate, realize, and practice this Dharma of the Precepts of the Ground of the True Mark (bhūtatathatā-cittabhūmi-śīla).
II. Exhortation to Contemplate the Essence of the Precepts:
Those who calculate a self and cling to signs cannot believe in this Dharma; those who seek realization by extinguishing their life-span are likewise not a ground for planting seeds.
One who wishes to cause the sprout of bodhi to grow and whose radiance illuminates the world should purify their observation of the true nature of all phenomena:
that they are neither arising nor ceasing, neither eternal nor annihilated, neither identical nor different, and neither coming nor going.
Thus, within this single mind, one should diligently adorn it through skillful means; these are the deeds a bodhisattva ought to perform, and they should be studied in their proper sequence.
Regarding those in training and those beyond training, do not give rise to discriminatory thoughts. This is called the foremost path, and it is also called the Mahāyāna.
All the evils of conceptual proliferation are extinguished from this source; the *sarvajñā* (omniscience) of all Buddhas emerges entirely from this source.
This is the meaning of observing the essence of the precepts as the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Since one is already a wise person, one should properly contemplate the nature of this essence of the precepts and practice without error. Why is this so? If one calculates...
My non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings who cling to signs—such persons as these are all bound by the faculties and their objects;
they are unable to believe in this pure dharma of precepts, which is received without receiving and maintained without maintaining. Why is this?
Because those who cling to a self and grasp at signs are incapable of correct reflection. It is not only ordinary worldlings and outsiders who are incapable of it.

Even those of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, who may indulge in emptiness and maintain silence, extinguishing their lifespans to attain realization, are not places where the seed of Bodhi can be planted;
they are of the class known as withered sprouts and ruined seeds. Nevertheless, the Buddha’s precepts are impartial.
How could one exclude them arbitrarily? Alas, such people fail to exercise proper discernment; therefore, they all lack a share [in this].

Even if ordinary beings or non-Buddhists wish to nurture the sprout of this bodhicitta so that the light of wisdom may illuminate and examine the world, they should, within these precepts of the mind-ground, give rise to unimpeded, pure insight and contemplate with stillness.
Observe with quiet discernment: within all phenomena, there is that which is true and without delusion—the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This is precisely the fundamentally perfect and pure precept-body (*śīlaskandha*) of our own original nature. This Dharma does not belong to arising through conditions, nor does it belong to ceasing through conditions;
for while all phenomena arise through the convergence of conditions, this true and non-delusive precept-body of the true mark is fundamentally [unconditioned].
Coming, there is no movement. All dharmas perish when their conditions are exhausted; this is the truth, free from delusion.

The essence of the precepts of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally non-inverted; therefore, it is said that they are neither born nor extinguished, unlike the birth and extinction of ordinary beings.
This nature of the precepts not only does not belong to the birth and extinction of ordinary beings, but likewise does not belong to external [phenomena].

The Way cuts off both permanence and annihilation. Because its fundamental moment is non-abiding, it does not belong to permanence; because it is eternally as it is throughout the ten thousand ages, it does not belong to annihilation.
Therefore, it is said to be neither permanent nor annihilated. Furthermore, it does not merely transcend the birth and death of ordinary beings.
The dharmas of the heterodox paths, such as those of eternalism and nihilism, and the dharmas cultivated and realized by the Two Vehicles, are entirely unrelated.

That is to say, their categories are distinct and difficult to reconcile, yet they are fundamentally not one; they are of the same substance and difficult to differentiate, yet they are fundamentally not different.

When one goes toward them, one knows not where they go, yet they fundamentally do not come; when one pursues them, one knows not whence they come, yet they fundamentally do not go. Therefore, it is said:
Neither identical nor different; neither coming nor going. Such a dharma does not belong to birth and extinction, to annihilation or permanence, to identity or difference, or to coming and going.
What kind of dharma is it? It exists solely within this single mind. One should diligently adorn this single mind through skillful means.
This single mind is precisely the Vairocana Dharma-realm, the mind of quiescent extinction. As for what is called "quiescent extinction":

This is called "single-mindedness. Having first realized this mind as the fundamental ground of practice (*ādikṣetra*), one further relies upon this mind to give rise to the path of skillful means (*upāyamārga*), diligently cultivating various gateways of practice (*caryāmukha*) to adorn unsurpassed bodhi.

Such wisdom and understanding, such wondrous conduct, are truly not something that can be accomplished through the deliberations of heterodox paths, worldly paths, or the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Rather, it is...
This is what all bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Great Vehicle and received the Great Vehicle precepts ought to practice.
Although it is called "Great," it cannot be accomplished by speaking of it all at once; one must study it well through the stages according to the Dharma before attaining correspondence with it.
What is the sequence of this study? It is precisely within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) that investigates reality and severs delusions.

This is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), where reality is fully exhausted and delusions are utterly ended. Regarding this, do not give rise to conceptualizations of existence or non-existence.
Because one does not give rise to such conceptualizations, it is called the foremost path that does not fall into the two vehicles;
it is also called the Mahāyāna, the Great Vehicle. The "foremost path" refers to the aforementioned single mind; the "Mahāyāna" refers to the aforementioned [state].

It is for this reason that one cultivates such a path. Thus, all the conceptual proliferations and unwholesome dharmas of ordinary beings, outsiders, and those of the Lesser Vehicle are entirely extinguished without remainder within this Great Path. It is here that the wisdom, supernatural powers, and samādhis of all Buddhas reside.
The wondrous fruit of sarvajñā (all-knowledge) is entirely manifested from this source, without the slightest deficiency.
Is it not through the skillful contemplation of this inconceivable ground-of-mind precept-dharma that one obtains the benefit of extinguishing transgressions and generating goodness?
III. Exhortation to Protect and Dedication.
Therefore, O sons of the Buddha, you should arouse great valor and courage; regarding the pure precepts of all Buddhas, you must protect and uphold them as if they were bright pearls.
The bodhisattvas of the past have already trained in this; those of the future shall train in it; and those of the present are training in it now.
This is the sphere of action of the Buddhas, praised by the Holy Lords. I have explained it in accordance with the truth; may this be a boundless mass of merit.
Returning it to bestow upon all sentient beings, may we together advance toward omniscience. May those who hear this Dharma swiftly attain the path of Buddhahood.
It is said that all evils are extinguished from this, and all virtues arise from this.

Truly, this is not something that can be reached by those of inferior faculties or meager roots in a single morning or evening. Therefore, you sons of the Buddhas who have received the precepts should resolve upon the Great [Vehicle].
With a courageous mind, one must protect and uphold the pure precepts of all Buddhas like a bright pearl, ensuring not even a hair’s breadth of damage or defilement;
only then is this the radiant Vajra-jewel precept within the Mind-Ground held by the children of the Buddha. [The section beginning with] "In the past... [is as follows].
This section cites scriptural evidence to conclude with an exhortation regarding the dedication and circulation [of this teaching].
It means that my exhortation to you all to courageously uphold this Dharma of the precepts is not without scriptural authority.

This Great Sūtra on the Precepts is that which those Bodhisattvas of the past who have already realized the fruit studied within; it is likewise that which those who will realize the fruit in the future shall study within.
"Study this. This refers to those who have realized the fruit in the present; they now study within this.
It is truly the ground traversed during the causal stage by all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and it is that which my own Master, the Holy Lord Vairocana, constantly extols and praises.
I, too, below, cite my own realization to exhort you, saying: "I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata..."
I have already followed what the Buddhas have taught, extolling and praising it; how much more so should you who are newly trained be doubly courageous and diligent in its protection and upholding!
The following four lines summarize the intent of the *Cittabhūmi-śīla-sūtra*:
within this *Cittabhūmi-śīla* thus expounded by me and the Buddhas, there lies vast, immeasurable, and boundless merit.
This assembly, in order to accord with the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), bestows this upon sentient beings so that each may take these precepts as the mind of the causal ground.
This is unlike ordinary worldlings and distinct from those of the two vehicles; together they shall advance toward the omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, it is vowed that anyone who hears this Dharma of the Mind-Ground Precepts shall realize the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment] not merely in a future life.

"Bodhi" means that one immediately and swiftly attains the perfect fruition of Buddhahood. As it was said above: "When sentient beings receive the Buddha’s precepts, they immediately enter the rank of all Buddhas.
How could this be empty talk? Thus, the thousand Śākyamunis and the hundreds of billions of Śākyamunis who appear [are manifested].

The manifestations transformed by the Radiant One are immeasurable and boundless. The Śākyamunis, as numerous as motes of dust, herein return to the fundamental Buddha, the *Sāmbhogakāya* (Sahaja), within the abode of one’s own mind.

Within this assembly, the thousand worlds, the hundreds of thousands of millions of worlds, and the worlds as numerous as motes of dust all return to the fundamental realm of the *Padmakośa* (Flower Treasury) of one’s own essence.
What is taught is sometimes profound and sometimes simple; it comprises immeasurable and boundless precepts.
Dharma. This is the dharma-gate of the self-nature śīla to which one returns in this assembly.

As for those to be delivered—whether monastics or laypeople, whether noble or lowly—all immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, these are the sentient beings who are the "sentient beings of self-nature" to which one returns in this assembly.
Such a wondrous precept of the mind-ground, this profound dharma-gate, is inconceivable and...

May it be so that all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma realm, in every life and every birth, may together resolve upon the indestructible vajra-mind, constantly follow and study under all Buddhas, and collectively realize the wondrous fruit of unsurpassed bodhi. May this be so!

This direct explanation of the meaning is intended solely for one's own contemplation. Those of great wisdom should consult the *Jieshu fayin* (Profound Revelations on the Vinaya Commentary) by the Great Master Yunqi, who was dedicated to the propagation of the Vinaya and held the Dharma-gate in the highest esteem; he personally composed this work.

The *Direct Explanation of the Brahma Net Sutra* has long been disseminated throughout the realm. On a winter day in the year Jiashen, at the Precept Platform in Kuaiji, I again exhausted my refined thoughts to revise and polish it further.
I commissioned Xian to collate and correct the text, while also overseeing the carving of the printing blocks, so that it might serve as a definitive edition forever.
It was completed in the middle month of autumn in the year Yiyou. I hereby respectfully record the date and time at the end.
Written by the Great Precept Disciple Yuanyun Jixian of Loudong as a Preface to the Direct Explanation of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Lower, Part Two (End).
